# Index of the books contained in this volume

<image-desc>A small woodcut initial 'M' containing two figures, possibly scholars or saints, looking at a book.</image-desc>Four volumes of divine and human wonders. The first, namely, concerns the wonders of Holy Scripture. The second concerns the wondrous propositions of the most blessed Apostle Paul. The third concerns the bulwark of the Christian religion. The fourth concerns the wonders of the world according to <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy was a 2nd-century mathematician and geographer whose works were foundational to Renaissance worldviews.</note>, clearly distinguished by Sir Symphorien Champier of Lyon, a nobleman and primary personal counselor to the most serene Duke of Calabria and Lorraine.

### The First Volume.
On the wonders of Holy Scripture, in which there are **4 books.**
The first is on the <term>Pentateuch</term><note>The first five books of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.</note> of Moses and the Prophets.
The second is designated for the New Testament.

### The Second Volume.
Theorems of the wondrous propositions of Saint Paul the Apostle, in **6 books.**
The first on the Epistle to the Romans.
The second on the First and Second Epistles to the Corinthians.
The third on the Epistle to the Galatians.
The fourth on the Epistles to the Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians.
The fifth on the Epistles to the Thessalonians, Timothy, and Titus.
The sixth on the Epistle to the Hebrews.

### The Third Volume.
The wondrous bulwark of the Christian religion, divided into **4 parts.**
The first, an apology <note>An "apology" in this historical context is a formal written defense of a belief system.</note> against the pagans.
The second against the Jews.
The third against heretics.
The fourth against the Muslims <note>original Latin: "Mahumetenses", referring to followers of Muhammad.</note>.

### The Fourth Volume.
On the wonders of the world, in **2 books.**
The first on the customs and wonders of the peoples and provinces of the world according to the tables of Ptolemy.
The second, a catalog of the cities of the whole world.

### Hieronymus of Pavia, of the Order of Saint
### Augustine, <term>Canon Regular</term><note>A member of a religious community of priests living under a rule (in this case, the Rule of St. Augustine) and sharing property, but also performing clerical duties in the world.</note>, to Symphorian 
### Champier, a nobleman of Lyon, a most famous man 
### of all good arts, medicine, and all literature. 
### Greetings.

Even though it would be completely inappropriate and foreign to the mouth of a Christian man (and much more for a religious man, especially a candidate for the <term>Sacred Spirit</term><note>original Latin: "sacri flaminis"</note>) to blame "ill fortune" for an unfortunate event—as if, according to the errors of the pagans, everything turned on a blind stroke of luck—I certainly believe I have enough cause to complain of the injustices I have suffered, my most distinguished Symphorian. For I traveled so that I might see you and that famous Jacques Lefèvre <note>original Latin: "Jacobum illū Fabrum." Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples (c. 1455–1536) was a pioneering French humanist and theologian.</note>, men renowned throughout the world in all branches of learning, whom I had come to know through your books and various monuments of philosophy.

Since certain matters for our most pious religion had to be pleaded under the leadership and auspices of the most reverend Lord Bishop of Paris in the court of the most Christian King, I was assigned as a companion to one of our superiors. I undertook this journey gladly, primarily for this reason: so that I might speak with you in passing. Nearly three years have now passed since I crossed from Italy <note>original Latin: "Latio"</note> into the lands of Gaul, not without great expense and labor, traveling through Alpine snows and long stretches of road.

And yet, although I saw that "sacred divinity" Lefèvre, I was not able to see you, O most illustrious Symphorian Champier, the pillar of the Gauls, and together with Lefèvre, the light, ornament, love, and delight of all literature. For when I arrived in Lyon, I immediately went to your home, asking if there was any way I could speak with the one I had so long desired to meet. I was answered most kindly by your servants that you were staying with the most illustrious Duke of Lorraine.

Alas, what stings of passion did I then feel! What torches burned in my breast and inmost heart! "Have the fates," I said, "so mocked my very best wishes?" O, the fleeting shifts of affairs! O, the threatening accidents and the crumbling hopes of deceived men! The die was cast, and I suffered a shipwreck in the very harbor. At last, I departed sad and grieving; yet because I often hoped that by some chance you might be found at home on our return, I proceeded further into <term>Celtic Gaul</term><note>A humanist term for the central regions of France.</note> to meet Lefèvre, who was staying in Paris <note>original Latin: "lutetie"</note> under a pleasant sky. I met the man, I gazed upon him, I spoke with him, I embraced him; at the same time, I was most humanely received and kissed by him.

Standing by him and tending to his side was a certain Charles, a most elegant youth of quite noble appearance, a follower and pupil of Lefèvre’s studies. You would have thought him a second <term>Alcibiades</term><note>The famous, handsome student of Socrates.</note> to Socrates, or a <term>Dion</term> to Plato, or a <term>Theophrastus</term> to Aristotle. Good God, with what unbridled joy did I then rejoice! I told them of my passion, my wanderings, my labors, the dangers and the journey I had undertaken; for having entered such a great city, the capital of the Gauls, I was seeking nothing else (in the words of Saint Jerome) but him. That most learned old man rejoiced along with me...

<vocab>Hieronymus of Pavia, Symphorian Champier, Jacques Lefèvre, Lyon, Gaul, Charles, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Theophrastus</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the introductory letter from Hieronymus of Pavia to the scholar Symphorien Champier. Having previously expressed his frustration at missing Champier in Lyon, Hieronymus now recounts his meeting with the esteemed Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples (referred to as "Fabrus") and their shared admiration for Champier's polymathic expertise.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>A iii</sig>

and in all things he was a host more sweet and refined than can be believed. He claimed that he had once traveled to us in Italy <note>original: "in latium"</note> so that he might see and speak with that most famous sanctuary of letters in the whole world, the illustrious prince **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, and **Hermolao Barbaro**, the Venetian patrician, who deserved so well of all literature. To these he added—as if to complete a <term>Triumvirate</term><note>A group of three men holding power; here used to describe the three greatest Italian scholars.</note>—that **Marsilio Ficino**, the first and legitimate propagator of Platonic philosophy among the Latins. After these, he especially commended the sharp genius of **Poliziano**, to pass over the others in the list, each of whom he honored with his own rightful praise. 

But when I brought you into the conversation among them, we both spoke much in your praise, almost in the manner of a <term>panegyric</term><note>A public speech or published text in high praise of someone.</note>, as one who had cultivated every branch of philosophy: **Orphic, Hermetic <note>original: "Trismegisticamq;"</note>, Asclepiadean, Zoroastrian, Magical, Pythagorean, Socratic, Platonic, Stoic, and Aristotelian.** Finally, you have stirred up and reduced to writing every Greek, Roman, and Gallic branch; you have examined all the papers of the philosophers; you know all the families, all the sects, all the schools. You have, in short, mastered all the opinions, all the dogmas, all the decrees, all the secrets, and all the mysteries. 

Behold, while these things were being discussed—and while I was following that venerable old man through countless questions to be explained—in order to test his genius (not as if I were demanding proofs from him, for his authority was already well enough proven to me, but seeking his mere judgment on what he himself felt with an open mind), I proposed to him many questions on natural philosophy, many on metaphysics, and many on theology. I asked how he could make **Aristotle** agree with **Plato** in so many points. But he, as he was prompt and succinct in all things, offered such solutions that were received by me certainly not as learned responses, but as if they were being drawn from divine oracles. And although he favors Aristotle greatly, he is "sworn to the words of no single master" <note>A famous quote from Horace: "nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri," meaning he is an independent thinker.</note>; he so mixed certain Platonic ideas among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note> that he did not defraud either of their proper praises. He is so devoted to both philosophers that he rejoices to be called neither a Platonist nor a Peripatetic. 

Rather, he is entirely **Apostolic** and a fellow-initiate of the faith. He overflows entirely with sacred doctrine; he is completely exuberant; he is entirely carried away to the "ambrosia" of **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic.</note>, to those sacred fountains of nectar, and even to the divine loves of **Hierotheus**. 

But as that fountain of nectar <note>referring to Lefèvre</note> knows no limit to love, it was already nearly the second hour of the night when I could scarcely be torn away from his holy embrace. However, the hour interrupted us for the dinner of the Most Reverend Lord Bishop. Having offered a book which he gave me as a remarkable pledge and monument of his love toward me, and embracing and kissing me again (for I do not recount every detail), he said: *"Be mindful of us in your prayers, Jerome my son; and you shall go to our Symphorien, to whom you will commend me most dutifully."* 

O, the hard and bitter condition of our departure! I finally withdrew like a groaning son from a father, weeping, wailing, and sighing for the love of the old man. I consoled myself for a little while, however, hoping that I could easily temper my grief if I should find you in your homeland of Lyon. What more? Having entered Lyon again, I heard that you were absent as before; and so I returned to Italy entirely frustrated, loathing myself because I did not deserve to see you. But what then? Can anyone go against his own <term>genius</term> or fate? *"Thus you willed it, O Gods,"* (as the poet says); I accept it. And so, my most famous Symphorien, though I have not seen you, my mind still burns to see you because of the "monuments" of your writing which I have read, and to embrace you (as I did Fabrus) before I die. 

Were I not bound by the bond of religion, I would come again to France by any means possible <note>original: "pedibus manibusq;" (with feet and hands)</note> to see my Symphorien, to speak with him, to embrace him, and to know him deeply. Therefore, since there is no hope (or certainly very little) of seeing you, it seemed best—out of the great love with which I have long been ensnared—to give this letter to you by my swift household messenger. Thus you may know how much your noble writings can deeply change the minds of strangers and foreigners, and how true is that sentiment of our **Marcus Tullius Cicero** in his *Laelius*: *"Nothing is more lovable than virtue; nothing more allures men to loving."* For indeed, because of virtue and integrity, we love in a certain way even those whom we have never seen. 

Farewell, my most famous Symphorien, and keep your lover continually in your heart; and when you write to our **Fabrus**, I pray you deign to impart a greeting to him in my name. And if ever you give yourself to the writing of histories (unless you are entirely a monk bound to Benedict), remember sometimes the sons of **Augustine**, namely the **Canons Regular**, among whom the most venerable are celebrated in France at Saint Victor in Paris and at the house of Saint Genevieve: our **Hugh**, **Richard**, **Adam**, and many others. Again, farewell, O perpetual glory of letters. 

From the city of Asti, the monastery of Santa Maria Nuova, of the order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine of the Observance. The eighth day before the Kalends of July <note>June 24th</note>.

<meta>This page continues a correspondence between the Italian scholar Hieronymus of Pavia and the French polymath Symphorien Champier. While the previous page saw Hieronymus praising Champier, this page appears to be Champier’s reply, written from the perspective of a host and fellow philosopher, returning the high praise and discussing the intellectual bonds that unite scholars across the Alps.</meta>

<page-num>A iij</page-num>

<margin>
The principal causes of goodwill.
</margin>

I might consider myself a product of most noble Italy, Hieronymus, because even though I have not known you in person, there is such great erudition in you: such a leaning toward study, and such a great love for me, as I have perceived from your letters. For the teaching of character, the sanctity of morals, and authority are accustomed to possess great power in reconciling minds and drawing them into goodwill—even those who are unknown to one another and separated by a vast distance of places. Indeed, the first of these qualities <note>the teaching of character</note> allured the philosophers; the second <note>sanctity</note> attracted Christians; and the last <note>authority</note> drew those devoted to an active life and occupied with business. Likeness produces the first bond; charity the second; and utility or convenience the third. And if all these things are present in one man, he draws other men entirely to himself.

<margin>
The most virtuous men of Italy.
Celtic Gaul, that is, Lyon.
Homer, the source of geniuses.
Ulysses's prudence regarding Troy.
Praise of Hieronymus of Pavia.
The Celts are more ingenious among the Gauls.
The wisdom of Saint Jerome. <note>original: "Diui hieronymi"</note>
Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>.
Sallust.
</margin>

Furthermore, since these qualities were present in **Hermolao Barbaro**, **Poliziano**, **Giovanni Pico**, and **Marsilio Ficino**, and since they once drew our own **Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples** <note>original: "fabrum nostrum stapulensem"</note> across those vast stretches of land for the sake of their friendship, it should not seem strange to you if Frenchmen living in <term>Celtic Gaul</term><note>A term used by humanists to refer to the region of France centered around Lyon (Lugdunum).</note> also move and attract you. For the nature of mortals is greedy for travel, and it is not only pleasurable to have recognized the worship of various peoples and the customs of nations, but it is also beneficial in life. Indeed, this knowledge not only delights a man, but also renders him prudent and highly learned. Hence **Homer**, the source of geniuses and the parent of antiquity, wishing to show **Ulysses** as a man of supreme prudence, sang that he had wandered through many cities and perceived the customs of many men. Similarly, he extols **Hieronymus of Pavia** with a proclamation of virtue as a most Christian and religious philosopher, who through much travel perceived not a few things wonderfully suited for forming the mind and instructing his life. He crossed the Alpine mountains, penetrated the innermost parts of Celtic Gaul, visited the Celts most learned in philosophy, and drank from the philosophy of **Aristotle** alongside them. He sought out the theologians of <term>Lutetia</term><note>The Latin name for Paris.</note>, and like a second **Saint Jerome**, he is regarded as a surveyor of the world, a purifier of souls, a tamer of vices, a thirster for knowledge, and a scorner of money. I have touched upon these cups, Hieronymus, so that while I was praising other studious men and our own, I might also show my approval of you. You will, however, grant me pardon that my duty has been interrupted for a long interval; you will bear it easily and modestly. First, I would not wish you to think that your letters were less pleasing to me because of that delay, since they were written so copiously and so ornately that they would be worthy to be sent to **Marcus Tullius Cicero** and **Sallust** (if only they were alive). They radiate the finest eloquence that your age allows. There happened, moreover, in that polished speech a certain indication of your special love toward me, so that I do not know whether I should praise your eloquence or admire your virtue. For friendship, especially when forged among good men, is not 

<column-break/>

only necessary—as the distinguished **Aristotle** says—and not only useful and healthy for the human race, but it is also a certain singular and extraordinary virtue. For what else is it that the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> call friendship, if not either a certain virtue or something combined with virtue? Indeed, it is worthy to have the name and character of virtue, as it proceeds from the purest and most abundant fountains of benefit and duty. As for those who measure friendship by profits or pleasures, or by any bodily or external things, they are certainly not far from the truth when they call that same virtue "honest." Therefore, I esteem and love you frequently, you who knock at the doors of friendship so humanely and with such decorated letters. But why should I discuss our friendship further, which is clearly visible and stands out? I come, therefore, to the response to your letter which you recently sent me. I do not know whether to admire its gravity or its sweetness more. I was wonderfully gladdened that you came into Gaul to see our **Lefèvre d’Étaples** and your **Champier** (whom you had known from books and the monuments of sacred philosophy). We read that **Orpheus** and **Musaeus** <note>Legendary Greek poets and musicians.</note> traveled through provinces and visited new people so that they might see in person those they had known from books. Thus **Pythagoras** visited the priests of Memphis. Thus **Plato** traveled most laboriously through Egypt and to **Archytas of Tarentum**. Thus you, sweetest Hieronymus, entered among the Celts and crossed the Alpine mountains. You penetrated the <term>Insubres</term> and <term>Allobroges</term><note>Ancient tribal names used here to describe the peoples of Northern Italy and the Savoy region.</note>, and the Celtiberians, the most opulent kingdoms of Gaul, and at last, having crossed the very wide Rhone, you arrived at Paris of the Parisians <note>original: "lutetiã parisiarũ"</note> so that you might hear our Lefèvre teaching among a few disciples about nature, about morals, and about the hidden mysteries of theology. Though the land of Gaul had not drawn him to contemplate himself, the fame of one man led you there. For Lefèvre is, out of the whole number in this most flourishing Gaul, like a certain light and ornament of integrity. For the goodness which nature bestowed upon him, he mixed with the elegance of Italy, so that no one is more famous than this one man, no one more excellent. For he possesses those choice words which savor not of the Rhone or the Liris, but of the Po, the Tiber, and the Capitol. It seems to me that the Tiber has begun to flow into the Rhone and the Seine; and although that ancient purity of Roman speech has not left Italy, the Gauls cultivate it with such great zeal that they almost yearn to steal it away. I return to Lefèvre, whom (as you write) you approved of; you set before yourself that celestial idea of his genius. You heard many things concerning natural, metaphysical, and theological questions, and how he made Aristotle agree with Plato in many points. And though Lefèvre favors Aristotle greatly, he has not sworn himself to the words of any one master; he so mixed certain Platonic things with the Peripatetics at times that he did not defraud each of his own proper praises (as you write). Thus he has access to both of these philosophers, so that he rejoices to be called neither a Platonist nor a Peripatetic. Instead, he is entirely apostolic and a fellow-initiate of the faith; he is entirely overflowing with sacred doctrine; he is entirely rapt toward the godly **Dionysius** <note>Refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a mystical theologian.</note>...

<summary>In this letter, Symphorien Champier responds to Hieronymus of Pavia, praising the intellectual and spiritual bonds of friendship that transcend national borders. He highlights the journey of Hieronymus across the Alps to study with the great humanist Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples in Paris, portraying the exchange of ideas between Italy and France as a revival of ancient wisdom.</summary>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page continues a letter discussing the intellectual landscape of the time, specifically focusing on the relationship between the teachings of Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples (often called "Faber" or "the Smith") and the two giants of Greek philosophy, Plato and Aristotle. The author transitions from personal praise to a deep dive into the "Symphony" or harmony between philosophy and Christian theology.</meta>

<margin>
A comparison of Plato and Aristotle.
</margin>

...as well as to the divine loves of Hierotheus. These are your thoughts regarding our **"Smith"** <note>original: "fabro nostro"; referring to the French humanist Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples</note>. But do not wonder that he favors Aristotle so much; for most of the ancients, both Greek and Latin, did the same. Some favored the reasoning of Aristotle, others that of Plato—approving of some points and rejecting others. There were even those who, relying on their supreme talent, strove to show that the two philosophers agreed with one another. Among the Greeks, **Simplicius** did this in many instances; among the Latins, **Boethius** promised he would do so; and **Giovanni Pico**, most famous throughout the world for his letters, also promised to do it—though whether he fulfilled it, I do not know. Indeed, no such work of his has come to light in our age.

We were hoping that we might eventually find some exposition and comparison by our "Smith" or by **Clitoneus** <note>likely Josse Clichtove, a student of Lefèvre d’Étaples</note> regarding both philosophers, whether on natural or divine matters, or those pertaining to ethics, or the method of discourse which they call **Logic**. We hoped to see how these two supreme men either agree or disagree, by what reasons this is proven, and what "matter and form" mean in Aristotle versus "the Great and the Small" in Plato; in what way **entelechy** <term>entelechia: the actualization or "completeness" of a thing</term> moves, or how the soul is moved by itself; whether the first or second substance is more powerful; whether there are any "separated forms" <note>Platonic Ideas existing apart from matter</note> or if they are entirely unseparated; and if they are separated, whether they exist as substances in themselves or in the secondary concepts of the mind. Furthermore, how "being" is predicated of entities—whether equivocally or univocally—and whether that method of "division" which Plato often calls the peak of philosophy is the same as the science of demonstration, or something different.

Is this structure of the world uncreated and eternal, or created and fleeting? Or is it perhaps both created and uncreated and eternal at once—and in what sense created, and in what sense uncreated? Furthermore, can it then be said to have a soul? Moreover, is God the cause and maker of substance itself, or merely the cause of the motion of natural things? Should the heavens be called a "fifth body" <note>the quintessence</note> among simple bodies, or one of the four elements? Furthermore, what should be considered the ultimate end? Is it virtue and honor, or the science of contemplation? Or—to use the words of the **Neoterics** <note>modern Scholastic theologians</note>—is happiness found in the "act of the intellect," as **Thomas** <note>Aquinas</note> believes, or in the "act of the will," as **Johannes Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus</note> says?

I used to think the books of our Lefèvre and Clichtove would be full of these and other such opinions of the supreme philosophers, so as not to dwell on each point. But since the "Smith" is entirely "Apostolic" (as you write) and overflows toward the ambrosia of **Dionysius** himself, as well as the divine loves of **Hierotheus**, he values these Platonic trifles at a straw <note>original: "floccipēdit"</note>, lest he lead Christians into the thickets of those who are called "worldly philosophers." That "Apostolic philosophy" is more useful, for it establishes life and morals; for Platonic philosophy only makes men learned, but this other makes them both learned and good. Yet, since he favors Aristotle in philosophy, it is a marvel that he can overflow toward the divine loves of Dionysius and Hierotheus. For that most holy man, **Dionysius the Areopagite**, who was the first and greatest author of Christian theology after the Apostles, had no writer on divine matters before him except for the Apostle

<margin>
Difficulties of Platonic and Peripatetic philosophy.
</margin>

<margin>
Saint Thomas.
Johannes Scotus.
The most holy men Hierotheus and Dionysius.
The utility of philosophy.
</margin>

<column-break/>

**Paul** and **Hierotheus**, the bishop of Athens. In the book he published *On the Divine Names*, where he used these men as his teachers, he wrote as follows:

<margin>
The golden words of Dionysius.
</margin>

"The substantial infinity remains above all substances; and the supra-mental unity remains above minds; and to all intelligences, that which surpasses all intelligence is unintelligible. The One is ineffable, exceeding every method of discourse; and again, the life-giving unity is the supra-substantial substance of every unity. It is unintelligible mind, ineffable reason, unintelligibility, and unnamability; it bears the likeness of no entity, and it is the cause of all entities, yet it itself is 'non-being,' insofar as it is beyond all substance. Likewise, there is no sense of it, no imagination, no opinion, no reason, no science, no name." And a little later: "The supra-substantial divine principle, because it is supra-essence and supra-goodness, can be understood least of all."

My dearest brother Hieronymus, did not Dionysius take these things from Plato using almost the very same words? Plato, illustrated by the light of nature, wrote these things concerning the One and the first principle of all, and concerning the simplicity and unity of God. Our most holy doctors, the leaders of the Christian religion, taught these things while inspired by the Divine Spirit. This fact seems to testify clearly enough that Plato at some point both felt and wrote truly regarding divine matters. 

<margin>
The agreement of Saint Dionysius with Plato.
</margin>

But we omit these for the sake of brevity. I openly profess this: I do not defend the opinion of Plato as if it were to be approved in every part, or as if I think it should be compared directly with our Christian doctrine. For I do not approve of that pre-existence of souls, nor the number of the gods, nor the souls of the heavens and the stars, nor many other things for which the Gentiles are condemned by the Church. 

<margin>
The author of the letter does not hold with Plato in many things.
</margin>

However, I have decided to explain what the two philosophers felt and what the distinction is between them in our **Symphony**—that is, the "Harmony of Plato with Aristotle and of Galen with Hippocrates." For even if both are Gentiles and far from our faith, it will still be worthwhile to declare which of them felt more rightly and more in accordance with our religion. This is especially true since I will be doing no injury to Aristotle if I seem to prefer Plato to him; indeed, I did not approach this comparison of my own accord, but was compelled by your letters because of the opinion of the "Smith," who puts the student <note>Aristotle</note> before the teacher <note>Plato</note>.

<margin>
The Caperlan Symphony.
</margin>

<margin>
Labeo.
A comparison of Aristotle to Plato.
</margin>

In my opinion, Aristotle is to be praised for his doctrine, in which he was most brilliant, and for his study, by which he deserved well of the human race. "Aristotle," says **Labeo**, "was a student of Plato of the highest genius, yet in wisdom he was inferior to Plato." But if we praise and admire Aristotle, as is certainly worthy, we shall not for that reason detract anything from the glory of Plato; rather, if one judges rightly, we increase it. For although thanks must be given to Aristotle for the benefit of so many works which he left to us and to posterity, no less thanks must be given to Plato, who made it possible for Aristotle to provide them. That is to say, Plato gave us such a man as Aristotle; he cultivated his genius; he adorned him with all disciplines. Aristotle used only this one teacher—and not for five or ten years...

<summary>The author discusses the ongoing intellectual project of reconciling the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology, citing early Church figures like Dionysius the Areopagite who utilized Platonic concepts. He defends his preference for Plato over Aristotle, arguing that while Aristotle was brilliant, he was ultimately a product of Plato's superior mentorship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a letter from the French humanist and physician Symphorien Champier to his friend Jerome. It expands on the relationship between master and student, the limits of secular philosophy, and provides a catalog of Champier's own intellectual output during a period of war between France and England.</meta>

<margin>Demosthenes</margin>...but he listened for twenty continuous years. For as **Demosthenes** <note>An ancient Greek statesman and orator.</note> says: the one who commits the seed to the earth is the cause of the crops arising. How could **Aristotle**, a man of such outstanding talent, have listened to **Plato** for so many years unless he felt he was perceiving the greatest fruit from Plato's doctrine—unless he considered Plato’s knowledge something to be proven and sought after? Therefore, 

<margin>Theophrastus</margin>**Theophrastus** <note>Aristotle's successor in the Peripatetic school.</note> is to be praised, for he wrote much more, and of no less quality, than his teacher Aristotle; but Aristotle is to be praised even more. Even if none of his books survived, it would be enough that he was the teacher of Theophrastus. In the same way, our own **Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples** <note>original: "Iacobus stapulensis"; a pioneering French humanist and theologian also known as "Faber Stapulensis."</note> is most greatly to be praised and admired as the teacher of the unlearned <note>original: "indocti"; likely a humble rhetorical device or a reference to their status before his instruction.</note> **Josse Clichtove** and **Charles de Bovelles**, and the parent of their learning. Even if no trace of his disciplines remained, he would still deserve the highest credit for the works written by Clichtove and Bovelles, as he was their author <note>in the sense of being the source or inspiration.</note>.

But whatever I may judge concerning Plato or Aristotle, that precept of the Apostle in the third chapter of **Titus** must be held, where he says: *“Avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law. For they are unprofitable and vain.”* <note>original: "Stultas autem questiones et genealogias r contentiones et pugnas legis deuita..."</note> He gave a similar command to **Timothy**, saying: *“But avoid foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they do gender strifes. And the servant of the Lord must not strive.”* And to the **Colossians** in the second chapter: *“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.”*

Therefore, those who believe they give light to the truth through **paralogisms** <term>paralogismos: a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</term> and clever absurdities are in error. For it is not the night that brings the day, nor is it Aristotle or Plato who brings faith, but the light that radiates from above. Indeed, the "empty philosophers" against whom Paul argues were Jews who reasoned fallaciously based on the signs and elements that had been handed down to them, to which they added their own human perceptions rather than divine ones. For circumcision, the **Passover** <note>original: "phase"; from the Hebrew Pesach.</note>, the lamb, the sprinkling of blood, the red heifer, and that whole genre were to the Hebrews like letters and elements; but in truth, the "elements of the world" are Christ. Divinity does not dwell in those old elements as it does in His own body. In Christ, the fullness of divinity dwells bodily; indeed, the body of Christ (of which He is the head) is most full of divinity. By His mercy, He has made us, as members of His body, bodily participants in that divine fullness.

I return for a moment to the "Smith" <note>Referring again to Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples.</note>. I praise the fact that you have embraced him and Charles de Bovelles so in friendship, and I am most grateful. As I have learned from your letters, you are greatly loved by them; both praise your virtue, learning, and kindness, and hold you in high regard. Why say more? Though there were already many reasons for mutual love, you act in such a way that more serious ones are added daily. Something might be added to the reasons, but nothing can be added to the height of that love. Regarding what you write about me: you attribute much more to me than is proper. Stop, Jerome, extolling me with such marvelous praises.

<column-break/>

Love deceives you. I have wandered too far; I would not deserve to see Jerome among the Gauls <note>Referring to the French people.</note>, and I am pressed by great grief. Finally, Jerome, there is little in me, but whatever there is, understand that it is all yours. I do not promise you gold or silver, nor Corinthian vases, nor shining pearls; but I promise good faith and a true and sincere love in our **Symphony** <note>original: "simphonia"; Champier’s preferred term for the intellectual harmony between different philosophical and medical traditions.</note>.

Concerning my trifles, these few things give me confidence in the "Symphony" between Plato and Aristotle. We are now putting the finishing touches on the "Symphony" of **Galen** and **Hippocrates**. As for the works of mine which we have already completed, they are these:
1. *On the Miracles of Holy Scripture*, in two books.
2. *On the Customs and Wonders of Nations and Provinces*, in one book.
3. *Theorems on the Miraculous Propositions of the most blessed Apostle Paul*, in six books.
4. *On the Christian Religion against Pagans, Jews, Heretics, and Muslims*, in four books.
5. *Periarchon* <note>Greek for "On First Principles."</note> *on the Principles of Platonic Disciplines*, in three books.
6. *Epitomes on the Books of Hippocrates*, in six books.
7. *The French Rose* <note>original: "Rosa gallica"</note> *on Maintaining Health*, in eight books.
8. *The Bulwark of France*, in three books.

These are the works, besides others, which still remain unfinished in my hands. There is nothing else to write now. War was being waged with the **King of the English** <note>King Henry VIII, who invaded France in 1513.</note>. But we hope that a treaty will be struck and peace composed as soon as possible; the ambassadors on both sides promise as much.

Farewell, best of men, and keep this admitted **Symphorien** <note>The author, Symphorien Champier, referring to himself.</note> in your heart for a very long time. Since you were the first to approach this friendship, see to it that you make it firmer every day through both familiar habit and frequent letters. Again, farewell; remember us in your prayers, for we have dedicated ourselves and all our things to your will.

From our library at **Maixe** <note>original: "Mancelum"; a town in Lorraine.</note>, the primary town of **Lorraine**. August 4, in this year 1513.

<margin>Books which he himself composed and those he has not yet sent out.</margin>

<margin>A treaty between the Most Christian King <note>The King of France.</note> and the Britons, whom they commonly call the English.</margin>

---

¶ The division of the books of the whole of Holy Scripture and the authors whom we have followed in this work: having placed them before your eyes in this form, we do not pass over them ungratefully, but name them in their proper places so that we are not caught in manifest theft <note>meaning plagiarism.</note>. To this is then joined another common partition of the same books, taken according to another reasoning.

<summary>In this letter, Symphorien Champier discusses the intellectual lineage of Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, warns against the vanity of secular philosophy outside of Christ, and lists his own extensive bibliography of works on theology, medicine, and philosophy. The text concludes with a mention of the ongoing war with Henry VIII's England and a wish for peace.</summary>

On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture. Book One.
a

<image-desc>A full-page woodcut illustration divided into six panels, each depicting a day of Creation. Each panel is labeled at the top: ON THE FIRST DAY (Creation of light/separation of land), ON THE SECOND DAY (Creation of the firmament), ON THE THIRD DAY (Creation of plants), ON THE FOURTH DAY (Creation of the sun, moon, and stars), ON THE FIFTH DAY (Creation of birds and sea creatures), and ON THE SIXTH DAY (Creation of land animals and man). ### Lord Symphorien Champier of Lyon: On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture.

### Concerning the Creator and the constitution of created things, and whether God created all things at once. Chapter 1.

<margin>On the creation of the world.</margin>
<margin>Varro.</margin>
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
<margin>Crowds of philosophers.</margin>
<margin>Lucretius.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Democritus.</margin>
<margin>Averroes.</margin>
In the beginning, Moses says, God created heaven and earth. He "created," I say, rather than "begat" <note>original: *genuit*; the author emphasizes that the universe is a work of God's will rather than a biological or necessary emanation of his essence</note>. Indeed, that heaven and earth were created means, in my opinion, that this statement implies the whole world was founded by God out of nothing. For Marcus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar renowned for his vast knowledge</note> says the entire mass of the world's structure consists of heaven and earth; and the philosophers divide the whole world into two parts. One is the "elementary" part containing the four natures <note>the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire</note>, from which all things are born. The other is the "ethereal" part, which is also called the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>also known as "aether," the celestial substance ancient philosophers believed made up the heavens</note>. The Moon marks the boundary between these two parts; below it, as Cicero says, nothing exists except what is perishable and mortal—I always exclude the souls of men. Above the Moon, however, all things are eternal. The earth is the home of mortals, while heaven is rightly considered the dwelling and seat of the immortals. Therefore, God created both heaven and earth, perfecting the universal workmanship of the whole world out of nothing. 

But crowds of ancient philosophers cry out against this, asserting that "nothing is made from nothing" <note>original: *de nihilo fieri omnino nihil*; a fundamental principle of ancient Greek physics that challenged the Christian doctrine of creation</note>. This is a sentiment certainly more worthy of the Epicureans and Cyrenaics <note>schools of philosophy that focused on materialism and sensory pleasure</note> than the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>. We can bear with Titus Lucretius <note>Roman poet and philosopher, author of *On the Nature of Things*</note>, who was a poet and toyed with the opinion of Epicurus, beginning his poem thus: "I shall never allow that any thing is born from nothing by divine power" <note>original: *Nullam rem ex nihilo gigni diuinitus vnquam*</note>. And we can bear with the rest of the poets, whose custom it is to spare neither good men nor the gods. But the philosophers have asserted it as an indubitable opinion, establishing so firmly that "nothing is born from nothing" that nothing was ever held more tightly by them, or more accurately defended, or more constantly affirmed. Various schools of philosophers converge, and almost all of them agree with one voice on that same opinion. On one side stands Aristotle and the whole faction of Peripatetics; on the other, Democritus surrounded by a crowd of atoms <note>the OCR reads "atbo: morum," likely a corruption of "atomorum"; Democritus was the father of atomic theory</note>; and over there the clever and old-fashioned Averroes <note>the 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle</note>. Battalions of philosophers come forward from every direction, and with distorted and empty arguments, they try to prove that it is entirely impossible for anything to be procreated out of nothing. From this, they conclude that neither the rational soul nor the angel was created out of nothing—as if God did not have so much power! Yet who is so barbaric as not to know He is almighty? Who is so insane...

<summary>This page introduces Symphorien Champier's exploration of the Creation, specifically defending the Christian doctrine of creation 'ex nihilo' (out of nothing) against the classical philosophical consensus that "nothing comes from nothing." Champier cites figures like Varro, Cicero, Aristotle, and Lucretius to establish the traditional cosmological divide between the mortal earth and eternal heavens.</summary>
<keywords>Creation, ex nihilo, Genesis, cosmology, Aristotle, Averroes, Lucretius, elements, fifth essence, Moses</keywords>

Folio 2.

# On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture. Book One.

<meta>catchword: a ij</meta>

<margin>Agathon</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>The majesty of the supreme principle.</margin>
God is deprived of this alone (as Agathon <note>Agathon was a Greek tragic poet; this quote is famously cited by Aristotle</note> says, and Aristotle does not deny): he cannot make those things that have already happened not to have happened. Yet why should he not be able to do all other things? Truly, antiquity recognized the difficulty regarding the majesty of the supreme principle, whom it was nonetheless accustomed to call the "Best and Greatest" in solemn prayer. For why would they call him "Best" if they denied he was perfect? Why "Greatest" if he could not yet bring all things to pass? O remarkable wisdom! These philosophers <note>literally "the upright ones," used sarcastically here</note> deny that anything can be made from nothing. If one refers this sentiment perhaps to the nature of fleeting things or to the art that produces fragile works, one might perhaps agree that nothing comes from nothing. But when they apply this to God, the author of all things, they should not so much be called back from error as bound in the shackles of Hippocrates <note>meaning they are insane and need medical/mental restraint</note>. Oh, the unspeakable and detestable impiety of such philosophers! Who could tolerate that man called "Thrice-Greatest Hermes" <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> saying the following in his book *On the Power and Wisdom of God* <note>The *Poimandres*</note>: "Nothing comes from nothing, for things that are not at all have no nature by which they might be able to be made." And who can endure Aristotle—who is judged above others to study wisdom and profess truth—when he denies that anything can be made from nothing? Being entirely immersed, as he says, in the contemplation of nature, he either did not know how or was not able to lift the sharper edge of his mind to encompass God’s supreme power. He relies on the foundation that "everything which is made is made from some underlying subject." We are neither ignorant of this, nor do we deny it, if we are looking at nature; but if we wish to refer this to God himself, we must necessarily be convicted of both impiety and ignorance. Let this remain fixed for now (says the Blessed Augustine) that, having completed the creation of natures, on the seventh day God rested from his work; and now, thereafter through all time, he does not cease from the governance of the entire creation. But although it is taught that every creature was established through the alternation of seven days, this alternation of days is not understood as a span of time, but rather the succession of works is declared therein. For the narrator of the history <note>Moses</note> divided in speech what God did not divide in the perfection of his work. For God created all things together at once <note>original: *simul*</note> when, by a single will, he arranged for the manifold variety of all species to be made, in which he made those things which have not ceased to develop from their very origin. Augustine intends to explain this from that saying of the wise oracle in Ecclesiasticus 18: "He who lives forever created all things together." It should be understood, however, that through those words of the wise man, Augustine—in his *Literal Commentary on Genesis* and in *The City of God*—seems to feel that those six days of creation which Moses enumerated in Genesis are one single day repeated seven times. In this, he is generally not followed by the Doctors of the Church. Whence the Blessed Ambrose says: we can assert by the sequence of the reading that on the first day the Lord made day and night, which are the successions of time, and on the second day he made the firmament, by which he divided the water which

<margin>Against the philosophers</margin>
<margin>Mercury Trismegistus</margin>
<margin>In the *Poimandres*</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>An Aristotelian principle</margin>
<margin>Augustine in the book *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture*, chapter 1.</margin>
<margin>Blessed Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book 1, chapter 6.</margin>

<column-break/>

is beneath the sky and the water which is above the sky. Yet it is enough for the present assertion that in the beginning he made heaven, which is the prerogative and cause of generation, and he made the earth, in which the substance of generation exists. Thus says Ambrose. Augustine, however, explains that saying of the wise man differently when he says, "He who lives, etc. created, etc.," so that "together" <note>the word *simul*</note> does not refer to the instant of creation, but to the instant of arrangement, which is eternity; so the sense is: "He created all things which he arranged together from eternity." But if some troublesome caviler asks what Augustine’s final opinion was, it is answered that his final intention was that which is written in the books *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture* <note>A work traditionally attributed to Augustine in the Middle Ages, though now known to be by an anonymous Irish author</note>, because it is believed he wrote that book last.

### Concerning the Sin and Fall of the Angels. Chapter 2.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a standing figure in robes, possibly a saint or scholar, holding a book or object, set within a rectangular frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>John of Damascus, book 2, chapter 3.</margin>
Among the properties of the fallen angels and demons, John of Damascus first proposes that the chief angel who fell and provided the occasion of ruin for the others had been in charge of the terrestrial order, and the guardianship of the earth had been entrusted to him by God. From this, he seems to feel that this angel was from the lowest hierarchy of angelic spirits and the final order. However, this does not seem correct to many of the Holy Fathers. Indeed, the most holy Gregory feels that the fallen angel (who is expressed by the name Behemoth) was the most excellent of the celestial spirits and the most eminent of the supreme order. Blessed Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note> likewise seems to denote that the fallen angel was the most excellent among the others. Furthermore, the most holy fathers of our religion say that the angelic power—that is, the one which fell into the depths—was not made evil in its nature. It must undoubtedly be held that it was created good by a good Creator, and by its own will it fell away from the good and slipped into evil. Yet it is not to be thought that any of the nine orders of angels <note>The traditional ranks: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, and Angels</note> fell entirely, such that no angels of that order remained in their integrity; rather, those who fell are found called by the names of various orders in the scriptures. For example, in Paul's letter to the Ephesians, in the last chapter, they are called "Principalities and Powers," and in Ezekiel, chapter 28, a "Cherub." To the heap of the devil's sin, according to Augustine, is added the fact that immediately after he sinned, he fell into the pit of despair. For if he had not despaired of having pardon for his crime, he would never have procured the loss of salvation for man by enticing him. For he who desires to have pardon for his own sin in no way prepares to increase it by another. Through this despair, therefore, he not only found a pit of perdition for himself, but he also stood as the cause of perdition for man when he sinned. This, however, may occur to lighten the sin of man: that he did not devise the transgression of the commandment solely by himself, but consented to the serpent’s persuasion; and furthermore, he drew another rational creature <note>Eve</note> into the offense against God.

<margin>Gregory, *Moralia*, book 33.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius in the book *On the Divine Names*.</margin>
<margin>Paul</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
<margin>Blessed Augustine in the book *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture*, chapter 2.</margin>

### On the Justice of Abel and Enoch, who hold the Primacy among Men. Chapter 3.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a scholar or saint at a desk with a book.</image-desc>
Two questions have arisen (says Ambrose) under the names of the two brothers, who are fighting each other and are contrary to one another. One perspective considers everything as belonging to man, as if he were the primary author of all thought, sense, and movement; that is, it ascribes all inventions to human genius. The other perspective defers everything to God as the worker and creator of all, and subjects all things to His governance as the parent and ruler. That former perspective is signified by Cain; the latter is called Abel. One soul gives birth to these two "sects." And so they are considered siblings because they are founded in one womb, but they are so contrary that it is necessary for them to be divided and separated once they have been brought forth by the soul's labor. For one house cannot perpetually hold two combatants. However, I (says Ambrose), following the mystery of the scripture in this place, understand this more as a representation of two peoples: how God, by adding faith to His Church, took away the treachery of the law-breaking people from His pious folk. Indeed, the words themselves seem to signify this when God says: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your bowels" <note>Genesis 25:23</note>. This is a figure of the Synagogue <note>representing the Old Law/Jewish people</note> and the Church <note>representing the New Law/Christians</note>. In these two brothers, Cain preceded Abel; by Cain is understood the parricidal people of the Jews, who pursued the blood of the Lord, their author and—according to the birth from the Virgin Mary—their brother (so to speak). By Abel, however, is understood the Christian people adhering to God, just as David said: "But for me, it is good to adhere to God." From these few (says Augustine), Abel is chosen as the first prince of all human justice, and after him, the most distinguished Enoch from before the Flood. To these two, the sum of justice is committed at the very beginning and end of the world. For one [Abel] was received immediately at the beginning of justice, even at the very start of the world, crowned with martyrdom in the dance of his own blood. The other [Enoch] is still reserved without death as a testimony for the final age. But because of this, the Lord Jesus Christ committed the primacy of human justice to Abel, saying: "From the blood of righteous Abel even unto Zacharias" <note>Matthew 23:35</note>. He did not add the word "righteous" to Zacharias, showing that it is Abel, not Zacharias, who holds the inheritance of justice. Just as it is written in the genealogy of the Savior: "Jesse begat David the king; David the king begat Solomon." The word "king" is not added to Solomon, although Solomon did not hold a lesser kingdom than his father; rather, it is understood that he did not possess his father David's kingdom

<column-break/>

by hereditary right alone, and that the honor of the kingdom pertained more to David, who was the first from that generation to obtain the kingdom. Just so, Abel held the primacy in human justice because he was the first on earth to begin being righteous; thus, all others succeed the fathers as if by hereditary right. So all follow the footsteps of Abel in all parts of justice. For the whole of justice consists of these three: virginity, priesthood, and martyrdom. This triple justice was in Abel: first, he offered gifts pleasing to God [priesthood]; he left no lineage of his race in the world [virginity/chastity]; and he earned the crown of martyrdom by the shedding of his blood. Enoch, however, is preserved without death, removed from the company of men for nearly the entire duration of the world, so that in him it might be shown how men—if they had not sinned—would have been transformed into spiritual life without death after producing offspring. But although he has been preserved for a long time and still lives, he will not be able to avoid the debt of death which we all took on in Adam. Certainly, this also provides the occasion for writing: why a life is shown to last so long beyond the limits of human age. Yet in this, a "new nature" is not created for one man; rather, the original and general governance of all men is maintained. For it appears to those considering the history of the books of Genesis that it was implanted in man in his first condition not only to live for a time, but to live perpetually, had not the sting of sin terminated the boundaries of nature with death. It is written in the Epistle of Jude the Apostle <note>Jude 1:14-15</note> concerning Enoch: "And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying: Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment upon all, and to convict all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against God."

### On the Location of Paradise and the Four Rivers: A Question Worthy of Note. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' depicting a figure, possibly Moses or a prophet, holding a scroll or book.</image-desc>
God planted a paradise of delights: that is, in Eden. This was not near Ethiopia because of the course of the Nile, as some believe, but toward the East; and He placed there the man whom He had formed. For so it is written (says Augustine). Why was it done thus? Some have imagined paradise as only a sensible [physical] place; others as only an intellectual [spiritual] one. However, I believe that just as man was created as both a sensible and intellectual being, in this same way was His most sacred temple created. But a difficulty arises among the mathematicians <note>in this context, "mathematicians" refers to geographers or those using logic to map the world</note>. <margin>The arguments of heretics.</margin>
These are indeed the inventions of heretics; but who among mortals, unless imbued with Christian discipline, could unlearn such things? There are some most learned and famous theologians who deny a sensible <note>meaning "perceptible by the senses" or physical</note> Paradise and have imagined only an "intelligible" <note>symbolic or spiritual</note> one. From their flock seems to come the blessed 

<margin>The Blessed Ambrose is not held [as authoritative] on this point.</margin>
Ambrose of Milan, that otherwise most learned man, who says in his forty-second letter to Sabinus: "All others agree that in Paradise are the tree of life and the tree of knowledge, which discerns good and evil. The other trees also are full of vigor, full of life-giving breath, and rational." From these things (he says), it is gathered that Paradise itself cannot be seen as earthly, nor in any specific soil, but in our principal part [the mind/soul] which is animated and quickened by the 

<margin>Saint Augustine, eagle of the doctors. On the literal meaning of Genesis, book 8, chapter 7.</margin>
virtues of the soul and the infusion of the spirit of God. Thus he says; and in his book *On Paradise*, chapter one, he says: "We should not estimate this Paradise to be material <note>original: "hylen," from the Greek for matter</note>, and therefore let us leave it as Paul's secret." Blessed Augustine, however, thinks quite differently in the thirteenth book of *The City of God*. For he says of the Paradise in which the first humans lived, that something spiritual can rightly be understood by its significance, provided that the truth of that history is believed as a most faithful narration of actual events in a physical place. And in the eighth book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*,

<column-break/>

he says: "Regarding these rivers, why should I labor further to confirm that they are real rivers and not spoken of figuratively? They are not as if the names themselves merely signify something, since they are very well known by the regions through which they flow and are famous among almost all nations."

<margin>That the four rivers are real rivers.</margin>
Indeed, it is established from these things that they truly exist. For antiquity changed the names of two of them, just as the river once called Albula is now called the Tiber; so Gihon is the one now called the Nile, and Pishon was the name of the one they now call the Ganges.

<margin>Gihon, Pishon, Tigris, Euphrates. Worthy of note regarding the literal sense of sacred scripture. Luke 10[:30]. Two cities of Judea.</margin>
The other two, the Tigris and the Euphrates, have kept even their ancient names. We ought to be admonished to accept everything else primarily according to the literal property of the text, and not to think there is figurative speech in them, but that the things themselves which are narrated both exist and also signify something else. It is not because a parable of speech could not assume something about a thing that did not properly exist—as the Lord speaks of that man who 'went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among thieves.' Who does not feel and plainly see that this is a parable and that the whole speech is figurative? Yet the two cities named there are demonstrated to be in their proper places today. We would accept these four rivers in that [figurative] way if any necessity forced us to accept the other things narrated about Paradise as figurative rather than literal; but since nothing prohibits us from understanding the things themselves as literally true, why do we not rather simply follow the authority of Scripture in the narration of events? Let us first understand the events as they happened, and only then search out whatever else they might signify. Or shall 

<margin>Worthy of note from Augustine.</margin>
we be moved because it is said of these rivers that the sources of some are known while others are entirely unknown, and therefore it cannot be accepted literally that they divide from one river of Paradise? Rather, it should be believed that because the place of Paradise itself is most remote from the knowledge of men, the four parts of the waters divide from there, as the most faithful Scripture testifies. But those rivers whose sources they say are not [in Paradise] may flow somewhere underground and, after traveling through many regions, burst forth in other places where they are known as if at their own sources.

<margin>Cavernous and porous earth. Augustine, On the literal meaning of Genesis. The author’s response to the objections of astronomers. The usefulness of Mosaic philosophy.</margin>
For who does not know that several waters do this? But this is known only where they do not run for a long time under the earth. Therefore, "a river went out of Eden"—that is, from a place of delights—"and irrigated Paradise"—that is, in [our] language, all beautiful and fruitful things that occupied all the land of that region. Thus says Augustine. To those things said above, we respond that if the location of Paradise were proven by astronomy and mathematics, it would no longer be a matter of faith; but it is proposed to us as something to be believed. But lest I leave you empty-handed, I will bring some things forward so that I do not lead you into the thickets of the astronomers (whom our people call cosmographers). Mosaic philosophy <note>theology based on the writings of Moses, i.e., the Pentateuch</note> is more useful: it institutes life and morals. The former [astronomy] has sometimes made men deceitful, but the latter [theology] makes them both learned and good. It is...

...rather blindness in the judgment of astronomers and rashness in the judgment of men, than falsehood in Moses. Astronomers seemed not to care for Paradise, because they had nothing explored of it, and they judged that business to be above the human capacity for reasoning. John of Damascus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and scholar</note>, a man of sharp wit—whose skillful intellect, exquisite doctrine, and sweet speech illustrated his genius—having discussed much regarding Paradise and the Garden of Delights, finally says there are <margin>Damascene, book 2 of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 4. Two seas around Egypt.</margin> two seas, one of which surrounds Egypt, being itself in the middle between two seas, and so forth. Various mountains, islands, reefs, ports, various bays, continents, and tracts of shores were established; the shores are said to be sandy. Truly, the rocky shores are deep at the very beginning, having depth immediately; similarly, to the east is the sea which is called the Indian, and to the north that which is called the Caspian; and pools are gathered here. There is also the Ocean, like a river indeed surrounding the whole earth, <margin>The Ocean according to Damascene: what it is.</margin> about which the divine scripture seems to me to have spoken, saying that a river proceeds from Paradise having potable and sweet water. This Ocean provides water to every sea, persisting and remaining unchangeable; however, the sea becomes salty because the sun and others (like <term>Siphons<note>original: "Syphones"; here referring to the ancient belief that invisible tubes or columns of vapor drew water up from the sea to form clouds</note></term>) draw up the finest parts, whence clouds consist, and clouds produce sweet water from the evaporated water. This Ocean is divided into four beginnings, that is, into four rivers: <margin>Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, Euphrates</margin> the name of one is Pishon, this is the Indian Ganges; and the name of the second is Gihon, that is the Nile descending from Ethiopia into Egypt; and the name of the third is Tigris; the name of the fourth is truly Euphrates. There are, however, many other very great rivers, some of which vanish into the sea, while others are consumed in the earth; whence also the whole earth is porous and cavernous, as if having certain veins through which, receiving water from the sea, it produces springs. According to the quality of the earth, therefore, the water becomes filtered and purified; the sea water is strained through the earth and thus becomes sweet. If, however, the place from which the spring is returned is either bitter or salty, the spring is reduced to the nature of the earth. For water <margin>How water becomes sweet. Augustine, question 26. He notes here and weighs those who hold the opinion of the blessed Ambrose, and you should consider.</margin> that is frequently narrowed and breaking out with force grows warm; and hence waters are returned to their natural state. By divine command, therefore, cavities were made in the earth, and thus the waters come together in their gatherings; hence also the mountains were made. These are the words of Damascene. 

Saint Augustine, in the first book of *Questions on Genesis*, when discussing the land of Sodom and Gomorrah before it was deserted, said it was like the Paradise of God. He says that the land of Sodom and Gomorrah, before it was destroyed, is compared to the Paradise of God because it was well-watered like the land of Egypt which the Nile irrigates; it shows enough, as I think, how that Paradise which God planted where he placed Adam should be understood. For I do not see what other Paradise of God might be understood; and certainly, if the fruit-bearing trees in Paradise were to be taken as virtues of the soul—as some think—with no corporeal Paradise established on earth with true kinds of wood, it would not be said of that land: "like the Paradise of God."

### ¶ Whether Lamech killed Cain as it is thought. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure in a landscape, perhaps a scholar or saint, holding an object while surrounded by foliage.</image-desc> [E] Concerning Cain and his death, Ambrose, following the determinations, says: God drove Cain from his face and banished him from his parents to a separate habitation in a kind of exile, because he had passed from human <margin>Saint Ambrose, book 2 of *Cain and Abel*, chapter 10.</margin> gentleness to the cruelty of beasts. Nevertheless, he did not want a homicide to be avenged by homicide—He who prefers the correction of a sinner rather than his death. Whence Lamech was avenged seventy-seven times, because his fault was heavier; he did not correct himself even after the condemnation of the other. Cain had sinned before by a certain unforeseen impulse; Lamech certainly ought to have been careful of what he had observed in the response to the other. Indeed, by his own judgment, he ought to have held the sentence so that no one would think a guilty person should be struck down everywhere. And to come to the mystery: he ought not to have killed him who had the space for penance until the natural end of his life; he could have been excused if he had redeemed himself even by a late act of penance, had not a premature punishment snatched him away. These are the words of Ambrose. 

The blessed Augustine also feels far differently about the death of Cain. For he denies that Lamech <margin>Saint Augustine in the book of *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 6.</margin> committed the killing of a kinsman. Whence he says thus: those who think Lamech said this about Cain think so in vain: "I have killed a man to my wounding and a young man to my hurt" <note>quoting Genesis 4:23</note>. For Lamech was already born in the fifth generation from Cain, that is, from Methushael, the great-great-grandson of Cain. Lamech records this, however, to show that he who sins under a manifested law should be more sharply bound; and through this, if after Cain, his imitator was avenged sevenfold—whom neither the deed of Cain nor the correction nor the sentence later passed upon him terrified into turning his will from such an impious and most cruel crime. After Cain, therefore, Lamech perpetrated this homicide, who without doubt, according to what was said above, paid sevenfold punishments; and what would be for him who followed this after Lamech, he shows saying: "But of Lamech seventy-seven fold," so that because penance does not follow an evil work, he may be struck with seventy-seven blows of plagues. Whence also the <margin>Matthew</margin> Savior commanded that seventy-seven times be forgiven to a sinner who turns <note>referring to Matthew 18:22</note>. But it is not thought that another committed homicide after Cain and before Lamech, because it is said: "Vengeance was taken for Cain," as if Lamech says of himself what was already done. How, however, could he say that vengeance was taken on him when the homicide he confessed he had committed was still recent, since it is certain that every deed carries its sentence with it? For when there is no other hope except that which is known to be worthy of the completed work, he holds the future for the deed.

<margin>Augustine alone holds this opinion.</margin> Finally, it was said to Adam and Eve: "on the day you eat of it, you shall die the death"; and yet they certainly did not die immediately, but after a long interval of time. This is because they had already lost the hope of immortality. A future death was spoken of as present because it began to be held in expectation. Therefore, when Lamech confesses that he killed a young man, and Cain (as has been shown) could not have survived until that time—or if he did survive (which seems impossible), he was an old man and Lamech did not kill him. These are the views of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a primary Father of the Western Church.</note>, though this opinion is not commonly held.

### Whether Woman is Called the Image of God. Chapter 6.

<margin>Saint Ambrose, book on *Noah and the Ark*, chapter 26.</margin> It puzzles most people why God said "He made man in the image of God," and did not say "in my image," since He Himself is God. But understand (as Ambrose says) that there is both the Father and the Son. Although all things were made through the Son, we nevertheless read that the Father made all things and made them through the Son, just as it is written: *You have made all things in wisdom.* Whether, therefore, the Father is speaking, He made him in the image of the Word <note>The "Word" or "Logos" refers to Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity.</note>; or if the Son is speaking, He made him in the image of God the Father. And for this reason, he demonstrates that the nature of man is a certain familiar and domestic thing to God: that is, the <term>rational man<note>original: "rationabilis bois" (rationabilis hominis). The idea that humans are defined by their capacity for reason, which reflects God’s nature.</note></term> according to which we were created in the image of God. This is the view of Ambrose.

But a great difficulty arises: namely, whether a woman is called the image of God just as a man is. For the same Ambrose, in his book *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*, wrote: "Dearest son, it seems to me justly said that the <term>inner man<note>The spiritual or soulful part of a human, as opposed to the physical body.</note></term> is the image of God. For the soul is called the inner man, because that <term>clay-like mass<note>original: "lutea illa massa." A vivid reference to the physical body being made of earth or clay.</note></term>, moistened by fluids so that it does not dissolve from being dried out, is quickened, ruled, and contained by it. Therefore, the Creator made the soul of man (as has been said) in His own image; and the whole is called the soul." Thus he says; and since a woman possesses a rational soul just as a man does, it would seem that if the man is called the image of God, the woman should be as well. 

Contemplating the holiness and doctrine of Ambrose compels me to think so. However, the eminence of Augustine’s doctrine often moves my mind to the contrary. In his book *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, chapter 21, he says: "this is what it means for man to be made in the image of God: because one [God] made one [man], so that just as all things are from one God, so the entire human race is from one man." This likeness is such that just as the Son is from the Father, so the woman is from the man, so that the authority of a single principle might be preserved. But the Son was born of God the Father in an ineffable and incomprehensible way. The woman, however, was made from the man corporally, as we read, so that birth might arise through her. Indeed, the Son was born so that through Him the creation might be made. In this, therefore, they are dissimilar. For God was born of God, but a female from a man; because in the former there is <term>simplicity<note>The theological concept that God is not composed of parts, but is a single, unified essence.</note></term>, and only a simple thing could be born of a simple thing—spirit from spirit, God from God. Therefore, the man is the image of God. For it is written: "And God made man; in the image of God He made him." 

Whence the Apostle <note>The Apostle Paul, specifically in 1 Corinthians 11.</note> also says: "A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God." But the woman (he says) "should cover her head." Why? Because she is not the image of God. Again the Apostle says: "I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to have dominion over a man." Thus says Augustine. And in the same book, question 23, he adds: "The man and woman are indeed of one substance, both in soul and in flesh. But the man is greater in rank, because the female is from him, as the Apostle says: 'The head of the woman is the man.'" He made the man greater by cause, not by substance. For even in one body there are greater and lesser members; not by nature, but by <term>ordination<note>The hierarchical arrangement or "ordering" of things by God.</note></term>. 

Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> also seems to agree with the blessed Ambrose when he says: "It seems worthy to ask in this place according to the literal sense: how is it that, with the woman not yet made, the Scripture says 'He made them male and female'?" Perhaps (as I judge) he says this because of the blessing with which He blessed them, saying "Increase and multiply and fill the earth," anticipating what was to come. He says "He made them male and female" because a human could not increase and multiply in any other way except with a female. So that His blessing might be believed to be certain to happen, He said "He made them male and female." 

Let us see (he says) through <term>allegory<note>A method of interpretation that looks for a hidden spiritual or symbolic meaning behind the literal text.</note></term> how man, made in the image of God, is male and female. Our inner man consists of spirit and soul. The spirit is called male. The soul can be named female. If these have harmony and agreement between themselves, they increase and multiply through their internal suitability; they give birth to sons—that is, good senses and intellects, or useful thoughts—through which they fill the earth and rule over it. This is from Origen. Augustine, in his book *Seventy Questions to Orosius*, question 18, says: "When the soul acts upon and thinks about those things which are temporal, it is called 'woman'; then it is not to be called the image of God, and for that reason, it must cover its head, lest there be too much of a progression toward lower things."

### On the General Flood and Noah’s Ark. Chapter 7.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a king or patriarch (likely Noah) seated on a throne holding a scepter, representing authority and the start of a new lineage.</image-desc> Before the famous disaster of the waters (as Berosus <note>Berosus was a Babylonian priest and historian from the 3rd century BC whose works were often cited by early Christians.</note> reports), in which the entire world perished, many ages passed which were preserved by the Chaldeans. But this flood of Noah submerged all lands; and therefore it is called an absolute inundation of the earth by barbarians, Greeks, and Latins alike. Whence Moses also noted this when he said: "All
