Berosus <note>Berosus was a 3rd-century BC Babylonian priest and historian whose works, though mostly lost, were frequently cited by ancient scholars to corroborate Biblical events.</note> shows in his third book how the human race was preserved through the preparation of the ark. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> also uses this passage against Apion the grammarian, saying that Berosus the Chaldean and the Phoenician historians name Noah and his sons by their proper names, as well as the flood and the ark. He says that some part of his ship, which came to Armenia near Mount Gordyene, still exists, and that some people take bitumen from there. Moreover, Maseas of Damascus <note>Maseas (or Nicolaus) of Damascus was a historian and philosopher during the Augustan age.</note> says the following in his 96th book of histories: "There is a high mountain in Armenia above Myriada called Baris, in which it is said that many people fled and were saved at the time of the flood, and that a certain man was carried to the summit of the mountain in an ark, and the remains of the timbers were preserved for a long time." 

This man was the same one whom Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, writes about. Maseas records that Noah (whom our writers call Noe) was a man who worshipped God and was just; and while everyone else turned toward impiety, he alone received the command to build the ark. Before the flood, he prepared the wood for 120 years because of its great size, as Moses indicates. Indeed, for forty-two years he prepared the timber due to the immensity of the work to be done, and so in the following year—which was seventy-eight years before the flood—he began the construction of the massive ark, as Berosus suggests. 

Because it is said that the flood happened unexpectedly, this should not be applied to Noah and those who knew and recorded it on baked clay tablets and stones, but to the mockers who neither believed nor hoped that it would come. This first flood lasted nine months, as Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman geographer.</note> asserts in his collections, as do Moses in Genesis chapter 8 and Xenophon in his work *On Equivocals*. It exceeded all the highest mountains of the world by fifteen cubits, as Moses testifies; and as he says, all flesh under heaven was destroyed, except for Noah and his family. 

From this, it is clear that the Talmudists <note>The author uses the term "Taluindistas," likely referring to Jewish scholars of the Talmud.</note> are speakers of falsehoods and liars, acting against the divine scriptures according to their custom, when they claim the flood did not reach Mount Zion. Their argument is that the seed of the Giants was found as food after the flood, not realizing that Noah and his sons (as Berosus believed) were themselves giants. He says the Titans <note>In classical mythology, the Titans were a race of giants; here, the author syncretizes them with the Biblical Nephilim or giants.</note> fathered giants, and as Moses testifies, they established a city of Titans in Egypt which they call Tanis <note>original: "Tanum"</note>, dropping the first letter, as is clear from Numbers chapter 13. 

Berosus then continues regarding the reasons for the other surnames of Noah and his wife Titheia. He provides the reasons for the three surnames in his third book: Noah, Ham, and Titheia. Regarding Noah, he says that the surname **Janus** was attributed to him from *Jain* <note>original: "Jain"; this refers to the Hebrew 'yayin,' meaning wine.</note>, which among the Arameans and Hebrews sounds like "wine." From this comes Janus, that is, the "wine-bringer" or the "wine-drinker," because he was the first to discover wine and became intoxicated, as Berosus says. Propertius likewise suggests this, as does Moses in Genesis chapter 9, where he also calls wine *Jain*. There we have it: *when Noah awoke from his wine.* Cato also in the *Fragments of Origins*, and Fabius Pictor <note>Fabius Pictor (3rd century BC) was the earliest Roman historian.</note> in his *On the Origin of the City of Rome*...

<column-break/>

...say that Janus was called the "Ancient Oenotrian" <note>Oenotrian derives from the Greek word for wine, 'oinos'.</note> because he discovered wine, and also grain for religious use rather than for common consumption. These are not things we have received from outsiders as if from unjust possessors; nevertheless, we believe Moses alone.

Therefore, when God saw the world filled with malice and crimes, He decided to destroy the human race with a flood, whereby all flesh under heaven was wiped out. However, that plague did not touch any of the creatures that can live in the waters; it only killed the land animals. At this point, as Augustine says, a question arises for those searching shrewdly, which requires a solution: **Why do land animals succumb to human punishment more than aquatic ones?**

Since the earth from which man had tasted was immediately cursed by divine miracle, it was said: *Cursed is the ground in your work,* etc. Then another question arises: **Why did God not also curse the waters in the curse of Adam?** To which it is easily answered: because man did not drink the water against the Lord’s prohibition, but ate of the fruit of the earth. Beyond these reasons, God spared the waters from Adam’s curse because He had prepared to wash away that curse through water, which was done in the flood and is now granted through **Baptism**. For in water and the spirit, all human things—both physical and spiritual—are purged. 

Because of this, when the Lord had laid aside the curse of human death by rising again, he did not eat the flesh of land animals, but of aquatic ones. To confirm his resurrection, he ate a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb before his disciples. On this point, those who claim that the "waters of the firmament" <note>A reference to the "waters above" mentioned in the creation account in Genesis.</note> arrived before the flood do not believe there were rains in the world before the flood, because of the sign of the rainbow <note>original: "arcus"; literally "the bow."</note> which was placed in the clouds after the flood. 

Guided by this estimation, and investigating the nature of the creatures themselves, they argue that no rainbow would occur in a clear sky before the flood. The **Iris**—that is, the rainbow—appears in clear clouds and is always created by the sun and moist, clear clouds. It is not only produced by the sun, but is also sometimes seen in clear clouds by the moon. Therefore, it is possible that the first age of the newly created world existed without any turbulent changes in the air or rains, but was sustained by morning and evening dew. Just as it had long-lived men and those vigorous in bodily health in its own strength, so too the world itself, moved by no disturbances yet, stood firm, bearing fruits suitable for those being born. From the second age, just as it began to live with turbulent morals, so too did it begin to flourish with the turbulent storms of nature. 

In the same way, even now in the land of Egypt, it is not clouded by rains, but is nourished by the "sweat" of the earth itself, the mildness of the air, and the rising of the Nile river. But how this investigation should be accepted as certain, let the learned and the Catholics see. In these opinions, however different they may be, and...

<margin>Genesis 8</margin>
...through many convoluted paths of our ancestors: we hold this fixed in our minds, that whatever waters had come from above, a wind blew so that the earth might be bared of the waters. For thus it is written: *The Lord sent a wind over the earth, and the waters were diminished.* <note>original: "Immisit dominus ventum super terram: et diminute sunt aque"</note> Whether the wind had gathered those watery seas into clouds, or whether the space of the heavenly firmament had taken them back, let the learned decide for certain. However, those waters which had flowed abundantly from the disrupted fountains of the deep returned by the same paths from whence they had come, at the Lord’s command. 

Indeed, the islands—which many assert did not exist from the beginning of the created world—were formed in the process of time, when nearby promontories were divided from the mainland by the boundaries of the sea. By this, it is understood that the wild animals found in the island forests were not carried there by human diligence, but were discovered to be there when the islands were divided from the mainland. For who, for example, would carry wolves, deer, wild boars, foxes, badgers <note>original: "tarones"</note>, hares, and squirrels <note>original: "serquirolos"</note> into **Ireland** <note>original: "Hybernia"</note>? Or how could they have escaped the hand of a tamer if they were being transported, given that all these kinds are now seen wandering through the woods? 

Some authors say that the earth itself brought forth these kinds of beasts and wild animals; they believe these animals trapped on islands were not from the Ark, but were procreated from the earth itself. Even if someone believes this opinion regarding the receding waters of the Flood to be acceptable and sufficient, that question still remains renewed in our minds. For with the daily floods and retreats of the ocean, this question is always reborn. Just as we do not know the manner of this daily tide—where it comes from or where it retreats—so also we are ignorant of the retreat of the Flood. 

For he who desires true wisdom should hasten to the eternal kingdom where there is no ignorance, and in the meantime say with the distinguished teacher of the nations <note>St. Paul the Apostle</note>: *We know in part, and we prophesy in part.* <note>original: "Ex parte cognoscimus et ex parte prophetamus"</note> Indeed, all things we possess, we know only in part. We are still ignorant of how the surface of the earth upon which we labor is sustained. The sun is given for the service of our needs by day, but how it completes its journey at night is hidden from our knowledge. In ourselves, we know the day of our birth, but we are ignorant of the day of our death; though we know for certain it is coming, we do not know when. Even the physical things we see, we can only consider in part. Therefore, we know in part as long as we are in this world. But if we come to that light of the Father of Lights, there will be nothing in creation that we do not know. 

However, to follow our purpose regarding this great Flood, it is shown that nothing was done against nature that would seem a miracle to the creatures; for nothing seems to have been brought upon them that God had not already made in the first condition of creatures, except that the water was gathered from a more abundant supply of the sea and the rains. I would, however, confirm nothing in these matters with absolute authority, lest I be caught in a defensive argument.

### On the Division of Tongues. Chapter 7.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'C' featuring a man in profile wearing a cap, possibly a scholar or king, looking towards the text.</image-desc>
As the increase of human propagation proceeded, the very multitude of mortals became proud of their own multiplication. According to the height of their own choosing, they desired to build a structure reaching toward heaven. The judgment of Divine Justice was wonderful in restraining this insolence. **Ambrose** says that God confounded the single speech of those people—which had been harmonious with mutually understood meanings—into a variety of seventy-two languages. This was done so that, as the harmony among the workers perished amid dissonant voices, the machine of their insane construction would be dissolved, and a timely dispersal of that evil gathering would provide inhabitants for the whole world. 

These are the words of Ambrose. **Moses**, however, in the tenth chapter of Genesis, does not name all the leaders of the languages, but only those who had a distinct tongue. This is because Moses does not distinguish the nations—according to Ambrose and **Augustine**—except into seventy-two; according to others, seventy-four. They say there was no distinct language except through seventy-two (or seventy-four) separate speeches, even though there were distinct ways of speaking within the same language and speech. Yet these were intelligible under the same language. 

Therefore, Moses describes as many leaders as there were languages. The **Chaldeans** <note>meaning the Babylonian or Aramaic traditions</note>, however, claim there were as many leaders as there were founders of kingdoms and nations. Delirious in their usual fashion and with no certain author, they say there were only seventy languages. Because of this, the good **Brother Nicholas of Lyra** <note>A famous 14th-century Franciscan biblical scholar</note> erroneously explains (as it seems) that passage in Deuteronomy 32: *When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel.* 

He says that when the Most High divided the nations in the confusion of tongues, He established the boundaries of the peoples into seventy languages according to the number of the children of Israel, who were seventy, as stated in Genesis 47: *All the souls of the house of Jacob which entered into Egypt were seventy.* 

And Nicholas of Lyra did not see (as I think), or rather was ignorant, that there were seventy-two languages according to Ambrose and Augustine, and seventy-four according to others. For as is clear in the tenth chapter of Genesis, there were four primary leaders: namely **Noah**, **Shem**, **Ham**, and **Japheth**. And from Japheth there were fourteen leaders of languages. From Ham, thirty-one. And from Shem, twenty-six. If we wish to look at this more strictly and exactly...

<sig>b</sig>

<margin>Peleg</margin>
At the time of the division of languages, there were only sixty divisions. This is because if the father, **Peleg** <note>original: "Phaleph"; Peleg's name means "division" in Hebrew</note>, was born at the time of the division of languages—as appears in Genesis chapters 10 and 11—then he and his brother **Joktan** <note>original: "Jetan"</note>, who was born after him, and the thirteen descendants of Joktan, were either not yet speaking or not yet born. Therefore, they were not confused in their language. And so, removing these fourteen leaders from the seventy-four, only sixty remain. However, **Augustine** says that many authors agree there were seventy-two languages, which were used in the building of that tower in the land of **Shinar** <note>original: "Sannaar"</note>. It is also related in the Gospel that the Lord chose seventy-two disciples—excluding those primary apostles—through whom the same Gospel would later be preached to all nations.

<margin>Augustine, Book 1</margin>
In a prefiguration of these, the spirit of **Moses** himself was bestowed as a gift of prophecy upon seventy elders, and two others who had remained in the camp, namely **Eldad and Medad**. Their hereditary successors, as it were, were the seventy wise men descended from the stock of Israel sent to **Ptolemy Philadelphus**, the king of Alexandria, by the high priests (namely **Eleazar** and others who at that time were in charge of the Jewish people and the Temple). These men translated the ancient scriptures of the Law into the Greek tongue. Truly, God did nothing against the nature of human speech in this, even though He once disposed of languages by dividing and consuming them among men. The same nature of speech remains in men, except that habit eventually teaches different languages from one another, not naturally, but by custom. For a Latin or a Greek person born or raised among barbarians speaks a barbarian tongue; conversely, the son of a barbarian, taught by Greeks or Latins, speaks in beautiful discourse. From this, it is understood that God did not change the nature of men, nor did He create anything new in them, but only divided the modes and forms of speaking among the different races.

### On the Sodomite Vengeance. Chapter ix.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'A' depicting a figure in a landscape, possibly a traveler or shepherd, within a decorative frame.</image-desc>

<margin>Augustine, Book 1 of the Wonders of Sacred Scripture.</margin>
Before Sodom sinned, while it still kept the simplicity of an incorruptible life, it was like the paradise of God. But where—as **Origen** says—it began to be corrupted and obscured by the stains of sin, it became like the land of Egypt. Regarding that Sodomite vengeance, the blessed Augustine writes: After a great interval of time, five cities situated on the border of Arabia and Palestine—Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Zoar—enjoying the habitation of a most fertile soil and an abundance of all things, were joined in an unseemly desire for luxury. This provided an opening for the Lord's vengeance, so that the entire region, with its inhabitants and animals, was set ablaze by a downpour of fire and sulfur poured from above. Thus, those who made their sin public not only by doing it but also by preaching it, consumed an infamous life with a famous penalty. 

In this Sodomite punishment, God is seen to do nothing against nature, since the heat of an unusual desire was inflamed from that fiery aerial space above. **Lot**, the servant of God, was rescued from the plague of sinners by angels; but his wife, commanded not to look back, was solidified into a pillar of salt when she did so. Thus, she whose sight was not immune from sharing in the guilt could not escape death, even though she was rescued from the fire for the sake of her righteous husband’s company. 

But as we have maintained that nothing in God’s creation is against nature, but that an indwelling nature is always governed in all things: how is Lot's wife turned into a pillar of salt against the human nature of the body? In this mutation, no one who has confirmed the saltiness of tears doubts that the government of a salty nature exists in the human body. These tears, as physicians say, emerge from the disturbed gall, conceiving a salty nature in the depths of their hidden nature; when they flow from the eyes, they prove this by the test of taste. And not only in tears, but also in phlegm and the spit coughed from the chest, one tastes that the nature of salt is inserted through the human body. Therefore, the powerful Governor of things, when He wishes to turn the whole into a part, pours throughout the whole that which was hidden in a small part. And for this reason, when He wished to turn Lot’s wife into a pillar of salt, that very thin part of salt which was in the flesh infected the whole body. And so it happened that He who finished establishing all natures on a certain day added nothing from one nature into another, but governs each thing within itself, just as He established it in the first creation.

**Sedulius**: As Lot fled the chaos of Sodom, his wife looked back; changed into a pillar of salt, she remained frozen. ### On Melchizedek, and what the faithful think of him, and whether he was a man, an angel, or God. Chapter x.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'B' depicting a king or high priest (Melchizedek) holding a chalice and bread, within a decorative frame.</image-desc>

**Melchizedek**, the priest of the most high God, met **Abraham** returning from the defeat of the kings; he brought out bread and wine, offered it to him, and blessed him, saying: "Blessed be Abraham by the most high God, who made heaven and earth, who delivered your enemies into your hands." And as the Apostle added: the lesser is blessed by the better. Finally, he offered a sacrifice and gave tithes. For this reason, Melchizedek (which in Latin interpretation means "King of Justice" and "King of Peace") blessed him. For he was the priest of the most high God. "Who is the King of Justice and priest of God," says **Ambrose**, "except He to whom it is said: 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek'? This is the Son of God, the priest of the Father, who reconciled the Father to our sins by the sacrifice of His own body." Now, as to whether Melchizedek was God or an angel...

<margin>Ambrose, Book 3 on the Faith, chapter 5.</margin> Whether he was an angel or a man, hear the same **Ambrose** writing in his third book *On the Faith* regarding that **Melchizedek**: through whom **Abraham** offered his sacrifices. The Church does not understand him to be an angel—contrary to the Jewish fables—but a holy man and a priest of God who, bearing a <term>type<note>In medieval theology, a 'type' is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows or prefigures Jesus Christ or New Testament events.</note></term> of the Lord, is described as being without father, without mother, and without an account of his genealogy, having neither beginning nor end. This was to show that the eternal Son of God was to come into this world, who was born without a father according to the <term>incarnation<note>The Christian doctrine that God took on human flesh in the person of Jesus.</note></term> and without a mother according to his divine generation. He is without an account of his generation because it is written: *Who shall declare his generation?* <note>original: "Generationem autem eius quis enarrabit"; a reference to Isaiah 53:8.</note> Therefore, <margin>Ambrose, Letter 82 on Melchizedek</margin> we receive that Melchizedek as a priest of God in the prefiguration of Christ. Nor does Ambrose stop there; in his eighty-second letter, he says: "Since the succession of the lineage drawn through **Aaron** held the heirs by the bond of their ancestry rather than by their shared justice, the **True Melchizedek**—the true King of Peace, the true King of Justice—came according to the prefiguration of that Melchizedek whom we read of in the Old Testament." This is indeed what the interpretation of his name signifies: without father, without mother, without an enumeration of his genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life. This refers to the Son of God, who knew no mother in that divine generation <note>referring to Christ's eternal existence from God the Father</note> and ignored a father in this birth from the Virgin Mary—born from the Father alone before the ages, and arising from the Virgin alone in this age. He who is the end of all things certainly could not have a beginning of days. But he is set forth as an example so that a priest ought to be as if without father and without mother; in him, the nobility of lineage is not chosen, but rather the grace of character and the <margin>Augustine, Against the Questions of the Old and New Testament.</margin> prerogative of virtues. On this matter, the blessed **Augustine**, a man of subtle intellect whose exquisite learning illuminated his mind, seems to have wished that Melchizedek himself was not a man nor an angel, but the **Holy Spirit**. For he himself writes in the *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testament*, in the one hundred and ninth question: "This Melchizedek is certainly not understood to have blessed Abraham in the way that human priests do—that is, giving a blessing through the office of an embassy with solemn words—but as a property <margin>The same priest.</margin> which he received substantially by nature, and not through words, so that it might be his own. For he was the priest of God, but he blessed and the effect followed; certainly not by the merit of a priest, but by the merit of that soul whose clean heart God inspected. Therefore, Melchizedek is not called 'greater than Abraham' solely because of the office of the priesthood, but he is placed before him by nature, so that he is understood to be beyond men. For <margin>Notable from Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews.</margin> it can in no way happen that one who is placed above such a friend of God—and a man of such faith that he did not hesitate to kill his own most beloved son out of love and fear of God—should be thought a mere man. For by what justice or by what works could anyone merit more than Abraham merited? For there was nothing more he could do for the commendation of merits than what Abraham had already done. The scripture says, therefore, that Melchizedek is without father, without mother, and without genealogy. And lest

it be understood otherwise than is fitting, it added: *having neither beginning of days nor end of life.* By this, it shows that Melchizedek was neither born nor died. What can human subtlety argue against such manifest things? For what craftiness of the mind is so deceptive that it dares to resist the manifest facts, so as not to take the meaning from the reading, but rather to impose a meaning upon the reading? For some say that Melchizedek should not be believed to be as he is reported in the <margin>Ambrose notes this opinion.</margin> scriptures, and by this, they turn the scriptures to their own sense. First, it says 'without father, without mother.' For whoever you are who strives for contention: it is better for men to be defeated by the truth than to conquer for falsehood, for to lose the truth is not to win. If there were a Melchizedek who taught the fear of the one God on earth, Abraham was chosen in vain so that from him the people of God might be named. This Melchizedek, therefore, appeared as a precursor of the future sacred Son of God, because he who follows in order precedes in service. Therefore, the things we have said about Melchizedek are not to be wondered at, since the scripture—to the confusion of those who clamor against it—adds more and says, after all things worthy of praise, to confound the malevolent: <margin>Melchizedek</margin> 'But having been made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.' But he cannot be like the Son of God unless he is of the same nature. And what seems incredible if Melchizedek appeared as a man, <margin>The third person of the Trinity is Melchizedek according to Augustine.</margin> since he is understood to be the third person? For if Christ, who is the second person, was frequently seen in the habit of a man, why doubt what has been said? Christ is the High Priest; Melchizedek is the second. Now both are read to be alike, and in every way the authority of the one God is to be preserved; therefore, the third person <margin>Saint Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 9.</margin> is also subject to the paternal name. Christ is the vicar of the Father and the high priest, and by this, he is also called a priest. Similarly, the Holy Spirit <margin>Melchizedek is to be understood as the high priest existing for the Lord, most friendly to those existing and non-existing.</margin> is called the high priest of the Most High God. And although Christ and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, the order of each must be preserved. Priests or messengers are so called because they show in themselves him whose messengers they are; for they are his image. And by this, Christ and the Holy Spirit, naturally having the image of God, are called his priests; in them, God is seen, just as the Lord says: *He who sees me, sees also the Father.* And if the Lord was seen in the acts of God, the acts of the Holy Spirit are works signified by the Lord. Behold, now two different ways of interpretation have been brought forward, by which **Ambrose** and **Augustine** are accustomed to interpret **Paul’s** words concerning **Melchizedek**. Besides these, others still remain according to the opinions and perceptions of different men. But truly, it would be a laborious task and less suited to this present place to recount all the opinions of authors regarding that high priest Melchizedek, whom the Apostle mentions in the Letter to the Hebrews; nor can it be sufficiently clear to us which of them is to be preferred over the others. Therefore, we ought to confess that the Scripture is true, but as for its understanding, we must either attain it through reading or obtain it from God through prayers. 

Listen, however, to what **Ambrose** himself spoke elsewhere regarding Melchizedek, saying: "This is he in whom **Abraham** blessed the most high God who made heaven and earth. You see," says Ambrose, "that no man discovered this, but God announced it. For Melchizedek is God, who is the King of Peace and Justice, having neither beginning of days nor end." <note>original: "Deus est enim Melchisedech qui est rex pacis et iusticie"</note> 

On the other hand, **Joannes Annius** <note>Annius of Viterbo (c. 1432–1502), a scholar famous for his controversial "discoveries" of ancient texts.</note>, the interpreter of **Berosus the Chaldean**, asserts that **Osiris** taught **Samus**, the son of **Janus**—whom the Hebrews call by the surname Melchizedek, that is, "King of Justice," as if it were a title for Janus. For Samus lived five hundred years after the Flood, as **Moses** asserts. Therefore, he was living in this age, and since (as the same Moses claims) he was a priest of the most high God, it is a strong argument that he gave thanks to God for the first discovery of bread in Palestine. He instituted the offering of bread and wine to God in sacrifice because, on account of the discovery of bread, the human race had been raised up from mutual slaughter—as **Diodorus** writes in his first book. This prefigured the slaughter of the **Messiah**, and that through the "deific bread" and a priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, the world was to be liberated from the death of the blindness of souls. 

But truly, it would be laborious to reconcile this opinion of Annius with Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews and to respond to Augustine. Therefore, we must obtain the understanding of Scripture from God through prayers, for it cannot be certain which opinion concerning that priest Melchizedek is to be preferred. I marvel, however, at Augustine, since in his *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testaments* he held this opinion concerning Melchizedek; yet why among the heretics did he name the "Melchizedekians," as appears in his book *On Heresies* in the chapter *To What God Wills*? <note>original: "ad quod vult deum"</note> In that place he says: "The Melchizedekians: these priests of the most high God think that Melchizedek was not a man, but the Power of God." Therefore, I leave the judgment of such matters to the doctors of the church. 

However, **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, in his commentary on the said Apostle’s Letter to the Hebrews, explains it thus when the Apostle says "without father," etc. He sets up a <term>similitude<note>A comparison or likeness used for teaching.</note></term> regarding those things which are kept silent about him: because in Scripture, no mention is made of his father or mother, nor of his genealogy. Hence, from this (he says), some of the ancients took up the material of error, thinking that since God alone is without beginning and end, they should say this Melchizedek was the Son of God. But this is condemned as heretical. His genealogy is not placed in Scripture for a double reason: one, to designate that the generation of Christ is ineffable—Isaiah 53: *Who shall declare his generation?* <note>original: "Generationem eius quis enarrabit"</note> The other, to designate that Christ, who is introduced as a priest, does not belong to the **Levitical** tribe or to the genealogy of the Old Law. 

And this (he says) is the intention of the Apostle; hence he adds, "having neither beginning of days nor end of life." But the Apostle says this (he claims) not because Christ was not born in time nor died, but on account of his eternal generation, in which he was born without the beginning of any time whatsoever. Hence, John 1: *In the beginning was the Word,* <note>original: "In principio erat verbum"</note> that is, before any given time, the Word already was, as **Basil** explains. For he is before all days, because through him the world was made, with which days began. Likewise, he has no end of life, truly as to eternity; even as to his goodness he has no end of life, because Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more (Romans 6). And later in chapter 13: *Jesus Christ, the same yesterday and today and forever.* 

Then, when he says "resembling the Son of God," etc., he shows the likeness in regard to the priesthood. It should be known (he says) that it is common to say that later things are likened to earlier things, and not the reverse. And therefore, lest it be believed (he says) that the priesthood of Christ is later than the priesthood of Melchizedek, the Apostle removes this concern: for although Christ as a man was born after him and in time, nevertheless as God and the Son of God, he is from eternity. And therefore, in all these things, Melchizedek was likened to him who is the Son of God. And this is insofar as he remains a priest forever, which can be explained in two ways. One way, because no mention is made of the end of his priesthood, nor of a successor—Hosea 12: *In the hands of the prophets I have been likened.* <note>original: "in manibus pphetarū assimilatus sum"</note> Likewise, he is a priest forever because that which he prefigured—namely, the priesthood of Christ—is forever. Hence in Scripture it is frequently found as a "perpetual rite"—Exodus 27: *It shall be a perpetual worship;* Leviticus 23: *By a perpetual worship and rite,* because that which was prefigured by this shall be perpetual. So says Thomas. 

But it is a thing to be wondered at concerning Thomas himself, **Nicolaus de Lyra**, the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard, author of the standard medieval theology textbook.</note>, and others who commented on Paul, that they made no mention of the opinion of blessed Augustine recounted above. Therefore, it must be said that either they did not read Augustine, or they preferred to remain silent out of respect for his sanctity. Thus, we must confess that Paul’s Scripture is true, and as for its understanding, we must either follow it legitimately or obtain it from God through prayers.

# On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture.

<margin>Augustine, Book 2, *Against the Enemies of the Law and the Prophets*.</margin>
<note>While attributed here to Augustine, this work, *De mirabilibus sacre scripture*, is now generally attributed to an anonymous 7th-century Irish author known as Pseudo-Augustine.</note>
Sarah, the barren wife of Abraham, gave birth at ninety years of age to a son named Isaac, even though she had been sterile through the entire span of her life until that age. But this was very fitting: for the son she was laboring to bring forth bore the very figure <note>In theology, a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> of Christ, who would be born of a virgin alone without the desire of human lust. And this (says Augustine), although it was against custom, was nevertheless not done against nature; for even if it is against custom for a woman to give birth from such material <note>Refers to her aged and barren body.</note>, it is not against nature for a son to be born in a servant’s womb at any time. After this son was born and the servant-girl Hagar was cast out with her son Ishmael (who was born first), she wandered through the desert. When the water failed and Ishmael was dying of thirst, she wept as she walked with the boy. But an angel urged her on, saying: "The Lord has heard the voice of the boy." Then her eyes were opened, and she saw a well in the wilderness. Concerning this well, it is reported either that it burst forth from the earth at that moment, or, if it had been there before, that Hagar’s eyes were then opened so that she might see what she could not see before.

<margin>Genesis 21.</margin>
<margin>On the ram which Abraham offered in place of his son.</margin>
<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, Chapter 22.</margin>
Furthermore, so that it might be revealed even to men that Abraham remained faithful in God’s friendship, God commanded him to offer his son Isaac (who was by then a young man) to Him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that God had shown him. Being obedient, Abraham went quickly to the place God had indicated; and taking his son, he prepared to sacrifice him then and there. Nor, when he had done this, did he bring out a ram for the sacrifice by chance (as **Josephus** says); but truly, they embraced and kissed one another beyond all hope, for they had heard the promises of such good things. But this ram raises a question: where did it come from in the wilderness? Did the earth produce it in that hour, as some assert, just as it brought forth cattle in the beginning? Or, lest God be said to have created that work from the earth after the sixth day <note>Refers to the belief that God ceased creating new species after the six days of Creation.</note>, do we believe (on the authority of Augustine) that an angel brought this ram from elsewhere? This would be similar to how the angel transported Philip from the eunuch to Azotus, and how the angel is said to have carried Habakkuk to the lions' den to reach Daniel in Babylon.

### On the Burials of Jacob and Joseph: One in the Promised Land, the Other in Egypt. Chapter 12.

Joseph, a prophetic man, foresaw that the Egyptian race—given over to idolatry—would eventually want to worship him, as he had been the author of their earthly abundance and had delivered them from danger; and indeed they did so. For they set up a statue of an ox in honor of Joseph, because the ox is the helper of man in agriculture. For this reason also, when the children of Israel wanted to worship an idol in the wilderness, they made no other statue than a calf—that is, an ox. This was largely because he <note>Joseph</note> was being worshipped near his tomb. Therefore, lest Joseph’s memory should fall into the idolatry of the Egyptians, he foresaw the departure of the children of Israel and said: "God will surely visit you; carry my bones up from here with you." Now, Joseph desired to come to the burial place of his fathers, the tomb of Abraham and Isaac. Yet, dying later in Egypt, he did not wish to be carried to his father’s tomb immediately after death, but accepted a burial place in Egypt for the time being. He later commanded the people concerning his bones when they left Egypt, saying: "Carry my bones with you." 

For Jacob never mixed with the women of foreign nations, except for those who came with him from Mesopotamia; therefore, he was carried to his father’s tomb with his body intact immediately after death. Joseph, however, had taken Aseneth—daughter of Potipherah the priest of Heliopolis—as his wife and had been mixed with foreign blood; for a time after death, he was laid in the soil of a foreign land. Why, then, did he wish to be carried to the land of promise later, while first being hidden in Egypt? I have placed this explanation here not because it should be counted among the wonders, but so that I would not omit so great a span of time between Abraham and Moses without some worthy commemoration.

### On Moses, the Bush in Horeb, and the Unconsumable Wood. Chapter 13.

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 2, Chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>
**Sedulius** wrote:
"Once a bush appeared burning with harmless fires,
Glowing but not consumed; nor did the voracious void
Devour its vital nourishment or change its color.
The fire licked the leafy branches with a gentle heat,
Yet the wood remained unburnt."
</margin>
The Egyptians, being given to luxury and idleness while others labored, and being greatly subject to other lusts, also happened—out of a love for gain—to treat the Hebrews very poorly out of envy for their prosperity. Seeing (as **Josephus** records) that the race of the Israelites was increasing and that they were highly ennobled by an abundance of riches due to their virtue and industrious labor, the Egyptians suspected they were growing too strong. Forgetting the benefits they had earned through Joseph due to the long passage of time, and the kingdom having passed to another house, they cruelly oppressed the Israelites and sought to inflict various miseries upon them. They went so far as to throw their male infants into the river so the race would not grow beyond measure, and commanded they be slaughtered by various deaths.

At that time, Moses, son of Amram, was born in that storm. Fathered from the Levite lineage, he rose up to avenge his people. Seeing an Egyptian man oppressing an Israelite, he killed him and fled from Egypt. For forty years he was an exile in the land of Midian, tending sheep. When the time of the promise made to the fathers had passed, as he was driving the flock to the pastures of Horeb, a bush appeared to him burning with fire but not being consumed. And when he desired to investigate such a vision—why the bush did not burn up while it was on fire—the Lord spoke from the midst of the bush: "I am," He said, "the God of your fathers; I will send you into Egypt, that you may release their offspring from the yoke of the slavery that oppresses them." 

In this horrible vision, the first thing that strikes our work is: how did the fire appear to burn, and yet that in which it burned was not consumed? If the fire took its nourishment from that material, why did it not consume the source from which it grew? And if it did not...

As noted previously, this is Pseudo-Augustine.</note> Regarding this matter, the flame which was seen to have risen in the bush was shown so that what was necessary might be revealed. For (says Augustine) there is a certain type of shrub whose nature is such that however much it burns, it is not consumed; rather, <margin>Saint Jerome.</margin> by burning, it is rendered more pure. Saint Jerome, in his explanation of the wooden altar shown to Ezekiel in a vision of the Lord in the city, reports concerning this wood that although it has the color of wood, it retains the name because he was indicating its nature. If, therefore, that fire shown to Moses burned in a bush of that tree, what wonder is it if it was in no way consumed? Thus, the nature is preserved in both: that is, when the fire and the tree are considered together, the fire naturally burns from the tree, and the tree burning with fire is naturally not consumed. Certainly, in that bush, that fire did not appear to be an enemy of the tree, but rather that fire of which it is said: "Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire." <note>Psalm 104:4.</note> <margin>Incorporeal fire.</margin> Truly, an incorporeal <note>A fire without a physical, material body.</note> fire is declared in the bush; since it was shown to a physical man, it was necessary that it be demonstrated through some physical matter.

and commanded it to turn into a serpent. Obeying him, it even devoured the staffs of the Egyptians which appeared to be dragons, leaping upon them until it had consumed them all. They were not moved until they underwent these experiences and until God willed that Moses be shown as no liar in any of the things he had predicted; and because it would benefit men to learn to observe and do those things by which the Divinity might not be offended, lest He be turned to wrath and take vengeance on their iniquities. <margin>Bloody River.</margin> For by the will of God, the river flowed bloody for them, so that it could not be drunk. Although it appeared naturally changed in this miracle, the king, fearing and hesitating, permitted the Hebrews to depart on account of the Egyptians. But when the evil had been somewhat relieved, he changed his mind again and did not permit them to go. But while he persisted after the removal of the calamity and was unwilling to restrain himself from his malice, God sent another <margin>Frogs of the Egyptians.</margin> plague upon the Egyptians. For an infinite multitude of frogs fed widely upon their land; the river was also full, and their drink was polluted. As the animals rotted there, a stench harmful to all exhaled from the water. The whole region was full of this kind of evil, with frogs bubbling up and moving everywhere. They even greatly vexed their domestic dwellings, as they were frequently found in food and cups and walking about in their beds. The stench was cruel, and the frogs were abominable and troublesome, both living and rotting. While the wretched Egyptians were thus pressed, the king ordered Moses to take the Hebrews and depart. When he had said this, the multitude of frogs was suddenly exterminated, and the land and river together returned to their own nature. Pharaoh, however, as soon as the land was deprived of these sufferings, forgot that calamity and again held back the Hebrews. Therefore, by the stroke of another evil, the Divinity wounded his deceit: for an infinite multitude of lice sprouted upon the Egyptians, <margin>Lice of the Egyptians.</margin> bubbling up even from their inner parts, by which the wretches were miserably consumed. They were unable to exterminate this kind of pest by washings or by the ointments of medicines. Because of this plague, the king of Egypt was troubled, fearing for the plague of his people. Although he thought he would be seen as a defeated man before such shame, he was nevertheless compelled to temper his evil and granted the Hebrews their departure. But when this was lightened again, he decreed that they leave their children and wives as hostages for their return. Wherefore he provoked God even more, believing he could deceive His providence just as he had Moses.

### On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture. Book One.

...punishing Egypt for the sake of the Hebrews. For He first filled the region with many kinds and various modes of beasts whose appearance no one had encountered before; by these the people were consumed and the land was stripped of the farmers' cultivation. If anyone escaped the destruction of the first sufferings, they succumbed to this languor and the death of those sustaining such things. And when Pharaoh still did not obey God's commands, God did not fail to find ways to chastise him further, with diverse and greater evils coming upon him anew by His cleverness. For their bodies were cruelly wounded, being corrupted from within; and with the king still not moderating himself despite this plague, a violent hail fell. Nothing like it had ever been produced by the air in Egypt before, nor had a similar storm ever descended upon them in winter time. Then a species of locusts devoured the sprouts that had not been battered by the hail, so that generally all hope for the fruits of the earth perished for them. Pharaoh, as foolish as he was malicious, sensed the cause; nevertheless, he continued to contradict God. Deepest darkness, having no part of light, was spread over the Egyptians; because of this, their eyes were closed by the thickness of it, and they were forced to die miserably. For they feared lest they be swallowed up together by the gloom. The king, however, being angry at the things said to him by Moses, threatened to take off his head. Then Moses said he would speak no more words about these things. But God showed that the Egyptians were yet to be struck by one more plague, so that they would release the Hebrews.

<margin>
The death of the firstborn.
</margin>
For the death of the firstborn happened to the Egyptians in such a way that many of the nobles gathered around the royal palace to persuade Pharaoh to release the Hebrews with all speed. He, having summoned Moses, ordered them to go, judging that if they left the province, the imminent punishment of the Egyptians would cease. Others urged the Hebrews on so they might exit more quickly, while others did so because of their long-standing acquaintance as neighbors. And so they went out while the Egyptians wept and performed penance because they had been so cruel to them. They stayed at the place called Baal-zephon; then they came to the Red Sea. Because they could have no food from the land on account of the desert, they ate unleavened bread made from fermented flour that had been thickened for only a short time; they used this for thirty days. For this reason, the Jews hold a festival of eight days—the days of unleavened bread—in memory of that scarcity. Those who were of a suitable age for the expedition numbered six hundred thousand, and they left Egypt in the month of Xanthicus <note>original: "rantico," likely a transcription error for Xanthicus, the Greek name for the month of Nisan/April used by Josephus.</note> on the fifteenth day of the moon, as the author Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> attests, four hundred and thirty years after Abraham had come into Canaan, and two hundred and five years after Jacob was brought into Egypt. Moses was then in his eightieth year, while his brother Aaron was three years older; he also carried the bones of Joseph, as Joseph had commanded his sons to do. The staff into

<column-break/>

<margin>
The opinion of Augustine regarding the staff of Moses turned into a snake.
</margin>
The staff turned into a snake (as Augustine <note>This refers to Pseudo-Augustine's "On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture."</note> suggests), and the snake changed back into wood, is a labor for those who investigate nature. This is because both the staff and the snake are clearly shown to be made from the earth. Therefore, that which arises from the same earth is changed back and forth by the power of God the Governor. If we concede that all things made from the earth can be changed into one another—such as an animal into a tree, bread into a stone, or a man into a bird—then nothing could be certain of remaining within the boundaries of its own nature. We would seem to be giving our assent to the ridiculous fables of magicians who say their ancestors wandered through the ages in different forms. By this, we would not be calling God a "governor" in these matters—far be it from us—nor would we believe Him to do anything new after the first creation of all things that does not retain its own nature. For there is "nothing new under the sun," <note>Ecclesiastes 1:9.</note> nor can anyone say, "Behold, this is new." And therefore many doctors (he says) go further and say that the staff was a real staff which always remained a piece of wood in Moses's hands. However, it was turned into the form of a snake *imaginarily* <note>As a vision or symbolic appearance rather than a physical biological change.</note> several times as a sign, especially since it was not necessary for any use except the demonstration of a sign. For if it had been a true snake, it would have remained a snake; and indeed, it was a true staff which Moses used to begin striking Egypt with plagues, and it had never been changed into a snake but always remained a staff. By it the sea was divided and the rocks in Horeb and Kadesh were struck. If, therefore, that snake was shown only as a sign through imagination, why were the other snakes of the magicians devoured by it in the presence of Pharaoh? To this, the learned could easily respond: that the snakes which were devoured were also themselves imaginary. Therefore, the imagination of the divine sign could devour that which was made through the diabolical incantations of the magicians. According to this estimation, the staff is not changed into the nature of a snake, but is commuted for the sake of the sign's appearance. For nothing is found in the nature of a tree that could make a snake; and therefore, unless it is seen as the sign of the staff which it naturally was, it is seen as a snake spiritually. But indeed, we must ask (the same Augustine says), regarding the purpose of the present work, how God, the governor of nature, naturally changed water into blood. Water, being the matter for all liquids, is daily changed into various things through the very administration of nature, while it is continuously and naturally drawn into the food and refreshment of every single nature. For when it is poured through the vine, it is changed into the taste and color of wine. And when it rises to the high summits of the olive tree, that same water makes the richness of the oil. When it is gathered into honeycombs by bees, it works the sweetness of honey. When it passes through the trunks of palms, it produces dates and reaches a sweetness pleasant to the palate. And when it is assigned as food for different animals, it is turned into blood...

fo. xv.
# On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture. Book One.

this same [substance] is distinguished through the flesh: for it prepares milk of white color and most pleasant sweetness in the breasts to nourish offspring, and through all other members of the flesh, it darkens the red color of blood. There are many aforementioned types of blood through the same flesh which the natural philosophers <note>original: "physiologi"; these were early writers on the nature of animals and the physical world</note> number up to twenty-three: from which they announce urine, semen, bile, black bile, saliva, and tears, and others to be; nature prepares this through various parts with water in its daily operations. What therefore stands in the way of capable minds if He, the most powerful Governor, should naturally effect in a moment that which He does through a longer time in other things? Water turned into blood does not act against nature: but what He would effect through time in other things, at the Lord's command, He works immediately in itself. Regarding the other plagues with which God through Moses and Moses through Aaron had chastised Pharaoh and his land and his servants: the simple narration of the plagues itself manifests that nothing exceeded the boundaries [of nature]: since (as the same Augustine writes) even if then more frogs than usual are always born from the waters, and gnats <note>original: "cynifes"</note> arise from dust by the heat of the sun in summer time, and locusts and flies, solidified by the sun's fervor, gather from everywhere; and beasts of burden, for various reasons, complete the term of their life by a customary death; disturbed dust from the earth often obscures the air; and infected air generates blisters and ulcers in humans and beasts; hail also and lightning rush down from frozen and violently disturbed clouds; the absence of light when it has receded hinders the gaze of the eyes more than darkness; death also, first sown in Adam, is shown to all his children: through which the firstborn offspring of all in Egypt were then more strictly condemned.

### On the receding and drying of the sea and the harmonious song of the children of Israel. Chapter XV.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a bearded figure (likely Moses) holding a staff, set within a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>

Furthermore, when the departure of the Hebrews from the Egyptians occurred: they took it heavily as if those signs of Moses had been by sorceries, and they deliberated on rushing upon them; taking up arms, they pursued. Moses led the Hebrews to the sea while the Egyptians watched. When indeed Moses had reached the shore, taking his rod, he asked God and called upon his Helper and Assistant: and when he had prayed, he struck the sea with the rod. Suddenly cut by the blow and divided within itself, it left the ground bare: so that there was a path for the Hebrews and a flight from Pharaoh’s army; the sea entered after Israel: but it was a refuge for one and a snare for the other. Therefore, when all the army of the Egyptians had entered the sea, it was poured out again, and the descending storm of winds overtook all the Egyptians: rains and also

<column-break/>

most heavy thunder descended from heaven. And these indeed, says Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, were so destroyed that none of them remained. In this miracle so remarkable among the works of God (says Augustine), this is required by the intention of our present task: how nature is preserved in the dried and receding sea from the shores. But we believe we find this not so with difficulty, God helping us: we who very often consider the backs of ponds covered with ice by freezing waves. Therefore, what is very often naturally effected in waters by winds and rains—not without a whirlwind of air while frost takes hold of the lower parts—is proved to have happened there then by God's command through a glacial wind suddenly acting on the sea. But just as the dry sea is suddenly returned at the Lord’s command, so by the same command, it is dissolved from dryness into fluid waves. Regarding its receding, we have already spoken before concerning daily administration: because we are accustomed to seeing it happen incessantly through the estuaries of the ocean sea. From which we can gather that the sea naturally leaves the shores every day, not against nature, although then, with God governing, it uncovered its own shores in a far different and dissimilar way. After crossing the Red Sea, the children of Israel sang, all the old men with the boys: and all ages, inspired by the same utterance <note>original: "famine"</note>, as if with one mouth, taught by no previous instruction, chanted the same fitting words together as one. But in these singers, the same Spirit is known to have effected nothing against nature. In whom breath and voice and words are moved through mouths and tongues. And thus it is held that that song, "Let us sing to the Lord," which is wrongly attributed to Mary <note>Miriam, the sister of Moses</note> on the fifth day [of the week] as if she herself had been its maker: because that song was not made by human means, but inspired by God.

### On the sweetening of the waters at Marah and the Manna. Chapter XVI.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a standing figure in robes, possibly a prophet or saint, within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

Therefore, having been granted such salvation unexpectedly, the Hebrews were again heavily saddened while they were led toward the mountain, and the region was a desert, lacking necessary food, and the water was difficult; it was not only in need of providing something for the people, but it was not even suitable for nourishing any animals continuously. Therefore, fatigued by labor and complaining with the heat of thirst, they found very bitter waters in Marah: prohibited by their saltiness, they were unable to have any solace for their thirst; but a piece of wood is shown to Moses by the Lord: by the touch of which the bitter water of the river is sweetened, and then the people, intoxicated with the heat of thirst, put aside its flavor <note>its bitterness</note> which until then had incessantly fatigued them with fury. But how will the investigator of nature prove it was done naturally that bitter waters in a moment...

It also discusses the divine inspiration behind the Song of Moses and the sweetening of the bitter waters at Marah.</summary>

immediately they are sweetened by the touch of the wood. "Regarding which," Augustine says, "what was the nature of that wood that seemed to possess such sweetness, that once dipped, the most bitter wave of the river became sweet and savory?" For if someone were to throw a honeycomb into bitter water now, would not the honeycomb become bitter rather than the water becoming savory? From this it is understood that the wood did not then make the water sweet against its nature, but by the command of the Creator and the Governor of nature, He changed the water into a flavorful state. For that which is achieved through human effort or the long cultivation of things is worked by the will of God when nature itself has need. Sailors frequently prove that bitter waters or even the saltiest ones can be turned into a sweet flavor; they filter them through the best soil <note>original: "humum optime terre"; this refers to an early method of desalination through soil filtration</note> and by this craft, having often sweetened them, they temper their thirst. The Creator and Governor of creatures himself uncovers the hidden nature in the thing itself, which would otherwise be manifested through another thing.

Having entered the wilderness, the Hebrews—nearly six hundred thousand foot-soldiers, excluding the "mixed multitude" <note>original: "purgamento erranti"; literally "wandering refuse," referring to the non-Israelites who left Egypt with them in Exodus 12:38</note>, that is, the cloudy and promiscuous crowd that had ascended from Egypt—God satisfied them for forty years with manna, which is to say, with heavenly bread. For Moses taught the Hebrews that the dew did not descend from heaven according to their own opinion, but had come for their salvation and food; and when they tasted it, as Josephus says, it provided them with the faith to believe. They, imitating their leader, took delight in the food; indeed, it had a very pleasant sweetness and delight. It was similar to aromatic plants <note>original: "aromitibus scipulis"; likely a corruption of "aromaticis dactilis" (aromatic dates) or related to spices</note> and its size was like coriander seed. Finally, the Psalmist, remembering that bread later, said: "He gave them the bread of heaven. Man ate the bread of angels." It descended with the dew through the night (always excepting the night of the Sabbath) around the area of the camp, showing the whiteness of snow. 

If indeed someone left any of it until the morning of another day, it swarmed with worms. Therefore, it was born in that upper part of the earth where hail and snow are produced (as Augustine records), and it was administered to men in the lower parts of the earth as food by the angels. From this it is easily discerned that God did not seek sustenance from somewhere outside of nature, but commanded it from the earth. It was not that God could not provide them with common bread every day even in the desert, but so that man, fed from the clouds, would know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. For just as He commanded nature so that man should be satisfied by bread, so also regarding any other thing, if He had so ordered it as He possessed it; and then He rained down wholesome sustenance from the clouds. Therefore, He made manna generated from the air through the ministry of angels, and for that reason it is called the bread of angels.

### On the rock struck in Horeb and on the turning of waters into stones. Chapter 17.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'A' featuring a seated figure pointing towards a landscape, framed by decorative foliage.</image-desc> And so they were provided for with food, the children of Israel, for forty years—the length of time they were in the desert. When they moved on from there, they came (as Josephus relates) to Rephidim <note>original: "rasim"; a misspelling of Rephidim</note>, having suffered the newest miseries of intolerable thirst. Moses then turned to God in prayer, asking that just as He had promised food to such a great multitude when they could not hope for it, He might provide for them now. God commanded that he strike with his staff the rock that was placed there, and from it he would receive an abundance of the things he lacked. Moses struck the rock with his staff, and it having been split, water flowed out copiously and very clearly. They wondered at the unexpected deed, and to those drinking, the draft was sweet and most pleasant. 

Regarding water being made into stones in the beginning: how can one be ignorant of this, who does not doubt that the nature of crystal proceeds from snow freezing over a long time into the immutable hardness of stone? Especially since we often observe clumps (as Augustine reports) not made from the soil of the earth itself, but from the growth of the first-fruits of hay on the tops of trees or cliffs, in which we find small stones already created by the pouring in of rains and the movement of the soil of the hay itself. We have also seen some clay-like <note>term: "argyllosas" (argillaceous); refers to soil containing high amounts of clay</note> lands, soaked by the accustomed course of flowing waters, converted into the hardness of stones. In these we also notice harder stones inserted, as if of an older age, which the earth itself had previously held within it. In the same way, we see some stones containing hollow shells <note>term: "cauos ostros"; a medieval recognition of fossils</note> that were interposed when the earth was soft, now inserted without their natural hardness. Many marine reptiles are also covered with leathery shells <note>original: "testudinibus cortaneis"</note> which have a hardness greater than many stones. 

From all these manifest proofs, no learned person denies that stones are now created from water alone, and some from water and earth. Just as the nature and custom of "weeping marble" <note>original: "lachrymosi marmoris"; likely referring to condensation on cold stone surfaces</note> indicates, the nature of salty liquid is also turned, having been condensed, into the hardness of stone, and is turned back again to be dissolved into liquid. Also stone, as the history in the books of Job tells, is turned into copper when dissolved by heat; which cannot happen unless it is first moved into the nature of a liquid. Furthermore, every metal, of whatever hardness it may be, is revealed to be of a stony nature: once dissolved by fire, it liquefies. Since, therefore, it is proven that the nature of stone is born from the moisture of water, what stands in the way if, by the will of God the Governor, the stone is changed back into water? It does not act against nature, but hastens to return to its own origin when God commands the rock to provide water for His people.

After these things, Augustine says that Moses’s relative <note>original: "cognatus"; referring to Jethro, his father-in-law</note>, who had brought Zipporah, the wife of Moses, and his two sons to him, hurried to meet Moses in the desert. Through his advice—even though he was a gentile—tribunes, centurions, leaders of fifties, and leaders of tens were established among the people of God <note>This describes the first administrative hierarchy of the Israelites, suggested by Jethro in Exodus 18</note>. But a question arises concerning the sons of Moses: why are they not the heirs to their father's leadership of the people, and why are they even excluded from the priesthood? For the Psalmist says, "Moses and Aaron were among his priests." It is taught that, in a sense, a false claim is made when the sons of Moses are born of a gentile mother for the sake of his wandering. For this is what is recorded of Moses when his firstborn was born: "and he called his name Gershom <note>Latin: "Gersan"</note>, saying: because I have been a stranger in a foreign land."

<margin>On the forty-day fast.</margin>
After the people of God were rescued from the ten plagues of the Egyptians, on the fiftieth day from when the Passover was celebrated in Egypt, Moses brought down the Law of the Ten Commandments from Mount Sinai on two stone tablets. When he was offended by the crime of the sinning people <note>The worship of the Golden Calf</note>, he shattered them at the foot of the mountain. After replacing them with the same number of tablets, he earned the right to receive the same commands again through the gift of God the Giver, after fasting for forty days. During this time, contrary to the custom of human nature, he was twice burdened by no hunger or labor, as I have said: he ate no food of earthly life, for sustained by the company of the Divine Word, he was able to endure such a long period without hunger.

### On the Ethiopian wife of Moses and the leprosy of the murmuring Miriam. Chapter XIX.

Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Moses, who had crossed the waters of the sea on foot with her brothers, bristled with the spots of leprosy because she had murmured against her brother Moses—not yet knowing the mystery of the "Ethiopian woman" <note>Moses's wife, mentioned in Numbers 12</note>. She would not have been freed from such a great contagion unless she had pleaded with Moses. As Ambrose suggests, that murmuring refers to a "type" or symbol of the Synagogue, which, being ignorant of the mystery <note>original: "sacramentum"</note> of the Ethiopian woman—that is, the Church gathered from the gentiles—murmurs with daily insults and envies that people. Yet, by the faith of that same people, the Synagogue itself shall be rescued from the leprosy of its own faithlessness, according to what we read: "that blindness in part has happened in Israel until the fullness of the gentiles should come in, and so all Israel would be saved." But when God called only those three into the tabernacle, Aaron was corrected by the word of God and protected from punishment by the oil of his anointing; but the leprosy tore at Miriam’s body with a white pallor. For this reason, she was ordered to stay outside the camp, but through the prayer of Moses, she was called back, healthy again, on the seventh day. Indeed, Moses’s Ethiopian wife had been in the house of Pharaoh, from which Moses departed at age forty; she waited for him through many days of his wandering. Having been brought out of Ethiopia, she was led with him through the desert; unless perhaps, as Augustine says, Zipporah is called an "Ethiopian" because the Ethiopians once came forth from the land of Midian.

### On Korah and his brothers consumed by fire and swallowed by the earth, and on the people demanding meat in the wilderness. Chapter XX.

When Korah <note>Latin: "Chore"</note>, Dathan, and Abiram incited two hundred and fifty men against Moses and Aaron so that they might separate themselves and rise up against the others, they said: "Let it be enough for you that the whole congregation is holy and the Lord is among them." Whereupon the Lord, being angry, spoke to the whole congregation: He considered and knew who were His, and He brought the holy ones to Himself. And He commanded that they choose censers <note>original: "arulas"; literally "small altars," used here for incense burners</note> and put incense in them—Korah and all who had risen with him against Moses and Aaron, the priests of the Lord—so that he who was chosen by the Lord might be confirmed as holy among the Levites of the Lord. And Moses said to Korah: "Hear me, sons of Levi: is it a small thing to you that God has separated you from the congregations of Israel?" and further (as Ambrose says), "You seek to perform the office of the priesthood. Thus you and all your congregation gather against Aaron; who is he, that you murmur against him?"

Consider, therefore, that the cause of the offense was that they, being unworthy, wished to perform the priesthood; and for that reason they were distrustful, murmuring and disapproving of God's judgment in the selection of His priest. Therefore, a massive fear seized the whole people; terror almost enveloped everyone. However, at the pleading of all, lest everyone perish through the insolence of a few, those guilty of the crime—the two hundred and fifty with their leaders—were separated from the body of the whole people. The roaring earth split in the midst of the crowd; the gulf opened to the depths and snatched away the guilty ones. They were so removed from all the supporting elements of the world that they were not contaminated by the breath of the air, nor the sight of the heaven, nor the touch of the sea, nor the earth as a grave <note>A poetic way of saying they were completely erased from the living world</note>. The punishment ceased, but the malice did not. From this very event, a murmuring arose among the people that the people had perished because of the priests. In this indignation, the Lord would have destroyed everyone, had He not been moved first by the prayers of Moses and Aaron. Afterwards, through the intervention of His priest Aaron, He preferred to grant the ungrateful ones the shame of forgiveness for their evils through those to whom He had granted grace. But whoever thinks the earth performed that office of vengeance against its nature (as Augustine says), let it be known without doubt that nothing is entirely without life; the earth is perceived to be insensible, yet those things which are seen to move in it—the growth of trees and the thickets of herbs—run like veins of blood throbbing in living flesh. Thus also, the rivers of "living waters" flow through the earth, through which life flows into the insensible by God’s command. The earth "opened its mouth" when it served as a threat against the sins of the good <note>original: "bonum peccatorum"; likely meaning the earth acted as a deterrent for the sake of the righteous</note>.

<margin>Ambrose, Epistle 82, to the church of Vercelli.</margin>

<margin>On the people demanding meat in the wilderness. Numbers 11.</margin>
...the mystery of vengeance swallowed the tents of the sinners. Furthermore, the faithless people, burning with a craving for meat, murmured and preferred the onions of Egypt over the heavenly manna. But when the matter seemed unbearable even to Moses, the Lord said, "Sanctify the people for tomorrow. For I will feed them with meat for an entire month." Moses, moved by human weakness, replied that there were six hundred thousand foot-soldiers—not counting the countless common people among them—and asked: "Shall a multitude of sheep and oxen be slaughtered to satisfy them? Or shall all the fish of the sea be gathered together in one place?" Therefore, so that nothing which the fragile human mind of Moses could conceive should be used to feed the people, a wind went out from the Lord. It brought quails across the sea and carried them to the site of the camp. They flew two cubits high in the air around the camp, as far as a day's journey <note>original: "oxigometram"; a Greek-derived term used here to mean a day's journey or a specific measure of distance</note>. The people gathered them and ate for an entire month—that is, thirty days. But the vengeance for their unbelief followed this transformation; for in that place, before the people departed, those who had craved the meat were struck down by the Lord’s wrath and buried. Certainly, in this (says Augustine), the Lord contributed nothing new or contrary to nature; He simply provided for the necessity of His people by bringing forth a creature of birds created long ago and hidden in some secret corner of the world. For as it is written in the Book of Wisdom, they saw a "new kind of bird" <note>Wisdom 19:11</note> shown to them, not newly created. What God had established in the beginning along with other creatures, He administered to His people in their time of need. But while quails had been provided once before alongside the manna and had caused no harm to those who ate them, this time He brought them again so that no one would think the meat of birds caused death without the fault of murmuring; for in this punishment, those who ate with a clean conscience were kept safe, just as when the manna was first given, it caused no harm to the whole multitude.

### On the rod of Aaron which blossomed, the waters of contradiction, and salvation in the sight of the bronze serpent by the command of God. Chapter 21.

<margin>Numbers 17.</margin>
Let us observe that in priests, divine grace operates more than human effort. One rod out of many which Moses had received from the tribes and stored away—the rod of Aaron—blossomed. Thus the people noticed the spectacular sign of divine judgment regarding the priest, and they ceased to claim for themselves by human judgment that grace which they previously thought they were equally entitled to. But what else does that rod show (says Ambrose), except that priestly grace never withers? In its highest humility, it holds the flower of the power of the faith committed to its duty. Or perhaps because the mystery is also referenced here: Aaron’s rod showed buds of almond blossoms, by which it was revealed that Aaron was chosen above all others for the Lord's priesthood. However (as Augustine says), it is not suggested that the rod did anything against nature in this display.

After some time had passed, the thirsty people in the wilderness of Kadesh <note>The Latin "cades" refers to Kadesh-Barnea</note> rioted heavily against Moses and Aaron. When Moses brought this matter before the Lord, he was commanded to strike the rock with the rod. But Moses, disturbed by the murmuring of the unfaithful people, wavered in his faith in the Lord’s command. Before the people, he and Aaron struck the rock <note>original: "saxum"; transcribed as "fazum"</note> twice, and the thirsty people drank the water flowing abundantly. Yet, because of this, Moses did not enter the Promised Land. Once before, at Horeb, the rock was struck, where only the people's faithlessness was noted; but in the wilderness of Kadesh, the rock was struck twice, for there faithlessness was recognized in both the people and their leader. In that same place, as the people murmured, the Lord sent fiery serpents with burning breath among them. By their breath, many of the rebellious murmurers were killed. The rest, terrified by the punishment of the dying and moved to a spirit of penance, cried out to Moses and the Lord that this plague might cease. Therefore, moved by the tears of the penitent, the Lord commanded Moses to lift up a bronze serpent, stretched out on a rod, in the sight of the people. When this was done, the bronze serpent was immediately raised, and by looking at it, the wounds from the first serpents were healed. However, just as we said regarding the rod and the wood by which the bitter water was sweetened, the healing was in the serpent, but it was held within the Lord's command. For whatever He Himself commanded would then be salvation for the people; but the history of these preceding events is now contained as a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality in Christian theology</note> in Christ and in the Church.
