### On Balaam, the donkey, and the pillar of cloud. Chapter 22.

<image-desc>A decorative letter 'S' featuring a seated king with a scepter.</image-desc>

It is difficult to explain the history of Balaam himself: how God is said to have come to Balaam at night first and asked who the men were who had come to him. When he replied they were sent by Balak, son of Zippor, saying, "Come and curse this people for me," God answered him, "You shall not go with them, nor shall you curse the people, for they are blessed." Again, a second time, God is said to have come to him at night and told him to go with them, but to observe this: that he should speak only the word God put in his mouth. And yet again, a third time, as he was going, the angel of God met him. To the angel, Balaam's way seemed so ungraceful and inopportune that he even wished to kill him, had the donkey—seeing the angel whom Balaam could not see—not turned aside. And yet, after he is blamed by the angel for wanting to go, he is again permitted by the same angel to go, provided only that he guards the word God puts in his mouth, to utter that alone and nothing more. Therefore, not everything (says Origen) has an easy explanation. The angel who met him is undoubtedly the one who was present with the children of Israel. He opens the mouth of the donkey so that he might rebuke Balaam through her, and the mute...

<meta>catchword: c iij</meta>

...is confessed through the voice of a beast <note>Referring to the miracle of Balaam's donkey (Numbers 22), where the animal spoke to its master.</note> by one who is considered divine and wise. From that same Balaam, it is said that the race of the Magi and their teachings began to flourish in the eastern regions. From these events, we understand (as Augustine asserts) that the Lord changed nothing inherent in the animal's nature; rather, He restrained the ignorance of the prophet through the air of the animal's mouth, even while the animal remained ignorant of what was happening. This was done so that the Spirit of the Lord might speak through the animal, and that the prophet—who was puffed up with pride—might be humbled by finding that even a senseless, brute, and mute animal subject to him could speak. For the Spirit of God breathes where He wills, even if it does not align with the will of the speaker. Just as Saul, driven by an evil will, came intending to kill the prophets but was seized by the Spirit of the Lord and began to prophesy among those he was persecuting; so too Balaam, who had been brought to deliver a curse and desired to fulfill it, was unable to curse the people of God. Instead, against his own will, he was compelled by the Spirit of the Lord to bless them. For these two reasons, Balaam was permitted by the Lord to come: so that his foolishness might be confounded by a mute animal, and so that the arrival of Christ—who was to be the Savior of the gentiles—might be recorded in the Law of God by a gentile prophet. Throughout the entire journey of the people of Israel, the column of cloud was never absent by day, nor the column of fire by night. Thus, they were protected from the cold of night and illuminated amidst the darkness as they traveled with the fire; and by day, they were shielded from the heat of the sun under the cloud. The Lord, the guardian of Israel, truly protected them so that neither the sun by day nor the moon by night could harm them.

### On the Death of Moses and His Unknown Burial. Chapter 22.

<margin>Augustine in Book 1 of the Wonders.</margin>
[image-desc: Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a figure, possibly a scholar or saint, seated at a desk or lectern.] When the people of Israel reached the mountain called Abarim—which is high and situated opposite Jericho, offering a view of the excellent and vast land of the Canaanites to those looking upon it—Moses dismissed the elders. While he was saying farewell to Eleazar and Joshua, and still speaking to them, a cloud suddenly stood over him (as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> believes) and he was taken up into a certain valley. It is written in the sacred books that he died, for fear that because of the excellence of his virtue, he might be thought to have departed into divinity. He lived a total of one hundred and twenty years, of which he was the leader for one-third, minus one month. He died in the last month of the year, which is called <term>Dystrus</term> <note>original: "distris"; a month in the Macedonian calendar equivalent to February/March.</note> by the Macedonians, but among the Hebrews, it is the beginning of the month of <term>Adar</term> <note>original: "adan"; likely a typo for Adar, the twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar.</note>. With his teeth not loosened and his eyes not dimmed, and with his body intact, he paid the <term>common debt of all mankind</term> <note>A poetic way of saying he died.</note>. As many believe, he took away the staff with which he had performed signs so that it would not be worshipped, since the children of Israel later came to worship even the bronze serpent he had made. His entire life (as Augustine writes) is divided into three forty-year periods: for forty years in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh, he learned letters <note>He received a formal education.</note> from infancy; for forty years he was an exile from Egypt in the house of the priest of Midian; and for forty years he provided leadership for the people through the desert.

## Second Treatise of the First Book on the Wonders of Sacred Scripture.

### On Joshua the Son of Nun: On the Drying of the Jordan, the Shoes and Clothing of the Children of Israel, and the Overthrow of Jericho. Chapter 1.

[image-desc: Large decorative woodcut initial 'N' with floral and foliate patterns.] After Moses <note>original: "Nyse"; likely a scribal error or variant spelling for Moyses (Moses).</note> had departed from among men in the manner described, Joshua the son of Nun—once all the funeral rites for him had ended and the mourning had ceased—commanded the people to be prepared for the expedition. He sent spies to Jericho to learn of their strength and what sort of resolve they seemed to have. He himself was organizing the army as if he were to cross the Jordan at the opportune time. Strengthened by the word of the Lord, he ordered the camp to be moved from the plains to the River Jordan. Then, so that the <term>Ark of the Covenant</term> <note>original: "arce onere testamenti"; literally the 'vessel of the burden of the covenant'.</note> might honor the rest of the people, the priests went before them into the first waves. From the place where they stood all the way to the sea, the entire bed of the river was immediately emptied of its waters, and the mass of water above, which was increasing from the springs, rose up into the air like a mountain until all Israel had crossed the riverbed on dry feet. As a miraculous testimony to this, twelve stones—as many as twelve men could carry—were taken from the bottom gravel of the Jordan to the site of the camp; and an equal number of stones from the dry land were placed in their stead. Certainly, in this sign also (says Augustine), one must ask how the river naturally did not permit the Ark of the Lord to pass. Even if some part of the water that flowed to the sea followed its natural accustomed course—leaving the higher ground and sliding down through the slopes according to the custom of a river—human industry has also been known to bare riverbeds. We have read and heard how the Emperor Titus <note>A historical error in the text; this anecdote actually describes King Cyrus the Great at the River Gyndes, as recorded by Herodotus, but medieval authors often confused these figures.</note>, on his expedition to conquer Babylon, camped by the River Ganges <note>Another likely geographic error; the Gyndes was a tributary of the Tigris.</note>, which is said to be second in size after the Euphrates. There, the vortex of the greedy riverbed drowned a most beloved man and his horse, after the horseman was persuaded by the audacity of crossing the river. Infuriated by this deed beyond belief, the Emperor decided to take revenge on the river as if it were a sentient creature. Throughout an entire year, he used his whole strength to divide the immense river into four hundred and sixty ditches; once the bed was bared, he left a path passable for women only wetting their knees. Later, when the same army and king were besieging Babylon during that same expedition, they were repelled by the immense height of the walls; they then turned the upper shallows of the Euphrates river... Those men, being well-taught in the aforementioned skill...

...turning aside through a different boundary: by entering through the exposed walls of Babylon, they captured the city. <note>The author likely refers to the historical account of Cyrus the Great diverting the Euphrates to enter Babylon, using it as an analogy for how God uses natural means to achieve His ends.</note> Therefore, what human industry achieved through a laborious struggle, God accomplishes more easily by the power of His own virtue. But does human diligence not often achieve this? It compels water to climb a high mountain from opposing valleys and forces it to return to its sources when obstructed. And truly, if men—being earthly and made of coarse earthly matter—frequently do such things, why could the angels (by whose service all these wonders are performed) not do the same through the river? Just as it is the natural work of the air and its own proper office to hold waters in the clouds—as the learned and unlearned alike know through daily observation—so then, at God's command, the air prevented the river's course, so that the Ark of God and the priests might pass through the waves.

Therefore, having entered the land after the long labor of their journey, the multitude of people ate from the fruits of the region of Canaan, and the food of manna provided from the clouds ceased. In this long journey, however, a thing worthy of great admiration occurred: that for forty years, neither the shoes nor the clothing of anyone among the entire people failed. In this, the Lord did not create a new nature in the shoes and clothes, but rather preserved that which had been created long ago. Then, having departed from the bank of the Jordan, Jericho, the first of the cities of Canaan, stood in their way.

In that famous earthquake, one hundred cities of Libya collapsed, and in the earthquake of the Lord’s Passion, eleven cities in Thrace were subverted. Furthermore, what the efficacy of human action carries forward, the time of destruction or even old age eventually consumes. Yet (says Augustine), in saying this, I do not mean to show that the walls of Jericho fell by chance. Rather, we show that it was done within nature, just as in other miracles. For we do not doubt that this, like the others, was effected by the command of God and administered by the work of angels.

### On the standing still of the sun and moon in the time of Joshua. Chapter 2.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' featuring a figure in a landscape, possibly a scholar or saint.</image-desc>
Now the King of Jerusalem, a Jebusite by name, took it heavily that the Gibeonites had made a pact with Joshua <note>original: "iesu naue" — Jesus son of Nun, known in English as Joshua.</note>. He asked the kings of the neighboring nations for assistance to fight against them. While they were providing help—for there were four of them camping with him near a certain

<column-break/>

fountain (as it pleases Josephus to say) <note>Referring to Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian.</note> not far from the city, and while they were already preparing a siege, the Gibeonites called upon Joshua as an assistant. It had come to this: they thought they would be destroyed by their own kind, yet they believed they would be saved by those who were camping for the destruction of the Canaanite race, because of their friendship. Joshua, however, hastening with his whole army to their aid and traveling day and night, came upon the enemy at dawn. They fled, and he followed them, proceeding down the descent of Beth-horon, where he also recognized the operation of God signified to him by thunders, lightning, and a fall of hail greater than usual. Furthermore, as the day grew, lest the succeeding night should restrain the momentum of the Hebrews, Joshua came upon the kings hidden in a certain cave near Makkedah and punished them all. That the day was then extended in length and grew more than usual is plain through the Scriptures. For then Joshua, seeing the divine right hand fighting with him and all things proceeding with prosperous success, raised a certain new and wonderful prayer to heaven, saying: "Let the sun stand still over Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Ajalon <note>original: "Elom"</note>, until I conquer this people." And the sun and moon stood in their place until the Lord overcame their enemies. And the sun stood in the middle of heaven and did not proceed to its setting for the space of one day. There was no day like it before this, nor did God ever so listen to a man, because the Lord fought for Israel. By this command (says Augustine), the luminaries did not rest by the authority of a human command, but they obeyed the command of the Lord who ordered them to stand. For the creatures of God do nothing because of the word of a commanding man, but they do what the Lord, obeying the arrangement of His servant, has commanded. This behavior of the luminaries committed nothing new against nature, even if it showed something new occasionally arising in their service. But even that variation disturbed nothing in the course of the year or the remaining days, while the sun and moon each rested in its own order. For that delay or reversal left nothing hindered or unusual in the accustomed course of the luminaries and seasons; rather, they ran toward the limit of their setting just as they do throughout every day, after they had completed the space of that unusually glorious day. From this, it is seen that the long day contributed nothing to the length of the following night, since the moon—the ruler of the night—likewise rested there with the sun, the ruler of the day.

...moved him: in whose sight, while Gideon was preparing an offering, pouring the broth of the meat over it, celestial fire consumed the burnt offering. <note>original: "holocaustum"</note> And again, when he asked for a sign, there was dryness on all the earth and dew only on the fleece, and then dew on all the earth. Therefore, while historically this was shown in the burnt offering by a celestial flame rather than an earthly fire—to demonstrate that the coming war would be completed not by human strength but by celestial aid—the dew shown first on the fleece demonstrated that divine mercy, which was then in the fragile and soft people of Israel, could extinguish the fiery wrath of the nations just as water extinguishes fire.

<margin>Judges 13.</margin>
<margin>On Samson's strength.</margin>
¶ Likewise, when the Israelite people were serving the Philistines, an angel of God appeared in the habit of a prophet, first to the sterile wife of Manoah <note>The text reads "manne," a variant of Manoah.</note> of the tribe of Dan, and then to Manoah himself. He taught them concerning the son who was to be born to them and how he should be raised: that a razor should never pass over his head, and that he should not drink <term>strong drink</term> <note>original: "siceram," referring to fermented beverages other than wine.</note> or wine, nor anything that can inebriate. When Manoah, not knowing he was an angel, wished to offer him a meal, the angel said: "I will not eat of your food, but if you wish, prepare a burnt offering to the Lord." When Manoah prepared it at his command, and the burnt offering was consumed with fire before them, the angel immediately ascended into heaven, demonstrating that God had prepared the liberation of the people through the strength of the man to be born. Thus Samson was born and raised according to the command; he possessed the greatest strength in the seven locks of his head. This was proven for certain when, having been stripped of them, he also lost his power. For when he fell in love with a foreign woman named Delilah in the valley of Sorek—who had accepted money from the Philistine princes and received the price of his destruction—he revealed to her that the secret of his strength lay in the preservation of his hair. While he slept in her lap, she called a barber and shaved his head. Led away by the Philistines and deprived of his eyes, Samson turned a millstone by hand until his hair grew back to its former length. Then, while the Philistines were feasting, he was brought out to be mocked; he said to the boy who guided his steps to lead him to the two columns upon which the whole house rested, so that he might lean against them as if tired. Grasping both with each hand and invoking the help of the Lord, he shook the entire house. It quickly collapsed, striking down three thousand Philistines along with Samson himself. But to those investigating the laws of nature, Augustine says it causes no small difficulty to understand how the whole sensible body possessed the movement of strength in the sensible hair, especially since Samson suffered no loss of pain when the barber separated the hair from the rest of the body with a sharp iron tool. Augustine responds that the strength was not *in* Samson’s hair, but rather the observation of the Lord's command preserved his strength. As for why he recovered that strength as his hair grew, he responds that, afflicted by penance, he gradually obtained by prayer what he had not lost by his own will. Therefore, that excellence of strength in Samson was not naturally born within him but was infused from above.

### ¶ Concerning the capture of the Ark by the Philistines and its return to Bethshemesh: and concerning the terror struck into the Philistines by the prayers of Samuel. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a figure in profile, possibly a saint or prophet, within a gothic architectural frame.</image-desc>
In the Books of Kings <note>Known in modern Bibles as 1 Samuel.</note> we read the account of where the Ark of God was captured by the Philistines and taken to Ashdod. There they brought it into the house of Dagon; and Dagon was found to have fallen face down on the ground before the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord. And the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the people of Ashdod, and he scattered them and struck them in their secret parts. <note>original: "in natibus," likely referring to the plague of tumors or hemorrhoids described in 1 Samuel 5.</note> After this, the Ark entered Ekron, and the people of Ekron gathered all the lords of the Philistines, as well as their priests and diviners, saying: "What shall we do with the Ark of the Lord? Tell us how we may send it back to its place." The priests and diviners responded: "If you send back the Ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty, but give him a guilt offering, and then you will be healed and it will be made known to you why his hand does not depart from you." And after a few words, they said: "Now make a new cart and take two milch cows upon which a yoke has never been placed; hitch the cows to the cart and lead their calves back home. Take the Ark of the Lord and place it on the cart, and put the golden vessels which you offered as a guilt offering in a chest beside it. Let it go where it will, and watch: if it goes up the road to its own borders toward Bethshemesh, then he has done us this great evil. But if not, we shall know that his hand did not touch us, but it happened to us by chance." Finally, the account follows: "And when they had placed the Ark of the Lord upon the cart, the cows went straight along the road that leads to Bethshemesh, turning neither to the right nor to the left." Observe therefore, says Origen, how the priests and diviners contemplated the cause of the evils that had befallen the Philistines—whether by the hand of God for the injury of the Ark or by chance—by the signs they had set forth, saying: "If it goes up the road to its own borders... he has done us these evils." Who then, looking diligently at this foreknowledge predicted regarding the direction of the cows, would call it either chance or something composed by art, and not rather a work administered by demons? For the demons feared the power of the Ark of the Lord. There is, therefore, a certain operation of demons in the service of foreknowledge, which is gathered through certain arts by those who have surrendered themselves to demons; sometimes through what they call "lots," and sometimes through what they called "auguries," and now...

### On Saul prophesying and by what spirit / on the raising of Samuel by the spirit-medium. Chapter 5.

It can indeed seem true (he says) if the name of Samuel is silenced: because Saul was going to be with the devil. For he migrated to him whom he adored. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the interpretation of biblical events, moving from the controversial scene of Saul and the medium at Endor to the theological understanding of how Scripture uses the names of real objects to describe visionary or symbolic things. It then transitions into the reign of King David and the early divided kingdom.</meta>

fo. xxiij.

# On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture. Book One.

<meta>catchword: prophet</meta>

Samuel described those things which were said and seen, expressing them while setting aside whether they were true or false—this is the view of Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), an influential theologian whose works often analyzed the literal versus symbolic meanings of the Bible.</note>. And elsewhere, it is likewise noted that in many places of Sacred Scripture, the names of real things are often ascribed to imagined things. In this way, the aforementioned rod imagined in the likeness of a serpent, and those phantasmal serpents of the magicians in Egypt, and that bronze serpent are so named. Two cherubim are also said to overshadow the mercy seat <note>The gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant.</note> by way of a likeness. Five mice or five rings <note>original: "anuli." While often translated as "tumors" or "hemorrhoids" in modern bibles, some medieval traditions interpreted the golden offerings of the Philistines as rings or tokens.</note> from the land of the Philistines are carried in a chest with the Ark of the Lord. Cherubim, palms, pomegranates, and nets are also described as being depicted in the building of the Temple: for although all these things are not the truth of the objects themselves but are received under these names through likeness, nevertheless Scripture itself, without any rule of uncertainty, places them here by name as if they were real things.

### On the numbering of the people by David's command and the plague that followed; and on the terrible signs at the dedication of the golden calves in Bethel. Chapter 6.

<margin>Exodus 25:5</margin>

And David, wishing to know how many thousands of people there were in total, forgot the Mosaic warning: in which it had been predicted that if the people were numbered, a <term>shekel</term> <note>original: "siclus," a standard unit of silver used for the sanctuary tax.</note> must be offered to God for each individual head. He therefore commanded Joab, the prince of the army, to go and number the entire host. When Joab said this was not necessary, David did not rest, but ordered the number of the Hebrews to be fully recorded. Joab, taking the tribunes and scribes and traveling through the province of Israel, considered how great the multitude was and returned to the king in Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days. He presented the number to the king, excluding the tribe of Benjamin. For he was not able to number this one, nor the tribe of Levi. However, David repented that he had numbered the people, because he had sinned against God. The number of the other Israelites was 900,000 men bearing arms and capable of performing military service; the tribe of Judah by itself had 40,000. When the prophets declared to David that God was angry with him, he began to supplicate and ask that He be favorable and grant pardon for the sin. Then God sent the prophet Gad (as Josephus says <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose *Antiquities of the Jews* provided extra-biblical details often cited by medieval scholars.</note>) to him, carrying three conditions of punishment, so that he might choose whichever of them he preferred: whether he wished for a famine to be created in the province for seven years; or to be conquered by his enemies in battle for three months; or certainly for a disease and languor to come upon the Hebrews for three days. David, falling into the anxiety of this choice between the worst of all things, was troubled; and in his mind he seemed to be greatly confused. Among these, however, he chose a common suffering for both the king and the subjects, in which the fear would be equal for all, saying: that it is much better to fall into the hands of God than into the hands of men. Hearing this, the pro-

<margin>Josephus, Antiquities, Book 7, Chapter 14.</margin>

<column-break/>

-phet reported back to the Lord. For the Angel of the Lord killed 70,000 men from all Israel as far as Beersheba and proposed to destroy the city of Jerusalem—not that the Lord wished to destroy the city which He has now dispersed, but so that the Angel, shown in the readiness of vengeance, might strike a worthy repentance into the king who saw him. From this (says Augustine), it is understood that David committed a lesser fault than the common people, who wiped out their sin through repentance alone. The sin of the people, however, merited the severity of death in their leaders <note>This suggests the people's collective underlying sins were being punished through the occasion of the King's census.</note>; thus says Augustine. And here an argument is taken by the <term>Neoterics</term> <note>original: "Neotericis," referring to "modern" or more recent theological commentators of the medieval period.</note> that where there is a greater penalty, a greater fault is argued. And then, when because of the sin of Solomon the kingdom of the people of Israel was divided from one into two, Jeroboam the son of Nebat, king of the ten tribes in the northern part, fearing lest the restoration of the temple which was in Jerusalem might again join the people to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, placed idols and altars in Dan and in Bethel. But at the dedication of the altar which was in Bethel, a man of God from Judah was sent by the Lord to prophesy against that altar. Upon his arrival, two terrible signs were shown. For the altar was immediately split into two parts at the hour of the burnt offering, and the king's own whole hand was withered and dried up. These two signs clearly suited the event and the deed: for they evidently showed what was then done in the king himself. For it seemed fitting that the altar which he had made for himself should be così split and dried up, just as he had divided the worship of God, which until then had been one in both altar and temple. And it was fitting that a withered hand should appear to him in that <term>schismatic</term> <note>Referring to a formal division or split within a religious body.</note> burnt offering, since he had made the hand of God's people "withered" so that they would not immolate offerings and burnt sacrifices to their Lord. A little while later, when David held the kingdom, the Ark of the Covenant was led from the house of Abinadab to Jerusalem by the king and all the people. Uzzah, the son of Abinadab, following the Ark, was suddenly struck with death and suffocated when he touched it as if to support it. In this deed, his rashness is condemned, since he touched it although he was not of the lineage of Aaron; and the whole people is warned that they ought to act cautiously in divine matters. But some think that a certain preceding sin in Uzzah was punished through this fault, for it often happens that smaller faults strike a vengeance for preceding sins.

He lived near a certain brook from which he received the help of a drink. For the ravens brought him food every day. And when the brook had failed due to excessive drought, he came to the city of Zarephath, not far from Sidon and Tyre; this city is situated in the middle of these two. For God (says Josephus) <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide historical context for biblical events.</note> had commanded a certain widow woman there to provide him with food. And when he was not far from the gate, he saw a widow woman gathering sticks for herself. When God had indicated to him that this was the one who was to minister food to him, approaching her, he greeted her and asked that water be given to him to drink. As she was going, he called her again and asked that bread also be brought to him. When she had sworn that she had nothing inside the house except a small amount of flour and a little oil—and for that reason, she had come out to gather sticks so that, having sprinkled the flour, she might make loaves for herself and her son, and once these were consumed, as nothing else remained, they would die of hunger—the prophet said: "Go forth with confidence and stand in better hope; first make a little for me and bring it. For I foretell that the jar of flour shall not fail you, nor the jug of oil, until the grace of God pours rain upon the earth." When the prophet said these things, she went and did what he had said. And she had a little, and from this, she served her son and the prophet alike, and none of these things failed them until the drought ended.

Even Menander <note>Menander of Ephesus (2nd century BC), a historian who wrote a history of Tyre; his mention of the drought is often cited by early Christian writers to provide secular evidence for the biblical narrative.</note> mentions this drought in the acts of the kings, saying: "And a drought came upon them from the month of Hyperberetaios <note>A month in the ancient Macedonian calendar, roughly corresponding to October.</note> until the same month of the following year. When he <term>supplicated to God</term> <note>original: "deo supplicaret" — referring here to the King of Tyre's prayers, though in the biblical context, it is Elijah’s prayer that ends the drought.</note>, many rivers were sent forth." Lest it move anyone that the land of the Sidonians suffered this same plague along with Israel, (says Augustine), since Jezebel, the wife of King Ahab and the persecutor of the prophets—and the cause of all the vengeance and crime—drew her paternal origin as the daughter of the King of the Sidonians. Certainly, even by this sign, no new nature was created by the Lord, but the nature already established was governed so that a small substance became not small. This is remembered as it was foretold concerning the shoes and clothes of the children of Israel <note>A reference to the Israelites' clothes not wearing out during the 40 years in the wilderness.</note>. For in all the other aforementioned miracles, nothing flees the reasoning of nature, as the event of things itself frequently shows.

And so the woman of whom we spoke a little before, who had provided food for the prophet: when her son had fallen into a sickness so that he gave up his spirit, weeping and scratching herself greatly with her hands, and emitting the cries that grief dictates, she accused God within herself that the prophet, being present with her, had done her an injury as if he were rebuking her sins, and therefore the boy had been extinguished. He, however, commanding her to be of calm mind, and taking the son from her, promised he would restore him to her alive. Through his prayer, Elijah called him back to life again. Concerning him, the Hebrews hand down (as Augustine writes) that he was later the prophet Jonah, whom the Lord released after three days from the belly of the whale that had swallowed him. For He who can kill His enemy in any safe place is able to rescue His servant whom He wishes to snatch away from any kind of distress. But indeed, that famous question which is discussed concerning those raised from the dead shall be reserved by us until we reach the account of Lazarus.

### On the burnt offering on Mount Carmel: and on the fast of forty days and the feeding of Elijah: and on the fire descending upon the captains of fifty: and on the crossing of the Jordan by Elijah and Elisha. Chapter 18.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a seated figure, possibly a prophet or scholar, holding a book within a floral and architectural frame.</image-desc>

After a short time had passed, by the will of God, he went to King Ahab to announce the coming rain. For distress and a lack of necessities had invaded the province so much that not only men were afflicted by the drought, but hunger also affected the other animals. Therefore, God commanded the prophet Elijah to go out to meet King Ahab. When someone reported to the king that he had seen Elijah, King Ahab soon met him, asking with an angry step if he were the one who existed as the author of impiety among the people of the Hebrews. Then the prophet, fearing nothing, said: it was he [Ahab] rather who had perpetrated all the evils, and his kin, who had introduced foreign gods into that province and had abandoned the God who is alone. "But now," he said, "command all the people to be gathered at Mount Carmel, as well as your prophets, and whatever number there are of your wife’s prophets of the groves, about four hundred and fifty." He gathered them on Mount Carmel. When they were gathered, the holy Elijah asked that two bulls be slaughtered as a <term>burnt offering</term> <note>original: "holocaustum" — a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire.</note>, one for the Lord and the other for Baal, on behalf of himself and the prophets of the idols, so that the Lord who answers by fire, He would be the God of all the people. When this was granted, the priests asked their bull, Baal, to consume the burnt offering by fire. But Baal, who was later delivered into the power of fire, was not able to give fire upon the burnt offering.

Elijah, however, cutting his bull into pieces and dividing it by its members upon the altar that had been constructed, and which he himself had repaired, then set it in place. He poured water abundantly over it, and as he prayed, suddenly fire fell from heaven which consumed the bull along with the altar, the stones, and the water all at once. And then he killed the priests of Baal who were delivered into his power at the brook Kishon; and all the people, having confessed, believed He was God. In this (says Augustine), nothing was done outside the nature of fire or water. The fire, descending from the ignited space of the air above under God’s governance, consumed the food for itself—a nature which it received on earth. For in that upper space, fire is pronounced to be burning on earth; fire which, from the higher place where its nature is, attempts to hold on ardently. Just as water does not ascend by itself unless through another substance, so also fire does not descend lower than itself unless through another substance. Thus, when the Lord rained down fiery showers upon the five cities <note>Referring to Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities of the plain.</note>, this same thing was done through sulfur, so that the fire might burn in the sulfur, and through the heavier nature of the sulfur, the same might fall to the earth. In this place, therefore (he says), where fire was upon the altar for the burnt offering...

...it descended through the air; it descended through sulfur: because fire by itself cannot descend unless God commands it to be mixed with some heavier matter. Therefore, Elijah, the servant of God, killed the priests of the idols without the guilt of homicide. This was because he lived under that Law which says: "You shall not suffer a blasphemer to live" <note>original: "blasphemum non patieris vivere." A reference to the strict laws against idolatry in the Old Testament.</note>. No master, therefore, worships an idol unless he has stood forth as a blasphemer of God. And because of this, he who had slaughtered the worshippers of idolatry was purging the land of blasphemers and sacrilegious men.

And after all these things, he who by praying had prohibited rain and the soaking of the earth for three years and six months, in a brief space of time by that same duty of his prayer, obtained from God abundant rain and a gentle drenching for the thirsty earth. This rain would by no means have come upon the earth unless he had first cleansed it by killing the worshippers of Baal. When Jezebel discovered that the priests of Baal had been killed by Elijah, she terrified the prophet with words threatening his own death; wherefore, moving into the land of Judah, Elijah sat in the shade of a juniper tree and fell asleep. 

<margin>Leviticus 24:16.</margin>
<margin>On the 40-day fast and the feeding of Elijah.</margin>
<margin>4 Kings 1 <note>Modern 2 Kings 1</note>. On the fire descending upon the captains of fifty.</margin>

An angel of the Lord, touching him in his sleep, woke him up; feeding him with bread and water, he refreshed him in his hunger and thirst. Refreshed by this food, in its strength he walked for forty days and forty nights without eating anything until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God. From there, relying on the company of the Lord's word, he returned again to the land of Israel. 

Concerning this bread and water administered by the angelic office—the strength of which carried the prophet through the labor of hunger for forty days—let us report the revealed understanding to those who know from whence it was, though we must defer the full explanation. In this bread, although we see a likeness of the whole work of human industry, we understand that it was not the power of earthly bread that fulfilled the need for forty days with a single satiation—unless perhaps, made by an angelic work from whatever earthly matter, it was made into a food stronger than the bread of men for the soul of the man living on earth. But if this bread made the anxious reader wonder by hiding its own nature, it still makes him feel secure regarding the forty-day fast; he sees how he endured that time of fasting when, through the power of a single meal, he lived for so long a time needing no other food. 

¶ Then, after a certain interval of time had passed, the prophet himself on the mountain [met] a captain of fifty with those who were under him, whom the king ordered to lead Elijah to him. He [the captain], filled with a haughty swelling of pride <note>original: "superbo tumore"</note>, said: "Man of God, King Ahaziah (that is, the son of Ahab) has commanded that you come down to him with us." Elijah replied to him, "As you say: if I am a man of God, let celestial flame burn against you now and against those who are with you." When this was done, the king ordered another man of the same rank with just as many companions to return to the same place; and when he uttered similar words as the first, the same vengeance consumed him following the same pattern. After this was done, a third captain of fifty, destined for the same danger, knelt humbly with his men before the prophet of the Lord. He asked through words of prayer that Elijah come into the king's sight. 

<column-break/>

But the angel of the Lord told Elijah to go with this man. Rising quickly and joining his step with the humble and suppliant man, he went to the king, though he had been proud with the others. Fire (as Augustine says <note>Referring to St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a primary authority for the author of this text.</note>) in this place, just as in the aforementioned burnt offering, fulfilled what was commanded in obedience to the word of the said prophet of God. And in these more serious matters, perhaps the avenging flame punished the number [of men] for a crime of sin committed before, just as we previously mentioned regarding Uzzah <note>Oza</note> and the numbering of the people. 

¶ Finally, when the Lord wished to take Elijah up, he and Elisha, the son of Shaphat <note>Saphan</note>, his minister, divided the river Jordan with Elijah’s cloak. They crossed over on dry feet, just as we previously said happened in the crossing of the children of Israel. For the explanation of this matter, the things previously said from the Book of Joshua are sufficient for this work.

### Chapter 9. On the ascent of Elijah in a fiery chariot and on certain virtues of Elisha.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a figure (likely a prophet or saint) holding a book or scroll, set against a background of foliage.</image-desc>When the opportunity was given to Elisha to ask what he wanted before Elijah was taken from him, he asked that a double portion of Elijah’s spirit might be within him. Then Elijah said, "You have asked a hard thing; but it shall be done for you." O precious inheritance (says Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan, noted for his eloquent sermons and writings on virginity.</note>) in which more is left to the heir than was possessed! He who receives gains more than he who gives possessed. A clearly precious inheritance: which, while it is transferred from the father to the son, is doubled by a certain interest of merits. 

Therefore, while Elijah himself possessed a single spirit of holiness, he left a double one to Elisha. In a wonderful way, Elijah left more of his kind on earth than he carried with him to the heavens; and although he himself was transferred entirely in body to the higher realms, a greater holiness remains with his "son." Elijah, the master of Elisha, was snatched up to heaven led by angels, and placed in a fiery chariot, he ascended as if in a triumph of victory. For he had stood forth as a victor, not over barbarian nations, but over worldly pleasures. 

For indeed, wicked morals are more serious enemies than hostile foes; wherefore Ambrose says elsewhere: "Elijah is found to have been mixed with no desires of bodily intercourse." For this reason, he was snatched to heaven in a chariot; for this reason, he appears with the Lord in glory; for this reason, he is to come as the precursor of the Lord’s arrival <note>Refers to the prophecy that Elijah will return before the final judgment.</note>. Elisha, asking for a double spirit, did not do so out of a desire for pride over his master; but seeing the innumerable sins of the people, he foresaw that they could not be restrained by a single spirit of Elijah, but only by a double one from the prophet who was leaving. For if he had asked for that which he was able to out of a mind wishing to exalt itself by vice, he would by no means have obtained what he asked from the Lord or from Elijah himself. 

Therefore, after these things were said, Elijah was snatched up into a fiery chariot as if to heaven, while Elisha watched. And thus far, he—just as Enoch—is preserved without death as a testimony of the final time; so that (as Augustine writes) the word of the final testimony might stand in the mouth of these two witnesses...

Elijah explains in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, chapter 29, saying that by explaining the Law spiritually and mystically, he [Elijah] will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the children to the fathers; that is, he will fulfill it in deed. ¶ Meanwhile, the sorrowful heir, Elisha, gathered the garments of Elijah falling to the earth; and likewise, invoking the Lord of Elijah, he crossed the Jordan with dry feet. Coming into Jericho, he healed the bitter and sterile waters by throwing salt into the spring—just as Moses healed the waters in the wilderness by means of wood. From there, coming to Bethel, the bald Elisha was mocked by small boys. When he cursed them in the name of the Lord, forty-two boys were torn apart by two bears coming out of the woods. In this place (Augustine says), the prophet did not curse the boys out of anger due to a personal insult, but because these sons—who were sacrificing to idols in Bethel—had turned away from the Lord and the law of their fathers. Perhaps even as small children, as was then the custom, they had been consecrated to idols; thus just vengeance was fulfilled in Bethel. For there stood one of the two golden calves which Jeroboam, son of Nebat (who made Israel to sin), had set up when he was made king. Then, in that expedition where Joram king of Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and the king of Edom went out against the sons of Moab: when the whole army was exhausted by thirst and labor in the desert, Elisha obtained water from God through a dried-up torrent-bed without rain. 

<margin>4 Kings 4 <note>Modern 2 Kings 4</note>.</margin>
There he ordered the people to make ditches and pits for the sake of the Israelites and the Gentiles who were together. Then, when he had returned to the land of Israel from that expedition, a widow of one of the prophets cried out to him tearfully, saying: "Behold, my creditor wishes to take my two sons, whom I bore to your servant, to be his slaves, because I have nothing else to pay him." Elisha said to her: "Tell me, what do you have in your house?" She replied: "I have a little oil for anointing stored in a vessel." 

<margin>The multiplication of the oil.</margin>
Elisha said: "Go, borrow empty vessels from your neighbors, and not a few." When she had done this, she filled them all from that little bit of increasing oil. This tiny portion of oil (says Augustine) was able to grow larger through divine power, not against nature. For it is fitting for all greatness in creatures to grow from smallness; especially since in liquids, nature—aided by the cupbearer's art <note>original: "pincer naria [pinciernaria] arte." Referring to the handling of liquids and fermentation.</note>—is seen to overflow and boil over into an abundance of liquid from a small amount of matter, as is proven in certain types of vessels through steam.

<column-break/>

Frequently leaving the city, this same man was often received with kind hospitality by a certain wealthy but sterile woman; he predicted that she would conceive by her own husband. But that child, having been born and raised, died prematurely as a boy from a severe and sudden illness. Then Elisha, restoring him to life through a symbolic order, returned him alive to his mother. Also at a certain time, when the sons of the prophets were gathered together, they unknowingly cooked deadly wild gourds <note>original: "coloquintidas." These are bitter, poisonous desert gourds.</note> among other wild herbs in a stew. When each had tasted it, they cried out that there was death in the pot. But when Elisha, with his own hand, threw a little flour into that same pot, the power of that flour—through its tasty, sweet, and healthy flavor—conquered the tasteless and deadly bitterness of the wild gourds. Also, ordering twenty loaves to be divided among a hundred men, he sated the crowd; and the servants gathered a superabundant supply of fragments. But we shall explain the meaning of this power more diligently when we discuss the five loaves and two fish in the second book, if the Lord permits.

### ¶ Chapter 10. On the healing of Naaman in the waters of the Jordan at the command of Elisha, and on the leprosy of Gehazi, and on the iron that floated.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'N' containing a portrait of a bearded man in profile wearing a cap, likely representing Naaman or the prophet Elisha.</image-desc>

<margin>4 Kings 5 <note>Modern 2 Kings 5</note>.</margin>
Naaman was a leper. A certain girl said to his mistress: "If my master wishes to be cleansed, let him go into the land of Israel; and there he will find one who can take away his leprosy." She told her mistress, the wife of Naaman, who was a general under the King of Syria. The king sent him [Naaman] to the King of Israel as if he were very dear to him. When the King of Israel heard that he had been sent to him so that he might cleanse his leprosy, he tore his clothes. Then Elisha the prophet commanded him: "Why have you torn your clothes, as if God were not powerful enough to cleanse a leper? Send him to me." He sent him; and the prophet said to him upon his arrival: "Go, go down into the Jordan and wash, and you shall be healed." He began to think to himself and say: "Is this all? I have come from Syria to the land of Judea, and I am told: 'Go into the Jordan, wash and you shall be healed,' as if the rivers in my own country were not better." Therefore his servants said: "Lord, why do you not do as the prophet says? Rather, do it and see." Then he went into the Jordan, washed, and rose up healthy; and all his skin was restored, soft and tender like a child's. Therefore, for the benefit of his health, he tried to offer gifts to the man of God. But the prophet refused them, preferring to give freely what he had received freely. From this event (says Augustine), it is most clearly shown that the mystery of power is contained in the command of the ordering God according to the prophet's word, and not in any material thing. Therefore Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, thought to himself that his master Elisha had spared Naaman for no reason; taking two boys with him...

Behold, by the same power Elisha the prophet had removed the leprosy from Naaman’s body, he now commanded it to cling to the flesh and the house of Gehazi. From this, it must be observed (he says) that all these miracles <term>virtutes: literally 'virtues,' but used here to mean miraculous powers or acts</term> are not performed through the effects of temporal things, but by the command of the one in charge. Against nature, nothing certain is perfected in the performance of these things; yet, in their perfection, the very will of the one who might otherwise despair—whether through itself, or through angels, or through men—requires those things which it knows beforehand to fit aptly in all ways with the symbols of things to come.

<margin>On the floating of the iron. 4 Kings 6 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 6.</note></margin>
<margin>Augustine, as cited above.</margin>

At another time, while the sons of the prophets were making a place for themselves in the presence of Elisha, the iron head of an axe slipped from the handle of one of them and fell into the river Jordan. He grieved very heavily at the loss of the iron tool, which he had received as a loan. Moved by the man's cry, Elisha sought the place where the iron had fallen and sunk, showing the affection of one who grieves. Having called out and thrown a piece of wood into that spot, he summoned the iron from the depths to swim to the surface of the water. Indeed, the thin substance of water is not strong enough to bear the heavy nature of iron. But He who later made the nature of the sea solid under the feet of Peter <note>A reference to Christ walking on the water and enabling Peter to do the same.</note> here commands the iron to rise from the depths. For the nature of water, though more fragile than earth, nonetheless appears more solid than air; it is shown here to have less strength than earth insofar as metals and stones are less supported by it. Yet it aptly retains more strength in that it can support the bodies of men and other animals and floating wood. Thus, even if water does not support metal entirely, it tolerates it in part when joined with those things that carry it—since it is often proven that a stone which two men can scarcely lift in the air, one man can hold in the water when it hangs from a rope. Hence Augustine says: it appears that water, if not entirely, can nonetheless support weight in part; and what a thing possesses in part, God can command to follow naturally in full. Because of this, the nature of water was able to support the floating iron, because God commanded the creature to do in full what it was accustomed to do only in part by itself.

### On the victory of the King of Israel against the King of Syria through the prophecy of Elisha. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a man's head in profile wearing a cap, set within a square frame with floral or foliate patterns.</image-desc>

"I remember having said often," (says Ambrose), "that I should not fear the warlike tumults of enemies, nor dread any large multitude of foes, because, as the Lord says, He who is in us is greater than he who is in this world." <note>1 John 4:4.</note> For the prophet says: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear Him and will rescue them." <note>Psalm 34:7.</note> A wondrous thing: holiness deserves more defenders from heaven than wickedness has brought forth attackers on earth. During a time of war, the King of Syria was setting ambushes for the King of Israel in many places. The prophet Elisha always revealed these to the King of Israel so that he might act cautiously. But when the King of Syria realized for certain that this was being done through Elisha, he sent a large army equipped with chariots and horses to Elisha's city. When the servant of the man of God rose in the night and saw this, he came to Elisha, terrified and confused with fear. Strengthening him, the prophet said: "Our helpers are more numerous than the enemy." And since the boy's mind was terrified beyond measure at seeing the large multitude of enemies, Elisha made visible to him the phalanxes of angels standing around the whole mountain in his circuit, equipped with fiery chariots and horses. From there, going out toward the enemies, he obtained from the Lord that He should strike that nation with blindness, just as He did before at the doors of Lot.

<margin>Saint Ambrose, Sermon 77, on not fearing barbarians. Psalm 33 <note>Psalm 34 in modern numbering.</note>. 4 Kings 6.</margin>

Therefore, promising the blinded enemies that he would show them the man they were seeking, he led them into the city of Samaria and there opened their eyes. When the King of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha whether he should kill them or not. The man of God commanded him not to kill them, but instead to refresh the enemies with food and let them go. "It was not," (says Augustine), "that this people was struck with blindness so that they could not see the light of day, but rather the recognition of the present Elisha and the places they were walking was hidden from their eyes." They were struck by this very blindness while they in no way understood the person they were looking at.

Meanwhile, after the death of Elisha, the servant of God: one day, when some people were carrying a dead man and saw a group of raiders, they became terrified and threw the corpse of the dead man into Elisha's tomb, which was nearby. When the body touched the bones of Elisha, the man revived and walked. Thus, it is said through the written word: "Let the spirit which is in you be doubled in me." <note>2 Kings 2:9. Elisha’s request to Elijah.</note> This necessarily had to be fulfilled. Elijah is recorded to have raised one person; Elisha is now seen to have done the same. But also another: that is, this one after death, namely in the tomb, he is seen to have brought back to life. But this "double grace" does not appear to be established by the act alone. For what Elijah had done once, he could have repeated twice or thrice if it were necessary. Rather, he announces that there is a double grace of Elijah in Elisha because Elisha obtained things by commanding, whereas Elijah did so by praying and petitioning; or because Elisha [possessed] the gift of miracles and prophecy with great honor and worldly dignity, whereas Elijah lived as a fugitive in the mountains and caves, held back from the company of men.

### Chapter 12: On the captivity of the people of Israel and the striking down of Sennacherib; and on the illness of King Hezekiah of Judah and the regression of the sun.

<margin>
On the regression of the sun in the time of Hezekiah.
Sedulius <note>Coelius Sedulius was a 5th-century Christian poet. These lines are from his *Paschale Carmen*.</note>
Taking pity on the final moments of the fading light,
God once added fifteen years to the king;
Closing the paths of death by His own right,
He turned life back from its setting toward the dawn.
<note>original: "Ultima labentis miseratus tepora lucis. / Terquinos quondā regi de? addidit ānos / Alus iure suo patefacta claudēs / Mortis ab occasu vitā cōuertit in ortum."</note>
</margin>

For a long time, the people of Israel lived in transgression of God's law and the sayings of the prophets, worshiping idols and despising the Lord, and so they were handed over into the power of the nations. However, God at that time still preserved the tribe of Judah and the city of Jerusalem, which the Lord had chosen; at that time, the just king Hezekiah governed this kingdom. But Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, seeing that his predecessors had destroyed the kingdom of Samaria and the impious people of Israel, gathered an army to move against Judah. He was led by Rabshakeh <note>A high-ranking Assyrian messenger; the text uses the Latin "Rapsace".</note>, whom the Hebrews—as Augustine writes—call the son of the prophet Isaiah. Sennacherib commanded his army to storm the city of Jerusalem. But in that very attempt, God, the defender of His people and the humble-maker of the proud, sent a celestial soldier—namely, an angel—to the Assyrian camp. In the work of a single night, the angel slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand men from Sennacherib's army. Thus put to flight from the land of Judah, Sennacherib barely escaped with a few followers to his city of Nineveh; there, while staying in the temple of his idols, he was killed by one of his own sons whom he had fathered.

**P** <note>Decorative initial 'P' showing a figure in prayer or contemplation.</note> After a short time had passed, lest King Hezekiah of Judah become prideful over such a great victory, he fell into a disease of most grievous exhaustion. The prophet Isaiah, coming to visit him in this illness, said: "Set your house in order, for you shall live no longer, but shall die." Moved by this very sad news, the king immediately turned his face to the wall and poured out a tearful prayer for his life in the sight of the most merciful Lord. Again, the prophet Isaiah, moved by the pure Light <note>Refers to the Holy Spirit or divine inspiration.</note>, was sent back while still in the middle of the courtyard to announce health and peace to the king and the city; he confirmed that fifteen years would be added to his life by the very word of God. Then, so that the king might believe without doubt what was being said, God twisted the course of the sun back ten hours from the setting toward the rising, along a returning path. Thus, it began to hurry forward again as if it were morning, even though it had already consumed the space of the entire day except for two hours. I do not know if I have ever heard of a miracle greater than this; what can be more wonderful than that the divine order of the celestial spheres should be changed?

### Chapter 13: On the Babylonian captivity of the Jews and on Daniel interpreting dreams, and the three boys cast into the fire.

**A** <note>Decorative initial 'A' showing a figure, possibly a prophet or king.</note> In the third year of Jehoiakim <note>original: "Joachī"</note>, king of Judah, who had remained loyal to that point, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieged Jerusalem with an army as if it were an Egyptian colony. Jehoiakim surrendered himself voluntarily and gave hostages—namely Daniel, Ananias, Azarias, and Misael—and part of the vessels of the temple of the Lord. He was left in his kingdom until, weighed down by the burden of most heavy servitude, he turned again toward the king of the Egyptians. An army was sent again, and he was captured and dragged away; before he reached the city, in the field of Babylon in the eleventh year of his reign, he was killed. Daniel, however, became famous in Babylon from the illustrious stock of the Jews. Since he was full of the spirit of God and gifted with the boon of prophecy, God demonstrated to him things that were unknown to men. Thus it happened that Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream, and some memory of the dream remained with him even when he was awake. God revealed to Daniel not only the dream itself but also the very occasion of the dream that occurred before the king slept. This was done so that Daniel might instill the knowledge of the High Creator in the king, and so that the people placed in servitude and captivity might have some help and solace, however small.

But that king fell into such a state of forgetting God that he erected a golden statue of immense height in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon, and commanded it to be consecrated in his own name with divine worship. It happened then that the three men placed over the region of Babylon—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—who were of Jewish descent, were accused by the Chaldeans before the king because they would not worship the gods nor the recently consecrated image. The king, incensed with incredible wrath, commanded the furnace to be heated more than usual. In a fierce sentence, he ordered these men to be cast into the fire by the strongest men of his army, along with their clothes and ornaments. But when they were thrown into the furnace and fell into the midst of the flames, they did not feel the heat of the fire hurting them in any way. Then the angel of the Lord descended with Azarias and his companions into the furnace, and he drove the flame of the fire out of the furnace and made the middle of the furnace like a wind of blowing dew. For from the air (as Augustine says) he found spirit, and from water he found dew within our fire, just as he performed other wonders through the angel who descended into the fire together with the servants of God.

Daniel had made the lions hungry <note>This refers to the biblical account where the lions were kept starved to ensure they would eat anyone thrown into the den</note>, yet the lions instead received the criminal bodies of those who had shed Daniel's blood. Regarding this, Saint Augustine says it is certain that the Lord does not cause a creature to act against the boundaries of its own nature; rather, He disposes and governs the parts of nature as necessary—either to defend and comfort those He protects, or to punish those He judges. As for the story of the transport of Habakkuk into the lions' den <note>A reference to the story in the book of Bel and the Dragon, where an angel carries the prophet Habakkuk by the hair to bring food to Daniel</note>: because it is not found in the Hebrew canon, and in Augustine’s time it was not yet accepted into our own canon of Scripture, it is not included in this sequence of wonders. Meanwhile, as the time of captivity drew to a close—which the Lord had foretold through the prophets must be fulfilled—He prepared the return of His people and the end of their exile through the mercy of King Cyrus <note>original: "tyri regis." The Latin likely contains a scribal error, mistaking "Tyri" (of Tyre) for "Cyri" (of Cyrus, the Persian king who ended the Babylonian captivity).</note>. At that time, Ezra, the priest of God, restored the Law which had been burned by the Chaldeans in the temple archives; indeed, he was filled with the same Spirit by which the Scripture had first been written.

### Chapter 15: Whether God has ever been seen here, and how we know through the faith of the Scriptures that God can be seen.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'M' featuring a crowned figure (possibly a king or prophet) holding a scepter, set against a background of stylized foliage and architecture.</image-desc> It is a great question how there is no contradiction in the fact that the ancients "saw God," if it is true that "no one has ever seen God" and "whom no man has seen nor can see." Let us consider these few points, if you please. When the holy John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century monk and theologian</note> was explaining the Gospel at the beginning of his book *On the Orthodox Faith*, he began from that passage: "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared Him." On this occasion, see what sorts of things he discussed regarding the vision of God. He says that the divinity is ineffable <note>too great to be expressed in words</note> and incomprehensible; for no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father. Furthermore, the Holy Spirit knows the things of God just as the spirit of a man knows the things within himself. After that divine and most blessed nature, no one has ever known God unless He Himself revealed it—not only among men, but not even among the "supramundane virtues" <note>angelic beings existing beyond the physical world</note>, meaning the Cherubim and Seraphim themselves. Thus says Damascus. Therefore, Saint John of Damascus posits that the divinity is incomprehensible to every rational creature, both human and angelic; only the three divine <term>hypostases</term> <note>the three distinct Persons of the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</note> know it absolutely and fully. This is consistent with the sentiment of the most blessed Paul, who says of God: "Who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light; whom no man has seen, nor can see." And by these words (as the translator of Damascus says), it is proven that Paul himself did not see God even when he was caught up to the third heaven and heard

<column-break/>

secret words which a man is not permitted to speak; for in that general statement, he includes himself in the number of those who have not seen God nor are able to see Him. Similarly, he says, Moses must not be believed to have seen God when he received the Law and had frequent conversation with God, even though in the twelfth chapter of the book of Numbers, God offers such testimony about him: "If there be a prophet among you, I the Lord will appear to him in a vision or speak to him in a dream. But my servant Moses is not so; he is most faithful in all my house. For I speak to him mouth to mouth, plainly and not through riddles and figures he sees God." Furthermore, in the thirty-third chapter of Exodus it is said: "The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is wont to speak to his friend." Indeed, Moses (the translator says) asked the Lord for the sake of a great gift and as a pledge of free divine love: "If I have found grace in your sight, show me your face, that I may know you and find grace before your eyes." Now, if he had seen God clearly (as many contend), he would not have asked for the showing of the divine face to be granted to him, as one who had already obtained it according to his wish. But let us attend to what response he received from God in that same place. "You cannot," said the Lord, "see my face. For man shall not see me and live." Again, in the same place, the Lord adds: "I will take away my hand and you shall see my back parts <note>original: "posteriora mea." A famous biblical metaphor for seeing the effects or "afterglow" of God rather than His direct essence.</note>. But my face you shall not be able to see." Since, therefore, it was said to Moses when he asked for the divine glory to be shown to him, "you cannot see my face," how could it be that he was made a partaker of the divine vision and a companion of heavenly glory? Nor is there any room for the legalistic objection that Isaiah and many prophets saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, even before the time He took on human nature for us. For indeed, he says, this kind of portrayal was made through a "subject creature" <note>An image, angel, or physical manifestation created by God to represent Him, rather than His actual essence.</note>. The most blessed Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian</note> also confirms this in the fourth chapter of his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*. But why dwell on this? Let us attend to what Augustine—to whom I more closely adhere—confirms in the twenty-seventh chapter of his literal commentary on Genesis. He says that unless Moses had earned the right to see the desired and longed-for clarity of God, God would not have said to Aaron and Miriam (Moses' siblings) in the book of Numbers: "I speak to him mouth to mouth, in a vision and not through riddles, and he saw the clarity of the Lord." This is not to be understood as something presented to the substance of the body or the senses of the flesh; for it was in this spiritual way that He spoke to Moses "face to face," person to person. Thus says Augustine. Nor is there any room for the objection that God said to Moses: "You cannot see my face. For man shall not see me and live." For when He said "man shall not see me and live," Moses was then on the mountain. But afterward...

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of divine visions, specifically contrasting how Moses and the Apostle Paul were permitted to "see" God compared to other prophets, and introduces the concept of apophatic theology.</meta>

fo.xxx.

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book One.

Moses had desired to see God: certainly not just as he had seen Him on the mountain or in the tabernacle, but in that very substance which is God, without any created bodily form being assumed. He desired to see Him through His own likeness, as much as a rational and intellectual creature can grasp. Hence, Augustine says in the same chapter, when the Lord said to him, "Show me yourself" <note>original: "Ostende mihi temetipsum"</note>: and now also to those whom He rebuked, and to whom He preferred the merit of Moses, He spoke through a bodily creature presented to the senses of the flesh. Therefore, in that way and in that form which is God, He speaks in a manner far more ineffably secret and present, with an unspeakable speech where no one seeing Him shall live this life by which we live mortally in these senses of the body. But unless someone dies to this life in some way—either by departing entirely from the body, or being turned away and alienated from the carnal senses—so that he rightly knows not, as the Apostle says, whether he be in the body or out of the body when he is snatched up and carried into that vision. By this, the words of Paul to Timothy in the sixth chapter are resolved, when he says: "Whom no man has seen, nor can see" <note>original: "quem nullus hominu vidit: sed nec videre potest"</note>. Indeed, as Augustine says in the book *On Seeing God*, chapter thirteen: It is necessary to be abstracted from this life in mind, because He takes one into that ineffability of vision; and it should not be considered incredible that this excellence of His revelation was granted to certain saints who had not yet died such that their corpses remained to be buried. I believe this was what was thought by the one who did not wish to speak <note>Likely referring to Paul’s humility regarding his own vision in 2 Corinthians 12</note>. Certainly, because of the blessed Paul, who did not keep silent about his own ineffable revelation, and Moses, it must be said that either what he asked for was granted to him (as those who hold the view of Saint Ambrose and Damascene <note>Saint John of Damascus</note> are forced to say), or that the God-beloved Moses and most holy Paul were carried up more sublimely and higher than others to such visions of God through narrower and more perfect signs. And through a divine likeness formed more clearly in their minds by angelic ministry, they drew closer to the entrance and doors of the Divinity. Hence they are said to have seen God openly and to have been admitted to His gaze, in contrast to "enigmas" <note>dark or puzzling reflections</note>. For to that most faithful servant of God, Moses, while he was to labor in the wilderness and still rule that people, it was granted what he asked: that he might see the clarity of the Lord, to whom he had said, "If I have found grace before you, show yourself to me clearly" <note>original: "Si inueni gratiam ante te ostende mihi temetipsum manifeste"</note>. For he received then (says Augustine) a fitting response: that he could not see the face of God, because no one could see it and live—signifying in this way that such a vision belongs to another, better life. Furthermore, in the words of God, the mystery of the future Church of Christ was prefigured. Moses, he says, carried the type <note>a symbolic model</note> of the Jewish people who would later believe in the suffering Christ. Therefore it was said to him: "When I have passed by, you shall see my back" <note>original: "cum transiero posteriora mea videbis"</note>. And the other things said there foretell the future Church through a wondrous sacrament <note>a sacred mystery</note>. But regarding what I had begun to say: By his desire...

<margin>Exodus 33.
Augustine, *On Seeing God*, chapter 13.</margin>

<column-break/>

...it was shown later in the Book of Numbers that even what he had asked for had been granted, where the Lord rebukes the insolence of his sister <note>Miriam</note> and says that He appears to other prophets in a vision and in sleep, but to Moses "in form" <note>meaning clearly or directly</note> and not through enigmas. There He also added, saying: "And he saw the glory of the Lord." Why is it, then, that He made him such an exception? Unless perhaps because He held such a ruler and minister of His people worthy even then of that contemplation—he being faithful in all his house—and that he should see God as He is, just as he had desired, which is the contemplation promised to all the children of God in the end. These are the words of Augustine. Furthermore, when it is said that God alone is immortal, inaccessible, invisible, and impossible to be seen, this pertains to a "sacred ignorance" concerning Him, and a sacred silence not only on earth but in heaven, and to the Theology which Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note>, the leader of those who philosophize on sacred things, calls <term>apophatic</term> <note>Apophatic theology defines God by what He is NOT, acknowledging that the divine essence is beyond human words and concepts</note>. And all these things, as Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a Renaissance humanist and theologian</note> most clearly declares in his commentary on Paul's first letter to Timothy, chapter six, says that these qualities belong to God absolutely and "uncontracted" <note>meaning without any limitation or restriction</note>. However, if any of these things belong to others—such as blessedness, power, majesty, dominion, immortality, and invisibility—they belong to them through participation and in a "contracted" <note>limited or finite</note> way. Thus, things that participate agree with the absolute, and the contracted with the uncontracted, as the finite with the infinite. For sight is in the body, intellect is a contracted thing, and sensual appetite is a "contracted" will; and bodily sight is not intellect, and sensual appetite is not the will. Likewise, both angels and men—if you compare them to God in His absolute state—are infinitely more "not"; they are neither blessed, nor powerful, nor do they even "exist" in that same sense, nor can they be. Yet they do exist and have power in their own limited way. For the "way" of each thing is its limitation. Therefore, God is such absolutely, without "way" or measure, and beyond all measure. And as the intellect is limited in various ways—for it is one way in a vision and another in the imagination—so blessedness and power and other things of that kind, which are attributed to creatures only in a limited way, are limited differently in an angel and differently in a man. But (as is right) the Apostle attributes all these things, unlimited, to God alone. Behold, several ways have now been brought forward by which many are accustomed to interpret the sayings of the saints concerning the vision of God which Moses and Paul had; besides these, others still remain to explain the same senses according to the opinions of others, as will be more broadly declared in the second treatise, chapter seven, of this second book. But in truth, it would be laborious and less suited to this place to review at present all the opinions of authors concerning those visions of Moses and Paul; nor can it be sufficiently clear to us which of them should be preferred over the others. For nothing should be said of God except what Holy Scripture says; to which opinion the most blessed Dionysius clearly agrees in the first chapter of *On the Divine Names*, saying: No reason, therefore, should presume to say anything of the supersubstantial and most secret...

<summary>This page explores the unique nature of the divine visions granted to Moses and St. Paul, arguing they saw God's essence more directly than other prophets. It introduces apophatic theology, explaining that while creatures possess qualities like "sight" or "being" in a limited way, God possesses them absolutely and infinitely.</summary>

to speak or think about the divinity, except for those things which the sacred scriptures have piously and purely handed down to us. For if the Apostle [Paul], who experienced such a spiritual ecstasy toward God, did not explain the mystery of that vision, who would be capable of expressing it correctly unless they were taught by the revelation of the Holy Spirit?
