### ¶ Lord Symphorien Champier on the wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

#### ¶ On the seven appearances of the archangel Gabriel. Chapter 1.

<margin>Origen, Book Six against Celsus.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral motifs and a central figure or face within the letter's structure.</image-desc>
**W**e say that angels are certain ministering spirits sent for the sake of their service to those who, as Origen says, are to inherit salvation. These spirits indeed ascend so that they may carry our vows, prayers, and supplications to those celestial places which far exceed the world in purity; or even to those super-celestial places which are known to be twice as pure as earthly ones. From there, they descend again to provide something to the just according to their merits, for those who have been touched by God’s favor. We have learned that these angels received their name because of their ministry, and they are frequently called "gods" or "divine beings" in the sacred writings. Otherwise, nothing is enjoined upon us except that they, by ministering to us, <margin>Saint Ambrose in the book *On the Faith* against the Arians.</margin> bring the things that are of God, and we should honor them as divine. For all vows and prayers, and furthermore the giving of thanks, are to be transmitted to God through an angel, who has been placed in charge of the others through the High Priest, the living Word and the Angel of God. ¶ These are the words of Origen, who also says that even if they were often seen in the figure of the Lord (as Ambrose says), they are nevertheless nothing other than what they know themselves to be. They do not change their substance when

<column-break/>

they take on the form of a human body. How much more then our Lord himself, who made all things, and who granted to the angels by his own institution that they might be able to do these things. For Zacharias, when he had seen the angel, was terrified. Indeed, a new face (says Origen) presenting itself to human sight disturbs the mind and strikes the soul with consternation. The birth of John was full of wonder. For just as the archangel announced the coming of our Lord and Savior, so the archangel announced the birth of John. He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb, while the people of the Jews did not at all see our Lord performing signs and wonders and curing their infirmities. John, however, while still placed in his mother's womb, leaps for joy. John converts many, but the Lord converts not just many, but all; this is his work, that he may convert everyone to God the Father. And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah. He does not say "in the soul of Elijah," but in the spirit and power of Elijah. There was power and spirit in Elijah just as in all the prophets, and according to the dispensation of the body, also in the Lord Savior himself, concerning whom it was said to Mary: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you." Therefore, the spirit which had been in John and the power that was in him also appeared in this one [Christ]; the former was translated [to heaven], but this one was the precursor of the Lord. And he died before Him so that, descending to the underworld <note>original: "ad inferna," referring to the "Harrowing of Hell" where Christ was believed to descend to liberate the souls of the righteous dead</note>, he might also preach His coming to them. Not only at that time were the ways prepared and the paths made straight, but even to this day the spirit and power of John precede the coming of the Lord Savior. Oh, the great mysteries of the Lord and of His dispensation! Angels run before Jesus. Angels daily either ascend or descend for the salvation of humanity in Christ Jesus. One archangel, Gabriel, made all the announcements pertaining to the birth of Christ. For scripture records that Gabriel appeared seven times concerning the birth of Christ. First, when he announced the birth of John the Baptist to Zacharias. Second, when he announced it to the Virgin Mary in the first chapter of Luke. Third, when he appeared to Joseph in the first chapter of Matthew. Fourth, when he evangelized the birth of Christ to the shepherds in the second chapter of Luke. Fifth, when he appeared to the Magi in the second chapter of Matthew. Sixth, when he warned Joseph to cross into Egypt. Seventh, when he warned him to return from Egypt. And an eighth is added: when he warned him again to turn aside into Galilee, in the second chapter of Matthew. Gabriel, therefore, gave protection concerning the child conceived and to be born, and concerning the Virgin who was to receive him. Therefore, when the time was later pressing, she found that she had conceived a son without male seed and without the delight of carnal pleasure, and she gave birth without damage to her virginity. In this matter, Augustine asks: Who among all men can show a custom of conception where the work was done without the seed of a man? Yet He was not born outside of nature, as the substance of His flesh was taken from the womb of a woman. He was born naturally from nature.

### On the Magi seeking the Savior by the guidance of a star. Chapter 2.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'M' depicting two figures, likely Magi or scholars, in conversation within an architectural frame.</image-desc>
The Magi were the first of all to adore Christ immediately after His birth; for at that time when Jesus was born, they set out from the East to Jerusalem, asserting that they were certainly warned by a star that a boy was born at that time and in that region who would be the future king of Israel and worthy of adoration. From Balaam <note>Balaam was a non-Israelite prophet in the Book of Numbers who famously predicted a "star coming out of Jacob."</note> <margin>Origen in Homily 13 on Numbers.</margin> (says Origen), the race and institution of the Magi is said to have flourished in the parts of the East, who, having all things written down among themselves which Balaam had prophesied, also had this written: that a star shall rise out of Jacob, and <margin>The Magi recognized the star.</margin> a man shall arise from Israel. The Magi had these writings among themselves, and therefore when Jesus was born, they recognized the star and understood the prophecy to be fulfilled—more so than the people of Israel, who despised hearing the words of the holy prophets. Therefore, recognizing from those things alone which Balaam had left written that the time was at hand, they came seeking Him immediately; they adored Him, and to declare that their faith was great, they venerated the small child as a king. 

Concerning this star of the Magi (says Augustine), it is doubted whether it should be understood as a star, or an angel, or the Holy Spirit. And if nothing is repugnant to the Catholic sense when each is discussed, the judgment will allow the measure of our small talent the free choice of choosing among the greater authorities. For if <margin>Various opinions on the star of the Magi.</margin> someone should prefer to accept it simply as a star, how did it deviate from the other stars in this guidance? The nature of the stars, having been created from the beginning and established in the firmament of heaven, is known as is manifested by the authority of the book of Genesis. If, therefore, it remained in the firmament of heaven, how could it become a guide for those walking between Bethlehem and Jerusalem? And if it flew through the air like an arrow at a somewhat slower pace because of frequent stops, it would meanwhile desert its fixed place and course in the firmament. Scripture does not describe this happening even to the greater lights [the sun and moon], except when they stood still or reversed as signs. Unless perhaps that "aerial fire" received such a ministry and took the name of a star because of its likeness. Or if an angel performed this ministry in the habit of a star—which is not repugnant, since angels transform themselves into many forms when they show themselves to men: as the angel showed himself to Moses in Horeb from the bush with a fiery torch, and <margin>Exodus 3:a. Joshua 5:d.</margin> like an armed soldier to Joshua, son of Nun, outside the camp in Gilgal, he was shown

<column-break/>

just as angels performed the role of the chariot and horses of fire at the ascension of Elijah, and when Elisha opened the eyes of his servant. <margin>4 Kings 2:b. 4 Kings 6:d. <note>In the older Vulgate numbering used here, 4 Kings refers to what is now called 2 Kings.</note></margin> In those same conditions, angels are manifested in the form of guests to the sight of Abraham and Lot; and Manoah and his wife saw an angel speaking to them in a prophetic habit. Doubtless, on this occasion also, an angel is made the guide of the Magi, transformed into the likeness of a star and a most brilliant radiance for the astrologers; just as it is said through the image of things to John in his Apocalypse through a vision. Yet this understanding does not go against the fact that the seven stars of the seven churches are angels <note>original: "stelle septem ecclesiarum angeli"</note>, whence one may perceive it in the spirit; or certainly, if it was neither an angel nor a star, let it be granted that the Holy Spirit became this star. Who, just as he later descended in the bodily form of a dove upon the Lord Jesus in the Jordan, so led the adoring nations to the cradle of the Lord being born in the flesh in the likeness of a star. 

<margin>Homer-Centos. <note>These are "Homerocentones," poems constructed by repurposing lines from Homer to tell Christian stories.</note> As the star shone before, it lay behind, the last one higher; because of its beauty, the weary sun yielded. A splendor came to the sky; all the land smiled from every side. A most ruddy star, which shines most brightly, shines entirely in the heavens. And it showed a clear sign to mortals, but the flashes themselves were clear to him.</margin> Concerning this Spirit, the astrologer Balaam spoke through a parable: "A star shall rise out of Jacob"—namely, the red light of spiritual grace by which the darkness of the unbelief of the nations is illuminated. Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit later descended in fire upon the apostles in the upper room of Zion, so he led the Magi to the Lord in the form of a star. This is what Augustine says. If someone should object to us from Calcidius the Platonist <note>Calcidius was a 4th-century philosopher whose commentary on Plato was widely read in the Middle Ages; he was often cited to show that even pagans recognized the miraculous star.</note> that the star was one of those which, appearing rarely, portend great calamities, we will ask him, who brings forward various stories about stars which portend calamities; then he adds: "There is also another holier and more venerable history which relates the rising of a certain star, not by which diseases and deaths were announced, but the venerable descent of God for the salvation of humanity and mortal affairs, which he testifies was observed by the Chaldeans, who venerated the newly born God with gifts." Thus says Calcidius.

### On the baptism of Christ and the appearances. Chapter 3.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'A' depicting the Baptism of Christ by John the Baptist in the Jordan River, with a dove representing the Holy Spirit above.</image-desc>
On another day the Lord was baptized, and the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him, and a voice thundered from the heavens saying: "This is my beloved son in whom I am well pleased." It must be said (says Origen) regarding the baptism of Jesus: the heaven was unlocked; and for the dispensation and remission of sins—not of him who had not committed sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth—but for the whole world the heavens were opened and the Holy Spirit descended, so that after the Lord had ascended on high and led captivity captive, he might grant to us the Spirit who had come to him, which he had indeed given also at the time of the resurrection, saying: "Receive..."

God indeed made this manifest when he showed his son, truly received in a fragrant bosom. The Mother who bore him and nourished him was pure. He was clothed in fragrant garments and washed. Wherefore she also wondered at his nature and marvelous appearance. She kept him to nourish and raise him. Saint Ambrose, Sermon 41 on Matthew 3.
</margin>
the Holy Spirit. <note>original: "spiritumsanctus"</note> If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained. Moreover, the Holy Spirit descended upon the Savior in the form of a dove: a gentle, innocent, and simple bird. Wherefore we are also commanded to imitate the innocence of doves. Such is the Holy Spirit: pure, winged, and rising to the heights. For which reason we say when praying: "Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may rest?" <note>A reference to Psalm 55:6.</note>—that is, who will give me the wings of the Holy Spirit. And in another place, the prophetic word promises: "If you sleep among the middle sheepfolds <term>cleros</term> <note>The Latin 'cleros' refers to 'lots' or 'inheritances,' often interpreted by early theologians as the Old and New Testaments.</note>, the wings of the dove shall be covered with silver, and her feathers with the pale sheen of gold." For if we rest between the two testaments, the Old and the New, the silver wings of the dove shall be given to you—that is, the words of God—and her feathers radiating with the glow and greenery of gold, so that our understanding may be filled with the perceptions of the Holy Spirit. That is, let one's speech and mind be filled by His coming; let us not speak or understand anything except what He suggests. Let all sanctification, both in heart and in words and in works, come from the Holy Spirit in Christ Jesus. Thus says Origen. Therefore, brothers, we ought to be dipped in the same font as Christ, so that we may be what Christ is. For, if I may speak with faith intact (says Ambrose), although both baptisms are of the Lord, I think this baptism by which we are washed is more graceful than that by which the Savior was baptized. For this one is celebrated through Christ; that one was celebrated through John. In that one, the Master excuses himself; in this one, the Savior invites us. In that one, justice was only half-full; in this one, the Trinity is perfect. To that one, the Holy One came and departed; to this one, the sinner comes and the holy one departs. In that one, a blessing is offered to the mysteries; in this one, sins are forgiven through the mysteries. We know, however, that John the Baptist, being a just man, bore the type <note>A 'type' is a historical person or event seen as a foreshadowing of something later.</note> of the Law. It was right, therefore, that he himself should baptize the Lord, just as the Savior was born from the Jews according to the flesh, so according to the spirit the Gospel should be born from the Law. Each drew its origin from succession, and from there received the tradition of consecration. This is therefore what He meant: "For thus it becomes us to fulfill all righteousness." For it was right that He should fulfill the mandates of the Law which He Himself had established, as He says elsewhere: "I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it." Thus says Ambrose. And lest anyone neglect the sacrament of baptism, the Lord, who had been without sin, entered the waters of baptism; and lest anyone disdain being baptized by an inferior, the Lord sought to be immersed by His servant. And so that (as Augustine prefers) He might grant the devil the opportunity to attempt a temptation, He hid Himself, appearing to be washed in the waters among those polluted by sins, as if He were in need of cleansing. Indeed, He saw the Holy Spirit descending upon Him at His baptism. Not because the Son of God did not possess all these things before His baptism, but so that He might show the power of the sacrament of baptism. For He did not then begin to receive the Spirit, who is believed to have the same substance as the Holy Spirit. Nor did the Father then first profess Him to be the Son, to whom He said: "From

<column-break/>

the womb before the morning star I begat you" <note>Psalm 110:3</note>—plainly before every angelic creature, which is often referred to in the Scriptures by the name of the "morning star." Nor did the chamber of the heavens then first begin to open for Him, who says: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool." And although the Holy Spirit is said to descend upon the Lord in a bodily form, it is not doubted that He did not take a dove from among actual birds, but formed it from the air. But because the person of the Son was clothed in the body of human flesh, it was fitting that the person of the Holy Spirit should descend upon Him through a bodily form. And the bodily voice of the Father was heard from a cloud through the air by bodily ears. For while the Son on earth had chosen the creature of water for the mystery of baptism, it was necessary that the Father should also thunder through a watery cloud, and the Holy Spirit should simulate that body—which was made from water in the beginning—taken from that cloud, so that the whole Trinity might show that they possessed the same will.

The body of the dove. Air from the cloud.

### How Christ, being invited to the wedding, changed the substance of water into the appearance of wine. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' depicting a scene with figures, possibly at a table or in a religious setting.</image-desc>
Many record that miracles were performed by the Lord on the same day: such as when, invited to a wedding, He changed the substance of water into the appearance of wine; that He transferred certain springs to a better use by His blessing; that the servants, having drawn water from the wells, found wine in the water-jars and regained what they had lost in a more useful expenditure, having filled what was lacking; and that He then first declared the power of His divinity by this miraculous sign. Some, however (as Saint Ambrose relates), testify that on this holy day He was baptized by John in the Jordan, and that the voice of God the Father and the Holy Spirit descending were present at the grace of His washing. Nor is it a wonder if the mystery of the Trinity was not absent at the Lord's washing, since the sacrament of the Trinity completes our own washing. For the Lord could not fail to first exhibit in Himself what He was later to command to the human race, since He performed all things not for His own sake, but for the sake of our salvation. Or did He wish to be baptized for Himself, since He had no sin, as the prophet says: "Who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth"? But it was certainly for us, who are subject to the sins of many crimes and have need to be purged in the baptism of Christ. And therefore the Lord came to the washing, not to be purified Himself by the waters, but so that He might purify the flow of the waters in us. Therefore, with many testifying (says Ambrose), the Lord was baptized on that day in the Jordan. Although it may be believed by different people that one or the other happened <note>referring to whether the Baptism or the Wedding at Cana happened on this calendar day</note>, I nevertheless (he says) confirm that both happened, and that one sign is contained within the other.

Saint Augustine, Book Three of the Wonders of Holy Scripture.

...for this was done. For when the Lord was baptized, he instituted the mystery of the washing <note>The sacrament of Baptism.</note> and converted the human race, which was like cheap water, into the eternal substance of the flavor of divinity. Similarly, when he turned the water-jars <term>bydrias</term> <note>From the Greek 'hydria,' referring to the large stone water pots used at the wedding in Cana.</note> filled with the liquid of springs into wine, he accomplished two things: he provided a more necessary appearance for the wedding and demonstrated that the bodies of men were to be filled with substance through the washing of the Holy Spirit. The Lord himself declared this more clearly elsewhere, saying: "New wine must be put into new wineskins." <note>Matthew 9:17.</note> For in the "newness" of the wineskins, the purity of the washing is signified by the grace of the Holy Spirit. He is said to have performed this first miracle in wine: namely, changing water into wine. It is a clearly magnificent sign and sufficient for believing in the majesty of God. For who would not wonder that elements were translated into something else? Indeed, no one can change nature except the one who is the Lord of nature. It must be believed from this that mortal man can be converted into immortality, just as a cheap substance was converted into a precious substance. I do not want the listener to merely look at the names of "wine" and "water," but if you wish to prove his power, look at the virtue of the things themselves. Indeed, through this deed (Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), an influential Bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church.</note> says), something deeper is shown. For when the Lord turns water into wine, he does not do this so that those reclining at the feast should lack drunkenness, but so that those who believe should have eternity. 

<margin>Matthew 4:b. The first miracle of Christ.</margin>

For this sign contains the entire mystery of the resurrection. For cheap water—pale and cold—turned into wine (which is precious, red, or fiery) signifies that the substance of man—cheap by condition, weak in infirmity, and pale in death—is to be committed to glory in the resurrection. This glory is precious in its eternity, colored by grace, and ignited by the spirit of immortality. And if it is glorious to change water into wine, how much more glorious is it to change sins into righteousness, and to temper morals rather than cups? I dare to say that those water-jars minister that precious substance not only to that feast, but to the entire world—except that they minister even better to us. For it is certain that from those same vessels, they drank drunkenness, but we drink righteousness; they received a cup of wine, but we receive the cup of salvation. And if it is right to say so, among them passed away that which liberates; but among us, that which we have taken remains.

### On the temptation of the devil and the forty-day fast. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral motifs.</image-desc> After receiving baptism, the Savior—full of the Holy Spirit who had come upon him from the heavens in the appearance of a dove—was led by the Spirit. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God. But this man (says Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note>), beyond all others, was specifically the Son of God; therefore it was fitting for him to be led by the Holy Spirit. Indeed it is written: "He was led into the desert by the Spirit." For forty days Jesus is tempted, and we do not know what those temptations were. They were perhaps omitted for this reason: because they were greater than could be entrusted to letters. Let it suffice for us to know only this: that for forty days he was in the desert and was tempted by the devil, and he ate nothing in those days; for he mortified the senses of the flesh with a perpetual and continuous fast. And when the days were completed, he was hungry. Then the devil said to him: "If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread." "Tell this stone," he says—the devil was surely pointing out which stone he wanted to become bread. What kind of temptation is this, that a son should ask the father for bread, and he would not give him a stone instead of bread (which not even the "skin-shifter" <note>original: "versipellis," a term for the devil implying he changes his shape or is deceitful.</note> adversary himself wanted)? For this is what the devil wanted: that the stone should become bread, rather than turning the man into a stone—the man whom the devil had pointed out in place of bread. 

<margin>Origen on Luke, homily 28.</margin>
<margin>The first temptation of the Savior.</margin>
<margin>Worthy of note: why the temptation of the Savior is not written by the Apostle John, [but by] Matthew, Luke, [and] Mark.</margin>
<margin>The second temptation of the Savior.</margin>
<margin>Origen in homily 30 on Luke.</margin>

The Lord was tempted first according to the assumption of the flesh by every temptation with which men were to be tempted. He was tempted for this reason: so that with him conquering, we might also conquer. And he responds as if on behalf of man. It is written: "Man does not live by bread alone." From which it is manifest that he was tempted not as God (inasmuch as he is God), but as a man. Carefully sifting through the sense of Scripture, I believe I have found the cause why John did not describe the temptation of the Lord, but only Matthew, Luke, and Mark. For John, who had made his beginning from God, saying: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," could not wear down the order of divine generation; rather, he expressed only that which was from God and with God, then added: "And the Word was made flesh." Furthermore, because God as God cannot be tempted (of which his discourse was concerned), he did not introduce him being tempted by the devil. But because the book of the generation of Jesus Christ is narrated in Matthew’s Gospel, and his generation is described in Luke and in Mark, it is the Man who is tempted; therefore a similar response is reported: "Man does not live by bread alone." If, therefore, the Son of God—God for your sake—was made man and is tempted, you who are a man by nature ought not to be indignant if you happen to be tempted. Two kings, therefore, hurry to reign in competition: the king of sin over sinners, the devil; and the king of righteousness, the righteous one, Christ. And the devil, knowing that Christ had come for this purpose—to take away his kingdom so that those who were under him might begin to be under Christ—showed him all the kingdoms of the world. For the lord of this world [the devil] shows how some are ruled by fornication, others by avarice, and others are seized by the care of popular acclaim, or captured by twofold allurements. Nor indeed (says Origen) should it be thought...

Fo. xxxv.
# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.
e iij
<meta>catchword: e iij</meta>

...showing him the kingdoms of the world, for example, the kingdom of the Persians and the kingdom of the Jews. But he showed him all the kingdoms of the world—that is, his own kingdom—showing how he ruled in the world, so that by urging him to do what he wanted, he might begin to have even Christ as a subject. He said, in effect, "Look at these two domains where I reign." He showed him innumerable multitudes of men who were held under his command. And truly, if we are willing to simply confess our misery and unhappiness, the devil is the king of almost the entire world. Hence, he is called the "prince of this world" <note>original: "princeps istius seculi"</note> by the Savior. Therefore, the devil says to the Lord: "Is this why you have come, to fight against me and take from my empire those whom I now have as subjects? I do not want you to struggle; I do not want you to strive; I do not want you to have any trouble in the contest. There is only one thing I ask: fall down and adore me, and receive all the kingdom that I hold." 

But our Lord and Savior certainly wishes to reign, and he wishes all nations to be subject to him so that they may serve justice, truth, and the other virtues. Thus, Jesus speaks to him: "It is written, *You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.*" <note>Matthew 4:10; Deuteronomy 6:13.</note> "I want everyone to be subject to me for this reason," he says, "so that they may adore the Lord God and serve him alone; this is the desire of my kingdom. But you wish to begin with me in the very sins I have come to dissolve, which I also desire to take away from everyone else. Know and recognize that I stand by what I have said: that the Lord God alone is to be adored, and I will subject you all under my presence, power, and kingdom." 

<margin>Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253), an early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> in Homily 31 on Luke.</margin> Again, the devil brings Jesus into Jerusalem. This is "incredible," as Origen would have it: that the devil should lead the Son of God and that he should follow. Yet he followed plainly, like an athlete going voluntarily to a contest. He did not fear the tempter, nor did he dread the snares of the most cunning enemy; in a way, he was saying: "Lead me anywhere; test me as you please; I give myself voluntarily to be tempted. I endure what you suggest; I offer myself; in whatever way you test me, you will find me stronger in all things." 

<margin>On the third temptation of the Savior.</margin> He brought him, therefore, into Jerusalem and placed him upon the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down." He brought him to the peak, to the highest point of the temple, and urged him to cast himself down from there. 

<margin>Saint Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258), Bishop of Carthage and an early Christian writer.</note></margin> The divine martyr Cyprian, in the book *On the Cardinal Works of Christ* addressed to the holy Pope Cornelius, says: "It is doubted by many whether this was a physical transport—if Christ allowed himself to be moved from place to place in the same way that Habakkuk was carried from Judea to Chaldea, and as Philip was carried to Azotus to meet the eunuch who, returning from Jerusalem, was reading the book of Isaiah without understanding it." But that the devil should have carried him physically seems unbecoming—that the Savior should have sat upon his shoulders and used him as a vehicle, knowing him to be his attempted destroyer; or that he should have committed himself to be carried by one whose snares he recognized. It is therefore to be believed that he was led by his own spirit both into the desert and atop the temple, so that in both places the devil might take him up for temptation. 

And while the first temptation in the desert was indeed local, the rest were conducted by the cunning of the tempter (or rather, the patience of the Savior allowed them to be conducted) in the same way that Ezekiel, while sitting by the river Chebar, was snatched up in spirit to Jerusalem, where he saw the city being built and measured, and the walls and temple restored. Cyprian says in the same passage: "In this way, Christ was upon the summit of the temple in spirit, knowing what the spirit previously desired, and he prepared the opportunity for the enemy who was about to strike him with vain glory." 

When the devil proposed this deceitfully and strove under a show of glory, the Savior said: "It is written, *You shall not tempt the Lord your God.*" <note>Matthew 4:7; Deuteronomy 6:16.</note> At the same time, consider how the devil tempts. He does not dare to tempt from any other source but the divine books, and taking a testimony from the Psalms, he says: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written that *he has given his angels charge over you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone.*" 

Let us see, therefore, what the devil says to the Lord from the Scriptures. "For it is written: *He has given his angels charge over you, and they will bear you up in their hands,* etc." See how he is a "turncoat" <note>original: *versipellis* — literally 'one who changes skin,' meaning a shifter or deceiver.</note> even in these testimonies: for he wishes to diminish the glory of the Savior, as if he needed the help of angels and would strike his foot unless he were lifted by their hands. He takes the testimony and interprets it as being about Christ, though it was written not about Christ specifically, but about the holy people in general. 

Indeed, Origen contradicts the devil with full confidence regarding the person of Christ, saying that this cannot be understood of him. For he who is greater than the angels and has obtained a more excellent inheritance than they does not need their help. And to none of the angels did God ever say, "You are my son; today I have begotten you." He spoke to none of them as to a son—he who "makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire"—but specifically to his own Son, of whom he speaks innumerable things in the prophets. The Son of God, I say, does not need the help of angels; rather, learn this, O devil: unless Jesus helps the angels, they will strike their own feet. 

However, so that you may know he interpreted it poorly, and that what follows is to be understood not of Christ but of the holy ones, listen. It is not Jesus Christ whom God delivers from the "noon-day demon," but the holy ones. Read the ninetieth Psalm <note>Psalm 91 in modern numbering.</note>, which begins: "He who dwells in the aid of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven." You will find these things suit a just man more than the Son of God: "A thousand shall fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but it shall not come near you. But with your eyes you shall see and receive the reward of sinners," and the rest, interpreting it in the person of the just man. 

For when he had said: "He has given his angels charge over you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone," the devil was silent about what follows: "You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon." Why are you silent, O devil? Is it not because you are the basilisk? You are the "little king" <term>regulus</term> <note>The word *basilisk* comes from the Greek for 'little king'; it was a mythical serpent said to kill with a glance.</note> of all serpents, having more harmful poisons than the rest.

It features a scholarly debate between Origen and Cyprian on whether Christ was physically transported to the Temple or moved "in the spirit," and highlights the devil's selective quoting of Psalm 90 (91).</summary>

fo.xxxvj.
-># On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.<-
e iiij

You, who kill anyone as soon as you see them, and who take on another contrary strength that joins with you, which is called the asp: you are subject to the just man, and therefore you are silent about all things. You are the dragon; you are the lion; of whom it is written: *You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.* <note>Psalm 91:13. The author uses these beasts as allegories for the devil's various forms of malice.</note> But we know that we have the power to trample you, for the blessing was given to us by the Savior when he said: *Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.* <note>Luke 10:19.</note> Therefore, just as he who is a sinner is trampled by the Son of God, so on the contrary, he who is just tramples the lion and the dragon; he tramples every power of the enemy in the name of Jesus Christ. 

In the devil’s three propositions <margin>Saint Augustine, in the third book of *On the Wonders of Holy Scripture*, chapter 6.</margin> (says Augustine), there was total iniquity; but in Christ’s three responses, by which the devil was repelled, there was total justice. When the enemy is condemned and conquered, liberty and redemption are prepared for the human race. In this sight, while Satan wished to raise himself above the Author, the one who was under him—that is, man—grew beyond him through the help of the Victor's house. And while the devil tried to bind Him who was free from every impediment, he was conquered again, and the one he held in prison laid down the chains in which he was held. While the devil struggled against a stronger opponent, the one who was weaker [man] was strengthened against him. And the Lord commanded him, who had previously been cast out from heaven to earth in error, to migrate even from the earth to the infernal regions. 

The Incarnation of the Lord was able to sustain the hunger of forty days without danger to life, since the Word of the Lord had twice renewed Moses through the air for forty days. Nor did it fail to water the limbs and sinews of Christ from within. Why then is the Lord Jesus described as being hungry after forty days and forty nights were completed? Since Moses and Elijah sustained a fast of such a length of time, our Redeemer sustained a fast of the same number of days so that he might take away the opportunity from the Tempter and so that it might be known <note>The Latin suggests Christ fasted specifically to prove he had a real, physical body that felt hunger, unlike a phantom or spirit.</note> that he bore the true substance of human flesh. Hence, in this fast, he did nothing outside of human capacity; he did not exceed that span of time for which men had fasted previously in the Old Testament.

### On the mute, the deaf, the lepers, the paralytic, and the five loaves. Chapter 6.

Once the adversary was defeated and the forty-day fast perfected, He began to perform the greatest miracles <note>original: "virtutes," meaning powers or miraculous acts.</note>—not by magic tricks, which display nothing true or solid, but by heavenly strength and power, which had been sung of long ago by the announcing prophets. These works are so many that a single book would not be

<column-break/>

enough to fulfill them all. I will, therefore, enumerate them briefly and generally, without any specific designation of persons or places. His miracles were those which (according to Lactantius) Apollo called "portentous." <note>Lactantius was an early Christian author; "Apollo" here likely refers to a pagan oracle that supposedly acknowledged Christ's power.</note> Wherever he made his way, he settled the leprosy that had spread over the faces and bodies of some; he cured many whose feet were uselessly formed. He made all the sick and weak, and those laboring under every kind of disease, healthy in a single word and a single moment—so much so that those who had been seized in all their limbs, having suddenly received back their strength, carried their own beds in which they had been carried shortly before. 

To the lame and those afflicted with defects of the feet, he gave the ability not only to walk but even to run. Then, he restored the eyes of those whose blind lights were in the deepest darkness to their former sight. He also loosened the tongues of the mute into eloquent speech. Likewise, he instilled hearing into the opened ears of the deaf and cleansed those who were polluted and sprinkled with stains. And he did all things not with his hands or any medicine, but by his word and command, just as the Sibyl had predicted, saying: "Doing all things by the word, healing every infirmity." <note>The Sibylline Oracles were often cited by early Christians as pagan prophecies of Christ.</note> Nor is it a wonder that he did miracles by his word, since he himself was the Word of God, supported by heavenly strength and power. 

Regarding the paralytic carried by four men, four divine works are perceived (as Augustine reports): his sins are forgiven; he is released by a word from the plagues of his present sickness; he is answered in his thoughts by the mouth of God who searches all things; and it is shown in this man that some people suffer pain because of the stains on their soul. The mute man could not speak a word to ask for responses from the prophets of God; He who restored eloquence to the mouth of an ass <note>A reference to Balaam's ass in Numbers 22:28.</note> would surely strengthen a human tongue for words, even if it were mute. And when the Light of Justice which came into the world appeared, how could the blind man not see? And by what power could the devil remain in a man, when Christ came to cast him out—he who expelled that sinner from heaven? 

In the five loaves and two fish feeding five thousand, things worthy of wonder are contained, namely three: the smallness of the material, the multitude of the satisfied people of Israel, and the abundance of the fragments. These are the thoughts of Augustine. Because of these miracles and divine works, when a great multitude followed him—whether of the weak, the sick, or those who desired to offer their people to be healed—he ascended a certain deserted mountain to pray to the Father. When he had stayed there for three days and the people were suffering from hunger, he called his disciples to ask what food they carried with them. They said they had five loaves and two fish in a bag. He ordered these to be brought and the multitude to sit down, distributed in groups of fifty. And when he had commanded the disciples to set these before the people, five thousand men were satisfied, and moreover, twelve baskets were filled with the remaining fragments.

<margin>Lactantius Firmianus, *Divine Institutes*, book 4, chapter 15: Lepers are cured, the lame are healed, the blind see, the mute speak, the stained are cleansed. 

Sedulius: <note>Coelius Sedulius was a 5th-century Christian poet.</note> 
Following the high ridges of the mountain with the people following, 
Thousands of the blind and the lame, 
And the people of the lepers, and the crowds of the deaf, 
And the weak hands of the common people, whatever was feeble, 
He restores to their ancient use, healing their deaths, 
And tunes the recalled organs to their own nerves.</margin>

fo. 37.
-># On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.<-

Nothing can be said or done more miraculously. To this end, the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient pagan prophetesses. Early Christian writers often claimed their verses—known as the Sibylline Oracles—actually predicted the coming of Jesus to convince Greeks and Romans of the faith.</note> (according to Firmianus <note>Lactantius, whose full name was Lucius Caelius Firmianus, was a 4th-century Christian author often called the "Christian Cicero."</note>) had long ago foretold the future in these words: *With five loaves and two fish at the same time, he shall satisfy five thousand men in the desert: and you shall take up the remains and fill twelve baskets for the hope of many.* <note>original: "Panibus simul quinque et piscibus duobus hominum milia in heremo quinque sanabit: et reliquias tolles duodecim cophinos implebit in spem multorum."</note> I ask you, what could the magic arts achieve here, whose skill is worth nothing other than to deceive the eyes?

### Jesus walks upon the sea, catches the sinking Peter, and commands the winds. Chapter 7.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'E' depicting a man in profile wearing a hat, possibly a scholar or cleric.</image-desc>
When Jesus was about to depart for the sake of praying, as was his custom, he commanded the disciples to take a small boat and precede him. But they, setting out as evening approached, began to struggle against a contrary wind. When they had reached the middle of the strait, he then entered the sea on foot and followed them, walking as if on solid ground: not as the poets falsely claim Orion <note>A giant hunter in Greek mythology who was said to be able to walk through the sea with his head above the waves.</note> strode in the deep, whose shoulder stood above the waves while part of his body was submerged. And again, when the wind began to rage to the point of extreme danger, he immediately commanded the wind and the waves, which were being carried along at their greatest height, to be still; and immediately at his word, a calm followed. Sacred scripture teaches that such great power was in him: that by his command he forced the winds to obey, the seas to serve, diseases to yield, and wild things to be obedient. What of the fact that they <note>The Sibyls.</note> also (as Lactantius is the authority) taught this before in their poems? One of which, as he says: *will restrain the winds; and he will level the raging sea, treading with faithful feet.* <note>original: "ventos compescet: sternet autem insanum mare pedibus fidis calcans."</note> And again, another which says: *He will walk through the waves, he will dissolve the diseases of men, he will give life to the dead, and he will keep away sorrows from many. And from a living fountain there will be a satiating drink for many men.* Overcome by these testimonies, some are accustomed to flee to the claim that those are not the poems of the Sibyl, but were forged and composed by our own people. Certainly, no one will think this who has read Cicero and Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar from the 1st century BC who categorized the different Sibyls.</note> and other ancients who mention the Erythraean Sibyl and the others; from whose books we bring forth these examples, authors who died before Christ was born according to the flesh. Was the nature of the bodies of the Lord and Peter made light, so that the water would support them, or was the substance of the water made solid, so that it could support human bodies? 

<margin>Saint Augustine, in the third book of On the Wonders of Holy Scripture.</margin> Whatever he did (says Augustine), it would not be against nature at the Lord's command: whether the water solidified or human flesh became light at the Lord's bidding. Just as soldiers or merchants <note>The text here refers to specialized swimmers or performers (institorum) mentioned in ancient accounts who could perform feats on water.</note> outside, as the ancients tell, might perform feats upon the ears of horses; or those imbued with the art of swimming who can submerge half-way into the depths and yet support men—if such things are possible for those who are strong, what wonder if at the Lord's command the flesh was made light? Especially since the bodies of the resurrection will be made so light that they will be supported not only by dense water, but even by clouds and air, as the apostle says: *we shall be caught up to meet Christ in the air.* <note>1 Thessalonians 4:17.</note> Alternatively, he may have chosen that the nature of the water be solidified; since water has the density of earth, as when frost binds it into a hardness that stiffens with the solidity of that earth so it can support a multitude, and later a warm breeze melts it. Or certainly, if nature did not bind the liquid waves, it is implanted in the waters like wood, which by its nature is accustomed to support both human bodies, other animals, and Liburnian ships <note>A type of fast, light galley used by the Roman navy.</note>; that solidity was made at the Lord's command. It is no wonder if it did not support Peter when he doubted, since when the Lord willed it, even the earth did not support the unfaithful—as Dathan and Abiron <note>Biblical rebels who were swallowed by the earth as punishment (Numbers 16).</note> are found to be without reason in the natural administration of things. Then, the lower reason is understood as the daily administration of things: such as how blood is made from water in animals, and salt water; and through the clouds, the earth becomes sweet by its infusion. And let the superior reason be the inherent governance which is discerned in the miracles of things: as God changed water into blood in Egypt in a moment, and into sweetness with a piece of wood.

### On the Transfiguration of the Lord and the appearance of Moses and Elijah. Chapter 8.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'A' depicting a seated figure, possibly a king or Christ in majesty, holding a scepter or orb.</image-desc>
Jesus took Peter, James, and his brother John up a high mountain by themselves, and he was transfigured before them. Some understand it thus: since they had not tasted death, these three apostles, before they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom and in his glory—for seeing Jesus transfigured before them, so that his face shone like the sun and his garments became white like light—they saw the kingdom of God coming in power. For just as if armed men were to stand around an emperor, so Moses and Elijah were seen around Christ by those who ascended the high mountain, appearing in majesty and speaking with Jesus about his departure, which he was to fulfill in Jerusalem. Now this exposition (as Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria, a hugely influential 3rd-century theologian.</note> prefers) which we have spoken of is suitable for those who are such as Peter names: *newborn infants desiring rational and guileless milk.* <note>1 Peter 2:2.</note> To whom Paul also spoke, saying: *I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able; but even until now you are not able.* <note>1 Corinthians 3:2.</note> And all exposition which is explained according to the third level, and can build up those who do not grasp a stronger exposition, I think is rightly called the "milk" that flows from the holy land of the scriptures. Moreover, the Word of God has diverse forms, appearing to each person according to what he knows is expedient to be seen; and he shows himself to no one beyond what he can grasp. Concerning that vision of the Lord on the mountain with Moses and Elijah...
<margin>Origen in Homily 3 on Matthew.</margin>

fo. xxxviij.
-># On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.<-

While they were speaking together (Augustine says thus), although in this manifestation the Lord’s face shone with a solar splendor, it was not the flesh itself that shone; rather, the divinity hidden within the body allowed a small portion of its light to be seen outwardly by the onlookers, as much as they were able to bear. From where, then, did his garments receive a whiteness like snow, since they were neither made of flesh nor of divinity? Unless, perhaps, just as the divinity shone outward through the flesh, so the flesh, illuminated by the divinity, radiated through the garments.

Now, Moses and Elijah were brought to such a vision specifically as the leaders of the Law and the Prophets <note>In Christian tradition, Moses represents the Law and Elijah represents the Prophets; their presence at the Transfiguration signifies that Jesus is the fulfillment of both.</note> to lead them to their conclusion. Or perhaps it was so that Moses—whose face once possessed a glory that the children of Israel could not look upon—and Elijah—who was snatched away in a chariot of fire—might be overshadowed when compared to Christ. And yet, the Scriptures record that these two also fasted for forty days.

Regarding the Lord Jesus alone, a testimony was pronounced to them twice by the presence of the Father. But while Elijah, remaining in his body, came to such a gathering, what should be said of Moses? Was he present in his body once again for this manifestation, or was a likeness formed from the air, just as the spirit of Samuel appeared to have a body? <note>Referring to the biblical story of the Witch of Endor summoning Samuel's spirit (1 Samuel 28).</note> If he came clothed in his own body, did he complete his resurrection at this time—a resurrection which for others will not happen until the final day? On this question, authors have put forth the same opinion without variation: they do not doubt that the Lord met with his three disciples and Elijah not as images, but in true bodies, and that Moses himself was seen in his own true body, taken up from the grave. Yet the Lord Jesus is rightly believed to be the "firstborn of the dead," <note>original: "primogenitus mortuorum"</note> and so it is believed that Moses' body was committed back to the grave after this vision, so that he might hope to take it up again on the last day when the dead shall rise.

This teaching is taken from the text of Augustine: that those bodies of the saints (of whom the Evangelist speaks) who rose during the Lord’s Passion either rose after his resurrection, or if it is said they rose before, then—like Moses—they returned to the dust of the earth, because Christ is called the "firstborn of the dead."

But perhaps you ask: when he was transfigured before those whom Jesus led up the high mountain, did he appear to them in the form of God in which he had been previously? So that to those who were below, he had the "form of a servant," but for those following him after six days <note>A reference to Matthew 17:1, where the Transfiguration occurs after six days.</note> up the high mountain, he no longer had the form of a servant but the form of God? But hear, if you can (says Origen), as a spiritual person. For it does not simply say "he was transfigured before them," but adds a necessary detail which Matthew and Marcus wrote; for according to both it is said: *he was transfigured before them.* According to this (he says), you would say it is possible for Christ to be transfigured with this transfiguration before certain people, while at the same time not being transfigured before others, but remaining in the "form of a servant." <note>Origen, a 3rd-century scholar, often sought deeper "spiritual" meanings. Here he suggests that Christ's appearance depends on the spiritual maturity of the viewer.</note> If you wish to see the transfiguration of Christ happen before those who have ascended the high mountain, consider with me in the Gospels 

<column-break/>

how Jesus is understood simply by those who do not ascend through "ascending works" and through the exercise of spiritual words upon the high mountain of wisdom. To those people, he is not known according to the flesh, but is understood, believed in, and worshiped as God the Word, according to the form of God.

Therefore, Jesus is transfigured before these people, and not before those who are below, living in earthly conduct. But whenever he is transfigured, his face will shine like the sun, so that he may be found more clearly by the "children of light" who have stripped themselves of the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. They are no longer children of darkness and night, but have been made children of God; and as they walk honestly as in the day, he shines clearly for them, not simply as the sun, but is revealed to them as the "Sun of Justice." <note>original: "sol iusticie"</note> And he is not only transfigured before such disciples, but even his garments become white as light. These garments are the words and letters of the Gospels with which Jesus is clothed. Origen also thinks that those things said of him by the Apostles are the "garments of Jesus," which become white for those ascending the high mountain with Jesus. But since there are different types of whiteness, they do not become white in just any way, but "white as light." Therefore, whenever you see someone who is not only careful and perfected regarding the divinity of Christ, but also makes all the words of the Gospels manifest, do not doubt that for such a person the garments of Christ have become white as light. Origen wrote these and many other things in that place, to which we think the reader should be sent if he has the leisure.

### On Lazarus and the others raised from the dead. Chapter 9.

<image-desc>A woodcut initial 'M' featuring a seated king or noble figure holding a scepter, framed within a decorative square border.</image-desc>

Christ raised three people from the dead. The first was raised in her own house; this person signifies those who, enticed by evil thoughts, have admitted the poison of sin into their conscience, but are prevented from an external act either by the bridle of shame or some other cause. <note>Refers to the daughter of Jairus. The author uses these miracles to map the progression of sin: from private thought to public act to habitual vice.</note> The second, who was restored to life outside the city gate, represents those who have brought thought into action, becoming all the more unhappy the more they have achieved their desires. The third, who was stinking in the tomb and held in the prison of a four-day death, had already brought his friends to despair of his life; he signifies those who have turned thought into action and action into habit and character. Their lives are full of outrages, detestable to heaven and hell—that dark and unpraiseworthy class of men who subvert laws and rights, who observe neither limit nor modesty, and who cast away the severity of all discipline. Although such a person may preside over many and rule widely, he nevertheless serves vice and the devil, as the Apostle says to the Romans: *you are servants to the one you obey.* <note>Romans 6:16.</note> Regarding Lazarus and the other dead, Augustine reports thus...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of resurrection and divine will, specifically examining the mechanics of the soul in the eight individuals raised from the dead in Scripture. It then transitions into a famous medieval debate regarding the supernatural darkness that occurred during the Crucifixion.</meta>

fo. xxxix.
# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.
<meta>catchword: prophet</meta>

By His will, God has preordained the lives of all things to a certain end and limit. Therefore, the lives of those who are resurrected are seen to be interrupted by death, but only so that those who are raised might be held in higher honor—as people beloved by God—among their fellow humans.

<margin>John 11:a</margin>
Hence, the Lord says to the disciples regarding Lazarus: "This sickness is not unto death, but so that the Son of God may be glorified through it." <note>original: "non est ad mortem: sed vt filius domini per eam clarificetur"</note> That he was resurrected on the fourth day does not mean God changed the length of his life, but rather that the Lord, who acts without change, often appears to delay an outcome—just as He delayed the births of children to the wives of Abraham and Isaac—to make the gift more welcome. The Lord provides these opportunities so that He might grant through prayer what He already intended to give as a gift.

<margin>Deuteronomy 34:b, 2 Corinthians 12:b</margin>
For if any of the saints asks for something He has not preordained, He does not permit it to happen: as when Moses asked to enter the land of promise, and Paul asked that the messenger of Satan <note>referring to the "thorn in the flesh" mentioned in 2 Corinthians 12:7</note> might depart from him; though they prayed, they did not obtain it. Regarding all those who have died generally, it is understood that they die once; yet among these eight specific dead people whom the Holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments record as having been resurrected, they were raised so that the worthy might be glorified. We should consider what is said of the first of them, the son of the widow whom Elijah raised: "I beseech you, let the soul of the child return." <note>original: "reuertatur obsecro anima pueri"</note>

<margin>4 Kings 17:b <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 17:21.</note></margin>
Concerning the last of them—that is, Eutychus—in the Acts of the Apostles, it says: "He was taken up and found dead; but when Paul went down, he lay upon him and, embracing him, said: 'Do not be troubled, for his soul is in him.'" Both accounts must be understood carefully: the widow's son was dead, and the prophet requested his soul to return. The other was also dead, yet Paul says his soul was in him. In both cases, the Scripture is true, for it cannot lie. But by what reasoning can it be accepted that the soul of a dead man remains hidden within the members of the body, unless perhaps the soul—which is incorporeal—is believed to reside in the body in a hidden way? Some, wishing to avoid the labor of deep understanding, say of Eutychus that he died as the soul left him, but after a short interval the soul returned, and they believe Paul said "his soul is in him" at that moment. However, the Scripture remains silent on whether the soul had departed or returned. The other six who were raised provide evidence that they were truly dead and were brought back to life by divine operation. These are the words of Augustine.

### On the darkness of the sun during the Lord's Passion. Chapter 10.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring two figures, possibly scholars or religious figures, engaged in discussion or study within an architectural frame.</image-desc>

An eclipse of the sun has always happened according to its natural cycle since the beginning of time. But the darkening of the sun that occurs according to the usual course of time does not happen at any other time except during the "conjunction" of the sun and the moon—that is, when the moon, passing beneath, blocks the rays of the sun and obscures its light by its passage. However, at the time when Christ suffered,

<column-break/>

it is clear that there was no conjunction of the moon and the sun, because it was the time of Passover. Customarily, this occurs when the moon is at its full and shines throughout the entire night. It is therefore evident that this darkening of the sun, like the other portents, was something new and beyond natural custom. Indeed, it is well established that the other signs occurring then were not natural, but new and marvelous. For the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom; the earth shook; the rocks were split; the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the sleeping saints arose. Consider that this darkening of the sun occurred outside of natural custom in a recent time under the rule of the Romans, such that darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour. How is it that no Greek and no Barbarian recorded such a miraculous event at that time? This is especially strange for those who wrote chronicles and noted whenever any such new thing occurred. Only your own authors wrote of this. Phlegon did write in his chronicles that it happened during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, but he did not specify that it happened during a full moon. To this, Origen replied that when it is said, "The earth shook," it refers only to the land of Jerusalem, or if one wishes to extend it further, to the land of Judea. Likewise, the darkness that occurred from the sixth to the ninth hour over "all the land" should be understood as occurring over the whole land of Judea, or certainly over Jerusalem alone. Thus (says Origen), he who understands it this way understands it without fault; but if one wishes to show the magnitude of the miracle too grandly, he may fall into the laughter of the wise of this world <note>original: "risum sapientium seculi huius"</note> and cause more disbelief in learned men than faith. This is Origen's view. I do not entirely approve of this opinion of Origen, moved by the authority of Eusebius, who asserts that he read in the histories of the Gentiles themselves that a prodigious eclipse of the sun happened at the very same time as ours. Lucian of Antioch and Tertullian say the same before Eusebius. Moreover, Saint Dionysius the Areopagite and the philosopher Apollophanes—who were walking together near Heliopolis <note>A major city in ancient Egypt known for its astronomical learning.</note>—saw it clearly with their own eyes and proved it through subtle disputations. We read of this in the letter of Dionysius to the wise Polycarp. Concerning this matter, the prophet Amos testifies: "And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord, the sun shall go down at noon, and I will darken the day of light; and I will turn your feasts into mourning and your songs into lamentation." Likewise, Jeremiah says: "She that has borne children is terrified and her soul is weary; the sun has gone down for her while it was yet midday; she is confounded and cursed; the rest of them I will give to the sword in the sight of their enemies." And the Sibyl says: "The veil of the temple shall be rent, and at midday there shall be a very dark night for three hours."

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

### On the opening of the tombs and the appearance of those who were raised. Chapter 11.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a seated scholar or saint at a desk.</image-desc>

When Christ gave up His spirit, to show that He died for the sake of our resurrection, He set the sequence of the resurrection itself in motion. For as soon as He cried out again with a loud voice and gave up His spirit, the earth shook and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose. Coming out of the tombs after His resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many. He who opened the tombs gave a hand to those rising and showed them the way by which they might seek the holy city. It was a divine power that worked in the bodies of the dead; for divine mysteries do not lack human means. God commanded the heavens to be made, and they were made; He decreed the earth to be created, and it was created. Regarding the bodies of the saints coming out of their tombs—as Augustine says—after the resurrection of the Lord: they later returned to their tombs, just as I remember concerning Moses, and there they await the final resurrection of all, as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in Hebrews 11</note> says. All these, having been approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, as God provided something better for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us. If, therefore, these saints and Moses were to rise twice in this manifestation, they would certainly have to be believed to rise again in the final resurrection of all. But let this be far from the Catholic faith: that anyone should believe a person who dies once should rise twice. Unless, perhaps, someone says that Moses and these others died twice. But it is nowhere written of these that they rose in such a way, but rather that they lived, or appeared, or came out of their graves. The name of "resurrection," however, is applied either to those who lived in this life after death, or to the common and future resurrection of all. Such an appearance of these people pertains neither to human life nor to the future resurrection, but to the completion of the Lord's resurrection and to the belief of the souls rising from the underworld. Such an appearance moves the mind, just as in those raised from the dead, a likeness is seen rather than a continuous death. Thus, in these, a likeness of the resurrection—not the resurrection itself—was shown. From continuous death, no one returns to life except the Lord until the final day, and from a true resurrection, no one is ever pulled back into death again. Thus says Augustine. But a doubt arises: for then the Blessed Virgin would have been turned to ash; the opposite of which the same Augustine holds in his book *On the Assumption*. It can be said to this that Augustine tempered his opinion there.

<margin>Saint Augustine, Book 3 of *The Wonders of Holy Scripture*. <note>This text, though attributed here to Augustine, is a 7th-century work by an Irish author known as Pseudo-Augustine.</note> The Apostle.</margin>

### On the food of the Lord after the resurrection. Chapter 12.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure, possibly Christ or a saint.</image-desc>

Regarding the food of the Lord after the resurrection: learned men ask how the flesh of the resurrection received this carnal food, while all the faithful know that the bodies that are to rise will be spiritual, as it is said: "It shall rise

<column-break/>

a spiritual body." For this reason—Augustine says—it is believed by sound judgment that the bodies that rise will not taste food out of necessity, but will have the possibility of eating if it were necessary. Nor does he at all deny the examples of God: as when the angels ate near the oak of Mamre <note>original: "mēbre", referring to Genesis 18</note>; but they do not, like us, pass chewed food to the stomach and intestines. Instead, as soon as it is received and tasted, they transform it entirely—not just in part—into a spiritual nature. Augustine says: Therefore, the food which the Lord took after His resurrection did not pass into the stomach and intestines like our food, but as soon as it was taken, it was transformed into a spiritual nature. This must be understood soundly: that the "spirit" is taken for a subtle body into which that food was immediately resolved by divine power, just as Augustine exemplifies here with the angels eating at the oak of Mamre.

### On the appearance of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and tongues of fire. Chapter 13.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a figure in profile.</image-desc>

By a certain mystery, while the Son of God carried the Son of Man to heaven, that very "captivity" <note>Referring to Psalm 68:18, "He led captivity captive."</note> carries and is carried. As for what He says—"He gave gifts to men"—this is the mark of a victor; for after a triumph, the victors always distribute gifts, and residing in their own kingdom, they reward the joys of their servants. So Christ the Lord, the victor over the devil, residing at the right hand of the Father after His triumph, distributed gifts to His disciples on the day of Pentecost—not talents of gold, nor silver metals, but the celestial gifts of the Holy Spirit. And among other things—Ambrose says—the Apostles spoke in various tongues. This was so that the glory of Christ might be proclaimed with the eloquence of Roman oratory to the Hebrew nation, and so that foreign ears—which would not understand the preaching of Judea in its own tongue—might recognize the redemption of the human race in their own speech. Every tongue was loosened in the preaching of Christ, so that every language might confess His majesty, just as Saint David says: "There are no languages nor speeches where their voices are not heard." Hence, it is to be believed that Christ reached perfection when we see the Paraclete <note term="Paraclete">A title for the Holy Spirit, from the Greek for "advocate" or "helper."</note> descend upon the Apostles at Pentecost. For the Apostles were baptized, as the Lord said to His disciples when He was about to ascend to heaven: "John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you shall receive not many days from now." And therefore Luke says: "When the days of Pentecost were completed, suddenly there was a sound from heaven as of a mighty wind coming, and it sat upon each of them." Regarding the fittingness of the Holy Spirit appearing in a dove over Christ and in fire over the Apostles—as Augustine reports—these things are in the Scripture. We have also spoken of the division of tongues and the virtues of the Apostles after receiving the Spirit in the distribution of alms and the profession of poverty. This is why Peter said to the paralytic: "Rise and walk," keeping the Master's command: "Do not possess gold nor silver." While serving God alone and being unburdened by "wicked mammon," <note term="mammon">A biblical term for wealth or profit, often used to describe ill-gotten gains or the worship of money.</note> he quickly loosened by a word of command one who was bound by disease. Thus says Augustine. From these words of Augustine, four propositions can be elicited. The first is that pau...

### On the miraculous deeds of Peter. Chapter 14.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting a seated figure, possibly a saint or scholar, holding a book or tablet.</image-desc>
**[A]nanias** <note>The OCR reads 'Maniam,' but context identifies this as Ananias from Acts 5</note> cheated the apostles regarding the price of the fields, with his wife being aware; and for that reason, both ended up punished with an equal penalty. Behold (says Augustine), how great is the apostolic power in Christ! While Peter rebuked Saint Ananias, he bound him to death by the power of his word alone; and Tabitha <note>Also known as Dorcas</note>, who was bound by the chains of death, he released by that same power of command. Therefore, Ananias and Sapphira died quickly in the sight of the Church so that the extent of apostolic authority might be shown, and to demonstrate what a great sin it was to take back what had been offered to the Church, so that others might be corrected by this example. These are the words of Augustine. From this text of Augustine, as Franciscus de Maronis reports, some take a valid argument that the apostles had some temporal goods in common: because lands or their prices were given to the Church, and the apostles were then the leaders in the Church; hence (they say) the logic is formed thus: Whenever someone is the head of a "college" <note>A 'collegium' or college refers to a structured community or legal body of people</note>, it is impossible for them not to have the goods of that college in the same way the college has them. But Peter was the head of the Church. Therefore, he had such goods in the same way as the Church. However, this reasoning does not please Franciscus: for (he says) it errs in two ways. First, because it concludes against the fact: if a prelate holds goods in the same way as the whole college, since the whole college does not hold them as a private owner, the prelate would not be an owner either. That the whole college holds them as its own property is clear, because the goods of one college are not shared with any other. Second, it errs because it assumes something false: namely, that a leader always holds goods in the same way as the community subject to him. For it is certain that Christ is truly the head of the Church, yet He does not have temporal goods in the same way the Church does: because for whomever

<column-break/>

use is refused, ownership (which exists for the sake of use) is also refused. For Christ (he says), in the state in which He is now, the use of such things is refused; therefore, such ownership is also refused, as they argue. Therefore, Franciscus says regarding the argument that whenever someone has leadership in any city, that which belongs to the city by way of possession and true ownership belongs to the head by way of administration and office. In this way the apostles held things, as is clearly and expressly written in the Acts of the Apostles: that they distributed the goods of the Church and did not claim ownership for themselves. Thus says Franciscus de Maronis, whom his followers call the "Illuminated Doctor."

### Second Treatise of the second book.

#### On the name of Paul: why he who was called Saul is now called Paul. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
**[Q]uestion:** Our first question seems to arise regarding the name of Paul himself—why he who was called Saul in the Acts of the Apostles is now called Paul. We find in the Divine Scriptures that the names of some of the ancients were changed: so that from Abram he was called Abraham; and Sarai, Sarah; from Jacob, Israel. In the Gospel also, from Simon, Peter; and the sons of Zebedee were named "Sons of Thunder." But we read that these things were done by the command of God. We find that a great deal was done regarding Paul in such a manner. Concerning this matter, it seemed to some (as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note> reports) that the apostle took the name for himself from the proconsul <note>Sergius Paulus, converted in Acts 13</note> whom he had subjected to the faith of Christ in Cyprus. Just as kings are accustomed to be named after those they have conquered—for example, "Parthicus" for the Parthians and "Gothicus" for the Goths—so also the apostle was called Paul after subjecting Paulus. We do not think this should be entirely dismissed. However, because no such custom is found in the Divine Scriptures, let us seek a solution rather from those examples which are familiar to us. We find, therefore, in the Scriptures several people using two names, and others even three: as Solomon is also called Jedidiah; Zedekiah is the same as Joachim; Uzziah is the same as Azariah. And you will find many others in the books of Kings or Judges called by two names. Nor did even the Gospels maintain this same custom <note>Meaning they also use multiple names for the same person</note>. For Matthew himself reports of himself that when Jesus passed by, He found a certain man sitting at the tax office named Matthew. Luke, however, says of the same man: that when Jesus passed by, He saw a certain tax collector named Levi and said to him, "Follow me." According to this custom, therefore, it seems to Origen that Paul used a double name: and while he was specifically ministering to the Gentiles he was called Paul, which was more...
