it seemed to be his original, native name. However, he was called Paul when he wrote laws and precepts for the Greeks and the Gentiles. For even what the Scripture says—"Saul, who is also Paul" <note>Acts 13:9</note>—does not evidently show that the name of Paul was first imposed upon him then, but designates that it was an old name. Saint Ambrose says that he was first called Saul because of his "unrest" <note>original: "inquietudinem" — Ambrose often interpreted the name Saul in the context of Paul's restless persecution of Christians before his conversion</note>. Others, however, have argued that because he was short in stature, he had the Hebrew name Saul; but because he was also a born Roman citizen, he had from the start the Roman name Paul, which is quite close to the Hebrew name. This also happened with John, also called Mark; indeed, we read of both names in the Acts of the Apostles. For he says that John and Saul are Hebrew names, while Mark and Paul are gentile <note>Roman/Latin</note> names, just like Marcus Regulus, Marcus Antonius, Paulus Emilius, or Paulus Sergius. For thus Luke records in the Acts: "taking with him John, who was surnamed Mark" and again, "Saul, who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit." Therefore, since Paul knew himself to be the Apostle to the Gentiles, those who argue this say he rightly placed his gentile name first and called himself Paul. Origen felt that Paul was "binomium" <note>original: "binomium" — meaning a person with two names</note>, for in the sacred utterances, he is the youth in ecstasy <note>original: "adolescentulus iumentis excessu" — a reference to Psalm 67:28 in the Vulgate, often interpreted as a prophecy of the Apostle Paul</note>.

### That the apostles did not reject marriage. Chapter 2.

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, holding a book.</image-desc>
**O**rigen, that man of steel <note>original: "adamantius" — a nickname for Origen meaning "man of diamond" or "unconquerable," referring to his tireless work ethic</note>, writing in the first book of his letter to the Romans, says among other things: "Truly he is free who comes to Christ through the purity of continence without a wife. Yet he is made a servant of Christ while he serves the virtues with integrity." Paul, therefore (as some hand down), was called while he had a wife, concerning whom he says when writing to the Philippians: "I ask you also, true companion, help those women who are with her." By mutual consent, therefore, he was made free, and calls himself a servant of Christ. Truly Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius report in the third book of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 23: "Among other things," he says, "do they also disparage the apostles? For Peter and Philip both had wives and even gave their daughters in marriage to men. But even Paul the Apostle does not feel ashamed in a certain epistle to make mention or greeting of his companion, whom he says he does not lead around with him so that he may be more unencumbered for the preaching of the Gospel." Truly, since we have made mention of Clement, it will not be absurd to bring forth another of his memorable narratives, which he inserted in the seventh book of the same work. "They say," he says, "that the blessed Peter, when he saw his wife being led to her passion <note>martyrdom</note>, rejoiced because of the grace of her election and her return to her own home, and he called out after her as she was being led away, addressing her by her own name: 'O [wife], con-

<column-break/>

<margin>Saint Ignatius in the fifth of his letters, which is to the Philadelphians.</margin>
-sider the Lord!'" Such were the marriages of the saints, and so perfect was the affection of the blessed. These are the arguments against those who would strip Paul of his marriage. Regarding what he adds in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter nine, when he says: "Do we not have the power to lead about a sister-wife, just as the rest of the apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas <note>Peter</note>?" The blessed Ignatius, a contemporary of Peter and Paul, testifies that Paul had a wife, and a faithful one indeed, and therefore called her a "sister." He left her set apart for the work of the Gospel for the sake of the Gospel of Christ. Concerning her, we shall add something more in the commentary on the letter to the Philadelphians, if God permits. The other apostles—though not all, for John remained a virgin forever—also had wives, according to the testimony of the divine Ignatius: including those who were called the brothers of the Lord—James, Joseph the Just, Simon, and Thaddeus—as well as Peter. This is established by their victories <note>their martyrdoms/triumphs</note>, should the authority of the Apostle in this present place seem sufficient to anyone. To some, however, it seems Paul was without a wife. For as it pleases Ambrose: "All the apostles except John and Paul had wives." These men were not eloquent, for they were without formal letters <note>uneducated</note>, yet being full of the Holy Spirit, they were able to offer a greater grace. These are the words of Ambrose. Which opinion is truer remains in doubt. Now, since the Lord deigns to open the way for us, let us hasten more quickly to the explanation itself. However, because no certainty is found in the Holy Scriptures regarding this matter, let us seek a resolution rather from those things which are given as examples to us. We find, therefore, in the epistles of Paul, as was already said above, that he made mention of a wife quite often; as in the first to the Corinthians when he says: "Do we not have the power to lead about a wife just as the rest of the apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?" Second, he writes thus to the Philippians: "I ask you also, true companion, help those women who are with her." According to the first opinion, then, it seems Paul was called to the Gospel while having a wife; and this opinion has very weighty authors: Ignatius, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Eusebius of Caesarea. In the Greek translation of Philippians chapter four, it is held thus: "I ask Enodia and I ask Syntyche to think the same in the Lord; I also ask you, noble spouse <note>original: "ingenua coniunx"</note>, help those who have struggled with me in the Gospel." In the common edition <note>the Vulgate</note>, however, it says: "I also ask you, true companion <note>original: "germane compar"</note>, help those who have labored with me in the Gospel." We say, therefore, that Paul was perhaps called to the Gospel while having a wife, and yet he remained in virginity <note>celibacy</note>. For when a marriage is initiated, then the name of "spouse" is adopted. For it is not the deflowering of virginity that makes a marriage, but the marital vow <note>original: "passio conjugalis"</note>. Finally, when a girl is joined, she is joined; she is not known <note>sexually</note> only upon masculine admission. That Paul was betrothed in marriage is read among many; concerning his virginity...

folio xliij.

# Book Two.

<margin>Polycrates, Bishop of Ephesus</margin> We do not read that he <note>Referring to Paul, from the previous page's context</note> had daughters. However, we do read that Philip and Peter had daughters. Regarding Paul, we read of neither sons nor daughters. Polycrates, writing to Victor, the bishop of the city of Rome, mentions both Philip the Apostle and his daughters equally, saying (as we have already inserted above) that "great lights have fallen asleep in the parts of Asia, whom the Lord will raise up on the last day of his coming, when he shall come in glory and gather all his saints." "I speak of Philip," he says, "who was one of the apostles, who fell asleep at Hierapolis <note>An ancient city in what is now Turkey, famous for its hot springs</note>, as did two of his daughters who grew old as virgins; and another of his daughters, filled with the Holy Spirit, lived at Ephesus." Furthermore, Gaius, in his dialogue written while disputing with Proclus, mentions the daughters of Philip and his death in similar words, saying: "after this, there were four prophetesses, the daughters of Philip; his tomb is at Hierapolis, a city of Asia, along with those of his daughters." Luke also mentions these in the Acts of the Apostles while they were still staying at Caesarea. 

Regarding Paul, however, we nowhere read that he fathered sons or daughters, and therefore some have thought he remained in a state of virginity—although it is also read that he had a wife, and that he merely preferred others to doubt his marriage rather than his virginity (if he had any). Thus we are taught (as Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> says) that the virtue of chastity is threefold: one of marriage, another of widowhood, and the third of virginity. For we do not praise one so as to exclude the others; these are profitable according to each person’s profession. In the rich discipline of the Church’s faith, she has those she prefers, but she has none she rejects; and would that she never might. We therefore praise virginity in such a way that we do not reject widowhood; we honor widowhood in such a way that its own honor is reserved for marriage. These are not our commands, but the teachings of divine testimonies. Let us remember how Mary, how Anna, and how Susanna are praised. And since not only their praises are to be preached, but their disciplines are to be followed, let us remember where Susanna, where Anna, and where Mary were found. And let us observe how each is preached with appropriate praises, and where they dwell: the married woman in paradise, the widow in the temple, the virgin in the secret chamber. But in the former, the fruit is slower; in the virgin, it is more mature. Old age proves the former; virginity is the praise of one's age, nor does it seek the help of years, for it is the fruit of all ages. Therefore, we have discussed these matters concerning the marriages of the apostles, and especially Paul, as far as we could from the gathered scriptures; yet it cannot be sufficiently clear to us which of these opinions is to be preferred.

### Whether it is true, as is said of John the Baptist, that he is Elijah. Chapter 3.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a portrait of a bearded man in profile, possibly a prophet or scholar, wearing a cap.</image-desc>Some people indeed have held the opinion, based on the saying "He is Elijah who is to come," <note>Matthew 11:14</note> that the soul of Elijah was the same as that of John. For they thought that what he said (as Origen <note>A prolific 3rd-century Christian scholar from Alexandria</note> notes)—"he is Elijah"—referred to nothing else but the soul. From this single speech, they almost introduced the dogma of the "transmutation of souls" <note>original: "transmutationē aiarum" — reincarnation or metempsychosis</note>, as if Jesus himself were confirming it. But it ought to have been observed that if this were true, something similar should be found in many other writings of the prophets or the Gospels. 

Furthermore, the speech added to this shows that a more secret or hidden meaning is to be sought in these words, rather than the literal understanding those people took, for he says: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." It must also be added that if the transmutation of souls happens because of sins (as they believe), for what sins was the soul of Elijah transformed into John? For he was announced by an angel to be born—how could he, who was so perfect that he did not even taste common death, come to a transmutation of the soul, which according to their assertion cannot happen except from sins? Finally, how can one explain what was said to John, "Are you Elijah?" and he says, "I am not"? But to show that this also agrees with the word the Lord spoke—"If you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come"—Origen says that "he is Elijah" must be referred to the "spirit and power" of Elijah himself. For John went before in the spirit and power of Elijah to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. But some of them say: if the soul of John was not that of Elijah, why did the Savior call him Elijah? Origen responds that Gabriel, in the words he spoke to Zechariah, demonstrated what it was of Elijah that was transferred into John. For he says: "And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the incredulous to the wisdom of the just"; he does not say "he shall go before him in the soul of Elijah."

### Whether Scripture clearly teaches that the soul is one thing, but the spirit is another. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' containing a portrait of a man, likely St. Paul, holding a sword and a book.</image-desc>Paul designates that there are three things in man when writing to the Thessalonians, saying: "that your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ." <note>1 Thessalonians 5:23</note> And David says: "Praise the Lord, you spirits and souls of the just." Isaiah, however, omitting the lowest part, mentions two: "My soul," he says, "has desired thee in the night; but also with my spirit in my heart I will watch for thee in the morning." Augustine, in his book *On Church Dogmas*, says: "There is not a third substance in the spirit of man, as Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind, a 4th-century Alexandrian theologian</note> contends; rather, the spirit is the soul itself, named for its spiritual nature. It is called the soul, however, because it animates the body to give it life." A third part, however, is introduced by the apostle along with the soul and body...

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

f iiij
<meta>f iiij</meta>

...the grace of spirits—that is, we understand it to be the "spirit" for which the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> prays, asking that it persevere whole within us, lest by our own fault it be diminished or driven from us; for the Holy Spirit will flee from a deceptive soul. From these passages, Origen <note>An influential and controversial early Christian scholar from Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD)</note> concludes, not without reason, that there is a threefold portion of man. First is the **Body** or the **Flesh**, the weak part of our nature, upon which that "old serpent" <note>The Devil</note> inscribed the law of sin through the fault of our birth, by which we are provoked to shameful acts and, once defeated, are bound to the devil. Second is the **Spirit**, by which we express the likeness of the divine nature; in this part, the best Creator, following the archetype <note>The original pattern or model</note> of His own mind, has engraved that eternal law of honesty with His finger—that is, by His own Spirit. Through this, we are glued to God and made one with Him. Furthermore, the third part, placed in the middle between these two, is the **Soul**, which is capable of natural sense and motion. Therefore: the spirit makes us like gods; the flesh makes us like beasts; the soul makes us men. The spirit makes us pious; the flesh makes us impious; the soul makes us neutral. The spirit seeks heavenly things; the flesh seeks sweet things; the soul seeks necessary things. The spirit carries us up to heaven; the flesh weighs us down toward hell; the soul is credited with nothing on its own. Whatever is of the flesh is shameful; whatever is of the spirit is perfect; whatever is of the soul is middle and indifferent.

For Scripture clearly recognizes (says Origen) that the soul is one thing and the spirit is another, as Paul testifies when he says: "May the God of peace sanctify you wholly, and may your whole **spirit**, **soul**, and **body** be preserved at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." <note>1 Thessalonians 5:23</note> And in the Book of Daniel: "Bless the Lord, you spirits and souls of the righteous." <note>From the 'Song of the Three Holy Children,' a portion of Daniel found in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles</note> Therefore, John the Baptist was not called "Elijah" because of his soul, but (as he says) because of the **spirit and power**; the virtue of Scripture is not troubled if the spirit was first in Elijah and afterward was made present in John. As the Apostle says: "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" <note>1 Corinthians 14:32</note>—not that the *souls* of the prophets are subject to prophets.

<margin>The spirits of the prophets.</margin>

To further confirm what the angel said—"And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah"—let us take an example from the Fourth Book of Kings <note>Known as 2 Kings in modern Bibles</note>, which is as follows: "And it came to pass, when they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha: 'Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee.' And Elisha said: 'I beseech thee that thy **spirit** may be double in me.'" And Elijah said: "Thou hast asked a hard thing; nevertheless, if thou see me when I am taken from thee, it shall be so unto thee; but if not, it shall not be so." Scripture wishes to show that it happened for Elisha just as he had asked; it adds that Elijah went up by a whirlwind as if into heaven, and Elisha saw it, and he cried out: "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel!" and he saw him no more. Because he saw him, therefore the **spirit**—not the soul—of Elijah rested upon Elisha.

Likewise, after Elisha struck the waters of the Jordan and they were divided, Elisha passed over; and the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho saw him and said: "The spirit of Elijah hath rested upon Elisha." And they came to meet him and worshipped him on the ground. We have said this (says Origen) so that we may understand that John was called Elijah not because they shared the same soul, but because of the same spirit. Christ's disciples understood this as well; for while the spirit of Elijah merely rested upon Elisha, John went before Christ not only in the spirit but also in the **power** of Elijah. For this reason, Elisha was not called "Elijah," but John was said to be Elijah himself.

**Blessed Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan</note> says the following in his book *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*: "The Creator made the soul of man in His own image." When I speak of the "mind" (*mens*), it does not signify something other than the soul of the man; rather, it is called "soul" for one reason and "mind" for another. For all that lives in a man is the soul. When the soul acts within itself, from itself, and through itself alone, it is usually called the **Mind**. But when it is occupied with the customary duties of the senses, it is called the **Soul**. The Mind, therefore, brings forth knowledge, and it loves to know what it knows.

<margin>

</margin>

Again, in his 23rd Letter to Horatianus regarding the Spirit, he says: "Does it not seem to you that this Spirit is our helper? Just as the one to whom it is said: 'Thou art my helper, forsake me not, nor despise me, O God of my salvation.'" Who else is the spirit that could teach Paul what he should pray for? For the Spirit of Christ the Son, or Christ Himself, teaches His disciples to pray. But who can teach Christ, except His own Spirit, whom He sent to teach and direct our prayers? For we pray in the spirit and we pray with the mind, so that one may pray well. The Spirit goes before and leads the soul into the right way, lest carnal things—or things too small or even too great for one's strength—creep in. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for their benefit.

Saint John of Damascus <note>An 8th-century Syrian monk and theologian</note> said that the **Mind** is in the soul as its purest part; whence (he says) just as the eye is in the body, so is the mind in the soul. Yet it is not a "composing part" in the way an eye is a part of the body's structure; rather, it is a particular virtue and power of the soul, devoted to a specific operation—namely, understanding—just as the eye is devoted to vision. In this, a comparison is made between the two.

### On the blasphemy of the spirit which is not forgiven here nor in the future, and whether there are some crimes that cannot be kept from the house of grace. Chapter 5.

Several people are accustomed to raise the objection found written in Matthew: "Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. And whosoever shall speak a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but he that shall speak against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come." <note>Matthew 12:31-32</note> John the Apostle says in his first epistle, chapter 5: "He who knows his brother to be sinning a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life shall be given to him; but there is a sin unto death, and I do not say that anyone should pray for that."

Likewise Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, writing to the Hebrews in chapter 6, sang thus: "For it is impossible for those who were once illuminated, have tasted also the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit—who have nonetheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come—and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again to themselves the Son of God and making Him a mockery." <note>Hebrews 6:4-6</note> Likewise Hermas, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, whom the Apostle mentions when writing to the Romans: "Salute Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas..." <note>Referring to the *Shepherd of Hermas*, a 2nd-century Christian literary work</note>

folio xlv.

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

...and those who are with them, the brothers, in the book of the one called the *Shepherd* <note>Referring to *The Shepherd of Hermas*, a popular early Christian work from the 2nd century often treated as scriptural by early fathers</note>, which, according to Jerome, is read publicly in some churches of Greece. In the fourth mandate, he writes: "I tell you that after that great and holy calling <note>Original: *vocationem*, referring to baptism or conversion</note>, if anyone is tempted by the devil and sins, he has one opportunity for penance. But if he sins repeatedly and does penance, it will not profit a man doing such things, for he will live for God only with difficulty." And I said: "Lord, truly, since I have heard these mandates so carefully, I know that if afterward I add nothing to my sins, I shall be saved." These are the words of Hermas. 

<margin>Saint Pamphilus from the second book of Origen’s *On First Principles*</margin> 

Pamphilus, indeed, a Christian martyr, in his apology for Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) was a prolific but controversial theologian; Pamphilus wrote a defense of his orthodoxy</note>, says on his authority: "I think it follows that he who sins against the Son of Man is worthy of pardon; for he who is a partaker of the Word or Reason <note>Original: *verbi vel rationis*</note>, if he intends to live rationally, seems to have fallen into ignorance or folly, and because of this earns pardon. But he who has already been deemed worthy of participation in the Holy Spirit and has turned back, this man is said to have blasphemed in reality and by deed against the Holy Spirit." 

These are the authorities of illustrious men by which some affirm that sin against the Holy Spirit and blasphemy will be unpardonable. 

<margin>Ambrose, Book 3 on Penance, Chapter 4</margin> 

To whom Saint Ambrose responds: "That which is found written in Matthew concerning the blasphemy of the Spirit is understood to be about heretics and schismatics <note>Those who create divisions or split away from the established Church</note> who separate the Church; to whom indulgence is denied because they have not laid down the merits of such a great crime for so long." For it is written: *Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to men; but the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven to men. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but he who speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the future.* 

By this example, all their assertion is destroyed and resolved. For it is written: *Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to men.* Why then do they not forgive? Why do they bind chains that they do not loose? Why, he asks, do you tie knots that you do not loosen? Forgive the others; deal with those whom you think are bound forever by evangelical authority as sinning against the Holy Spirit. 

And yet, let us understand whom he binds. The Jews were saying, "He does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub <note>A name for the prince of demons or the devil</note>, the prince of demons." Jesus responded: "Every kingdom divided against itself will be destroyed, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. For if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand? But if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?" 

Regarding these, we clearly see that they were saying the Lord Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebub, to whom the Lord responded: that the inheritance of Satan was in those who compared the Savior of all to Satan and placed the grace of Christ in the kingdom of the devil. And so we might know what he said about this blasphemy, he added: *offspring of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?* You, therefore, who speak these things...

<column-break/>

...he denies that you pertain to pardon. Finally, Peter said to Simon <note>Simon Magus, a practitioner of magic who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit, giving us the term 'simony'</note>, who, corrupted by the practice of the magic art, thought that he could purchase the grace of Christ through the imposition of hands and the infusion of the Holy Spirit with money: "You have no part nor lot in this faith, for your heart is not right before God; therefore, do penance for this your wickedness, and pray to the Lord if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you; for I see that you are in the bond of iniquity and the bitterness of gall." 

<margin>Acts 8</margin> 

You see that he condemns this man who blasphemed in the Holy Spirit by apostolic authority—and all the more because he did not have a pure conscience of faith—and yet he did not close off the hope of pardon for him, whom he invited to penance. 

The response, therefore, was from the Lord to the blasphemy of the Pharisees, and he denies the grace of his power to all these, which is for the remission of sins, because they would claim heavenly power was supported by the devil's help. He also asserts that those use a diabolical spirit who would separate the Church of God, including the heretics and schismatics of all times, to whom he denies indulgence; because every sin is concerning individuals, but this is concerning the whole. For they alone are those who wish to undo the grace of Christ, who tear apart the members of the Church, for which the Lord Jesus suffered and the Holy Spirit was given to us. 

The same Ambrose also says in the book *On the Calling of All Nations*: "Just as there are no crimes so detestable that they can exclude one from the home, so no works can exist so illustrious that this [grace], which is granted freely, should be owed through the judgment of retribution; for the redemption of the blood of Christ would become worthless." 

<margin>Ambrose, Book on the Calling of All Nations, Chapter 5</margin> 

Divine father Augustine also feels quite differently about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit; whence in the book which he entitled *On the Same Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*, he says: "It seems to some that only those sin against the Holy Spirit who, having been washed in the bath of rebirth <note>Baptism</note> in the Church and having received the Holy Spirit, have afterwards, as if ungrateful for so great a gift of the Savior, immersed themselves in some deadly sin, such as adultery or homicide, or even a departure either entirely from the Christian name or from the Catholic Church; but from where this sense can be proven, I do not know, since the place for penance of any crimes whatsoever is not denied in the Church." 

"Therefore," he says, "let us seek the light of exposition from the Lord. Rise up then, brothers; lift up your ears to me, your minds to the Lord. I tell your brightness <note>A formal honorific address to his audience</note> that perhaps in all the holy scriptures no greater question, no more difficult one is found; whence, to confess something about myself to you, I have always avoided the difficulty and trouble of this question in the sermons I have had for the people." 

"I advise you to notice and understand that the Lord did not say: 'All blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven,' nor did he say, 'Whoever has spoken any word whatever against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven him,' but *whoever shall speak a word*. For if he had said the former, nothing at all would remain for us from which we could dispute. It is necessary, therefore, that there be some [specific] blasphemy and some [specific] word which, if spoken against the Holy Spirit, earns no pardon or remission; for if we begin [to think any word], how will anyone be able to be saved? But if again we think there is none, we contradict the Savior. What then is this blasphemy?"

<margin>Augustine</margin>

folio xlvi.

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

...the way of the world, or rather its lack of moderation. Regarding what that blasphemy might be, and how it is a word against the Holy Spirit, I will no longer delay your expectation. I say, therefore, that impenitence itself is the "spirit of blasphemy" <note>original: *spus blasphemie*</note>, because it will be forgiven neither in this world nor in the future. For in impenitence <note>The OCR reads *beato*, likely a transcription error for *quia* (because) or similar</note> no remission is held, neither in this world nor in the future: because penance obtains remission in this world that it may be valid in the future. Concerning this impenitence, or an impenitent heart: as long as anyone lives in this flesh, he cannot be judged [finally]. For no one is to be despaired of as long as the patience of God leads to repentance—nor does He snatch the impious from this life, He who does not wish for the death of the impious so much as that he should return and live. 

Whoever, therefore, is guilty of impenitence against the Spirit in which the unity and fellowship of the communion <note>original: *omnionis*, likely *communionis*</note> of the church gathers: it will never be forgiven him. This is because he has closed off for himself the place where forgiveness is granted; and he will be justly damned with the spirit that is divided against itself—divided, too, is he against the Holy Spirit, who is not divided in Himself. Hence, when it is said "a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven him," but to him who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit it will not be forgiven, this refers to the blasphemy of an impenitent heart. By this, one resists the remission of sins which is performed in the church through the Holy Spirit. 

This blasphemy did not possess Peter, who repented as soon as he wept bitterly. He was a victor through the Spirit, though he had been divided against himself and the truth when he was questioned—the Lord had prayed for him, so that his faith might not fail. In this reading of Saint Matthew, the Lord revealed much more clearly what he wished to be understood: that is, when he himself speaks of a "word against the Holy Spirit," he means that which resists the unity of the church with an impenitent heart. Since the remission of sins happens in the Holy Spirit, that blasphemy of the spirit which occurs in an impenitent heart—resisting such a great gift of God until the end of this life—will not be forgiven. Indeed, a "word against the Holy Spirit" is spoken when one never comes from dispersion back to the congregation, for the church received the Holy Spirit for the purpose of remitting sins. 

There is, therefore, one refuge: let an impenitent heart be avoided so that the blasphemy is not irremissible. Let penance not be believed to be profitable in any other way than by holding to the church where the remission of sins is given, and where the fellowship of the Spirit is guarded in the bond of peace. These are the things that Augustine feels concerning the spirit of blasphemy. 

Regarding the authority of the [Epistle to the] Hebrews, chapter six, when it is said "it is impossible for those who were once enlightened..." <note>Hebrews 6:4</note>, I respond that it does not say "impossible to be renewed to penance" in a simple sense. Rather, it is impossible to be renewed to penance for those who are "recrucifying in themselves the Son of God and making him an example of shame." This is certainly what those would be doing who, having fallen after the enlightenment of baptism, thought they could be renewed through a repeated baptism—just as the Jews did. After committing crimes, they would return again to the foundations of faith, penance, baptism, and the laying on of hands as if they had never been baptized before, coming anew to the knowledge of Christ and faith when they should not have done so. 

Rather, in baptism we die <note>original: *rimur*, likely *morimur*</note>, are buried, and rise with Christ: which can only happen once, for the Lord died once, was buried once, and rose once. Come now, if there is a place for penance after a lapse following baptism: what sort of place is it if it is not through the washing of purification? <note>original: *ablutionis lauacrum*</note>. There is, without doubt, a place for penance. For if there were not, the Apostle would not have handed over the incestuous fornicator to Satan for the destruction of the flesh so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord. If there were not, the Holy Spirit would not say what we have heard in the Epistle to the Ephesians: "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you." For what else is this than calling one from dead works to penance? 

What else does Paul mean when he writes to Timothy, that he should correct those who resist with gentleness, lest perhaps God give them penance leading to the knowledge of the truth, and they may recover themselves from the snare of the devil? Behold how, for the faithful, a place for penance is undoubtedly left after a lapse. You will say: "Since it is not through the washing" (for that, as said, is impossible, and we are forbidden to attempt it), "how is it done?" Without doubt, by approaching with confidence the throne of grace, so that I may receive mercy and find grace in a time of need. 

In the Apocalypse, the seven angels of the seven churches (who were the bishops and pastors of those churches) are admonished to perform penance if they had any "dead work." Wherefore John, the eagle of heavenly secrets, says: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." 

But truly, if any—after such great grace from God in the pouring out of the washing—always roll back into all evil things after multiple lapses and divisions, never performing anything good (like a sterile field or soil producing only harmful weeds), these show themselves to be children of a curse, reserved for the justice of God in the fire of Gehenna and eternal punishment. Wherefore Paul adds, saying: "For the earth that drinks the rain often falling upon it, and brings forth herbs fit for those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God; but that which brings forth thorns and thistles is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is to be burned." 

<margin>
Ambrose,
book two
on penance,
Chapters
4, 5, 10, 7.
</margin>

Regarding the authority of Hermas, I respond that he spoke of a *difficulty*, not an *impossibility*, when he said: "For he will live for God only with difficulty." For John says: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world." And therefore (says Ambrose), return to the church, you who impiously separate yourselves. For He promises pardon to all who turn back, because it is written: "Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." Finally, even the Jewish people—who said of the Lord Jesus, "He has a demon," who said He casts out demons by Beelzebub, and who crucified the Lord Jesus—are called to baptism by Peter’s preaching, so that they might lay aside the deserts of such a great crime. 

For I believe that even Judas could have been not excluded from pardon by such great mercy of God, if he had performed penance not before the Jews, but before Christ. But let those who perform penance hear how they ought to act: with what zeal, what affection, what intention of mind, what striking of the innermost heart, and what conversion of the soul. "See," he says, "O Lord, because tri..." <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the folio</note>

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

<margin>Lamentations 2:C</margin>...I am troubled. My bowels are troubled by my weeping; my heart is turned within me. You have known the intention of my soul; know now the faith of my mind and the condition of my body. The elders of the daughter of Zion sat upon the ground; they were silent and threw dust upon their heads; they girded themselves with haircloth. The princes bowed their heads to the earth; the virgins of Jerusalem wasted away in tears; my eyes have grown dim. <note>original: *venter meus turbatus est... oculi mei caligauerunt*. A poetic description of deep grief and penance from the Book of Lamentations.</note>

<margin>Jonah 3:D</margin>My bowels are troubled; my glory is poured out upon the earth. In this way the people of Nineveh wept, and the announced destruction of the city was avoided. For so great is the medicine of penance that God is seen to change His sentence. It is within you, therefore, that you may escape; the Lord wishes to be asked, He wishes to be hoped in, He wishes for man to supplicate Him. You are a man and you wish to be asked so that you may forgive, and do you think God will forgive you if you do not ask? The Lord Himself wept over Jerusalem, because He did not want her to have to weep, so that the Lord's tears might lead to her pardon. He wants us to weep so that we might escape, just as you have it written in the Gospel: "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves." <note>original: *filie hierusalem nolite me flere: sed vos ipsas flete*. Refers to Luke 23:28.</note> David wept and earned the removal of divine punishment by mercy when the people were dying, after he chose the one option among three where he might experience the greater mercy of the Lord. Why do you blush to weep for your sins when God commanded the prophets to weep for the people? Finally, even Ezekiel was commanded to weep for Jerusalem, and he received a book in the beginning of which were written lamentation, a song, and woe: two sad things and one delightful thing—for he shall be saved in the future who has wept more in this world. For "the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools is in the house of feasting." And the Lord Himself says: "Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh."
<margin>Luke 23:D; 2 Samuel 24:B; Ezekiel 2:D; Ecclesiastes 7; Luke 6:D</margin>

### Why in Luke the father of Joseph is written as Heli, and in Matthew as Jacob. Chapter 6.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a man's face in profile within the letter's counter.</image-desc>Since the Evangelists Matthew and Luke have handed down the generations of Christ to us in various ways, they are thought by many to say things contrary to one another. In this matter, several of the faithful, through ignorance of the truth, try to apply certain fabrications according to their own opinions; therefore, let us bring forth the history of this matter into the open. Africanus, <note>Julius Africanus (c. 160–240 AD), an early Christian traveler and historian who wrote a letter to Aristides to reconcile the two genealogies of Jesus.</note> writing to a certain Aristides about the harmony of the Gospels and about the genealogies which are reported differently by Matthew and Luke, refutes the opinions of others who wander far from the truth of God. He himself, however, brought forward the history he had discovered in these very words:

"Among the people of Israel," he says, "the names of generations are numbered sometimes according to nature and sometimes according to the order of the Law. According to nature, successions are held which descend from the truth of seed or blood; but according to the Law, a son is substituted for another man who fathered him, under the name of a brother who died without children." <note>This refers to 'Levirate Marriage' (from the Latin *levir*, meaning 'husband's brother'). If a man died childless, his brother was required to marry the widow to continue the deceased brother's lineage.</note> Since, therefore, the orders of generations of this kind were preserved among them—so that some were from the actual lineage and others were generated by others through substitution, yet were deputed as sons of the former by the benefit of the Law—the succession of both types was commemorated by each of the Evangelists. That is, so that one of them set forth the one who had fathered him [naturally], and the other set forth the one who was seen as if he had fathered him [legally]. And thus it happens that neither Gospel lies, since one follows the order of nature and the other follows the Law.

For Jacob and Heli were made uterine brothers <note>original: *vterini fratres*. Brothers born of the same mother but different fathers.</note> from a different line of fathers. One of them, namely Jacob, taking the wife of his brother Heli (who had died without children) according to the mandate of the Law, fathered Joseph. By nature of the lineage, Joseph was his own son, which is why it is written "Jacob begat Joseph"; but according to the precept of the Law, he becomes the son of Heli, for whom Jacob (because he was his brother) had taken the wife to raise up seed for his brother. And through this, Africanus says, the genealogy is found to be rare and intact: both that which Matthew enumerates, saying "Jacob begat Joseph," and that which Luke designates with careful observation, saying he "was thought to be the son of Joseph, who was of Jacob." <note>The author is reconciling Matthew 1:16 and Luke 3:23.</note> He [Luke] also, by the resonance of that same distinction, was thought to be the son of Heli, who had been the son of Melchi. For the Evangelist, observing with sufficiently competent judgment, designated this legal succession (which consists more in a kind of adoption toward the deceased than in the truth of the lineage), lest he should name someone as having fathered another in such successions. Through this worthy distinction, not descending but ascending all the way to Adam, he reached even unto the Lord. Concerning this opinion, you will see more in the first book of the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius, <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note> chapter six, if you have leisure.

<margin>Eusebius; Augustine.</margin> The blessed Augustine also feels similarly about the genealogy of Joseph in the *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question fifty-six. He says: "It is not doubtful that the father of Joseph was Jacob; for the order holding its path from David through Solomon arrives by a straight course to Jacob, whose son is Joseph. Heli, however, the son of Nathan, holding the order from David through Nathan (the son of the same David) down to the time when the Savior arrived—from which the individual Evangelists followed the orders of generations of the individual brothers from David—fled as if by stealth: so that Matthew might descend from David through Solomon to Joseph, while Luke ascended from Heli (who was in the time of the Savior) through the lineage of Nathan, the son of David." He joined the tribe of both, namely Heli and Joseph, showing both to be of one lineage, so that when he associates Joseph with Heli, he shows they do not differ in generation but are brothers. And by this, the Savior is not only the son of Joseph himself, but also of Heli; for by the same reasoning that the Savior is called the son of Joseph, he is also the son of Heli—the son also of all others who are of the same tribe. Hence it is that the Apostle says: "Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh." For Luke was moved by divine nod to ascend from Heli through the lineage of Nathan to David, and through Terah his father to ascend to Shem the son of Noah, and reaching back before the flood to Seth the son of Adam (who was given in place of Abel), and by the same reasoning he made the Savior the son of Adam as he was called the son of Joseph.

folio xlviii.

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

...and by ascending above Heli or Adam, he might assign that before all flesh, Christ is the Son of God. This is what some believe: that Heli had taken the wife of Jacob, as the law commanded that if anyone died without children, a brother or kinsman should take his wife to raise up seed for his brother. <note>This refers to the "Levirate Law" (Deuteronomy 25:5), where a man was required to marry his deceased brother's widow to continue the family line.</note> And so it happened that Heli fathered Joseph for Jacob, whose wife he had taken; and through this joining of generations, Joseph is not undeservedly said to have Heli as a father. This is what Augustine says. <margin>Augustine</margin> Nor is it improbable, nor does it serve any other purpose than what was said above: that it joins two brothers through generation and shows Christ to be the Son of God before every generation. For the Evangelist, when he recounted this, said: "And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was the son of Heli." <note>original: *Et ipse iesus erat incipiens fere annorum triginta filius sicut putabat Joseph qui fuit Heli.* Refers to Luke 3:23.</note> That is, Jesus was estimated to be the son of Joseph. And not only was he the son of Joseph, but also of Heli. Not that he calls Joseph the son of Heli, but in the same way that Joseph was called the son of Jesus <note>The translator likely means "Jesus was called the son of Joseph"</note>, so was he also the son of Heli. Because of this, Joseph and Heli were sons of brothers—namely, of Solomon and Mathan, the sons of David—so that by ascending through David to Abraham, Noah, Seth, and to Adam himself, he might teach that above Adam, Christ is the Son of God when he says: "Who was the son of Seth, who was the son of Adam, who was the son of God." <note>original: *Qui fuit filius Seth qui fuit filius Ade qui fuit filius dei*</note> He certainly speaks of Christ as the son of Adam in the same way he spoke of him as the son of Joseph. These are the words of Augustine.

Now, Origen says these same persons are in the generation of the Savior when he is said to descend and when he is said to ascend. <margin>Origen</margin> For he who made him descending to the heavens for you did not seek out [perfect] women, but introduces sinful women and those whom Scripture had reproached. However, when he narrates him as baptized, he makes no mention of any woman. In Matthew, therefore, in the generation of the descent, there is Tamar, who lay with her father-in-law by trickery; and Ruth the Moabite, so she might be of the lineage of Israel; and Rahab, of whom I cannot know from where she was taken; and the wife of Uriah, who violated her husband's bed. <note>The author is highlighting that Matthew's genealogy includes women with "sinful" or "irregular" backgrounds to show Christ's mercy.</note> For our Lord and Savior came for this: to take upon himself the sins of men, and he who had done no sin died for us. Therefore, Origen says that in descending into the world, he assumed the persona of sinful and vicious men; <margin>Origen</margin> and he willed to be born from the stock of Solomon, whose sins are written down, and Rehoboam, whose crimes are reported, and of others who did much evil in the sight of God. But when he ascends from the "washing" <note>Referring to the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan.</note> and the second order is described, they are not born through Solomon but through Mathan, who reproached his father concerning the death of Uriah and the birth of Solomon. But in Matthew, the name "generation" is always added, while in Luke it is completely silent. In Matthew it is not written "he was beginning," but in Luke, because he was about to ascend from baptism, the Scripture says: "And he himself was beginning." For when he was baptized, he assumed the mystery of the second generation, so that you also might destroy your former birth and be born in a second regeneration; and then he is said to have "begun." And just as the Jewish people, when they were in Egypt, did not have a beginning of months, but when they returned from Egypt it was said to them: "This month shall be the first month for you among the months of the year," so he who is not yet baptized is not narrated to have begun. Thus says Origen.

<column-break/>

Perhaps someone will say: what is the proof that Mary, the mother of the Lord, is of the tribe and seed of David, since it is not her genealogy, but Joseph’s, that is described by Matthew and Luke? I respond: let us bring forth the speech of a fit witness. For the angel says to Mary, among other things: "And the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end." <note>original: *Et dabit illi dominus deus sedem Dauid patris sui...* Refers to Luke 1:32-33.</note> How could David be called "his father" by a fit witness if Mary were not of the seed of David?

### ¶ Whether the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, as is read in Matthew, Luke, and John, or truly at the third hour, as Mark says. Chapter 7.

The Evangelists spoke with one mouth and one reason. How did it happen that while three lead—namely Matthew, Luke, and John—saying that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, Mark on the other hand says the Savior was crucified at the third hour? Augustine responds that it is not good to wrap true treasures in obscurity. <margin>Augustine</margin> For the three Evangelists had one sense. Mark, however, wished to intimate a matter that had been passed over by them, knowing it to be necessary. For he who followed the examples of the authors could not be deceived; he learned those things he wrote with great devotion and industry, and he did not do so without the Holy Spirit. Therefore, what he wished to show by this must be resolved. It must be considered, then, that the Savior was crucified not by Pilate, but by the Jews. For as far as Roman laws are concerned, Pilate himself continued to pronounce the Savior innocent. For Pilate said to the Jews, "I find no cause in him." And when they said, "Crucify him," he responded, "For what evil has he done?" Finally, persisting and wishing to lead him out of their hands, he suffered their false accusations as they said: "If you let this man go, you are not Caesar’s friend; for everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar." Thus it happened that he delivered him to their judgment; therefore Pilate did not give the sentence, but the Jews did. Finally, they were warned by the chief priests to say, "Let him be crucified." Mark wants it understood that this sentence was given at the third hour, in which they persisted with constant voices; after an interval of about three hours, during which there was a going to and returning from Herod, they crucified the Savior. For everyone who is sentenced to death is already counted as dead from the moment he receives the sentence. Mark, therefore, manifested that the Savior was not "crucified" by the judge's sentence [alone]. For it is difficult to prove a man innocent who is punished by a judge's sentence. Therefore, he allowed himself to disagree in the word so that he might teach that what was fulfilled at the sixth hour began at the third hour—not as we read of the physical act, but by the persisting malevolence of the Jews.

folio xlix.

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

<margin>Mark 1:d, 1 Corinthians 2:b</margin>
If perhaps someone should ask how <term>Mark</term> <note>Mark the Evangelist, traditionally symbolized by the lion.</note> the Evangelist says that the demons knew and confessed Jesus, while on the other hand the Apostle [Paul] denies that the "princes and powers of this world" knew the divinity of the Lord Jesus. For <term>Mark</term> says among other things: "For they knew him to be the one." Yet the Apostle says: "Whom none of the princes of this world knew; for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty." If the demons knew, how were the "princes" ignorant?

<margin>Augustine in Book 1 of *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, question 65; Acts 3:c</margin>
To some (says <term>Augustine</term>), it seems that the "princes of this world" signifies the elders of the Jews, according to what the Apostle <term>Peter</term> says: "For you know, brothers, that you did this evil through ignorance, just as your princes did." Therefore, they were princes of the Jews, but they were not truly the "princes of this world." <note>The author is distinguishing between earthly Jewish leaders and the spiritual "rulers of darkness."</note> Thus he says "not of this world," since the Jews said they had no king but Caesar, under whose power they had been reduced. But those other ones are the true "princes" whom the Apostle signifies in another place,

<margin>Ephesians 6:b</margin>
saying: "Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the princes and powers of this world, against the rulers of this darkness." Rightly, then, one asks: if these spiritual powers did not know Jesus, how could the demons recognize him? It is one thing to say that the demons recognized Christ, and another to deny that the princes of this world knew him. For the demons knew him to be the one promised through the Law. They saw in him all the signs that the prophets said would come to pass—such as that the redeemer of Israel would come from the seed of David and be born of a virgin—but they were ignorant of the *mystery* of his divinity, just as their princes were. Finally, even the crafty devil questioned the Savior, saying: "If you are the Son of God..." etc. For seeing at times divine power and at other times human weakness, he was tormented, doubting what was true. Therefore, the scriptures are in concord according to what has been revealed; for it is impossible for men of the same Spirit to disagree.

### Whether Anyone Has Seen God. Chapter 9.

<margin>Genesis 32:b, Isaiah 6, John 1:b</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, at a desk.</image-desc> Why is it that Jacob was called "the man who sees God," and Moses "saw God face to face," and Isaiah said, "I have seen the God of Hosts with my own eyes"? Yet on the other hand, John the Evangelist says: "No one has ever seen God." This seems contrary (says <term>Augustine</term>), but as far as faith is concerned,

<margin>Augustine</margin>
no one has ever seen God, neither the Father nor the Son. For when he is said to have been "seen," it refers to understanding. He was seen as if in an image, just as when we do not know the emperors ourselves but see them in a portrait, not in truth. So too was God seen so that he might be understood to exist by the one to whom he appeared through reason, not through his actual substance; for in his own nature, God cannot be seen. And to more truly open the secrets of the proposed question, let us strive to explain the sense of the Evangelist. John

<column-break/>

indeed wished to bring forth something hidden that he knew pertained to the doctrine of salvation; therefore he said: "No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father; he has revealed him." Wherefore <term>Augustine</term> says in his treatise: "I am who I am," says God. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are by their own nature invisible. He appeared when he willed—not as he is, but as he willed—to whom all things are subject. He appeared in fire, but he is not fire; he appeared in sound, but he is not sound. These things are not God, but they point to God. Let us consider the Evangelist’s meaning: to show that it is true that no one has ever seen God, he teaches that the Son has revealed this, who certainly cannot be deceived because he is in the bosom of the Father. And what is the "bosom of the Father" but his affection? It is the love of the true Father for the Son through the unity of nature. Therefore, no one has seen God except the only Son. John the Apostle heard the Son of God saying among other things: "Not that anyone has seen the Father, except him who is from God; he has seen the Father." Thus, to further the condemnation of the Jews who refused to hear or believe in Christ the Son of God, the Evangelist shows that this Christ is the one who appeared to the patriarchs as God; but that he who is the Father is never seen except by the Son. For when he denies that God the Father was seen, but confesses that God appeared to the fathers, he wants to manifest the Son of God; because he, the Son, was always seen by the fathers as God. Whence, among other things, he says to the Jews concerning the Father: "Neither have you ever heard his voice, nor seen his shape." Behold, there is no contradiction in God being both seen and unseen. God (says <term>Ambrose</term>), even if he was seen by Abraham, was seen in the form of a human body so that he might demonstrate that in the latter times he was to come as a man. And if we approve that the Son of God was seen by the fathers, it was not so that the whole of what God is was seen, but rather the arrangements of future things that were to be fulfilled in their own times were perceived in him through an image. For who would have seen the Son of God if he had not deigned to take on humanity? You see, therefore, through all the characteristics of the divine scriptures, that God was shown to the fathers in honor, yet God himself was not revealed as he properly is. Finally, while Moses prayed that he might see the face of God purely, God immediately said to him: "You cannot see my face; for man shall not see my face and live." By this very denial of sight, love is assigned—which is as great as must be believed of that which is judged invisible. Therefore, although Moses (who described the position of the heavens, the orders of the world, the changes of the elements, and finally the ornaments of the whole globe) was one to whom the Lord himself bore witness, saying: "There shall be no one among the prophets like my servant Moses, to whom I have spoken face to face, mouth to mouth," nevertheless, God could not be seen purely. This was right, for although he was the most worthy of all prophets, it was not to the extent that he had the power to gaze upon God, because he was only a man. For God was not so revealed to human sight that the total deity appeared in him; but rather, like a mirror, when he wishes to include faces within his light as if in a full image of a man, so does his majesty.

<margin>Saint Ambrose in the book *On the Faith Against the Arians*, chapter 8.</margin>

<margin>Exodus 33:d</margin>

<margin>Numbers 12:b</margin>

folio l.

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.

g ii

<margin>The three heavens according to the blessed Paul.</margin>
Ambrose says that by the preceding brightness, that which was seen was an image of truth, which did not demonstrate God himself as He is. On the other hand, others think those "three heavens" (to the third of which <term>Paul</term> <note>The Apostle Paul, who describes being "caught up to the third heaven" in 2 Corinthians 12:2.</note> writes he was caught up) should be understood according to a triple grade of knowing divine things. Truly, the human soul knows divine things first by the contemplation of the nature of physical things; even the philosophers, though lacking our faith, arrived at this path. And this is the **first heaven**. Second, through faith and the belief in those things which are handed down in Scripture to be believed; this is how Christians in this life acknowledge God. And this is the **second heaven**. Third, the soul knows divine things by the direct intuition of the things themselves through the "light of glory," just as the blessed in that heavenly fatherland acknowledge God. And this is the **third heaven**. 

To this last one, it is said, Paul was caught up: for he was carried forth to that third kind of knowing God by divine indulgence and gift. Saint <term>Augustine</term> <note>A foundational Christian theologian (354–430 AD) whose works shaped Western philosophy.</note> seems to be of this opinion, for he says explicitly in Book 12 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 27 and 28, that 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Moses and Paul saw the divine essence just as the blessed in the fatherland see it. Whence it is said that they saw "not through a glass darkly" <note>original: *non per speculum in enigmate*</note> but "face to face." What was said of Moses—"mouth to mouth"—means that those with a pure heart shall see God through His "species," which is what God is and whatever He is. And a little later: Why should we not believe that for such a great Apostle and teacher of the nations, caught up to this vision, God willed to demonstrate the life in which he would live forever after this life? 

However, it must be understood that when speaking of this perfect vision in the same book, chapters 26 and 27, he says: "In the fatherland, the brightness of the Lord will be seen, not through a bodily vision as on Mount Sinai, nor through a spiritual vision such as <term>Isaiah</term> and 

<margin>Isaiah, John.</margin>
<term>John</term> saw in the <term>Apocalypse</term> <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>; but through His essence and not through riddles, as much as the human mind can grasp it according to the grace of God taking it up." I think it should be understood (he says) that what is written of Moses—that he might see God more fully—did not mean as he had seen Him on the mountain or in the tabernacle, but in that substance which is God, with no physical creature assumed to be presented to the senses or to the likeness of bodies, but through His own essence, as much as a rational and intellectual creature can grasp. 

But perhaps someone might ask: 

<margin>A Question</margin>
Were Moses and Paul "blessed" <note>In the sense of attaining the 'Beatific Vision' usually reserved for the afterlife.</note> at that moment in which they saw the divine essence? It must be answered that they were; for according to Augustine in Book 7 of *The City of God*, essential happiness consists in the perfect vision of the divine essence, taking "happiness" as an **act**, but not as a **state**, because they did not remain there. 

Again, another might ask: 

<margin>Another question.</margin>
When such a vision departed, did they remember what they had seen? I answer that every perfect vision naturally leaves some disposition in the memory through which we remember past sights. Therefore, since that experience was most perfect, there is no reason why it would not leave an intellectual disposition through which one could remember what was seen. That most perfect disposition recalled the sights to the memory most distinctly, and these things are represented in the manner of an essence. 

Hence he says: Unless Moses had earned the right to see the occupied and desired clarity of God, God would not have said to his siblings Aaron and Miriam in the Book of Numbers: "Hear my words. If there is a prophet among you, I the Lord will be known to him in a vision and I will speak to him in a dream; but not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I speak to him, in appearance and not through riddles; and he saw the brightness of the Lord." This is not to be understood according to a physical substance presented to the senses of the flesh. For indeed, He spoke to Moses "face to face" <note>original: *facie ad faciem*</note>. Yet Moses said to Him: "Show me yourself." And even to those whom He was rebuking—and to whom He preferred Moses's merit—He spoke through a physical creature presented to the senses of the flesh. Therefore, in that appearance which is God, He speaks far more ineffably, secretly, and more presently, with an ineffable speech where no one seeing Him shall live this life which is lived mortally in these senses of the body. 

But unless a person somehow "dies" to this life—either by departing the body entirely or by being so turned away and alienated from the carnal senses that he rightfully "knows not," as the Apostle says, whether he be 

<margin>The Apostle</margin>
in the body or out of the body when he is caught up and carried into those visions. Wherefore, if the Apostle called this third kind of vision (which is above not only all physical sensing but also all spiritual vision where likenesses of bodies are seen) the "third heaven," in this is seen the brightness of God. By seeing this, hearts are purified; whence it is said, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." They see not through any physically or spiritually figured sign, nor "through a glass darkly," but "face to face"—which was said of Moses as "mouth to mouth"—namely, through the essence of what God is. The mind, as much as it can, captures that which He is, alienated and snatched away from every body and every earthly worldly stain and likeness of a body. We wander from this vision while weighed down by a mortal and corruptible burden, as long as we walk by faith and not by sight, even when we live justly here. 

Why then should we not believe that for such a great Apostle and teacher of the nations, caught up to this most excellent vision, God willed to show the life in which one must live forever after this life? I, however (he says), have not been able to know or teach any kinds of visions or sights beyond these three: by body, by spirit, or by mind. But how many and why there are differences in each kind—so that in each one something is carried above another by degrees—I confess I do not know. 

Finally, for the Apostle snatched from the senses of the flesh into the third heaven and paradise, one thing was certainly lacking for the full and perfect knowledge of things which belongs to the angels: he did not know whether he was in the body or out of the body. This will certainly not be lacking when, having received our bodies in the resurrection of the dead, "this corruptible shall put on incorruption and this mortal shall put on immortality." For all things will be evident without any falsehood and without any ignorance, distributed in their orders: physical, spiritual, and intellectual, in a whole nature and perfect happiness. It is therefore clearly evident that Augustine himself posits that Paul’s knowledge was **intuitive and beatific**, because he does not consider it to differ from that of the angels or saints, except by the fact that he did not know if he was in the body or...

# On the Wonders of Holy Scripture.

Hence, Paul is said to have been "snatched up to the third heaven." For some think those "three heavens" should be interpreted according to a triple vision: namely, of the senses, of the imagination, and of the intellect. Thus, they understand the **first heaven** as a judgment of things in a certain sensible way, by which we perceive them so that we either feel them or seem to feel them, as Moses did at the burning bush. The **second heaven** (which belongs to the imagination) we understand as a kingly judgment. When we behold the things themselves as if in an image, presented and placed before us—just as usually happens either in an "excess of mind" (which the Greeks call **ecstasy**) or in sleep, when not the bodies themselves but the images of things are seen, as Pharaoh of the Egyptians, while sleeping, saw the cows and the ears of grain in a dream. In all these things that have been proposed, there is not just one cause. For briefly, the "forms" of the individual causes are signified: because the Spirit is indeed one, but He has many gifts. Therefore, when one reads "Holy Spirit," his office <note>The specific role or function being performed.</note> in which He is signified ought also to be understood. For there is no doubt that the Spirit was not given to believers except as the Evangelist testifies: after the Lord, having conquered death, rose again and was glorified. However, so that the Apostles could perform miracles while the Lord was present, power was

given just as it was previously given to the Prophets. Therefore, **three forms of the offices of the Holy Spirit** in the Apostles are shown. The **first** is that which pertains to ecclesiastical right in regenerating or other duties. The **second** is that which was given at Pentecost, which is general. For the Holy Spirit fell not only upon the Apostles, but truly upon all believers. The **third form** is that which was granted to the Apostles alone for performing signs and miracles until the seeds of faith were made to grow. For the "seeds of faith" were the miracles performed by the Apostles. For they themselves were appointed as the overseers of this truth, who by signs and wonders might testify that our faith is not irrational.

### On the resurrection, and that there will be a resurrection of all people, and concerning those who will be found alive. Chapter 11.

<margin>Saint Ambrose, book on the faith of the resurrection, chapter 10.</margin> <image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, holding a book or object, set against a background of foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc> From three things <note>The OCR reads 'Pribus', a likely error for 'Tribus' (Three), matching the decorative initial 'P'</note> most evidently (says Ambrose) is the faith of the resurrection gathered: by which all things are understood through the reason of the universe; by example; and by the testimony of what has occurred, because many have already risen. The reason is evident: because since every experience of our life exists in the partnership of body and soul, and since the resurrection must hold either a reward for good acts or a punishment for the wicked, it is necessary that the body—whose actions are weighed—should rise again. For how shall the soul be called to judgment without the body, when an account must be given of its shared life with the body? There will be a resurrection for everyone, but it is believed with difficulty because it is not our own merit but God’s gift. Therefore, the first evidence for faith in the resurrection is the common practice of the world and the state of all things: the series of generations, the cycles of successions, the setting and rising of the stars, the passing of day and night, and their daily succession as if they were being brought back to life. Also, the logic of this life-giving balance could not persist unless its own fluids (from which all earthly things are generated) were restored by divine arrangement through the nightly dew, just as much as the heat of the sun might dry them out during the day—this he says. And as the divine Augustine says: there will be a resurrection of all people, and if it is of all, then all must die, so that the death brought by Adam may rule over all his children. And let that privilege remain in the Lord which is specifically said of him: <note>original: "Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem"</note> *You will not allow your holy one to see corruption.* For his flesh did not see corruption; we have received this reasoning through the tradition of the great crowd of the Fathers. But because there are (says the same Augustine) other equally Catholic and learned men who believe that those found alive at the coming of the Lord will be changed into incorruption and immortality while the soul remains in the body, and that this is accounted to them as a resurrection from the dead—that they set aside mortality by transformation, not by death. Whoever one might agree with (he says), provided they are not a heretic—unless through 

<column-break/>

contention they become a heretic. For it is sufficient to read in the Church that we believe the resurrection of the flesh will come from death. Thus says Augustine; and a little later he says: When we say in the <term>Creed</term><note>The "symbolo," referring to the Apostles' Creed or Nicene Creed</note> that the living and the dead are to be judged at the coming of the Lord, it does not only signify the just and the sinners, as Diodorus thinks, but we believe "the living" are those who are to be found in the flesh. These are believed to be either yet to die or to be transformed; or, as others wish, they are to be immediately raised or reformed, as if they were judged as having previously died. Therefore, we shall either pay the penalties for our sins or receive the grace for our good deeds. They shall rise again (says Ambrose) in the same nature, now receiving the wages of the first. Then, we who are alive (he says) shall be caught up together with them in the <margin>Ambrose, book on the faith of the resurrection, chapter 9.</margin> clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord—those first, and the living second. Those are with Jesus; the living are through Jesus. To those, life is sweeter after rest; to the living, though it is a welcome shortcut, the remedy is nonetheless unknown. There is, therefore, nothing we should fear in death, and nothing over which we should grieve; if either the life that was received is paid back to nature when she asks for it, or if it is spent in the service of one who asks, in which there is the practice of religion or the exercise of virtue. For no one has ever successfully wished for themselves to remain as they are. Such a promise was thought to have been made to John <note>The Apostle John, whom some believed would not die until Christ's return</note>, but it was not believed; we hold the words, but we derive the meaning. In that very book, he denies that he was promised he would not die, lest anyone be misled by a vain hope based on his example. But if it is an insolent hope to want such a thing, how much more insolent is it to grieve beyond measure when that which is unavoidable occurs? What if Christ (as some wish) does not want some to be dissolved in the body, such as those who might be found alive at his coming? And if it pleased him to do the same for Enoch and Elijah, and if anyone else is reserved for his coming? Will they not then die who are found alive? Paul expresses the prophecy to us: that they are caught up to meet Christ in the air. Nor (as our <term>Stapulensis</term><note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536), a French humanist and theologian who used the Latin name Jacobus Faber Stapulensis.</note> writes) does this contradict the article of faith left to us <margin>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples in the commentary on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter 4. For since all humans come to the predefined limit of death, it is appointed for them once to die. Is it any wonder if, at that time, with those who have not reached that limit (which by God’s decree cannot be passed over), it is dispensed by Christ's presence that they do not die? Truly (says <term>Origen</term><note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note>), a twofold resurrection is understood: one of the mind, purpose, and faith, when we rise with Christ from earthly things to think on heavenly things and seek things to come. The other is the general resurrection of the flesh which will be for all. Therefore, the resurrection of faith according to the mind is seen fulfilled in those who savor the things that are above, where Christ is at the right hand of God. But that general resurrection of the flesh, which pertains to all, is still to come; because the former is fulfilled in the first coming of the Lord, and the latter in the second.
