### Whether God is invisible and what difference there is between seeing and knowing: and how the blessed see God. Chapter 12.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a figure, likely a scholar or saint, seated at a desk or lectern, surrounded by architectural elements.</image-desc>
Nothing is to be believed to be invisible and incorporeal by nature except God alone: that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is called incorporeal and invisible because He is infinite, uncircumscribed, simple, and in every way sufficient unto Himself and within Himself. And although He is everywhere, He is known to be invisible and incorporeal within Himself. But we must ask how God is said to be invisible, and yet Abraham, Moses, Isaiah, Jacob, and finally Paul sometimes saw Him. For Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a high and elevated throne under <note>the Latin "abrozemebre" appears to be a corrupted term, likely referring to a prophetic vision or a specific Hebrew name for a vision</note> what in our language is interpreted as "vision." Abraham also offered a feast to the Lord and His angels, and the vision delighted him; for the clarity of Abraham’s heart was pure so that he could see God. Moses, moreover, saw God, of whom the Lord says: "I speak to him mouth to mouth, in a visible form and not in riddles," <note>original: "Os ad os loquar ad eum in specie: et non in enigmate" - see Numbers 12:8</note> and he saw the glory of the Lord. And Paul was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which a man is not permitted to speak; and Jacob was called "the man who sees God." <note>A traditional medieval etymology for the name 'Israel'</note> Since God was seen in this manner, I do not see how He can be called invisible. Therefore, lift up your ears, brothers; lift up your minds to the Lord. I tell your charity that perhaps in all the Holy Scriptures, no greater question and perhaps none more difficult can be found. Therefore, let us ask the Lord for the light of exposition. Let us see what the "vision of God" means to those who understand it—even if our understanding is far inferior and unworthy due to the weakness of human intelligence. But indeed, it would be laborious and not at all appropriate for this place to review all the opinions of authors at this present time regarding that vision of Paul when he was caught up into paradise. For if the Apostle, who suffered such an ecstasy in God, did not explain the mystery of that vision, who would be sufficient to express it correctly unless he were taught by the revelation of the Holy Spirit? Let us see, however, what Origen thinks about the vision of God and whether God can be seen. For in the first book of *On First Principles* <note>original: "periarchon" - the Greek title of Origen's work</note>, in the first chapter, he says: "See if the Apostle

<column-break/>

<margin>Origen</margin>
does not say this very same thing when he speaks of Christ, saying: 'Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.' <note>Colossians 1:15</note> For he does not say (as some think) that the nature of God is invisible to some and visible to others. The Apostle did not say 'the image of the invisible God to men' or 'invisible to sinners,' but he pronounces quite consistently about the very nature of God, saying: 'The image of the invisible God.' Even John in his Gospel says: 'No one has ever seen God,' <note>John 1:18</note> clearly declaring to all who can understand that there is no nature to which God is visible. It is not as if He is visible by nature and merely escapes the sight of a more fragile creature; rather, it is because it is naturally impossible for Him to be seen. If you ask me," he says, "what I think even of the Only-Begotten Himself—whether I would say the nature of God, which is naturally invisible, is visible even to Him—lest it immediately seem impious or absurd to you, we will give the reason following. It is one thing," he says, "to see, and another to obtain knowledge." <note>original: "Aliud est videre: aliud est cognoscere"</note> Seeing and being seen belong to bodies; knowing and being known belong to an intellectual nature. Whatever is a property of bodies, therefore, must not be thought of regarding the Father or the Son. But that which pertains to the nature of the Deity is established between the Father and the Son. Finally, even He Himself in the Gospel did not say 'No one has seen the Father except the Son,' nor 'the Son except the Father,' but He said: 'No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son.' From this, it is clearly judged that whatever is called 'to see' and 'to be seen' among corporeal natures, is called 'to know' and 'to be known' between the Father and the Son through the power of knowledge, not through the fragility of visibility. Because, therefore, in an incorporeal and invisible nature, one does not properly speak of seeing or being seen, for that reason, neither the Father is said to be seen by the Son in the Gospel, nor the Son by the Father, but they are said to be known. And if someone should propose," he says, "the verse: 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,' our assertion will be even more strengthened by this. For what else is it to see God with the heart, except to understand Him with the mind and to know Him? For the names of the sensory members are frequently referred to the soul, so that it is said to 'see with the eyes of the heart'—that is, to behold something intellectual with the power of intelligence. Thus it is said to 'hear with ears' when it directs the sense of deeper intelligence. So too we speak to those who desire to use it, when one 'tastes and eats the bread of life' that descended from heaven. Similarly, it is said of the other offices of the members, which, being transferred from corporeal names, are adapted to the virtues of the soul—just as Solomon says, 'you shall find a divine sense.' <note>Proverbs 2:5</note> For he knew there were two kinds of senses: one mortal, corruptible, and human; the other kind immortal and intellectual, which he now called 'divine.' By this divine sense, therefore—not of the eyes, but of a pure heart, which is the mind—God can be seen by those who are worthy. For 'heart' stands for 'mind,' that is, for the inner...

...nourished by the power of the **intellect**; you will find this named in all the scriptures, both New and Old, in great abundance. These are the words of **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was one of the most influential early Christian theologians, though some of his views on the soul and the nature of God were later debated.</note>. And again, in the fourth chapter of the second book of his *On First Principles* <note>original: "periarchon," from the Greek "Peri Archon"</note>, he says that Moses must be thought to have seen God not by beholding Him with carnal eyes, but by understanding Him with the sight of the heart and the perception of the mind. This is partially manifest from the fact that He said: "You shall not see my face" (He who gave the responses to Moses), "but my back parts" <note>original: "faciem meam non videbis... sed posteriora mea" - a reference to Exodus 33:23</note>. 

These things are surely to be understood as a mystery <note>original: "sacramento"</note>, in the way it is fitting to understand divine words, by rejecting and scorning those "old wives' fables" which the unskillful imagine regarding God’s front and back parts. For we have said that it is one thing to see and be seen, and another to know and be known, or to recognize and be recognized. Therefore, "seeing" and "being seen" is a matter of bodies, which certainly cannot be properly applied to the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit in their relationship to one another. For the nature of the Trinity exceeds the manner of vision for those who are in the body. While God grants the quality of mutual vision to all other creatures, nothing else is fitting for an incorporeal and primarily intellectual nature except to know and be known, just as the Savior himself announces, saying: "For no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him." It is manifest, therefore (says Origen), that He did not say: "No one has *seen* the Father except the Son." 

Again, the same Origen, in his second homily on John, says: "And we saw his glory, as of the only-begotten from the Father" <note>John 1:14</note>. Where did you see, O blessed theologian, the glory of the incarnate Word, the glory of the Son of God made man? How did you see it? With what kind of eyes did you look? With bodily eyes (as I believe) on the mountain at the time of the Transfiguration. For then you were present as the third witness of the divine glorification. You were present (as I estimate) in Jerusalem and heard the voice of the Father glorifying His Son and saying: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again." 

And again, in the seventh homily on **Numbers**, he says: "Before Moses took the **Ethiopian woman**, it is not written that God spoke to him in appearance and not in riddles <note>original: "enigmate"</note>. But when he took the Ethiopian woman, then God said of him: 'I speak to him mouth to mouth, in appearance and not in riddles.'" For now, when Moses comes to us and is joined to this Ethiopian woman of ours <note>Origen frequently interpreted Moses' Ethiopian wife as a symbol of the Church gathered from the Gentiles</note>, the law of God is no longer recognized in figures and riddles as before, but in the very appearance of truth. And those things which were previously designated in a riddle are now fulfilled in appearance and truth. Previously, baptism was in a riddle—in the cloud and in the sea; but now, regeneration is in appearance—in water and the Holy Spirit. Then, the manna was food in a riddle; but now, the flesh of the Word of God is true food in appearance, just as He himself says: "For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed." Thus, therefore, now that Moses is placed among us and joined to this Ethiopian woman—either he speaks to us, or God to him—He does not speak in a riddle, but in appearance. To these things is added: "and the glory of the Lord," he says, 

<column-break/>

"he saw." When did Moses see the glory of the Lord? I say (says Origen) it was when the Lord was transformed on the mountain, and Moses was present there with **Elijah**, and they spoke with Him. And therefore, He rightly adds in the following words: "And why were you not afraid to detract from my servant Moses?" This (he says) is clearly directed at those who seem to accept the Gospels but disparage Moses; they are deservedly accused because, while they learn through the Gospel that Moses saw the glory of the Lord together with Elijah, they strive to disparage the Law and the Prophets. And so, let us not detract from Moses, nor disparage the Law, but let us be not only hearers of the Law but also doers, so that we may deserve to be glorified together with Moses himself. These are the words of Origen.

Again, in his first homily on **Isaiah**, he says: "On account of the death of King **Uzziah** <note>original: "Osie"</note>, after whose death the prophet says he saw visions. But what vision? 'I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and elevated throne,' etc. Not everyone who sees God sees Him sitting upon a high and elevated throne. I know another prophet saw the Lord, and saw Him sitting upon a throne, but not a high or elevated one." Differing from the Scripture, **Daniel** says: "Thrones were placed," and that throne was not high; and "I will come to sit for judgment of the people in the **Valley of Jehoshaphat**." Therefore, here He sat in a valley, and in a valley He is to judge the one whom He is to condemn. But it is another thing to see Him sitting upon a high and elevated throne. And in **Micah**: "Go forth, and God descends." And to see **Sodom**, He descends. "Descending," He says, "I will see if they have completed their deeds according to the cry that has come to me." Therefore, God is seen sometimes above and sometimes below, according to the dignity of the business at hand. "I saw the Lord" (Isaiah says) "sitting upon a high and elevated throne." If I see God reigning in these things that are here, I do not see Him upon a high and elevated throne. If I see Him reigning over the heavenly powers, I see Him sitting upon a high and elevated throne—upwards, where His throne is elevated and the house is full of His glory. I do not think that this house which is on earth is full of His glory; "the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof," but you will not find the fullness of God's glory in the present age. But if anyone builds a temple to God, the glory of God will be seen. These are the words of Origen.

->### On the Wonders of Holy Scripture. Book Two.<-

He alone is invisible because He is not fully intelligible to any creature. Indeed, the souls of the blessed and the angels see Him always in their own way, not ours; not through intervals of space as we perceive bodily things, but they behold Him both within themselves and outside themselves in every creature, and beyond every creature. Yet, even they do not, by any gaze of the intellect, exceed the vastness of His clarity. Because He is not seen or understood as fully by them as He is by Himself, He is said to be "alone invisible." And a little later, in chapter 43, it is said: 

Three visions—namely the **sensual** <note>original: "sensualis" - referring here to the five physical senses, not in a modern moral sense</note>, the **spiritual**, and the **intellectual**—are recognized by the wise. A **sensory** vision is when we perceive colors and forms of things outwardly, but understand that something is hidden within, just as we understand the meaning within written letters. The second vision is **spiritual**: by this, we see not the things themselves, but images similar to things in a spiritual way, as we are accustomed to in dreams, and as we know John saw many things in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> and the prophets did as well. The third vision is **intellectual**: when we behold neither external things nor the images of things within, but rather the substances themselves as they truly are, with colors stripped away, perceived by the intellect; and we discern the differing quality of each thing by reason. 

This third vision is called the "third heaven," because the truth of things is hidden in it, as if from the foolish. And if the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> was "caught up in the body," then he was led to the bodily heaven, namely to the firmament. But if he was "outside the body"—which seems more likely—then he is believed to have been caught up to the **intellectual heaven**. In this state, he is known to have seen the essence of the Godhead as it is, and the angelic substances as they are; not through the senses (which cannot happen except through the body), nor spiritually (which happens only through images like things), but truly, which happens only through the intellect itself. 

Angels or the righteous are called "heaven" by a certain similarity, because in the secret place of God they are hidden from human <margin>Augustine</margin> use; and conversely, demons or the wicked are called "darkness" because they are hidden from us in their torments. 

**Augustine** says again, in his book *On the Soul and Spirit*, chapter 30: "The soul, stripped of the flesh, lives, sees, and hears, and holds all its senses and powers vividly, being pure, subtle, swift, and perpetual. And just as God is everywhere in Himself, so the soul is everywhere, in a way, in itself. Because of this, the soul will be in that place after the body where it was active while in the body; God is now where He was before the world was made, where He would also be if the world ceased to exist." The soul is incorporeal, yet it can have a likeness of the body—not a physical one, but one similar to a body—and of all its limbs when it departs from the body. Thus, it is carried toward spiritual things according to its merits, or to places of punishment similar to bodies, such as have often been shown to those who were caught up from the senses of the body and lay like the dead; while they themselves carried within them a certain likeness of their own body, through which they could be carried to those places and experience such things with similar senses. For souls that are accustomed to bodies and are affected by images of visible things through a delight in the physical, suffer torments in those same images when they depart from their bodies; for they can be held there by physical

<column-break/>

suffering because they were not purified from the corruption of physical affections, which they drew from the thick love of the flesh. 

Some souls, however, are punished in the very places where they committed their faults; others are held in hidden receptacles until the final resurrection, according as each is worthy of rest or misery. But our true delights will be when we come to Him and "we shall see Him as He is" and we shall be like Him. Then there will be manifest vision, full knowledge, true love, firm union, inseparable society, perfect likeness, and a <margin>Augustine, *On the Creed, to the Catechumens*, Book 3, Chapter 3.</margin> blessed life forever, and beyond into perpetual eternities. 

These are the words of **Augustine**. And in the third book of *On the Creed, to the Catechumens*, he says: "Listen to the Apostle Paul describing what kind of God our sacred scriptures preach: 'To the King of ages, immortal, invisible, incorruptible, the only God, be honor and glory' <note>1 Timothy 1:17</note>. Our God is not seen with the eyes of the flesh, but is seen with the eyes of the heart; He is not seen for a time, but is seen for eternity." 

But the pagan says: "Show me whom you worship." I answer: "Indeed, I have one to show you even now, but you do not have the eyes to see Him." For our Savior says: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" <note>Matthew 5:8</note>. Wherefore, elsewhere **Augustine** sang: <margin>Augustine, in the book *On the Conflict of Vices*, chapter 26.</margin> "Let the love of the present world depart, in which no one is born who does not die; and let the love of the future world succeed, in which all are so brought to life that they do not die thereafter. There, no adversity disturbs, no necessity constricts, no trouble disquiets; but perennial joy reigns. If you ask what is there, where such and so great a beatitude persists: it cannot be said otherwise than that whatever good exists is there, and whatever evil exists is not there at all." 

"What is that good?" you ask. Why do you ask me? It has been defined by the prophet and the apostle: "What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him" <note>1 Corinthians 2:9</note>. 

For this happiness, **David**, though surrounded by many riches of the world, sighed when he said: "What is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from You upon the earth?" <note>Psalm 73:25</note>. Abounding in sweet royal feasts, he said: "I shall be satisfied when Your glory shall be manifested" <note>Psalm 17:15</note>; and again: "My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" <note>Psalm 42:2</note>; and again: "Woe is me, that my sojourn is prolonged" <note>Psalm 120:5</note>. Hence also **Paul** says: "I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for it is much better" <note>Philippians 1:23</note>. 

And in the book of *Soliloquies of the Soul to God*, he says: <margin>Augustine, in the book *Soliloquies of the Soul*, chapter 36.</margin> "For You are the light, in whose light we shall see light: namely, You in Yourself, in the splendor of Your countenance, when we shall see You face to face. What is it to see face to face, except what the Apostle says: 'To know even as I am known' <note>1 Corinthians 13:12</note>? To know Your truth and Your glory; this is to know Your face. To know the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, the mercy of the Holy Spirit: the one and indivisible essence of the supreme Trinity itself. For to see the face of the living God: this is the highest good, the joy of angels and the reward of all the saints in eternal life, the glory of spirits, and perpetual joy..."

...of heart, <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page: "Blessed are the pure in heart."</note> an everlasting crown of glory, the prize of happiness, a rich rest, the beauty of peace, the innermost eternal joy, the paradise of God, the heavenly Jerusalem, the blessed life, the fullness of beatitude <term>beatitudo: the state of supreme, spiritual happiness</term>, the joy of eternity, and the peace of God which surpasses all understanding. This is full beatitude: the total glorification of man to see the face of his God—to see Him who made the heavens, to see Him who made him, who saved him, and who glorified him. He shall see Him by knowing Him, love Him by delighting in Him, and praise Him by possessing Him. Therefore, Your vision is our entire reward, our whole prize, and the total joy that we await. This is eternal life: that we may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent. Furthermore, Augustine, in his 105th tractate on the Gospel of John, says: "If the knowledge of God is eternal life, we strive to live all the more as we progress further in this knowledge. However, we shall not die in eternal life. Then, therefore, the knowledge of God will be perfect when there is no death." Then shall be the highest "clarification" of God, because it is the highest glory. Among the ancients, however, "glory"—by which men are called "glorious"—was defined thus: "Glory is frequent fame regarding someone, accompanied by praise." But if a man praises when he believes in fame, how will God praise, He who Himself sees? Because of this it is written: "Blessed are they who dwell in Your house; they will praise You forever and ever." There shall be the praising of God without end where there will be full knowledge of God; because there is full knowledge, there is the highest clarification or glorification. Again, in his 7th tractate on the Epistle of John, he sang thus: "No one has ever seen God." He is an invisible thing; He is to be believed in not with the eye but with the heart. But just as if we wished to see this physical sun, we would purge the eye of the body so that the light could be seen; so, wishing to see God, let us purge the eye by which God can be seen. And where is this eye? Hear the Gospel: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." But let no one, through the lust of the eyes, imagine God for himself. For such a person makes for himself either a huge form or some inestimable magnitude; he imagines Him descending through places like this light which he sees; he expands Him through the fields as much as he can with these eyes, or he makes for himself someone like an old man of venerable form. Think of none of these things! There is something for you to think of if you wish to see God: "God is love" <note>original: "Deus dilectio est"</note>. What kind of face does love have? What kind of form? What kind of stature? What kind of feet? What kind of hands? No one can say. Yet it has feet, for they lead to the Church; it has hands, for it stretches them out to the poor; it has eyes, for by them it understands the one in need. "Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor." It has ears, of which the Lord says: "He who has ears for hearing, let him hear." These are not members distinct by location, but the intellect sees the whole at once. You who have clarity, you shall dwell in it; stay, and it shall stay in you. But whether God is seen with physical eyes in the fatherland <note>referring to Heaven</note>, the same Augustine shows in the 22nd book, chapter 24 of *The City of God*, saying: "Although nothing prevents the 'eye of the heart' from being understood—about which eyes the Apostle says: 'To have the eyes of your heart enlightened'—yet no Christian doubts that God is seen by these, who faithfully accepts what that Teacher God says: 'Blessed are the pure...

<margin>In Augustine's exposition on the Gospel of John. The definition of Glory.</margin>
<margin>Augustine in the 7th tractate on the Epistle of John.</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>

<column-break/>

...in heart, for they shall see God.'" But it is also written: "And all flesh shall see the salvation of God." This can be understood without any knot of difficulty, as if it were said: "And every man shall see the Christ of God," who was certainly seen in a body and will be seen in a body when He judges the living and the dead. Indeed, that passage from Job can be accepted: "In my flesh I shall see God." There we shall rest and we shall see; we shall see and we shall love; we shall love and we shall praise. Behold what shall be in the end without end. For what else is our end but to reach the kingdom of which there is no end? I seem to have paid my debt for this great work with the Lord's help. To those for whom it is too little or for whom it is too much, may they forgive me; but to those for whom it is sufficient, let them give thanks not to me but to God with me, that God may make us participants in the true life and in the blessed life of all the living—He who leads us all to the highest good. Glory and honor to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the almighty God in the highest, forever and ever. Amen. This one thing I protest: that whatever has been said by me here or elsewhere, I wish it to be asserted only insofar as it is approved by the Roman Church.

# Preface of Symphorien Champier.
aa ij

### Prologue of Symphorien Champier to the Book
### on the Miraculous Propositions of the most blessed Apostle Paul, concerning the praises of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, addressed to the most noble, universally learned, and especially venerable Lord, Lord Gaspard de Tournon, Bishop of Valence and Prelate of the Church of Die. <note>Gaspard de Tournon (died 1520) was a prominent French bishop and patron of learning.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a central floral or pinecone-like motif surrounded by intricate foliate scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc>

**Since many things** have been written by ancient theologians concerning the epistles of the most blessed Apostle Paul, and several most learned men of our own age—especially Pietro Marso of Calabria <note>Petrus Marsus (1442–1512) was an Italian humanist known for his commentaries on the classics and scripture.</note> and our own Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples <note>Jacobus Stapulensis (c. 1455–1536) was a leading French humanist and pioneer of the Protestant Reformation in France; he produced a famous Latin translation and commentary on Paul's epistles.</note>—have committed to writing very powerful arguments to explain and spread Paul's thought, I nevertheless thought it not at all out of place if I were to bring forward certain proofs by which those "miraculous propositions" <term>propositiones: here referring to theological principles or "theorems" derived from Paul's letters</term> of Paul might be proven. Regarding these, Peter, the prince of the apostles, in the third chapter of his second letter, recorded a very difficult statement in the following context: "As also our most dear brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, has written to you, as also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which the unlearned and unstable wrest..." <note>A translation of 2 Peter 3:15-16.</note> and so forth. This effort will not only support the truth itself and our Christian faith in general, but it also serves as the best possible beginning for the work we proposed to build concerning the praises of the apostles Peter and Paul.

For while all the blessed apostles possess equal grace of holiness before the Lord, I know not how it is that Peter and Paul seem to excel above the rest by a certain peculiar virtue for the salvation of the faith. Indeed, we can prove this from the judgment of the Lord himself. For to Peter, like a good steward, He gave the key of the kingdom of heaven; to Paul, as a fit teacher, He enjoined the mastership of ecclesiastical instruction. Specifically, this was so that those whom Paul has instructed for salvation, Peter may receive into rest; and whose hearts Paul has opened through the doctrine of his words, to their souls Peter may open the kingdoms of heaven.

<margin>Ambrose, in his sermon on the birth <note>original: "natali" — referring to the "birthday" into heaven, or feast day</note> of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.</margin>
For as Saint Ambrose reports, Paul also received in a certain way the "key of knowledge" <note>original: "clavis scientiae"</note> from Christ. Indeed, it should be called a key by which the hard hearts of sinners are opened to the faith, the secrets of minds are laid bare, and whatever is held closed within is brought forth into the open by a rational manifestation. It is a key, I say, which opens the way through foresight to the confession of sin, and includes the mystery of salvation’s grace for eternity. Both, therefore, received keys from the Lord: the one of knowledge, the other of power. The latter dispenses the riches of immortality; the former bestows the treasures of knowledge. For there are treasures of knowledge, as it is written: "In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." <note>Colossians 2:3.</note> Therefore, the blessed Peter and Paul stand out among all the apostles and excel by a certain peculiar prerogative. Yet between them (as Ambrose says), it is uncertain whom one would prefer over the other; for I think them equal...

<summary>In this preface, Symphorien Champier introduces his study of St. Paul's complex theological principles, arguing that while Peter holds the keys to heaven's power, Paul holds the "key of knowledge" necessary for salvation.</summary>

equal in merits: because they are equal in suffering: and we see that they lived with a similar devotion of faith, just as we see them having reached the glory of martyrdom together. For we should not think it happened without cause that on one day, in one place, they endured the sentence of a single tyrant; they suffered on one day so that they might reach Christ together. They suffered in one place so that Rome might not lack either one of them under a single persecutor, and so that an equal cruelty might bind them both. Thus, the day was decreed for their merit, the place for their glory, and the persecutor for their virtue. How great the merit of the most blessed Peter and Paul truly is, we can understand from this: that while the Lord illustrated the region of the East with His own passion, He deigned to illuminate the region of the West with the blood of His apostles in His stead, so that it might be no less blessed. And although His passion is sufficient for our salvation, the martyrdom of these men also provides us with an example. But let us see the cause for which they endured these things: namely, that among other wonders, they also cast down that great Simon Magus <note>original: "Simonem." A sorcerer mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles who, according to legend, attempted to fly in Rome to prove his divinity but was brought down by the prayers of Peter and Paul.</note> from the void of the air by their prayers, prostrating him in his fall. Truly, there is no one who does not know how blessed the departure of the apostles from this world was. For this is the first blessing found in them: that both are known to have suffered on one day. Thus, those whom one faith had bound in service, one day crowned in martyrdom. Then, although the passion itself was different for each, how much it was filled with the holiness of grace! For Peter bore the end of the cross just like the Savior, <margin>Ambrose</margin> and he was not separated from the likeness of the Lord's devotion even by death: so that he might imitate in passion the One he imitated in faith. Regarding Paul’s neck (as the divine Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church.</note> relates), when the persecutor struck him with the sword, it is said that a wave of milk flowed out rather than blood, and in a marvelous way the holy Apostle stood forth in that very spot as splendid with the grace of baptism rather than being covered in blood. Indeed, this matter is not surprising in Saint Paul. For why is it a wonder if the nourisher of the Church abounds in milk? <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> As he himself said to the Corinthians: *I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.* This is clearly that land of promise which God promised to our fathers, saying: *I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey.* For He did not speak of this earth which involves mire and mixes in mud with stagnant waters, but of that land of Paul and those like Paul, which continually distills what is pure and sweet. For which of Paul’s epistles is not sweeter than honey and whiter than milk? Which epistles, like the breasts of the churches, nourish the people unto salvation. Therefore, we read that milk flowed from the apostle's neck instead of blood, <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> because *flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God.* Therefore, Paul already possesses the kingdom, since he lacks the blood which is said to hinder one from reigning. Thus, while still placed on earth, Paul was already being transformed into the substance of the heavenly kingdom. Concerning Paul, the divine Augustine says: <margin>Augustine in his treatise on Psalm 130.</margin> He who was made a preacher from a persecutor attained a more abundant grace in all apostolic labor than the other apostles, so that God might better show that what He gives is His own, and not man's. Just as physicians are accustomed to show the power of their art in desperate cases, so our Lord Jesus Christ,

<column-break/>

# Preface. Folio 3.

our physician and savior, showed the greatness of His art in a desperate man who had been a persecutor of the church, so that He might not only make him a Christian but also an apostle—and not just an apostle, but as he himself said, so that he might labor more than everyone else. <margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin> Therefore, he was of the most excellent grace; and you see, brothers, how Paul's epistles flourish in the church more than those of his fellow apostles. For others wrote, but they only spoke in the church. As for those things brought forward by erring men under their names—since they are not their own—they are rejected and not accepted by the church. Others who wrote did not write with such great grace. Since he was of such great grace and had earned great gifts from God, why does he say: *Lest I be exalted by the magnitude of the revelations,* etc.? For this reason Origen says: <margin>Origen, Homily 8 on Genesis.</margin> "See Paul, who from Jerusalem and the surrounding area as far as Illyricum filled the world with the Gospel of God; hear him saying: *How many things happened to me at Iconium, at Lystra, how many at Ephesus; how many times was I beaten, how many times stoned, and how many times did I fight with beasts.* But he remained until he reached the height—that is, until he established churches throughout the breadth of the whole world." But let these things concerning Paul suffice as a preface. Most holy prelate, and all you who are about to read the "theorems" <term>theozemata: Champier's term for the divine propositions or principles he extracts from Paul's letters</term> of the divine speech of Paul arranged in this volume, I would wish most earnestly that you attend not so much to Paul himself as to the understanding of Paul and the Giver of that understanding. And all the less, when they read whatever commentaries they might find, should they attend to human authors if they perceive signs of spiritual life and true food for the soul; but they must understand the power following from above, and recognize the true Author—and once recognized, follow Him with as much purity and piety of soul as they are able. For one is kindled to Him by these steps alone, He who works all things in all. Therefore, most kind Father, admit Paul as a guest; bring in the herald of Christ, the legate of Christ for the life of all nations, the orator of the world. If, moreover, you hide him in the sacred cabinet of your breast—keep him once hidden, meditate on him once kept, digest him, and cherish him—he will without doubt place you on the true path of blessedness. I ask, therefore, that you receive these theorems kindly, and according to your custom and humanity, both read and correct them, and be willing to remember me as your own. May you be well and happy, and live fortunately. At Nancy, the primary town of Lorraine, on the 13th day before the Kalends of July [June 19], 1514.

### Saint Damasus the Bishop on the praises of Paul the Apostle.

For a long time, Saul, following the commands of the authorities,
Preferred the laws of his fathers over the Lord.
He refused to believe the holy prophets had praised Christ.
With constant slaughter, he desired to scatter the people,
Blindly tearing apart the pious bonds of the holy Mother <note>The "holy Mother" refers to the early Church.</note>.
After the darkness, he deserved to know the true light.
Having been tested, he sensed what the glory of Christ could do;
When his ears received the voice and light of the Lord,
He turned his ways, following the precepts of Christ.
Changed, and thereafter pleased to be called by the name Paul,
By a wondrous faith of things, he was suddenly carried beyond the heavens
And deserved to know what the rewards of life could be.
The martyr ascended, reaching the inner sanctums of Christ.
The third light of heaven, paradise, held him as he went;
He enjoyed the conversations of the Lord, keeping His secrets,
Commanded to preach the truth to the nations and peoples.
To penetrate the depths of the sea, to see both night and day—
For whom it was enough to have lived a hidden life.
Beatings, chains, hunger, stones, and the rage of beasts,
The filth of prison, rods, torments, and bonds,
Shipwreck, tears, and the dire poison of the serpent—
He did not fear to carry the marks <note>original: "stigmata"</note> of Christ in his body.
He taught the believers how they might conquer death.
Worthy of the love of God, the teacher lives through the ages.
In these brief verses, I confess, most blessed teacher
Paul, that I, Damasus, wished to show your triumphs.

<column-break/>

### The theorems of the wonderful propositions of the most blessed Paul the Apostle: which the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, wrote about in his monuments in the third chapter of the Second Epistle of Peter, under this context of words: "Just as our most dear brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, has written to you, as also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are certain things hard to be understood, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do also the other scriptures, to their own destruction," etc. With the explanations of Lord Symphorien Champier of Lyon, gathered from various opinions of theologians.

->The Vulgate Edition.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a saint, likely Saint Paul, holding a sword and a book.</image-desc> Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he had promised before through his prophets in the holy scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made to him of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined the Son of God in power, according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead.

->Understanding from the Greek.<-

Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he had promised through his prophets in the holy scriptures, concerning his Son, made of the seed of David according to the flesh, defined <note>original: "definito." The Greek "horisthentos" can be translated as "defined" or "declared," whereas the Vulgate used "predestinated."</note> as the Son of God in power through the spirit of holiness from the resurrection from the dead.

->Exposition.<-

<margin>Origen</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' with leafy and floral ornamentation.</image-desc> Paul, who was previously Saul, was born in the town of Gischala <note>A town in Galilee; though the Bible says Tarsus, some traditions suggest his family moved from Gischala.</note> in Judea, from the tribe of Benjamin. When his homeland was captured in the Roman war, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus, which is in Cilicia. Soon after, in Jerusalem, he devoted his efforts to Gamaliel <note>A celebrated doctor of the Jewish Law.</note>, who was most skilled in the Mosaic law. Origen, however, felt that Paul had two names: because he was Hebrew, he had the Hebrew name Saul, and because he was a Roman citizen by birth, he had the Roman name Paul, which was quite similar to the Hebrew; this also happened with John Mark, as is read of both in the Acts of the Apostles. For as most assert, John and Saul are Hebrew names, while Mark and Paul are gentile <note>original: "gentilitia," meaning Roman or non-Jewish family names.</note> names, such as Marcus Regulus, Marcus Antonius, Paulus Sergius, or Paulus Emilius. <margin>Saint Ambrose.</margin> Among our ancestors, as Saint Ambrose testifies, names were given for a reason: just as Isaac was named for laughter and Jacob for the heel, so this man was called Saul because of his restlessness <note>The name Saul was etymologically linked by some medieval scholars to the idea of "tossing" or "restlessness" (inquietudo).</note>. But after he believed, he called himself Paul instead of Saul; this was a change. And because Saul, according to the sense mentioned above, is interpreted as "restlessness" or "temptation," when he came to the faith of Christ, he called himself Paul—that is, as if from a tempter he had become quiet, humble, or small—and also because our faith is "small" <note>original: "par," likely a play on "paulus" meaning small/modest.</note>. For whereas before he brought temptations out of the restlessness of Judaism upon the servants of God, afterward he himself suffered temptations for the sake of the hope which he previously denied out of love for Judaism. Paul in the Latin language is interpreted as "modest," and in the Greek as "quiet." Others say he was called Paul after the first spoil he brought to the Church from [the proconsul] Paulus—namely, Sergius Paulus, whom he converted to the faith in Cyprus.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul / Book One.
**Folio 5.**

<margin>Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.</margin>
Augustine also says that Paul chose this name for no other reason than to show himself to be small, as the least of the apostles, standing firmly against the proud and arrogant who presume much of their own works. For this reason, he was first called Saul and afterwards Paul; that is, first proud, then humble. For you know from where the name Saul is derived: it was the name of a king who was proud and unrestrained. The apostle did not change his name out of any boastfulness, but rather, from Saul he became Paul—from a proud man to a modest one. Hear how he was Saul and how he is Paul: "I was once," he says, "a blasphemer, a persecutor, and injurious." <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 1:13. The name 'Paulus' in Latin means 'small' or 'little'.</note>

<margin>From a treatise by Augustine on Psalm 72.</margin>
You have heard of Saul; now hear of Paul. "For I," he says, "am the least of the apostles." What does "least" mean, if not "I am Paul"? And it follows: "who am not worthy to be called an apostle." Why? "Because I was Saul." And what does "I was Saul" mean? Let him say it himself: "Because I persecuted the church of God." But then he says, "By the grace of God I am what I am." He took away all his own excellence; he was the least in himself, but great in Christ. And in another place: "I am the last and the least of the apostles," as if he were the fringe of the Lord's garment. What is as small as a fringe? Yet by touching this fringe, the woman was healed of her flow of blood. In that "small" man, a "great" one lived; in the "least," a "grand" one dwelt. And the less he was of himself, the more he excluded the "great" man <note>meaning his former ego</note> and the more the "least" man belonged to God; for he calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ.

<margin>From Augustine in a sermon on the Apostle Paul.</margin>
But in what sense is the word "servant" <note>original: *seruus*</note> used here? I believe it is used in nearly the same way that Plato, Aristotle, and the other philosophers use it. For Paul does not seem to have been lacking in philosophy or any human discipline, nor was he ignorant of divine matters, as the Holy Spirit made him more eminent than all. In the Sacred Scriptures, he is that "little young Benjamite" in an ecstasy of mind. Philosophers are accustomed to call a man a "servant" who is not his own, but belongs entirely to another; who does not live for himself, does not work for himself, and does not procreate for himself, but for his master. Thus, although Paul was the freest of all men, he calls himself a servant of our Lord Jesus Christ, testifying that he is not his own, but belongs entirely to Jesus Christ; that he does not live for himself, but for Jesus Christ (the truly living life); and that he does not work for himself nor generate faithful children for himself, but for Christ the Lord. And this servitude to Christ surpasses all liberty. What then is meant by that which is said in the Vulgate edition?

<margin>From a treatise by Augustine on the Gospel according to John.</margin>
"Who was predestinated the Son of God," etc. Hear the Apostle himself elsewhere: "We know," he says, "that for those who love God, all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose." These he also foreknew and predestinated to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. "And those whom he predestinated, he also called." Unless perhaps (as Augustine says) we are afraid to call Christ himself "predestinated"; for the Apostle seems to have said this about us, that we might be conformed to his image. As if, indeed, anyone faithfully looking at the rule of faith is going to deny that the Son of God was predestinated? One cannot rightly deny he was a man. Certainly, the Lord was not predestinated according to that which is the Word of God with God. For why would he be predestinated when he already was what he was, without beginning and without end, eternal? But that which was not yet was to be predestinated, so that it might come to be in its own time, just as it had been predestinated to happen before all time.

<column-break/>

Whoever, therefore, denies that the Son of God was predestinated, denies that this same person is the Son of Man. According to this predestination, therefore, he was glorified before the world was, so that his glory might be revealed from the resurrection of the dead before his Father, at whose right hand he sits.

### Theorem Second.

->The Vulgate Edition.<-

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who hold the truth of God in injustice: because that which is known of God is manifest in them; for God has manifested it to them. For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.

->Understanding from the Greek.<-

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who suppress the truth in injustice; because the knowledge of God is manifest in them, for God has manifested it. Not his invisible things from the condition of the world, but through his works they are understood and seen: that is, his eternal power and divinity; so that they are without excuse.

->Exposition.<-

Sicut <note>original: "Sicut" (Just as). The woodcut initial 'S' depicts a figure, likely a philosopher or prophet, pointing towards the heavens, illustrating the theme of finding God through nature.</note>
<margin>Saint Ambrose.</margin>
Just as the righteousness of God is revealed in those who believe, so also ungodliness and injustice are revealed in those who do not believe. From the very fabric of the heavens (as Ambrose says), God appears angry with them. For he created such beautiful stars so that from them, it might be recognized how great and how admirable their Creator is, and that he alone should be adored.

<margin>Psalm 18.</margin>
Hence it is written in the Psalm: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands." Therefore, through the natural law, he holds the human race guilty. For they were able to perceive this through the law of nature, with the fabric of the world testifying that God the Creator alone is to be loved. This is what Moses handed down in writing, but they became impious by not worshiping the Creator; and injustice appears in them when, seeing the truth, they ignore it, not making God one. That wrath of God from heaven is the sword, famine, and pestilence, and such vengeful plagues.

<margin>Isaiah</margin>
As it is said through Isaiah: "My sword is drunk in heaven," and through Jeremiah: "Behold, I will send upon them the sword, and famine, and pestilence." The knowledge of God is manifest from the fabric of the world; so that he who is invisible by nature might be known even through visible things. The work was made by him so that the Artisan might be made manifest by his own visibility; so that through the certain, the uncertain might be known; and so that through this work, which is impossible for others, he might be believed to be the God of all.

<margin>Wisdom 13:b</margin>
Solomon also says of the wise men of the world: "If they were able to know so much that they could speculate about the world, how did they not more easily find its Lord and Creator?" But those whom Solomon rebukes (says Augustine) did not recognize the Creator through the creature; those whom the Apostle rebukes did recognize him, but they were not grateful.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul
They acted; and claiming themselves to be wise, they were made fools: and they fell away to the worship of idols. For the Apostle clearly showed that the wise men of the nations <note>original: "sapientes gentium"</note> had found the Creator when he spoke with the Athenians. For when he had said, "In him we live, move, and have our being," he added, "As some even among you have said." <note>A reference to Paul's speech at the Areopagus in Acts 17:28, where he quotes Greek poets.</note> However, this intent more specifically argues against the impiety of the nations, so that from this it may be proved that even the perverse can come to grace. For it is just that they should undergo the penalty of impiety if they do not receive the reward of faith. For what (says Origen) is so foul, so obscure, and so dark as to turn the glory of God into the effigy of a bodily and corruptible human form—as is the custom of those who worship idols—and to equate the eminence of the divine majesty with birds, four-footed beasts, and serpents?

## Theorem Three.

->The Vulgate Edition.<-

¶ For through the law comes the knowledge of sin. But now, without the law, the justice of God is made manifest, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; even the justice of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe in him. For there is no distinction; for all have sinned and do need the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

->Understanding from the Greek.<-

<margin>Note that the law was not sufficient without grace.</margin>
¶ For through the law comes the knowledge of sin; but now the justice of God without the law is made manifest, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; but the justice of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe; for there is no distinction. For all have sinned, and do need the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus.

->Exposition.<-

<margin>Augustine in the explanation to the Romans.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial Q with a woodcut of a scholar (likely St. Paul) writing at a desk with a book and lectern.</image-desc>As for what the Apostle says—"Because no flesh shall be justified in the law before him, for through the law comes the knowledge of sin," and other similar things—these must be read quite carefully by those who think they should be cast as an insult against the law. This is so that the law does not seem to be rejected by the Apostle, nor that free will <term>arbitrium liber</term><note>The capacity of the human will to make choices, a central debate in Reformation-era theology.</note> is taken away from man. Therefore, let us distinguish these four stages of man written by Augustine: before the law, under the law, under grace, and in peace. Before the law, we follow the <term>concupiscence</term><note>In this context, concupiscence refers to disordered desire or the inclination toward sin.</note> of the flesh. Under the law, we are drawn by it. Under grace, we neither follow it nor are we drawn by it. In peace, there is no concupiscence of the flesh. Therefore, before the law, we do not fight, because we not only desire but we also sin; indeed, we even approve of our sins. Under the law, we fight but we are conquered; for we confess that the things we do are evil, which we certainly do not wish to do; but because grace is not yet present, 
<margin>Romans 4:d. Romans 3:c.</margin>
we are not helped. In this stage, it is shown to us how we lie prostrate; and while we wish to rise, we fall and are more grievously afflicted. Hence it is said: "The law entered in, that sin might abound." <note>Romans 5:20.</note> From this also comes what is stated here: "Through the law comes the knowledge of sin." For it is not the removal of sin, because sin is taken away only through grace. Therefore, the law is good, 

<column-break/>

since it forbids what ought to be forbidden and commands what ought to be commanded. But when anyone thinks he can fulfill it by his own strength and not by the grace of his Liberator, that presumption profits him nothing; rather, it harms him so much that he is seized by a more vehement desire for sinning, and in his sins, he is even found to be a transgressor. For where there is no law,
<margin>Romans 4:c.</margin>
there is no transgression. Thus, when a man lying prostrate has recognized himself, and finds he is not able to rise by himself, let him implore the help of the Liberator. Sin does not exist in our evil desires, but rather we sin in our personal assent <note>original: "prententione"</note> to them. This is the point of what the same Apostle says: "Let not sin reign in your mortal body, to obey the lusts thereof." 
<margin>Romans 6:c.</margin>
For here he shows that there are desires which must not be obeyed, so that we do not permit sin to reign in us. But since these desires of the flesh are born from the mortality of the flesh, which we draw from the first sin of the first man (whence we are born carnally), these shall not be ended except by the transformation of the resurrection of the body, which we have earned through the promise made to us. There, perfect peace shall exist, which we have placed in the fourth stage. For the peace is perfect because nothing resists us, nor do we resist God. This is what the Apostle says: "The body indeed is dead because of sin,
<margin>Romans 8:b.</margin>
but the spirit is life because of justice." Through faith, however, comes the abolition of sin. Therefore, faith must be followed. What is this law, let us see again, through which he says sin is known? And how is it known? For we see (says Ambrose) <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), the Bishop of Milan and a mentor to Augustine.</note> that the ancients were not ignorant of sin, because Joseph was sent into prison (though by a false accusation), and the cupbearer and the baker of Pharaoh were imprisoned 
<margin>Divine Augustine.</margin>
because of sin. How then were sins hidden? Indeed, the law is threefold: so that the first part is concerning the mystery <term>sacramento</term> of the divinity of God; the second is that which agrees with the natural law, which forbids sin; and the third is the law of deeds, that is, Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, etc. This is therefore the natural law which, being partly reformed through Moses and partly having its authority confirmed in restraining vices, made sin known—not that sin was hidden, but it showed that the sins which are committed would not go unpunished by God, lest perhaps someone escaping for a time might be thought to have mocked the law. This is, therefore, what the law showed. But now, without the law, the justice of God is manifested, having testimony from the law and the prophets. For it is clear that the justice of God appeared without the law—but without the law of the Sabbath, and circumcision, and the new moon, and of vengeance—yet not without the mystery of the divinity of God. And lest this should perhaps be thought to have been done against the law, he added that the justice of God has testimony from the law and the prophets. When he says "witnessed by the law and the prophets," he designates the Law of Moses. But if what we have said seems to you to be less than full, we will also add what Origen says, 
<margin>Origen in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 3.</margin>
if it seems good to you: that it is the same law of which it is said, "But now without the law the justice of God is manifested." What is this law? It is that of which he says: "witnessed by the law and the prophets." This law, which is manifested without the law, does not receive the testimony of the law; yet if it receives the testimony of the law, then it is not manifested without the law. Since this (he says) seems unsolvable and cannot be pulled apart by any reason...

<meta>This page continues the theological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, moving from the manifestation of God’s justice through faith (Romans 3) toward the origin of sin in Adam and the abundance of grace in Christ (Romans 5).</meta>

fo. vij.

<header>The Theorems of Saint Paul</header>

It must be understood that the justice of God is indeed manifested by Christ Jesus, providing testimony for him—not by the law of nature, which is still weak and small <note>The Latin "vngue... et parua" (literally "a fingernail and small") is an idiom for something of very little significance.</note>, but by the Law of Moses; not that which is according to the letter, but that which is according to the spirit. Concerning this, the same Apostle says: "for the law is spiritual." Therefore, the Law and the Prophets are witnesses of the justice of God, which is manifested through faith in Jesus Christ unto all who believe. Among them, there is no distinction whether they believe from among the Jews or the Gentiles. See (he says) that when he manifests the justice of God, he does not posit faith as the only cause, but he includes the Law and the Prophets. For neither (he says) does faith alone without the Law and the Prophets manifest the justice of God, nor again do the Law and the Prophets without faith. One, therefore, depends upon the other, so that there may be perfection in both. He says there is no distinction between Jews and Greeks, since it is clear that all were equally made subject to sin. And now the justice of God, supported by the testimony of the Law and the Prophets, is given equally to all through faith in Jesus Christ, because all had been made strangers by sin. Wherefore Ambrose says that this must be understood generally when he says: "there is no distinction." For he includes everyone here, even the saints, to show that the Law profited nothing without faith. For the Law was given in such a way that there would be faith in the Law, which would hope for the future salvation. Wherefore the death of Christ Jesus is effective, because here in this age he taught what must be believed and observed, and he snatched everyone from hell. For in Adam all have sinned (unless they were preserved, as is said of the glorious Virgin <margin>Augustine in the book *On Nature and Grace*.</margin> <note>A reference to the theological debate regarding the Immaculate Conception; the author notes the common exception for the Virgin Mary.</note>). For all, as Augustine writes, have sinned, whether in Adam or in themselves, and they lack the glory of God; therefore, the entire mass <note>original: "vniuersa massa" — refers to the "massa damnata," the Augustinian concept that all humanity is a "mass of perdition" due to original sin.</note> owes the penalty. And if the deserved punishment of damnation were rendered to all, it would undoubtedly be rendered without injustice.

->### Theorem Four.<-

->#### The Vulgate and Greek editions are the same.<-

<margin>Romans 5.</margin>
For until the law, sin was in the world; but sin was not imputed when the law was not. Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a figure of the one to come. But the law sub-entered <note>original: "subintrauit" — a technical term for the law entering "alongside" or "stealthily" to make sin visible.</note> so that the offense might abound; but where the offense abounded, grace abounded all the more; so that just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through justice unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

->### Exposition.<-

<margin>Saint Ambrose</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'P' containing a woodcut illustration of two figures, possibly saints or teachers, conversing in an interior setting with a window.</image-desc>
For men used to think they sinned before God but not before men. For, says Ambrose, the natural law had not entirely become numb, because they were not ignorant that they should not do to others what they did not wish to suffer themselves. The natural law is always present and was never unknown; but it was thought for a time to have authority only among men, and not to make them guilty before God. For it was unknown that God is going to judge

<column-break/>

<header>Book One. fo.vij.</header>

the human race; and because of this, sin was not imputed, as if sin did not exist before God, asserting that God was indifferent. But where the law was given through Moses, it is manifest that God cares for human affairs, and that those who do evil will not go unpunished, no matter the reason they escape in the present. For the natural law has three parts. The first is that, once acknowledged, the Creator <margin>Three parts of the natural law.</margin> should be honored, and His brightness and majesty should not be attributed to any of the creatures. The second part is moral: that is, to live well under the governance of modesty. For it is fitting for a person having knowledge of the Creator to restrain their life by law, lest the acknowledgment be frustrated. The third part is docile <note>original: "docilis" — relating to teaching or being taught.</note>, so that one may hand down the knowledge of God the Creator and the example of morals to others, so that they may learn how merit is established before the Creator. Nor is there true Christian prudence without this. However, when he says "until the law, sin was in the world," it must be understood, as Saint Augustine writes, "until grace should come." <margin>Augustine in the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans.</margin> For this was said against those who think that sins could be taken away by the Law. But the Apostle says that sins were made manifest by the Law, but not taken away, when he says "but sin was not imputed when the law was not." For he does not say "it did not exist," but "it was not imputed"; nor when the Law was given was it taken away, but it began to be imputed, that is, to appear. Therefore (he says), let us not think that "until the law" was said as if sin no longer existed under the Law; but it was said "until the law" so that the entire time of the Law is counted until the end of the Law, which is Christ. But death reigned (says Origen), which had entered through sin, until Moses: that is, as long as the Law remained over those who sinned according to the likeness of the sin of Adam, through whom death itself received entry. This Adam is a figure of the one to come: not according to his transgression, but according to this: that just as through him death entered, so through the newest Adam <note>A common title for Jesus Christ (the Second Adam).</note> life entered into this world; and just as through the former condemnation came upon all men, so also through Christ comes justification unto all men. But as for what he says—"the law sub-entered so that the offense might abound"—by that very word he sufficiently signified, as Augustine writes, <margin>Augustine on Romans.</margin> that the Jews did not know by what dispensation the Law was given. For it was not given so that it could give life, because grace gives life through faith; but it was given to show by how many bonds of sins they were held bound, those who presumed to fulfill justice by their own strength. Thus sin abounded when lust became more burning because of the prohibition, and for those sinning against the Law, the crime of transgression was added. He understands this according to the degree in those four degrees where the Apostle considers the law placed in the members <margin>Origen</margin> resisting the law of the mind. Does the Apostle therefore (says Origen) seem to have placed the law of the members in this place, which he says "sub-entered" so that sin might abound? For the very word he used seems to judge this most fully. For it is one thing to "enter," and another to "sub-enter" <note>This refers to the Greek *pareiselthen*, suggesting a side-entry or a secondary purpose.</note>, just as it is one thing to "lead" and another to "sneak away," one thing to "draw" and another to "withdraw." For "sub-entering" indicates this: when one has entered, another enters under a pretext. In...

fo. viij.

<header>The Theorems of Saint Paul | Book One</header>

...by which reason it is shown that under the pretext of the natural law—which the Apostle named the "law of the mind" <note>original: *legem mentis*</note>, which agrees with the law of God—there arose the "law of the members." This law of the members suggests the desires of the flesh and leads man captive to lust and the pleasures of iniquity; therefore, sin abounds. Thus, the law entered so that the offense might abound; but where sin abounded, he says, "grace did superabound." In this present passage, when he spoke of sin abounding, he used a most worthy expression: that grace should conquer that abundance, and so he positioned it as "superabundance." For the grace of Christ superabounded in this: that it not only absolves men from past sins but also fortifies them against future ones. Indeed, he shows two kingdoms within man: one in which sin reigned unto death, and another in which grace reigns over justice

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
unto life. And as Saint Ambrose writes, the Apostle shows what happened *after* the law was given, not what the law itself produced. How (he asks) did sins increase by a fault of the law, which threatens punishment lest one sin? It is said to have "entered" so that sin might abound; it is true that it entered as if to be helpful, yet with humility; afterward it began to dominate those whom it had commanded not to sin, and yet they did sin. For the law began to show the abundance of sins: and since they were now forbidden, they were committed even more than they had been before. Therefore, the law was given in this way so that the offense might abound. For the Apostle, commending the faith through which sins are surely deleted, said that the law acted to make sins abound; for (he says) it was not given to abolish sins, but to make them abound; since he showed they were "sinners" before the law, but after the law, he held them all as "guilty." It is manifest, however, that when sin abounded, the gift of God superabounded. This gift comes from the promise and crushes all sins, so that the Devil's envy may show he has achieved nothing. Grace superabounded, therefore, because sin reigned for a time, but grace reigns for eternity. For the kingdom of God is found where grace reigns, just as the kingdom of the Devil was sin reigning.

### Theorem Five.

->The Vulgate Edition.<-

For without the law, sin was dead. And I once lived without any law; but when the commandment came, sin revived.

->Understanding from the Greek.<-

For without the law, sin was dead; but when the commandment came, sin revived.

->Exposition.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'O' depicting a crowned kingly figure, possibly Moses or a biblical patriarch, holding a scepter or rod.</image-desc>
He shows those sins which were hidden, and which would not have gone unpunished before God. Once this was discovered, man was made guilty; and therefore he does not seem to give thanks to the law. For who would gladly welcome one who announces that punishment is imminent? But he gives thanks to the law of faith: because he who was made guilty through the laws of Moses is

<column-break/>

reconciled to God through the law of faith. Who then can show that the former law is just and good? Indeed, an imminent danger is a good thing to know. But he gives more thanks to the one through whom he was snatched from the danger and lives. When he said, "without the law sin was dead," it must be understood in two ways, as Saint Ambrose writes: both as the Devil being signified in sin, and as the act of sin itself, which he calls "sin." For he says the Devil was "dead" because he ceased from the deception of man before the law, but was, as it were, quiet; for he was secure in his possession of man. He said sin was "dead" because it was thought it would not be imputed <note>original: *non imputaretur*; meaning it would not be "counted against" the person</note> before God; therefore among men, it was dead, as if one could sin with impunity. For sin was not hidden, but it was unknown that God was going to judge it. But when the law was given, it became manifest that sin "revived." Why did it revive? Unless because it had lived before, and afterward, through neglect, it was estimated to be a dead master, even while it lived. For man thought sin was not imputed when it *was* being imputed; thus, the living was held for dead. But when he says, "I once lived without the law," what does it mean to have lived without the law, since the law was always there? It means that man lived without the fear of God, secure in the thought that God would not judge human acts. Origen says: he did not say "I did not have it," but "I did not know it," as if he were ignorant of what concupiscence <note>The strong desire for worldly or carnal things.</note> was. But when reason and natural law <margin>Origen</margin> found a place within us as we aged, it began to teach us what things were good and to prohibit the bad. This, therefore, is what it means when it says "Thou shalt not covet"; what we were ignorant of before, we learned from the law itself: that concupiscence is evil. This is the law of which he says: "I should not have known concupiscence unless the law said: Thou shalt not covet."

### Theorem Six.

->The Vulgate edition and the Greek are similar.<-

For what was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh: so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.

->Exposition.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'C' showing a tonsured monk or clerk seated at a desk with an open book on a lectern.</image-desc>
Since in the preceding sections he has named so many laws—for he spoke of the "law of the mind" and the "law of the spirit of life," and conversely <margin>Origen</margin> the "law in the members" and the "law of sin"—here we ask which of these laws he means when he says "what was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened." Behold, two parts: "through the flesh" (this is no small matter to deliberate upon). Origen believes, however, that here as in other places, the Apostle divides the law of Moses into two parts: he names one part "flesh" and the other "spirit." That part which concerns observances (he says), which carries a literal sense, he calls the "sense of the flesh," just as he said of such Jews that they were "vainly puffed up by the sense of their flesh." That...

It contrasts the "dead" state of unrecognized sin before the Law with the "revived" state of sin once the commandment "Thou shalt not covet" was introduced.</summary>
