<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, focusing on Chapter 8. It transitions from discussing the "law of the members" to the "spiritual law" and the "law of the spirit," drawing on the interpretations of Ambrose, Augustine, and Origen regarding predestination and the nature of Christ as the "firstborn."</meta>

The Theorems of Saint Paul. Book One. Folio 9.

<margin>The spiritual law.</margin> But that which is received spiritually he calls "spirit"; as he says elsewhere: "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life." <note>original: "littera occidit spiritus viuificat"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6.</note> In this place, therefore, he says that regarding what he calls the "impossibility of the law," in which it is weakened through the flesh, the understanding which is according to the letter <note>The "literal" or surface-level interpretation of the Mosaic Law.</note> can be taken; for it was itself impossible and weak if it were felt "according to the flesh"—that is, according to the letter. For what, he asks, is as impossible as the observation of the Sabbath according to the letter of the law? For it commands one not to go out from his house, not to move from his place, and to lift no burden. Because these things seem so impossible, the Jews, who observe the law according to the flesh, devise certain foolish and ridiculous commentaries with which they seem to patch up <margin>The spiritual law.</margin> the law's impossibility. Therefore, the "law of the spirit of life" (says Ambrose) is the law of faith itself. For even the law of Moses is spiritual because it forbids sin, yet it is not "of life," because it cannot remit the sins of those guilty of death so as to bring the dead to life. <margin>The law of sin.</margin> But the "law of sin" is that which he says dwells in the members, which strives to persuade us toward things that are adverse. The "law of death," however, is the law of Moses, because it puts sinners to death. <margin>2 Corinthians 3:b.</margin> For in another epistle, among other things, he says concerning the authority of the law: "If the ministry of death, carved in stone, was in glory," <note>original: "Si ministratio mortis formata in lapidibus fuit in gloria"</note> then it is no wonder if it is called both a "spiritual law" and a "law of death." For even the Gospel <margin>The spiritual law.</margin> is the same way; for he says in another place: to some it is an "odor of life <margin>The law of the spirit.</margin> unto life," and to others an "odor of death unto death." Let us now see what the difference is when he speaks of the "spiritual law" and the "law of the spirit." The difference is this: it is called the "spiritual law" because it gives precepts <note>Rules or commandments.</note> through which one may not sin (for he who does not sin is called spiritual), matching the higher celestial beings. But it is called the "law of the spirit" because God—whose faith it is—is Spirit. In the former, there are words; here, there is the reality. There, the things of God; here, God himself is most clearly manifest. Here the Apostle teaches, as Saint Augustine is the authority, that these same precepts of the law were not fulfilled because those to whom the law was given before grace were devoted to carnal <note>Worldly or physical.</note> goods. They desired to acquire happiness from these, and they feared nothing unless adversity threatened such goods. Therefore, when they were disturbed by those temporal things, they easily fell away from the precepts of the law. The law was therefore weakened by not fulfilling what it commanded—not by its own fault, but "through the flesh," that is, through those men who, by seeking carnal goods, did not love the justice of the law but preferred temporal comforts. And therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, our liberator, by taking on mortal flesh—that is, the "likeness of sinful flesh"—condemned sin. For death was assigned to sinful flesh, yet that death of the Lord was an act of favor, not a debt. Nevertheless, the Apostle also calls this "sin," referring to the taking on of mortal flesh; for although his flesh was not sinful, he acts as if it were sin when he, being immortal, dies. But "regarding sin," he says, "he condemned sin in the flesh." For the death of the Lord brought it about that death should no longer be feared, and temporal goods would no longer be sought, nor temporal evils feared, in which that "carnal wisdom" resided, through which the 

<column-break/>

precepts of the law could not be fulfilled. But with this "wisdom" distinguished and taken away in the Man of the Lord <note>Refers to the humanity of Christ.</note>, the justice of the law is fulfilled when one walks not "according to the flesh," but "according to the spirit." Whence it was most truly said: "I did not come <margin>Matthew 5:b. Romans 8:c.</margin> to destroy the law, but to fulfill it." For the fullness of the law is charity <note>Divine love.</note>, and charity belongs to those who walk according to the spirit; for this belongs to the grace of the Holy Spirit. For when there was no charity for justice, but only fear, the law was not fulfilled. Saint Ambrose also explains the authority of the <margin>Saint Ambrose</margin> Apostle in this way: "God, having sent Christ, condemned sin by sin"; that is, he condemned sin by his own sin <note>Here, "sin" refers to Christ's sacrificial offering or his taking on the likeness of sinful flesh.</note>. For when Christ is crucified by "Sin" (which is Satan), Satan committed a sin in the flesh of the Savior's body. By which act, he condemned sin in the flesh, in the very place where he had sinned.

# ¶ Theorem Seven.

## ¶ The Vulgate edition, identical with the Greek.

¶ Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, <margin>Romans 8:f.</margin> that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.

### ¶ Exposition.

<margin>Ambrose on predestination</margin> <image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'I' containing a woodcut of a hooded scholar pointing at a book.</image-desc> These whom it pleased him would be devoted to him in the future, he chose to receive the promised rewards; so that those who seem to believe but do not remain in the faith they began are denied to be "chosen" by God, because those whom God chooses remain with him. For there are those, as Saint Ambrose likes to say, whom he chooses "for a time," such as Saul and Judas—not from foreknowledge, but from their present justice. Regarding "becoming conformed to the image of his Son," he says this: that they are predestined for the future world so that they may become like the Son of God. Christ is rightly called the "firstborn" <note>original: "primogenitus"</note>, who was not made, but born before every creature. To his example, God deigned to adopt men as sons to himself. Christ is the firstborn in regeneration, and the firstborn from the dead, whose nature is unknown <note>Likely referring to the mystery of the Resurrection.</note>. He is also the firstborn ascending into the heavens after his victory. Therefore, the "Firstborn" in all things is called our brother, because he deigned to be born as a man. But he is "Lord" because he is our God, as the <margin>Jeremiah</margin> prophet Jeremiah says: "This is our God." <note>The quote "This is our God" is actually from Baruch 3:36, which was often attributed to Jeremiah in this period.</note> "And those whom he predestined, he also called." To "call" is to help one who is thinking about the faith, or to prick the heart of one he knows will listen. Above, he said: "those whom he foreknew, he also predestined"; and now he adds: "those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified." See (says Origen) into what an absurd opinion they fall who do not accept the foreknowledge of God, but act as if God only knows things <margin>Origen</margin> after they have happened.

<meta>This page continues the theological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, specifically addressing the chain of salvation: foreknowledge, predestination, calling, and justification. It transitions from a general discussion of these terms into "Theorem VIII," which focuses on the mercy and hardening of hearts as described in Romans chapter 9.</meta>

### Paul’s Eighth Theorem

<margin>A noteworthy point on predestination</margin>
...he did not predestine. And again, if we refer to the common understanding of what he says—"those whom he called, them he also justified" <note>original: "quos uocauit illos & iustificauit"; a reference to Romans 8:30.</note>—we would open a wide window to those who deny that it is within a person's power to be saved. For they say: if those whom God foreknew, he also predestined, and those he predestined, he also called, and those he called, he also justified, then those who are not justified bear no fault, because they were neither called, nor predestined, nor foreknown. Yet it clearly goes against us that not everyone who is called is also justified. For even the apostle Judas <note>Judas Iscariot, often used in these debates to show someone "called" who later fell.</note> was called, but he was not justified; for even if someone argues he was justified at the time he was called, he certainly was not "glorified." Furthermore, those of whom the Apostle speaks as having "suffered shipwreck of their faith" were indeed called, but they were not justified. According to the parables of the Gospel, those to whom the servants were sent and who made excuses were called, but were not justified; and he who entered the king's banquet without a wedding garment was called, but was not justified.

In this present passage (says Origen), it is clear that the Apostle followed the custom of Holy Scripture in using the word "knowing" <note>original: "cognoscendi"</note> to show that those were "foreknown" by God in whom God—knowing what sort of people they were—had placed his love and affection. This is also according to what is written: "The Lord knows those who are His." <note>original: "Cognouit dominus eos qui sunt eius"; 2 Timothy 2:19.</note> Since, as far as common knowledge is concerned, the Lord is not ignorant of those who are not His, he is nevertheless said to have "known" those whom he held in love and associated with Himself. Thus, therefore, those whom God foreknew, he also predestined; and those he predestined, he also called; and those he called, he also justified.

<margin>A noteworthy point</margin>
Therefore, Origen concludes that neither does the cause of our salvation or perdition consist in God's foreknowledge, nor does justification depend on the calling alone, nor is being glorified entirely removed from our own power. For if (he says by way of example) we imagine that God does not foreknow something that was undoubtedly going to happen—such as Judas becoming a traitor—and the prophets foretold this would happen, it was not because the prophets foretold it that Judas betrayed Him. Rather, because he was going to be a traitor, the prophets foretold those things which he was going to do out of the wickedness of his own purpose. Certainly, Judas had it in his power to be like Peter and John if he had wished, but he chose the greed for money more than the glory of their company. The prophets, or the records of their books, handed down the memory of this future will of his. So that you may know that God’s foreknowledge is not placed as the cause of salvation for anyone, but rather it lies in their own purpose and acts, look at Paul: fearing lest perhaps while he preached to others, he himself might become a castaway, he "buffeted his body" and "brought it into subjection." <note>1 Corinthians 9:27.</note>

<margin>Augustine in his exposition on the purpose: Romans and Matthew 20.</margin>
This is against those who throw such questions at us in this exposition. It can be asked (says Augustine) whether all who are called are justified. But elsewhere we read: "Many are called, but few are chosen." <note>Matthew 20:16.</note> However, because the chosen themselves are certainly "called according to His purpose," this pertains to the foreknowledge and predestination of God; nor did He pre-

<column-break/>

### Book One.
#### Page 10.

-destine anyone unless He foreknew that they would believe the calling of all those whom He also calls "chosen." For many did not come when they were called. But no one comes who has not been called. Those whom God foreknew to be "fit" for Him (as Saint Ambrose writes), these remain as believers. Because it cannot happen otherwise, except that those whom God foreknew, He also justified, and through this, He also magnified them, so that they might be made like the Son of God. Regarding the others whom God does not foreknow <note>In the sense of "acknowledging" or "choosing," rather than a lack of divine awareness.</note>, He has no care for them in this grace, because He does not "foreknow" them—even if they should believe or be chosen for a time because they seem good. Lest justice should seem to be despised, they do not remain so as to be magnified. Just like Judas, they departed from the Savior after having suffered. Therefore, God, foreknowing that they would be of an evil will, did not have them in the number of the good, even though the Savior says (as the same Ambrose notes) to those seventy-two disciples whom He had chosen in the second rank <note>The "seventy-two" disciples mentioned in Luke 10, distinct from the twelve Apostles.</note>, who later departed from Him:

<margin>Luke 10; John 6.</margin>
"Your names are written in heaven." But this was on account of justice, because it is just that a response be given to each person according to their merit. For because they were good, they were chosen for the ministry, and their names were written in heaven on account of their justice; but according to foreknowledge, they were in the number of the wicked. For God judges from justice, not from foreknowledge. Hence the Apostle John also

<margin>1 John 2.</margin>
says of such people in his first epistle: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us." <note>1 John 2:19.</note> There is no "respect of persons" <note>Partiality or favoritism.</note> in the foreknowledge of God.

<margin>The definition of predestination according to Ambrose.</margin>
For foreknowledge is that by which it is determined what the future will of each person will be, in which they are to remain, and by which they are either condemned or crowned. Finally, those whom He knows will remain in good are frequently evil beforehand; and those whom He knows will remain evil are sometimes good beforehand. Thus the complaint ceases, because God is not a "respecter of persons." For both Saul and Judas Iscariot were good before; as the Scripture says of Saul: "He was a good man, and there was not a better man than him among the children of Israel." And regarding Judas Iscariot, Peter the Apostle says: "He who obtained the lot of this ministry..." <note>Acts 1:17.</note> How could he have obtained a ministry of salvation unless he were good then?

->->### ¶ The Eighth Theorem.<-<-
->->#### ¶ The Vulgate Edition.<-<-

> For he says: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I will have mercy." <note>Romans 9:15; quoting Exodus 33:19.</note> Therefore it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth." <note>Romans 9:17; quoting Exodus 9:16.</note> Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.

<meta>This page follows the discussion of predestination and God's foreknowledge. The previous page established that God "knows" those who will respond to His call, and this page deepens that argument by addressing the difficult concepts of divine mercy and the "hardening" of hearts, specifically using the examples of Pharaoh, King Saul, and King David.</meta>

->Theorems of Saint Paul<-
->Book One<-

## Understanding from the Greek

For Moses says: "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion," etc. <note>original: "Miserebor cuius miserebor ⁊ miserebor quem miserebor"; a quotation from Exodus 33:19, cited by Paul in Romans 9:15.</note>

## Exposition

<margin>Saint Ambrose</margin>
<note>Ambrose of Milan (c. 340–397 AD) was an influential bishop and one of the four original Doctors of the Church.</note> "I will have mercy," He says, "on him on whom I will have shown mercy." This means (says Ambrose): I will have mercy on the one whom I foreknew would be a recipient of mercy. Knowing that he would turn back and remain with me, I will grant him mercy. I will provide mercy to the one whom I foreknew would return to me with a righteous heart after his error. This is to give to the one to whom it should be given, and not to deny it to the one who deserves to receive it; so that He calls the one whom He knows will listen. Now, to "call" means to prick the heart <note>original: "compungere"; to feel the "sting" of conscience or divine inspiration.</note> to receive the faith. Therefore, it is rightly said, "it is not of him that willeth," etc., because what is asked for ought not to rest in the will of the one asking, but in the judgment of the one giving. Whether something should be given must be weighed by the giver’s judgment. For when Saul sinned and asked for pardon, he did not receive it; but on the other hand, when David sinned and asked for pardon to be granted to him, he obtained it. In this, surely, the judgment of God as the giver (or non-giver) must be followed, because He who desires all to remain safe through justice does not judge unjustly. For He who inspects the heart knows whether the one asking does so with such a mind as to be worthy.

<margin>Origen</margin>
<note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar whose commentaries on Romans were foundational, though controversial.</note> Whence that saying of the Apostle: "It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth," etc. <note>Romans 9:16.</note> According to Origen, this must be understood just as David says in the Psalm: "Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it. Unless the Lord guards the city, he watches in vain who guards it." <note>Psalm 127:1.</note> In this, he shows not that the person building the house does nothing or is idle, but that while the person expends all the force of their care and labor as much as is within a human to do, the work reaches perfection only when all obstacles are removed by God. Therefore, while it is taught that a human should indeed apply labor and care, it is God who grants success and the outcome to the work. It is a pious and religious thing—and therefore a good one—to attribute the sum of the work more to God than to the human. Thus, even when Paul planted and Apollos watered, God is said to provide the growth. And it is added: "So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth." <note>1 Corinthians 3:7.</note> Therefore (he says), we can also say in the present passage: "So then, neither is he who runs anything, nor he who wills, but God who gives the outcome." For he who wills and he who runs seems to be the same as he who plants and he who waters; the Apostle says they are "nothing," not because they do nothing, but because in comparison to God, who gives the growth or the outcome to the work, they are said to be nothing. But let us see what is meant by that which is said to Pharaoh: "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power." <note>Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16.</note> For He says this, as it pleases Saint Ambrose,

<column-break/>

because while "Pharaoh" was the name of the kings among the Egyptians—just as among the Romans, emperors and kings are called "Augustus"—this particular Pharaoh was guilty of such great evils that he did not deserve to live. Lest he should think he lived by his own merit, or that God (whom he often thought he could deceive) was powerless to take vengeance, he hears from God: "For this purpose I have raised you up," etc., so that in this case, other nations might realize there is no other God besides the one who was the God of the Jews and who has now become the God of the Christians. 
<margin>Let us know according to Ambrose from whom Christ comes according to the flesh.</margin>
Who (he says) were also Christians then, just as we are now; and we are "Jews" because of Judah, from whom Christ comes according to the flesh <note>The author is playing on the name "Judaism" and the tribe of Judah to show continuity between the Old and New Testaments.</note>. For the ancient Jews, by hoping for the future Christ as Redeemer, were Christians. For Pharaoh was preserved so that many signs and plagues might be shown upon him as if he were already dead. He is said to be "raised up" because, although he was dead in the eyes of God, he received a little time to appear to live, so that he might be the one through whose punishment and various types of torments (even unto death) all those who were without God might be terrified by fear. They would then confess with the greatest admiration that He alone is God, from whom these vengeances come. This is also like what ancient physicians sought to do with men worthy of death, or those who had received a death sentence: they sought how they might benefit the living by opening these men up to understand the causes of sickness that lay hidden within, so that the punishment of the dying might contribute to the health of the living.
<margin>Galen, Celsus</margin>
<note>Galen (129–216 AD) and Aulus Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC – 50 AD) were the most famous medical authorities of antiquity.</note> As Galen in his book *On the Anatomy of the Living* and Cornelius Celsus in his books written *On Preserving Health* have passed down. Furthermore, what he says—"He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens"—he seems to take from those things written in Exodus. For it says there: "I will harden the heart of Pharaoh so that he will not let the people go." <note>Exodus 4:21.</note> "Pharaoh's heart shall be hardened," as 
<margin>Origen</margin>
Origen writes in this way: God did not want to give sudden and full vengeance upon him. For although his malice was complete, yet through His patience, God had not excluded the possibility of conversion. And therefore, He used at first lighter strikes, then gradually heavier ones upon him. But because of how God acted through patience, Pharaoh was hardened toward contempt, storing up greater wrath for himself; so that it is fitting to say to him what the Apostle writes: "Or do you despise the riches of His goodness and patience and long-suffering, not knowing that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath." <note>Romans 2:4-5.</note> Therefore (he says), it is not that God hardens whom He wills, but rather the one who refuses to patiently obey is hardened. It is therefore superfluous for you, the adversary, to say to the Apostle: "Why does He still find fault? For who resists His will?" <note>Romans 9:19.</note> It is certain that no one resists the will of God, but it is necessary for us to know that His will is just and right. Pay attention to what he says: that we are good or evil belongs to our own will. But whether the evil person is destined for certain punishments, or the good person for certain glory, belongs to the will of God.

<sig>bb iij</sig>

# The Theorems of Saint Paul
## Theorem Nine.

->The Vulgate edition and the Greek differ very little.<-

¶ God gave them a spirit of remorse <note>original: "spiritum compunctionis"; in many biblical translations this is rendered as a "spirit of stupor" or "slumber," but here the author emphasizes the "pricking" of the heart or conscience.</note>: eyes so that they may not see and ears so that they may not hear, even unto this very day. And David says: let their table become a snare before them, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a retribution to them. Let their eyes be darkened so they may not see, and forever bow down their backs.

### Exposition.

<margin>Origen</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' containing a scene of a scholar or saint seated at a desk within a room.</image-desc>
Regarding the phrase, "let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block": the word "trap" <note>original: "captione"; referring to being caught or taken.</note> is not written in the Psalm, nor is it found in the copies of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> nor in those of the Hebrews, as Origen points out. Furthermore, the Psalm says: "let their table become a snare *before them*." The Apostle Paul does not include "before them." What is their "table" if not their books? They believe they are reading the food for the soul from these books, wishing always to insist upon the works of the Law. But being blind, they do not see that they must flee to the grace of God. Therefore, their books are a snare and a stumbling block to them, as they walk always "bowed down" toward the lowest things—that is, looking only at the works of the Law. They never lift their backs toward the sublime things which are of the faith of Jesus Christ, who came into this world to save what was lost through God's mercy and grace. But was their blindness, their bowing down, and their fall permitted by God for this purpose: that they might deserve it? Oh, the ineffable goodness of God and His incomprehensible mercy, which these blind ones themselves flee from!

<margin>Saint Ambrose</margin>
Saint Ambrose says that he "curses" the table of the wicked because that is where the innocent are usually deceived. By trickery, they are called to a banquet so that they may be destroyed. This is how Amnon, the son of David, was deceived by his brother Absalom. And the wicked Holofernes thought he could deceive the holy Judith through a feast. And at the table of the criminal Herod, the wicked served up the head of John the Prophet. However, the "Table of the Lord" is the word of the Lord, and everything called the Old Testament is the "table of Israel." At this table, if anyone wished to eat the word of God, they were fed by the speeches of the Law and the Prophets set before them. 

<margin>Origen</margin>
Origen believes this is the table of which Solomon speaks: "If you sit to dine at the table of a ruler, understand diligently what is set before you and stretch out your hand, knowing that it is necessary for you to prepare such things." But when the Savior says, "When you eat and drink at my table," what else do we understand by "His table" except the place where He teaches the knowledge of things to those who are worthy and able to grasp the word of wisdom? Solomon testifies to this in Proverbs regarding Wisdom, saying: "Wisdom has built herself a house and sup-

<column-break/>

ported it with seven columns; she has slaughtered her victims, mixed her wine in a bowl, and prepared her table." Therefore, all of Scripture is the "table of Wisdom."

## Theorem Ten.

->The Vulgate edition.<-

<margin>Romans 11</margin>
¶ For who has known the mind <note>original: "sensum"; sense or understanding.</note> of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? Or who has first given to Him, that it should be repaid to him? For from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things: to Him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

->Understanding from the Greek.<-

¶ For who has known the mind <note>original: "mentem"; the Greek 'noun' is often translated as 'mind' or 'intellect'.</note> of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? Or who has first bestowed a gift upon Him, that it should be repaid to him? Because from Him and through Him and into Him are all things: to Him be glory forever. Amen.

### Exposition.

<margin>Origen</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' depicting two figures in an outdoor setting with a tree.</image-desc>
Concerning this, it is written in Isaiah that it is manifest that God alone is the one who knows all counsels, and thus He is the one who needs no one else, because all things are from Him. By this, His counsel cannot be grasped or measured by anyone. You see how, in these final words, he shows that in everything he said above, he has set apart the mystery of the Trinity. As it says in the present passage: "For from Him and through Him and in Him are all things." As Origen writes, this agrees with those words which the same Apostle mentions in other places when he says: "there is one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." And again, he says that all things are revealed by the Spirit of God. By this, he designates that the providence of the Trinity is in all things. So too when he speaks of the "depth of riches," he signifies the Father from whom all things come; and the "depth of wisdom" signifies Christ, who is His wisdom; and he shows the "depth of knowledge" to be the Holy Spirit, who knows even the deep things of God. Furthermore, when he says "from Him," it indicates our very existence; "through Him" indicates that we are in life through His providence; and "in Him" indicates that the perfection and end of all things will be in Him at that time when God will be "all in all." And then to Him be glory forever. Amen.

<margin>Augustine in the treatise on Psalm 5.</margin>
Therefore, do not say there are two or three gods. As Augustine says, the Trinity itself is one God. It is not that the same Trinity can sometimes be called Father, sometimes Son, and sometimes Holy Spirit—as the heretic who tells fables <note>A reference to Sabellianism, a heresy that claimed God is a single person who simply changes "modes" or "masks."</note> believes. Rather, the Father is nothing but the Father, the Son is nothing but the Son, and the Holy Spirit is nothing but the Holy Spirit. And this Trinity is nothing but one God. For when the Apostle said "From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things," it is believed he was suggesting the Trinity itself. Yet he did not follow this by saying "to *them* be glory," but "to *Him* be glory." This Trinity is one God, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things. Thus, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each have full substance, and together all are one substance. The Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son; but...

<margin>Augustine, Book 1 of On Christian Doctrine.</margin>

### ¶ The Eleventh Theorem.

#### ¶ The Vulgate edition agrees with the Greek.

<margin>To the Romans 14.</margin>
¶ Blessed is he who does not judge himself in what he approves. But he who wavers <note>original: "discernit"; implies one who hesitates or makes a distinction in his mind out of doubt</note>, if he eats, he is condemned: because it is not from faith. For everything that is not from faith is sin.

### ¶ Exposition.

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a portrait of a tonsured man in profile within a circular medallion.</image-desc> When you do anything / whether you eat / or drink / or approve anything else: that is, when you attempt to do or omit something. The Apostle calls one "blessed" if, out of the fullness of faith, you do not judge yourself to be acting badly / or do not doubt / or hesitate that you are sinning in the very thing you attempt. Each person is subject to their own judgment, as Ambrose wrote; the Apostle considers that person to be condemned who does what he feels he ought not to do. He calls that person blessed who does nothing other than what he approves as useful for himself. And he who judges that he should not eat, yet eats, is condemned. For he condemns himself when he does that which he asserts is useless to him. Certainly, he does not eat from faith who denies it should be eaten and yet eats. Rightly, the Apostle also calls this "sin": to act otherwise than what one has approved. For the Romans had been led into the Law <note>The Jewish Mosaic Law regarding clean and unclean foods</note>: but when those arrived who believed more correctly, questions were raised about eating or not eating meat. And the group among them who said it should be eaten (and not merely approved) seems better, because all things are very clean. He calls those "weak" <note>original: "infirmos"</note> who would deny meat should be eaten, whether from the Jews or the Gentiles: and he leaves them to the purpose of their own heart. For it does not hurt not to eat, nor does it profit toward God to eat: lest those bound by their own reasoning should sin by eating with a scrupulous conscience. But the Apostle says: "Whether you eat, or whether you drink: or whatever else you do: do all for the glory of God." But someone might ask (says Origen) whether the things heretics do—since they act according to what they believe—should be thought to be done "from faith." Or, because the faith among them is bad, should everything they do be pronounced as sin because it is not from faith? I think (he says) that their state should be called "credulity" rather than "faith." Just as false prophets are sometimes called "prophets" by a false name / and false knowledge is called "science" <note>referring to 'knowledge falsely so called' in 1 Timothy 6:20</note> / and false wisdom is abusively named "wisdom": so too is the credulity of heretics falsely named

<margin>Origen</margin>

---

<header>Book Two. folio 13.</header>
<page-num>folio 13</page-num>

faith. Whence (he says) it must be seen whether perhaps even if some good work seems to be done among them, because it is not done from faith, it is turned into sin. There is also sometimes a chastity that is not from faith, at least among those who attend to "seducing spirits and doctrines of demons," speaking lies in hypocrisy, having a seared conscience / "forbidding to marry and abstaining from foods which God created." There is therefore a false faith of those who have "suffered shipwreck concerning the faith." There is also a false wisdom, namely of this world, and of the prince of this world, which shall be destroyed. For just as pirates are accustomed to light a lamp at sea in shallow places and hidden rocks through the darkness of night, so that they may invite those sailing—under the hope of reaching a harbor of safety—to the shipwrecks of destruction; so too is that light of false wisdom or false faith lit by the princes of this world and the spirits of this air, not so that men might escape, but so that the men of this world might perish while sailing the waves and the sea of life. Concerning these pirates (he says) Job also said: "The arrows of his pirates <note>original: "pyratarum"; a variant or interpretation of the Hebrew "raiders" or "troops" in Job 19:12</note> have come upon me." For this reason, surely, the Apostle Paul himself says: "even Satan transforms himself into an angel of light." Therefore, we who are sailing the waves of this life must not believe every light—that is, every wisdom—but as the Apostle warns, "test the spirits, whether they are from God." Therefore, we ought to pray without ceasing for the help of the Lord, and hope that He will snatch us from the "snare of the hunters," so that we too may say: "our soul is snatched like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare is broken and we are delivered." And as it is held in the book of Sentences by Prosper: <margin>Prosper.</margin> All the life of infidels is sin: and nothing is good without the Highest Good. For where the knowledge of the eternal and immutable truth is lacking, there is false virtue even in the best of morals.

# ¶ The Theorems of Saint Paul

¶ For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing: but to us who are being saved, it is the power of God. <note>original: "potestas dei"</note> For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and I will reject the prudence of the prudent. ¶ The foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

-> Exposition <-

<margin>Saint Ambrose</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial M. Inside the letter, a crowned king (likely David) sits on a throne, holding a scepter.</image-desc>**I**t is clear: that those for whom the cross of Christ is foolishness are in a state of destruction: for they have not been rescued from the death below <note>Hell or the grave</note>: and to those who believe, it is the power of God. They believe in Him (as Ambrose says) not that the cross of Christ is a weakness, but a power. They understand that death was conquered on the cross; those who have its sign are saved, because they cannot be held by death. For He destroys the wisdom of the wise when He does the very things they deny can be done. Moreover, He rejects the understanding of the prudent who call God "unconcerned" <note>original: "incuriosum"; a reference to Epicurean or Stoic ideas that God does not interfere in human affairs</note>; He proves His involvement through those things they think are foolish: such as the Son of God being incarnated from a virgin and crucified for human salvation—a fact truly witnessed by power, not just words. ¶ Having said these things, He attacks both the Jews and the Gentiles: because the scribes of the Jews and the teachers of the law think it is foolish to believe that God has a Son. In a similar way, the Gentiles also consider this a matter for laughter. But the Jews distrust it because it is not so openly signified in the Law. The Gentiles, however, judge it foolish because the reasoning of the world does not accept it (it says nothing can be done without physical mixing <note>original: "commixtione"; referring to natural biological reproduction</note>). Yet here is the investigator of this age: who decides that the world is driven by the constellations, and that rising and setting are caused by the twelve signs of the zodiac, thinking through his calculations that nothing at all can happen without their motion. And the wisdom of this world has been made foolish: thinking itself to be wise, it has been found to be thick <note>original: "dens[a]"; meaning dense or spiritually dull</note>.

<margin>Augustine from Book 10 of *The City of God*.</margin>
For what he judged impossible has been declared possible. For God, as Saint Augustine writes, destroys and rejects from among them that wisdom which He Himself gave: but specifically that which those who do not have His wisdom arrogantly claim for themselves. Whence, having mentioned that prophetic testimony, the Apostle follows and says: Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. For indeed the Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom. But we (the Apostle says) preach Christ crucified—a stumbling block to the Jews, and foolishness to the Gentiles: but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. This "foolish" and "weak" thing they despise, as if they were wise and strong in their own power.

<margin>From a sermon of Augustine on the Gospel readings.</margin>
But this is the grace that heals the weak—not those boastfully flaunting a false happiness, but rather those humbly confessing their true misery. And if you ask: Who are these people? Perhaps they are those who, disputing much about God, said false things. Inflated by their own doctrines, they were least able to find and know God; and in place of God (whose substance is incomprehensible and invisible)

---

<header>Second Book. Folio 14.</header>
<page-num>Folio 14.</page-num>

they thought God was the air, the ether, or that God was the sun.

# ¶ The Second Theorem.

-> ¶ The Vulgate and Greek editions agree. <-

<margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin>
¶ We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery <note>original: "ministerio"; though the text says "ministerio" (ministry/service), the context and standard Vulgate "mysterio" suggest the hidden wisdom of God's plan</note> which is hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory: which none of the princes of this world knew; for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory—as it is written: what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love Him. But God has revealed them to us through His Spirit: for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God.

-> Exposition <-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial M. Inside the letter is a woodcut illustration of a man in robes looking upward, perhaps a saint or person in prayer.</image-desc>**I**t is manifest that this is not the wisdom of the princes of this world, who are destroyed by it. For Christianity extinguished the errors they inserted there—namely, idolatry, greed, and other vices; just as the Apostle John said, "For this the Son of God came, to undo the works of the devil." Therefore, he [Paul] testifies that he was sent to manifest the hidden meaning which neither princes nor powers knew, nor the world heard, and which it therefore considered foolish because it was unknown. However, it is rational and salvific, as witnessed by its power, to which all the intention of human reasoning yields.

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
Therefore, as Saint Ambrose writes, the wisdom of God is hidden, not in words, but in power: it is not possible by human reason, but believable by the efficacy of the Spirit. Indeed, it is so much the true wisdom, and is declared to have always been with God, that it is said to be predestined before the ages for our glory—we who believe. For God, foreseeing the future errors in the world He was about to make, decreed this for the confusion of those who would make foolishness their wisdom, but for the glory of us who were going to believe and do believe. Unless He were both the Son of God and the Son of Man because of the "form of a servant" which He took—He who is the Son of God because of the "form of God" in which He exists—the Apostle would not say (says Augustine) regarding the princes of this world:

<margin>Augustine in the first book on *The Trinity*.</margin>
"For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." For He was crucified from the form of a servant; and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For such (he says) was that assumption <note>The Incarnation</note> which made God man and man God. For behold, we have said: because according to that which is God, He glorifies His own; according to this, He is certainly the Lord of glory. And yet the Lord of glory was crucified, because it is rightly said that even God was crucified—not from the power of divinity, but from the weakness of the flesh. For in Him alone is our glory, and in Him alone does he choose to glory who is predestined by God for the glory of all. And Paul glories not in himself, but in Him, and everywhere teaches that one must glory [in the Lord]. And if Herod and Pilate and the princes of the Jews had known Him to be God, they would never have crucified Him. For He was God, but (as the prophet Isaiah says) truly a hidden God. The princes of this world are not only men...

### The Theorems of Saint Paul / Book Two.
**Folio 15.**

<margin>
Ambrose
Luke 4:b
John 14:d
Luke 22:b
Matthew 27:c
6:c
</margin>
**S**aint Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Milan, a 4th-century church father</note> was of the opinion that the "princes of this world" should be understood as the Jews and the Romans. However, he also identifies them as those "principalities and powers" <note>original: "principes et potestates"</note> against whom we struggle—the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly realms—because it was by their counsel and will that Christ was crucified. Indeed, after the temptations, the devil "departed from him until an opportune time" [Luke 4:13]. And the Lord himself said: "the prince of this world comes, and in me he finds nothing" [John 14:30]. Therefore, the "princes of this world" crucified the Lord of Majesty <note>original: "dominum maiestatis"</note> through ignorance. For how could the leaders of the Jews be understood as the "princes of this world" when they were subject to the Roman Empire? Furthermore, the Roman leaders did not truly crucify Christ of their own will, since Pilate said, "I find no cause of death in him," and even washed his hands, saying to the Jews, "I am innocent of the blood of this just man; see to it yourselves" [Matthew 27:24]. Moved by this reason, Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage</note> wrote in his *Apology* against the Gentiles (chapter 21, near the end) in favor of Pilate: "Pilate, who was already a Christian in his own conscience regarding Christ, sent word to Tiberius Caesar." He adds that the Caesars might have believed in Christ if either Caesars were not necessary to the world, or if Christians could have been Caesars. 

<margin>The Great Tertullian</margin>
These are the things Tertullian wrote in favor of the Christians. However, because I have found such things written about Pilate nowhere else, I do not think he should be believed. Indeed, Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History"</note> reported that he found in the histories of the Greeks and Romans that Pilate, deserving such an end to his life, killed himself with his own hand. Therefore, Ambrose says it was those "princes" whom Christ triumphed over in himself who crucified the Lord. Mark the Evangelist says of the demons: "they knew that he was the Christ, Jesus." They knew indeed who he was:

<margin>Saint Ambrose</margin>
the one who had been promised in the Law. Yet the "mystery" <note>original: "mysterium"</note> of him, by which he is the Son of God, they did not know. This is also what Peter the Apostle said to the Jewish people: "I know, brothers, that you did this evil through ignorance, just as your princes did"—though he does not say "princes of this world." If, therefore, the servants killed the Lord through ignorance, it should not be credited to the Father. But one is not permitted to be ignorant; and although they did not know he was the Lord, they were not unaware that they were doing a wicked thing. Nevertheless, the "Lord of Majesty" is said to be crucified, even though he cannot die. But because "the Word was made flesh" <note>John 1:14</note>—that is, the Son of God was incarnated and made man—death is ascribed to him. This is because the Jews were not merely pursuing the flesh, but the one who worked through the flesh. Thus, although the Lord of Majesty is a stranger to death, yet according to the desire of the Jews and the prince of this world, they killed the Lord in the flesh. And if the princes of this world did not understand God made man, how much less did ordinary men? But if his words caused offense or scandal, faith should not have been denied in the face of his powers and signs. For power should have been set before human weakness and ignorance, and that which seemed impossible to human reason should have been believed. Therefore, for those who love God—that is, those who believe—he prepared a home, of which the Apostle speaks through the prophet Isaiah: "What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him" [1 Corinthians 2:9 / Isaiah 64:4].

<column-break/>

<margin>Augustine in a sermon on the birthday of a martyr.</margin>
"The eye has not seen," says Augustine, "because it is not a color; the ear has not heard, because it is not a sound; it has not entered into the heart of man, because it is not an earthly thought." Understand in this way what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered the heart of man: those things which God has prepared for those who love him. "What more," he asks, "do you seek from me, O man? Ask him who has taken up residence within you." I also say this: we are asking what specific good God keeps for the righteous, if he distributes so many good things to both the wicked and the righteous. And when he said, "what eye has not seen," there are those who say, "What do you think it is?" Behold what it is that God keeps for the righteous alone, whom he himself has made righteous. Behold, our reward is defined briefly by the prophet: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people" [Jeremiah 31:33]. "I will be their God"—he promised us himself as our reward. Why look for anything else, if you have found something better? If I said he promised gold, you would rejoice; but he promised himself, and you are sad? If a rich man does not have God, what does he have? Do not seek anything from God except God. Love him freely; you will love him freely if you desire only him from himself. Do not fear poverty. He gives himself to us, and he is enough for us. He gives himself to us, and he is enough for us. Listen to Philip the Apostle in the Gospel: "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us" [John 14:8].

## ¶ The Third Theorem.

### ¶ The Vulgate Edition.

<margin>1 Corinthians 5</margin>
**I**t is widely reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles: that someone has his father's wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be taken away from your midst. For I, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, him who has so acted. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together with my spirit, by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, you being in agreement with my spirit, I would deliver him with the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### ¶ Understanding from the Greek.

**I**t is generally reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication that is not even named among the Gentiles: that someone should have his father's wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather groaned so that the one who admitted to this crime might be removed from the midst of you. For I, as if absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as if present, him who has so worked this: that in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, you and my spirit being in agreement, I would deliver him with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ to Satan himself for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

### ¶ Exposition.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul. Book Two.
**Folio 16.**

<margin>Ambrose: *On Duties*</margin><image-desc>Decorative initial C containing a woodcut of a crowned king holding a scepter.</image-desc>When the act of that fornication <note>Referring to the man in 1 Corinthians 5 who was living with his father’s wife</note> was known, the apostle willed that he should be expelled from the assembly of the brotherhood. Indeed, he publicly held his stepmother in the place of a wife; in which matter there was no need for witnesses, nor could the crime be managed by any evasion. Therefore, he says he is **absent in face [body], but present by the authority of the spirit** <note>original: "absens facie: presens autem autoritate spiritus"</note> which is never absent. Since all carnal pleasure is from the devil, it is through this that when one is released to this pleasure, he is **delivered to Satan**. For the flesh, as Saint Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Milan (c. 340–397), a Doctor of the Church</note> bears witness, has this in its nature: that it perishes. Therefore, when the soul joins itself to the desire of the flesh, weakening its spiritual vigor, it suffers destruction at the same time. Thus, if this man, having been seized for the disgrace he committed, were to feel shame at being cast out, he would not perish, as repentance would follow.

For by the consensus of all, he was to be cast out from the church not only by the presence but also by the power of the Lord Jesus—that is, by the judicial sentence for which the apostle acted as an ambassador. When he is cast out, he is **delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh**. Indeed, he destroys both soul and body when things are done against the law. But in this case, the destruction of the flesh is assigned to the Lord in another way. For although all sins produce a carnal man, this desire of the flesh is specifically that which delivers the soul, spotted with filth, together with the body to Gehenna <note>a place of spiritual punishment or hell</note>; because when the soul is conquered by the lust of the flesh, it becomes flesh—just as a rightly governed body is called spiritual. Yet it is the soul which, either conquered by allurements, makes the whole man fleshly, or remaining in the vigor of its own nature, provides for the flesh so that it may be called spiritual. The aforementioned contaminated man is delivered to Satan so that **the holy spirit may be safe** <note>original: "spiritussanctus salvus sit"</note> in the days of the church at the day of judgment. "Unless," says Ambrose, "he had been cast out, the spirit of the church would not be safe on the day of judgment." For the cause of contamination would desert everyone; so that on the day of the Lord, being found naked of the Holy Spirit, they might hear <margin>Matthew 7:d, Romans 8:b, Ephesians 4:g</margin> from the Lord Judge: **"Depart from me, I never knew you."** As he says to the Romans: **"If anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he is not his"**; and in another epistle: **"Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God."** For if he is grieved, he deserts, and one will not be safe—not certainly for himself, who is incapable of suffering, but for us to whom <margin>Augustine: *Against Faustus*</margin> he was given, so that through him we might be proven to be sons of God. For a thing that is lost is not safe—not certainly for itself, which must be wherever it is, but for the one by whom it is lost.

Thus plainly and not cruelly, according to the authority of Saint Augustine, the apostle delivered the man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh so that the spirit might be safe on the day <margin>This is from Augustine: *Sermon on the Mount*</margin> of the Lord Jesus. He delivered others as well, so that they might learn **not to blaspheme**. And if the heretics do not wish to understand "death" here (for perhaps it is uncertain), let them at least confess it to be some sort of vengeance enacted by the apostle through Satan. That he did this not with hatred but with love is made manifest by the addition: **"so that the soul may be saved,"** striking the one whom he delivered to the power of the demon so that the body which he had used badly might be visibly tortured as an example to others, and lest the soul—the image of God—which had been conscious of the evil deed, should perish for eternity. For who would not be deterred from committing some crime if he saw someone, on account of a similar

<column-break/>

deed, already being miserably tortured, possessed by the Lord? <note>i.e., by the Lord's judgment</note>

->### ¶ Theorem Four.<-

->#### ¶ The Vulgate Edition.<-

**All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> will be brought under the power of none. And elsewhere: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but not all things edify.**

->#### ¶ Understanding from the Greek.<-

**All things are in my power, but not all things are profitable: all things are in my power, but I will be brought under the power of none. All things are in my power, but not all things are beneficial: all things are in my power, but not all things edify.**

->#### ¶ Exposition.<-

<margin>From Augustine: *To Pollentius*</margin><image-desc>Decorative initial I with a woodcut of a scholar or evangelist seated at a lectern, holding or writing in a book.</image-desc> We can distinguish between that which is lawful and that which is not lawful, and therefore not expedient, by a certain boundary. Those things seem to me to be lawful according to the mind of Augustine, and yet not expedient, which indeed permit justice (which is before God), but on account of giving offense to men, they ought to be avoided lest they impede salvation. However, those things are not lawful, and therefore not expedient, which the very principle of justice forbids, so that they should not be done even if they are praised by those who have knowledge of them. If this is so, then unlawful things are forbidden by the Lord for this reason: so that those things which are lawful but not expedient might be avoided not by the bond of law, but by the free benefit of love.

According to the Greek translation, however, the apostle can be explained differently, as our Stapulensis <margin>Faber Stapulensis</margin> <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536), a French humanist and theologian who sought to reform the church through a return to the original Greek of the Bible.</note> wrote. For it was in the power of the apostle both to refresh his belly with a variety of food and drink, and to be distended by excessive eating, and to commit fornication, and other such things that belong to the flesh; but he was brought under the power of none of these. For he clung to reason and the spirit; and he who clings to the spirit clings to God; and also because those things are not profitable. For both the foods which are for the belly and the belly which is for the foods, God will destroy both. This opinion seems easier than the common one, because, as Augustine bears witness, it is difficult to define by any universal rule the difference between that which is illicit (and therefore not expedient) and that which is licit and yet not expedient. For someone might say that everything which is not expedient to do is a sin. Furthermore, sin is illicit. Therefore, everything that is not expedient is illicit. And where will those things be which the apostle said were lawful but not expedient, if everything that is not expedient is not lawful? Wherefore, because we cannot doubt that the apostle spoke the truth, and we do not dare to say that some sins are lawful, it remains that our Stapulensis has established his opinion upon a rock; or shall I say, with Augustine and Ambrose and others among whom the Vulgate edition is confirmed, that it is accepted that something may be done which is not expedient, and yet if it is lawful, it is not a sin—though since it is not expedient, it certainly ought not to be done. If this were absurd...

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of 1 Corinthians 6, specifically addressing the distinction between what is lawful and what is "expedient." # The Theorems of Saint Paul.

It seems that something may be done which is not expedient, yet it might be said that the one who did it has not sinned. This should be understood from the common use of reason, which is so broad that we even say pack animals <note>original: "iumenta", beasts of burden</note>—who lack reason—"ought" to be beaten when they "do wrong." However, sinning in the proper sense belongs only to one who uses the rational judgment of the will. Among all mortal living things, this has been divinely granted only to man. But it is one thing when we speak strictly, and another when we borrow or misuse words by transferring them from other things. Therefore, if we wish to find the mind of the apostle—since we cannot doubt that Paul spoke the truth as an apostle not from man but from God—we do not dare to contribute anything of our own. It remains for us to say, following the understanding of Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536), a pioneering French humanist and theologian</note>, that it is a general principle from the Greek <note>original: "ex greco esse catholicam"</note>, or to distinguish it by some certain end: as has already been said, between what is permitted and what is not permitted, and therefore what is not expedient. For that distinction of Augustine’s was piously devised, but perhaps does violence to the literal text. 

We ought, therefore, to rightly boast of our craftsman <note>referring again to Lefèvre d’Étaples</note>, who has published so many immortal monuments for our instruction and that of posterity—especially because he made the letters of Paul Latin, and now clarifies the understanding from the Greek, and now corrects the Vulgate interpretation. For we know in what thickest night <note>a common humanist metaphor for the "Dark Ages"</note> these things once lay hidden. O blessed city, not only for the fact that you will inhabit it, but o all of Gaul <note>France</note>, which is decorated by such a man! He is worthy of the greatest praises because he has restored philosophical eloquence—which Gaul had suffered through during the times of the Goths, Vandals, and "Owls" <note>original: "bubonum," likely a derogatory term for scholastic philosophers</note>—or rather (what is much worse), he has restored the best literature, which was in its greatest bloom before those calamitous ages. For it is more excellent to form the souls of citizens than to build their minds.

### Fifth Theorem.

### The Vulgate and Greek editions are similar.

<margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin>
Every sin, whatever a man does, is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body.

### Exposition.

<margin>Saint Augustine</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut historiated initial letter E containing a scene of a scholar or saintly figure seated at a desk or in a landscape, possibly studying or writing.</image-desc>It appears the apostle wished to emphasize the evil of fornication to such an extent that, in comparison to this fornication, he said all other sins are to be considered "outside the body." He said that whatever other sins exist, only in this evil of fornication does one sin against his own body. As Augustine writes, this is because the pleasure of the body holds its servant and makes him a captive with a greater heat of lust—than which there is none higher. These things are said concerning the specific fornication of this body; for in the Holy Scriptures, fornication is rebuked and named not only specifically, but also generally. And that is also a general

<column-break/>

**Book Two. Folio 17.**
<page-num>fo. xvii.</page-num>

fornication of the human soul, by which anyone who does not adhere to God adheres to the world. Whence John says: *If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.* And the apostle James says: *Do you not know that the friendship of this world is enmity with God?* Here the apostle shows, as Saint Ambrose writes, that this is the gravest 
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
sin, because from this the whole body perishes. In other sins, a portion perishes, not the whole. For the "whole body" is the man and the woman, because the woman is a portion of the man. Whoever commits any other sin, sins outside himself; but the fornicator sins against his own flesh. 

Consider if a man ends his life with a noose, or slaughters himself with a blade: he does not seem to sin against his own body <note>in the specific sense Paul means</note>, but rather against the soul to which he does violence. But to fornicate is a corporal offense, which touches both body and soul. For it is not without the desire of the flesh—since the flesh has its own movement—that the soul lusts so that it sins against the flesh, even though without the soul nothing can be done. Therefore, through that which he does against the flesh (which is of himself), he sins; for he has referred it back to its origin. He is said to sin against his own body so that he might cease from fornication as if sparing himself. Again, it seems to some that he who fornicates is said to sin against his own body because he is a member of the Church; thus, by contaminating himself, he sins against the Church of which he is a member. Therefore, it must be said to the one who is a member of the Church when he fornicates: that he sins not for himself, but against the Church. 

Furthermore, the apostle says that he who fornicates sins against his own body through that by which he offends against his own "portion" <note>his partner or his own physical self</note>. Other sins, even if they are generated through the body, do not—as Saint Ambrose says—
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
make the soul so stupefied and indebted to carnal concupiscence in the same way that the use of lust causes the soul to be mingled with the body itself in the act of carnal fornication. For the soul is glued to the body to such an extent that in that very moment, a man is permitted to think of or intend nothing else; for that very submersion and absorption of lust and carnal desire subjects the captured mind to itself.

And I do all things for the sake of the gospel, that I may be made a participant in it.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul
## Understanding from the Greek.

¶ For though I was free from all, I made myself a servant to all, so that I might gain more: to those who were under the law, I became as if under the law, so that I might gain those who were under the law; to those outside the law, I became as if outside the law—though I was not outside God’s law but within the law of Christ—so that I might gain those outside the law. To the weak, I became as if weak, so that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, so that by all means I might save some. Moreover, I do this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may become a partaker in it.

¶ Exposition.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or saint, within an architectural frame.</image-desc>

He says he has become a servant of all in this way: he always showed a humility similar to all those who were weak in mind, so that through patience he might strengthen them for future salvation. He nurtured the souls of those who were either sinning or following divine matters too slowly, so they would not take it harshly when they were corrected. This should not be seen as if he were merely pretending to be all things to all—as flatterers are accustomed to do—but it is not so. For a man of God and a spiritual physician, knowing the causes and wounds of everyone, nurtures them with great diligence and feels compassion for them. For we have certain things in common with all people.

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
He therefore became like a Jew to the Jews because (as Saint Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Milan (c. 339–397), an influential Latin Church Father</note> concludes) he circumcised Timothy to avoid offending them, and he entered the temple purified so they would not find an occasion to blaspheme because of him. He did something that ought to have already ceased, but he did it according to the law. For he agreed with them that the law was from God and the prophets, and from that point, he showed them that Christ is the one who was promised. To ensure his agreement was effective, those who are under the law are identified as Samaritans.

<margin>Who the Samaritans are.</margin>
For they receive only the Law, that is, the five books of Moses. They are, however, of Persian and Assyrian origin; the King of the Assyrians placed them there to inhabit the lands of Samaria after the children of Israel were taken into captivity. Therefore, they also worship fire according to the custom of the Persians. To these people, the Apostle—while not denying that the Law was from God—became as if under the Law. But through that law, he taught them that Christ was to be sent, or was sent in the Word, just as that Samaritan woman did who said to the Lord:

<margin>John 4:25</margin>
I know that the Messiah is coming—having been taught by the law.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Saint Augustine also says that it is one thing to be *under* the law, another to be *in* the law, and another to be *without* the law. The carnal Jews are *under* the law. Spiritual Jews and Christians are *in* the law. Thus, the former kept the ancestral law of Moses, but they did not impose unusual burdens on the believing Gentiles. Therefore, those who were circumcised did not try to undo it, nor were the uncircumcised forced to be circumcised. Those *without* the law are the Gentiles who have not yet believed, with whom the Apostle testifies he harmonized through merciful compassion, not through crafty deception. That is, he helped the carnal Jew or the pagan in the same way he would have wished to be helped himself if he were in need—carrying

<meta>catchword: carrying</meta>

---

<header>Second Book. leaf 18.</header>
<page-num>18</page-num>

their weakness through the likeness of compassion, not deceiving them with a false fiction—so he says. With the Jews, he made himself similar in food and drink and in all things that could not hinder the gospel, so that he might acquire the Jews for Christ. With the Gentiles, he also made himself similar in food and drink and other things, so that he might associate the Gentiles with the flock of Christ. And to those weak in the flesh, he was as one surrounded by the weakness of the flesh—though he was spiritual—in order to lead them toward the spirit. He conformed himself to all where there was no sin, so that he might save all, and above all so that he might be a partaker of the gospel. For this is the reward he expects from all these efforts. And as Blessed Ambrose writes: Paul agrees with them—that is, with the Gentiles—according to natural philosophy and reason.

<margin>Saint Ambrose</margin>
That the world was made by God, as were the things within it, and that the soul is immortal, and that we have our origin from Him. (As he said in the Acts of the Apostles: "And as some of your own have said: for we are also his offspring.") In this way, he became as if without the law, through which he introduced to them that Christ himself is the one whom God chose to judge the world, and that He is the one through whom He made all things. And he became weak when, for the sake of weak brothers, he abstained from lawful things so as not to cause them to stumble. This was the mark of a prudent and spiritual man: that though he became all things to all, he did not exceed the boundaries of religious purpose. For where he yielded, he yielded so that he might make progress; and he did nothing other than what the law commanded.

## ¶ Theorem 7.

### The Vulgate and Greek editions agree.

<margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin>
¶ A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God. But the woman is the glory of the man. For the man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man; for the man was not created for the woman, but the woman for the man. Therefore, the woman ought to have a veil over her head, also because of the angels.

¶ Exposition.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a figure in profile, likely a theologian, within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

Although man and woman are of one substance, nevertheless, because the man is the head of the woman, he is traditionally placed before her. He is greater by way of cause and tradition, not by substance. Therefore, the woman is inferior to the man. She is derived from him, and because of this, the woman is seen to be indebted to the man, being subject to his authority. He says the honor and dignity of the man prevent him from covering his head. For it is not fitting for the image of God to be veiled; it ought not to be hidden.

<margin>Stapulensis</margin>
But Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a French humanist scholar</note> does not explain Paul in quite this way. Man and the angels were created immediately by God; therefore, man should have no veil in the symbol of this relationship where he is connected to God, no differently than the angels. But the woman, he says, must have one not only because of the man, but also because of the angels. For it would be pride if she made her creation equal to that of the angels, since she holds this power through the mediation of the man. Man was made immediately by God as His image and...
