<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the Epistles of Saint Paul, specifically interpreting the eleventh chapter of 1 Corinthians. It follows a discussion on pastoral humility and transitions here into a debate regarding the "Image of God" and the necessity of ecclesiastical trials.</meta>

# The Theorems of Saint Paul

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
<margin>3 Esdras 4</margin>
...the likeness of God is for His glory; but the woman, with the man acting as a medium like a veil placed between her and God, has a sort of partition and covering. For the man is the first and immediate glory of God; the woman is the mediated and second glory, and the immediate glory of the man, created for the man's sake. So says that author. However, Saint Ambrose explains the Apostle differently, and I believe we should adhere more to him. Even if we owe much to our homeland, I believe truth must be placed before all things, which sacred scripture affirms is great and stronger than all else. <note>original: "magnã 7 prę omnibus fortiorẽ". This refers to the famous debate in the apocryphal book of 3 Esdras (or 1 Esdras in modern Bibles), where it is concluded that "Truth is great and strongest of all."</note> For the whole earth calls upon the truth; even heaven blesses it; and all works are moved and tremble at it; and there is nothing wicked with it. Someone will perhaps say: "Has not your Smith followed the truth here?" <note>The "Smith" (Latin: *Faber*) refers to Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a prominent French humanist and theologian whose commentary on Paul was highly influential and sometimes controversial.</note> To whom we shall respond that the Smith neither fights against the truth but defends it, though sometimes he has remained silent about it; for (as Horace says) "sometimes even good Homer nods." <note>A classical idiom meaning that even the most talented people make mistakes.</note> And according to that saying of Varro: "No one can ever know everything." While the Smith understands the "angels" <note>Referring to 1 Cor. 11:10, "A woman ought to have a veil on her head because of the angels."</note> to be spiritual substances, Ambrose says the "angels" are the bishops, just as is taught in the Revelation of John. And since they are indeed men, they are rebuked for not correcting the people, and what is right in them is praised. Therefore, he says, the woman must veil her head because she is not the [primary] image of God, but to show she is subject. And because transgression began through her, she must have this sign: so that in the church, out of reverence for the episcopal office, she does not have her head free but covered with a veil. Nor should she have the power to speak, because the bishop holds the person of Christ. Therefore, as if before a judge, so before the bishop, because he is the vicar of the Lord; because of the original guilt, she must appear subject. There is a great difference between the glory of God and the glory of man. For man was made in the image of God, not woman. Yet the image of God is in the man because one God made one man, so that just as all things are from one God, so all people would be from one man; thus one visible man would have the image of the one invisible God on earth. So that one God might be seen in one man to preserve the authority of a single origin, to the confusion of the devil, who—neglecting the one God—wished to usurp dominion and divinity for himself. This is what the prophet Ezekiel signifies. And the Apostle says the same: for he says, "so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God." If man alone is the image of God and not woman, what shall we say to this: if, in her own person, the woman fulfills the image of the Trinity? Why, when she is taken from the side of the man, is he still called the image? Or if even one person of a human can be called the image of God from three [faculties], just as in the supreme Trinity itself each person is God, why is woman not the image of God? Now, for this reason, she is commanded to veil her head; because he is the image, he is forbidden. But it must be seen, as it pleases Saint Augustine, how what the Apostle says is not contradictory (that the man, not the woman, is the image of God) with what is written in Genesis: "God made man in the image of God; he made him male

<column-break/>

**Second Book. folio 19.**
<page-num>xix</page-num>
and female (he made them and blessed them)." Indeed, he says that human nature itself was made in the image of God, which is completed by both sexes. Nor does he separate the woman from being understood as the image of God. I believe, therefore, it is what I have already said when I was dealing with the nature of the human mind: that the woman along with her husband is the image of God, so that the whole substance is one image. But when she is assigned as a "helper" (concerning that specific role), she is not the image of God; however, what pertains to the man alone is the image of God, as full and complete as when joined with the woman in one. Thus says Augustine.

### Theorem 7.
->**The Vulgate and Greek editions do not differ.**<-

<margin>1 Corinthians 11</margin>
First of all, when you come together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and I partly believe it. For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you.

### Exposition.
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting two men in a landscape, one holding a digging tool like a spade, appearing to be working in a field or garden.</image-desc>
<margin>Augustine in book 18 of The City of God.</margin>
The race of heretics is crafty: not with the spirit of wisdom, but of impatience, by which the beginnings of heretics usually boil over and disturb the peace of the saints. According to that word of the Apostle: "There must also be heresies," etc. Hence it is also said: "The learned son will be wise, but he will use an imprudent servant." For many things (Augustine says) pertaining to the Catholic faith, while they are stirred up by the crafty restlessness of heretics so that they may be defended against them, are considered more diligently, understood more clearly, and preached more urgently; and the question arising from the movement of the adversary provides an occasion for speaking. But the "bad brother" is a boy (that is, a servant) to his brothers in his own work: when the good knowingly use the bad for the exercise of patience or for the advancement of wisdom. I know, says Ambrose, that some <margin>Saint Ambrose</margin> who are corrupt in mind by the craftiness of the devil say: "It is necessary for there to be heresies." He did not certainly will it or hope for it, but because they exist, Paul said they would be in the future, just as the Lord did. He says, "It is necessary for scandals to come," and "the Son of Man must suffer," foreknowing that Judas was going to be the betrayer. God sometimes permits schisms and heresies to be among you, so that the worthy may be made manifest among you; for just as fire takes nothing away from gold but makes it more brilliant and proves it to be genuine and not at all counterfeit, so he who is not shaken among schisms and heresies but remains firm in the traditions of the Church is proven faithful.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul

<margin>Cf. 1 Corinthians 14</margin>

¶ He who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit. What then is to be done? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind.

¶ The spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets.

->¶ Exposition<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial N featuring a figure in scholarly or clerical robes holding a book.</image-desc>
For he who desires to speak in tongues ought to pray that he might receive the gift of interpreting, so that his study may benefit others. For it is manifest that our mind is ignorant if the tongue speaks what it does not know, just as Latin-speaking men are accustomed to chant in Greek, being delighted by the sound of the words, yet not knowing what they are saying.

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
The spirit—or as it pleases the divine Saint Ambrose—which is given in baptism, knows what the soul prays while it speaks, or when the tongue prays in words unknown to itself. But the God who is the mind is without fruit. <note>Ambrose is distinguishing between the "spirit" as a gift of the Holy Spirit and the "mind" as the human faculty of understanding.</note> For what fruit can he have who is ignorant of what he says? When someone speaks in a tongue that he knows, he prays both with the spirit and with the mind: for not only is his spirit given that which it says—which happens in baptism when one prays—but the mind is also not ignorant of the psalm in a similar way.

<margin>Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book 12</margin>
Here, however, this spirit, as the divine Saint Augustine writes, is distinguished from the mind by very evident testimony. "For if I pray," says the Apostle, "in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful." Wherefore, he says, it appears that prophecy pertains more to the mind than to that spirit (which in a certain proper way is called "spirit"), which is a certain power of the soul inferior to the mind, where the likenesses of bodily things are expressed. Therefore, Joseph was more of a prophet, who understood what the seven ears of grain and the seven oxen signified, than Pharaoh, who saw them in his dreams. For the spirit of the latter was formed so that he might see, but the mind of the former was illuminated so that he might understand. And through this, "tongue" was in the latter, but "prophecy" in the former; because in the one was the imagination of things, but in the other was the interpretation of those imaginations. In the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*,

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine writes thus: The spirit is not a third substance in man, as Didymus contends; but the spirit is the soul itself because of its spiritual nature. It is called "soul" (*anima*) because it animates the body for the sake of giving life. However, we understand the "spirit" introduced by the Apostle alongside the soul and body to be the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle prays may persevere whole in us, lest by our vice it be diminished or driven from us; for the Holy Spirit will flee from a deceitful person. When the Apostle says, "and the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets," he says this because it is one and the same Spirit who pours Himself out, according to the reason and quality of the causes, both upon the prophets who tell of future things and upon those who reveal the scriptures. Therefore, Ambrose says it is "subject to the prophets" so that He might kindle their talents and help the efforts of the spirit with hope. He assists the best desire for narrating the things of God, so that He may fulfill the will of a good purpose. For the same was said of the Savior: they drank

<column-break/>

# Book Two
<page-num>Folio 20</page-num>

from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ. This "being subject" is the same as "following." For He followed so that, when human help failed, He might be present to grant assistance. So too the spirit is said to be "subject" so that He may help good efforts when He suggests them. For he who perfects the beginnings of another is seen to be "subject."

### ¶ Theorem 1
<note>The original text uses "Theorema.r.", where 'r' likely stands for the first in a series or 'Responsio'.</note>

->¶ The Vulgate edition is the same as the Greek.<-

¶ When, however, all things shall have been subjected to Him, then the Son himself will also be subject to Him who subjected all things to Himself, so that God may be all in all.
<margin>Cf. 1 Corinthians 15</margin>

->¶ Exposition<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial F featuring a figure seated at a desk writing in a large book.</image-desc>
The Son, according to the dispensation <term>dispensation: the plan or arrangement of God's actions in human history, here referring to Christ taking on human flesh</term> of the flesh, will be subject; but according to His divine hypostasis <term>hypostasis: the distinct personhood of Christ as the second person of the Trinity, equal to God the Father</term> and the form of God, He reigns over all things with the Father as the Son of God, who is God. He is all things in all, God in God, and reigning over all. Those who contend that the Son of God is not equal to the Father are accustomed to use this testimony quite frequently. For no error could arise more pale under the name of Christian than from not understanding the scriptures. For they say: "If He is equal, how will He be subject?" Which is certainly similar to that question in the Gospel: "If He is equal, how is the Father greater?" For the Lord Himself said, "Since the Father is greater than I." The rule of the Catholic faith, as the most blessed Augustine writes, holds itself thus: that whenever

<margin>John 14</margin>
anything is said in the scriptures about the Son being minor to the Father, it should be understood according to His taking on of humanity. But when those things are said by which His equality is demonstrated, they should be accepted according to the fact that He is God. It appears, therefore, how it is said: both "the Father is greater than I" and "I and the Father are one"; and "the Word was God" and "the Word was made flesh"; and "He did not think it robbery to be equal to God" and "He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant." God is said to be "all in all" so that no one of those who cling to Him may love his own private will against Him. It is manifest to all what the same Apostle says in another place: "What do you have that you did not receive?" God the Father is "all in all," says Ambrose; that is, that

<margin>Saint Ambrose</margin>
every creature may feel as one, and with one voice every tongue of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth may confess that there is one God from whom all things are. When, therefore, he says "all in all," he signified this: because from Him...

# The Theorems of the Divine Paul / Book Two.

...are: and in them He is. From Him and by Him all things were created. In them, by the confession of all, God will be one. If, however, he had said "so that God may be in all," one might understand that He is indeed in all things, but only through affection or a common sense, and not that those very things are from Him. But when the Smith <note>original: "faber"; referring to the scholar Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples</note> says that the Son of God, who is God, is in all things—all things being in God—God reigns over all; and in the creatures He is a creature, subject to God as a creature, yet as the head of the creatures. I think the Smith, along with Propositivus, Nicholas of Cusa, and the ancient theologians, has posited Him as both Creator and creature. But since "Christ" is a name of a person <term>suppositum; a technical term in scholastic theology for a distinct individual substance</term> representing the second person of the Trinity, it does not seem possible to call Him a creature, but only the Creator. For He Himself said: "Before Abraham was made, I am." For that human nature according to which Christ is man is neither Christ nor the Creator, but is the nature assumed by God, according to which the Son of God is called man.

<margin>The Son of God, Christ, is called Creator, not a creature.</margin>
<margin>Cardinal Cusanus, in his work, says He is also a creature, but such a creature that He is also the Creator; Creator and creature without confusion. See his *On Learned Ignorance*, Book III.</margin>

### Theorem XI.

#### The Vulgate Edition.

> We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (for the trumpet shall sound), and the dead shall rise again incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For it is necessary for this corruptible body to put on incorruption, and this mortal body to put on immortality.

#### The Understanding from the Greek.

> We shall not all indeed sleep: but we shall all be changed, in an indivisible moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; it shall sound, and the dead shall rise again incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For it is necessary for this corruptible body to put on incorruption: and this mortal body to put on immortality.

#### Exposition.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'R' containing a woodcut illustration of a person's head and shoulders, appearing like a saint or scholar in profile.</image-desc>
The Greek codices, as the venerable Bede writes, have it thus: "We shall all indeed sleep, yet we shall not all be changed." This change <note>Latin: "commutationem"</note> must without doubt be understood as a change for the better, because both the just and the unjust are going to rise again. But as the Lord speaks in the Gospel: "those who have done good unto the resurrection of life; those who have done evil unto the resurrection of judgment," calling eternal punishment "judgment." Just as in another place He says: "He who does not believe is judged already." Therefore, those who are to rise for judgment will not be changed into that incorruption which cannot suffer the corruption of pain. For that belongs to the faithful and the saints. But those others will be tortured by perpetual corruption, because "their fire shall not be extinguished and their worm shall not die." What, asks Augustine, does this distinction mean: "and the dead shall rise incorrupt, and we shall be changed," unless it means that all shall rise incorruptible, but the just shall also be changed into that incorruption which no corruption can possibly harm? And because of this, those who are not changed into it,

<column-break/>

will indeed rise incorrupt in the integrity of their limbs, but not in a way that avoids the corruption of the pain of punishments when they hear: "Depart into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels." From which evil hearing the just man will not be afraid. Regarding that change of the just, when he had said "and we shall be changed," as if we were asking how this happens or what kind of change it will be, he adds and says: "For it is necessary for this corruptible body to put on incorruption, and this mortal body to put on immortality." Perhaps someone will say against the Smith <note>Lefèvre d'Étaples</note> that the Greek codices, as Bede reports, have it: "We shall all indeed sleep"; why then did the Smith put:

<margin>An answer on behalf of the Smith.</margin>
"We shall not all indeed sleep"? He himself will answer that in the Greek copies this is consonant with the words of the Apostle. For the Apostle, by the Lord's revelation, says in another place: "For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who live, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have slept," etc. Therefore, those who are snatched up alive will not die. For death is the separation of the body and the soul; but the coming of the Lord will be in a momentary instant, which the Lord Himself expressed saying: "For as the lightning comes from the east and appears even to the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be." And the resurrection is in a moment, in an indivisible point; for as the Apostle says here: "in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead shall rise incorruptible." Also, the divine Ambrose

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
says that all men shall rise, but only those who are to reign in glory will be changed. Or he says it thus: "We all shall rise who are found dead at the coming of Christ; not all who are found in the body will be changed, because the saints alone follow the glory of blessedness." The "last coming" of Christ is understood. "The dead" or "sinners" are to be understood as those who, even while living, are said to be dead; they rise to punishment or are immortal so that they rise without any diminution of limbs. Or certainly, he says simply that all the dead rise, and only the saints, along with those who are found just and living, are changed into glory, so that the causes of death having been emptied by divine victory, it is as if death were swallowed up and does not perish.

### Theorem I.

#### The Vulgate and Greek editions agree.

> To some indeed the odor of death unto death: but to others the odor of life unto life.

#### Exposition.

<margin>Divine Ambrose.</margin>

The Apostle says this because to the unbelieving, the preaching of the cross of Christ is the odor of death. Hearing the word of God, says Ambrose, they receive it as if it were a pestilence from which death arises; and it is necessary that it happens to them according to their faith. But because faith is the word heard, it is the messenger of eternal salvation, and it will happen to them according to their faith. Whether therefore in those who perish, or in those who are saved, the good [odor] of Christ...

### Theorems of Saint Paul

<margin>Ezekiel 3:17-21</margin>
The apostles were a sweet fragrance to God because they preached sincerely and without flattery. Those who did not believe were entangling themselves in a snare, even as they were free, just as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: "Preach; if they hear you, you will have gained their souls; if they do not, they will have seen to themselves, yet you are delivered from their perdition." The preaching of the truth is the "good odor of Christ," and he who serves and lives according to the good morals of the Gospel receives this odor unto life.

<margin>From the book of sentences by Prosper of Aquitaine.</margin>
But he whose life disagrees with his good words incurs death. As Prosper writes, this condition also binds the listeners: when right preaching is heard by some through unbelief, it is received unto death; by others through faith, it is received unto salvation.

# Second Theorem.
->The Vulgate edition is the same as the Greek.<-

<margin>2 Corinthians 5:20-21</margin>
**Be reconciled to God. For him who knew no sin, he made to be sin for us: that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.**

### Explanation.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring a male figure in a garden or forest setting.</image-desc>
Indeed, it is said "from sin" <note>original: "A peccato"</note> because the very thing offered for sin was itself called "sin." Hence we find that passage in the Apostle concerning Christ the Lord: "Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us." God the Father made his Son to be sin for us—that is, a sacrifice for sin. In the same way, the lamb in the burnt offerings was treated as the sin itself—meaning it became the sacrifice for sin. Just as it is said of the ram that follows in the story of the Savior: as if it were the "salvation" itself, when in fact it is

<margin>Augustine, Book 2 against Maximian.</margin>
the sacrifice of salvation, which he later makes clear by repeating it. For he also calls that "for sin" which he had previously called "unto salvation." For how (as Augustine writes) should we remember him saying that Christ, though he was not a sinner, was "made sin" for us? Read the Law more diligently, he says, and lest you perhaps encounter a faulty manuscript or a Latin translator who has erred, look at the Greek and you will find not that Christ *committed* sin for us, but that he was *made* sin by God the Father—that is, a sacrifice for sin. Therefore, he himself did not commit sin, but God made him sin for us; this is to say, He designated him a sacrifice for sin. For if you recall or read again, you will find in the books of the Old Testament that sacrifices for sins are called "sins."

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
As Saint Ambrose writes, Christ was made the "cause of sin" <term>cause of sin: here meaning the one who takes on the legal debt or penalty of sin</term>, though neither the chance nor the dignity of being born a man touched him. Because all flesh is under sin, he was therefore made flesh, and thus "made sin." And because he was offered for sins, he is not undeservedly said to be "made sin," because even the victim in the Law which was offered for sins was called "sin." This was so that we might become the righteousness of God in him who knows no sin, as Isaiah says: "He who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth," was killed as if he were a sinner, so that he might justify sinners before God in Christ.

# Third Theorem.
->The Vulgate and Greek editions differ little.<-

<margin>2 Corinthians 12:2</margin>
**I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago (whether in the body I know not, or**

---

<header>Second Book.</header>
<page-num>folio 22.</page-num>

**whether out of the body I know not, God knows) such a one caught up even to the third heaven. And I know such a man (whether in the body or out of the body I know not, God knows) that he was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.**

### Explanation.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' showing a man kneeling or sitting by a tree, possibly in prayer.</image-desc>
What is meant by the statement "he heard ineffable <note>original: "ineffabilia," meaning unspeakable or beyond description</note> words which it is not lawful for a man to utter"? I truly think that those words were of such a kind and such a nature that a mortal man could not express them. The Apostle says he was caught up twice (as Ambrose writes): first from here to the third heaven, and then into the celestial paradise, of which the Lord spoke to the thief, saying he would be with him in the paradise of the Father; there where the city of God, Jerusalem our mother, is said to be. What wonder is it then if, after the resurrection, a body already purified, refined, and made immortal is believed to be in the heavens, since the Apostle does not doubt that even a mortal body could be lifted to the heavens and taken into the celestial paradise of God the Father? This was for "such a man," meaning one who is already worthy of God. He says this so that he might be seen to glory in this experience, yet he does not wish to speak openly of himself, lest he seem to be praising himself. Even John the Apostle, when he knows he is speaking of himself, says "this is the disciple whom Jesus loved," who also leaned back on his chest at the supper, so that he would not seem to speak gloriously of himself.

Augustine raises the question of how the substance of God itself could be seen by certain people while still in this life, given what was said to Moses: "No one can see my face and live," unless the human mind can be divinely snatched <note>original: "rapi," the root of 'rapture'</note> from this life into the angelic life before it is released from the flesh by common death. For in this way, he was "caught up" so that he heard there ineffable words that it is not lawful for a man to speak, where there was such a turning away of the focus from the senses of this life that he did not know whether he was in the body or out of the body. That is, whether his mind was alienated from this life into that life by a more vehement ecstasy while the bond of the body remained, or whether a total dissolution had occurred such as happens in full death. Thus it remains true that "no one can see my face and live," because it is necessary for the mind to be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the ineffability of that vision. It is not incredible that for certain holy people, not yet so dead as to be corpses for burial, this excellence of revelation was granted. 

If we correctly understand the "first heaven" as everything corporeal—whatever is above the waters and the earth; and the "second heaven" as that spiritual realm perceived in bodily likeness (such as the vision where the vessel full of animals was let down to Peter in an ecstasy); then the "third heaven" is that which the mind beholds—so secret and remote, and so entirely snatched from the senses of the flesh and purified—that it is able to see and hear ineffably those things which are in that heaven: the very substance of God and the Word-God through whom all things were made, in the charity of the Holy Spirit. We believe not incorrectly that the Apostle was caught up there, and perhaps there lies the "paradise of paradises." For if the joy of a good soul is in good things among all creatures, what is more excellent than that joy which is in the Word of God, through whom all things were made?

# Theorems of Saint Paul

<margin>Galatians 1</margin>
### First Theorem.

-> The Vulgate and Greek editions are entirely similar <-

**Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father who raised him from the dead, and all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age <note>original: "seculo nequam"</note> according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.**

### Explanation.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'I' depicting a bearded figure, likely St. Paul, seated in an interior with arched windows, writing at a desk with a book and lectern.</image-desc>
In this letter, he writes to those who had already been warned by the authority of those coming from the Jews, who were compelling them to observe the Law. They had begun to believe those people, thinking that Paul the Apostle had not preached the truth because he did not want them to be circumcised. Therefore, he began in this way: **I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you into the glory of Christ, to another gospel.** Thus, in this opening of the case, he briefly suggested through the salutation itself—when he calls himself an apostle not from men nor through man, which he is found to have said in no other letter—that those who were persuading them of such things were not from God but from men. He also showed that he should not be considered unequal to the other apostles regarding the authority of the Gospel testimony, since he knew himself to be an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.

<margin>Augustine, Retractations, chapter 22.</margin>
Saint Augustine explained this letter in a single volume, in which he says that the earlier apostles were truthful in that they were sent not from men but from God through a man—specifically, through Jesus Christ while he was still mortal. However, the last apostle <note>referring to Paul</note> was sent through Jesus Christ who was already "wholly God" after his resurrection on account of his immortality. As Augustine writes in the first book of his *Retractations*, Christ is called "wholly God" because of what he began to have after the resurrection: not on account of his divinity <note>which he always had</note>, but because of the immortality from which he never departed. In that state, he was fully God, and yet he had still been the one who died. Now, however, the meaning of what follows is made manifest: he adds that the other apostles were sent through Jesus Christ while he was still partially "man," that is, mortal. The last apostle, Paul, was sent through Christ

<margin>Notably Augustine says: "as if he were not man"; because Christ is truly God-man, but he is seen as such only according to his humanity.</margin>
who was already wholly God—that is, immortal in every part. For he said this, Augustine explains, to expound on the Apostle's words: "not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father." It is as if Jesus Christ were no longer a man. It follows that "he raised him from the dead," so that it might appear from this why he said "not through man." Therefore, on account of his immortality, Christ the God is now "not man" <note>in the sense of being no longer a mortal man</note>; yet, because of the substance of his human nature in which he ascended into heaven, the man Christ Jesus is the mediator between God and men. For he will come in the same way they saw him going into heaven. Saint Ambrose also says that the Apostle testifies he was not chosen or sent to preach by men, as were some who, chosen by the apostles, were sent to strengthen the churches. Nor was he like others who were sent by the Jews

<meta>catchword: sent-</meta>

<column-break/>

<header>Book Three.</header>
<page-num>folio 22.</page-num>

to disturb the churches, whom he calls "false apostles." Instead, he was sent by the Son of God. In this context, he seems to deny that Christ is a "man" because he gave the commands as God, not as a man. Whomever Christ chose, he chose by divine judgment, by which Paul signifies that he is a fit and steadfast preacher. For it is certainly much better that God chose him rather than a man; and so it is true. By mentioning "the dead," he condemned two heresies: the Manichaeans and the Photinians. 

<note>The Manichaeans were a dualistic sect that often denied the physical reality of Christ's body; Photinians followed Photinus of Sirmium, who denied Christ's pre-existence and divinity.</note> 

The Manichaean denies that Christ is a man but does not deny he was crucified; the Photinian does not concede that Christ is God, yet he does not dare to deny that he raised his own body from the dead. Like the Manichaean, when he does not deny the crucifixion, he seems foolish for not confessing him as Lord; and the Photinian, through a certain impiety, denies the God who he confesses raised himself from the dead. For he had read the saying: **Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.** He was saying this, however, about the temple of his body. Therefore, by raising himself from the dead, he signified that he raised his own body; nevertheless, he is said to have been raised by his Father. This is because all power of the Son is from the Father, so that the deeds of the Son are the deeds of the Father, from whom all things come.

...knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but only through faith.

->Explanation.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a circular frame with two seated figures in robes, possibly scholars or saints, engaged in discussion near a window.</image-desc> After the harmony of their fellowship and the respect for primacy which they mutually granted one another through the grace of God, a cause now intervened. Out of concern for the church, Paul says, "I resisted him to his face." What does this mean, except that I contradicted him in person? And for what reason did he stand firm? Because, he says, "he stood condemned" <note>original: "reprehensus erat"</note>—condemned, as Saint Ambrose <note>Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD) was the Bishop of Milan and a major influential figure in the early Church.</note> says, by the truth of the Gospel, which this action opposed. For who would dare to resist Peter, the first of the apostles (to whom the Lord gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven), unless it were someone else of similar standing? Someone who, knowing by the confidence of his own election that he was not inferior, could constantly disapprove of what Peter had done without counsel. 

As the same Ambrose writes, all the Jews who agreed with the "simulation" <note>In this context, "simulation" refers to Peter’s act of pretending to follow the Law only when certain people were watching.</note> of Peter and Barnabas acted in good faith; but because of the scandal caused by those coming from James—for they were zealots of the Law who revered both the Law and Christ with equal right, which is against the discipline of faith—they would not mix with the Gentiles when these people were present. They feared the bold attack of those who championed the Law. Had this been the only issue, it would not have been blameworthy; but Paul shows how this error affected those under them. For Peter himself yielded to the animosity and audacity of the Jews, fearing (as easily happens) that a scandal might arise that would be difficult to settle. He had even purified himself according to the Law under compulsion and circumcised Timothy against his own will. 

It would not have been an error for Peter if he had simply hidden his association with the Gentiles while the Jews were present to avoid scandal. But the entire cause for rebuke is this: when the Jews arrived from James, he not only separated himself from those with whom he had been living like a Gentile, but he also compelled the Gentiles to "Judaize" <term>Judaize: To adopt Jewish customs and ritual laws, such as dietary restrictions or circumcision, as a requirement for salvation.</term> out of fear of those men, so that the Gentiles remained ignorant of what the true good was. For they knew that Peter himself had not lived as a Jew among them; but later, hearing from him that the Jewish customs were to be followed, they naturally hesitated as to what was the truth. If it were true that one should live as a Jew, they held Peter to be a transgressor because he had lived like a Gentile. If, however, it were better and true to live simply, then the Gentiles were being overturned through his cowardice. To those from whom a good thing had been taken, a laborious and heavy burden was being delivered. Even when the Apostle Paul yielded for a time, he did not do so out of conviction, but cried out that it was a superfluous and vain thing to do, performed only because of the fury of the Jews. He would not have succumbed to the matter unless a cause had intervened in which the audacity of the Jews was boasting loudly. 

Now, Timothy was the son of a Jewish woman but a Greek father; hence it happened that as an infant he was not circumcised according to the Law. Therefore, spies were lying in wait to see if anyone who was a Jew by nature would accept an uncircumcised man, which they considered unlawful for the Jewish race. Seeking an occasion to hold Paul as an overturner of the Law, he yielded to their fury for a time. But because Paul said this to Peter in front of everyone, necessity compelled it...

<column-break/>

<margin>Saint Augustine in the explanation of the Epistle to the Galatians. John 21.</margin> ...so that all (as Augustine says) might be healed by his rebuke. For it was not useful to correct in secret an error that was doing harm in public. To this is added the weakness and charity of Peter, to whom it was said three times by the Lord: "Feed my sheep." <margin>Matthew 16.</margin> Afterward, for the safety of the flock, he most willingly endured such a rebuke from the shepherd himself. For the one who was rebuked was more wonderful and more difficult to imitate than the rebuker. It is easier to see what you should correct in another and to fix it by blaming or rebuking than to see what needs correcting in yourself and to willingly accept it, whether through yourself or especially through another—and even more so, to accept it in front of everyone. 

This serves as a great example of humility, which is the greatest Christian discipline; for charity is preserved by humility. <margin>Saint Augustine in the letter to Saint Jerome. And elsewhere in the same letter to Jerome.</margin> Nothing violates charity faster than pride. And therefore the Lord did not say: "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me how I raise four-day-old corpses from the tombs and drive out all demons and diseases from people's bodies," and other such things. Instead, he said: "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart." 

Elsewhere, Augustine says: If Peter did what he ought to have done, then Paul lied; for when Paul saw someone not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, whoever does to him what he ought to do, acts rightly. Therefore, he who says Peter did not act rightly—when he knows Peter did what he ought to have done—speaks falsely of him. But if Paul wrote the truth, then it is true that Peter was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel. I indeed (says Augustine) believe that Peter acted in such a way as to compel the Gentiles to Judaize; I read that Paul wrote this, and I do not believe Paul lied. Therefore, Peter was not acting rightly, because it was against the truth of the Gospel to think (and to lead others to believe) that they could not be saved without those ancient sacraments. 

This was shown to him by the "Antilogies" <note>likely referring to contradictory arguments or legal disputes</note> of those from the circumcision who had believed. Now (he says), if any Christian (even one from the Jews) should wish to celebrate such things in the same way, it would be like raking up dead ashes; he would not be a pious caretaker of the body, but a violator of the burial itself. At that time, Paul had seen no other of the apostles except James, the brother of the Lord. He saw James in Jerusalem, because he had been appointed Bishop there by the apostles. <margin>This is Ambrose’s opinion regarding Blessed James, against those who say Joseph was a young man when he was with the Virgin Mother of the Lord, and she remained a virgin in the Gospel.</margin> As Saint Ambrose writes, James himself had previously been an unbeliever, as the Evangelist says: "For not even his brothers believed in him yet." 

In the Gospel, it is said that this James was the son of Joseph, and is therefore called the "brother of the Lord" because Joseph was called the father of the Lord. Thus Mary says to Jesus in the Gospel of Luke: "Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow and sadness." <margin>Luke 1.</margin> And in the Gospel of John, Philip says to Nathanael: "We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph." <margin>John 1.</margin> In this way (he says), James and the others are called the Lord’s brothers, because Joseph was also called his father. Some, led by madness, claim with an impious assertion that these were true brothers of the Lord born of Mary, since they say Joseph was called his father but was not truly so. <margin>Isidore’s opinion on James the brother of the Lord.</margin> If these were his true brothers, then Joseph would be his true father; for the same one who called Joseph his father also called James and the others his brothers. Thus he concludes. Saint Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), a scholar and archbishop.</note> writes in the seventh book of the *Etymologies*, chapter 9, that James the son of Zebedee was the brother of John, who was killed by Herod after the Lord’s ascension; and there is another James, the son of Alphaeus, for the sake of distinction...

## ¶ The Third Theorem.

### ¶ The Vulgate and Greek editions agree.

<margin>Galatians 3.</margin>
¶ For whoever are of the works of the Law are under a curse. For it is written: "Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law to do them." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 27:26.</note> But that no one is justified by the Law before God is manifest, because "the just man lives by faith." However, the Law is not based on faith, but "he who does these things shall live in them." Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree," so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

### ¶ Exposition.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial Q containing the profile portrait of a man wearing a soft cap, likely a saint or scholar.</image-desc>
Those who act under the Law are under a curse, because transgressors of the Law are sinners. It is written in Deuteronomy: "Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law to do them," because if anyone should neglect anything of the Law, he would be considered cursed. And the commandments are so many that it is impossible to keep them. Hence Peter the Apostle says in the Acts of the Apostles: "Why do you impose a yoke on the brothers which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?" These things were given to a negligent and proud people so that they might have a law for every part of their conduct. And through this, he teaches that one must withdraw from the Law, lest the righteousness sought through faith should perish. For the Law is not of faith. For, as it pleases Saint Ambrose to say, the Law commands nothing to be believed, since all its things are manifest, so that he who keeps the Law may live.

<column-break/>

Otherwise, he must necessarily be punished, because he who knew what was to be avoided and yet committed it can be confronted (he says) from the opposite side and told: "If no one is justified in the Law, why is it that he who neglects something of the Law is cursed?" This is true: because no one is justified through the Law *before God*. He is, however, justified *before the world* so that he may be secure in this present life. But if he wishes to be justified before God so that it may count toward his merit on the day of God’s judgment, let him follow faith. Otherwise, though secure here, he will be guilty in the future. Therefore, the Law is profitable, but only that which is written on the tablets <note>Referring to the Ten Commandments.</note>. For the rest were given as a burden. And since no one could fulfill the Law, all were subject to the curse of the Law, so that it might claim vengeance against them. But Christ, born a man and offered by the Father for us, redeemed us from the devil. For offering himself to a willing death for those who were subject to the curse of the Law, he made him "a curse" <note>The author uses the neuter noun "maledictum" (a curse) to distinguish Christ from a "maledictus" (a cursed person), suggesting he took on the state of the curse without being a sinner himself.</note> as Ambrose writes in this way: just as in the Law a sacrifice offered for sins was called "sin," so for the sake of the cursed, he who was offered became "a curse." For he was also made a curse by the Jews while he was killed as if he were a sinner. Therefore, he did not say he was made "cursed" for us, but "a curse." For everyone who was offered to death on account of his own sin became "cursed." He died for his own cause. And if you look closely, you will see Christ was made the "curse" of those by whom he was killed. For the cross of the Savior is the sin and the curse of the Jews, because it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." <margin>Moses.</margin> Moses said this in Deuteronomy regarding those guilty of death, so that it would be sufficient for those suspended on a tree to remain there until evening and then be taken down for burial; because he who was suspended died on the tree, lest if he remained suspended longer, his death should hold greater reproach and become a stain upon his lineage if his death were publicized further. And through this, the innocent Savior suspended on the tree is not "cursed," but is the "curse" of those by whom he was suspended. However, as far as it pertains to the Jews, by offering him to Pilate to be killed as a sinner, they made him a curse, so that he was killed like a guilty man although he was innocent: because one worthy of death is cursed according to the Law. Seeing many flocking to his teaching, they were jealous, saying: "Behold, the whole world has gone after him." <margin>John 12. c.</margin> And through this, he is said to have been killed for us. And he was killed for us in a twofold way: for while they thought he ought to be killed so that he might not teach, they accomplished nothing; for both his doctrine grew and he emptied death of its power in his passion. For descending into hell, he liberated the human race, for which cause he also permitted himself to be killed, knowing it was for us against the devil; so that in the nations the blessing of Abraham might be made in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the blessing of the Spirit through faith. And he says this because, once the Jews were reproached and cursed—while they were flattering themselves regarding the righteousness of the Law—by the killing of the Savior as if he were guilty of violating the Sabbath, the blessing of the promise made its transition to the Gentiles through the faith of Christ Jesus. Whence the Lord says to the Jews: "The kingdom shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits." <margin>Matthew 21. a.</margin> Saint Augustine in...

# The Theorems of Saint Paul

In his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, he explains the Apostle’s statement in this way: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us," because <margin>Deuteronomy 21</margin> it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." <note>This refers to the crucifixion; the "tree" is a common biblical metaphor for the wooden cross.</note> For those who understand the spiritual sense, this sentence is a sacrament of liberty. However, for those who perceive it carnally—if they are Jews, it is a yoke of slavery; if they are pagans or heretics, it is a profound blindness. For even some of our own people, being less learned in the scriptures and fearing this sentence too much while still approving of the Old Testament scriptures with due piety, do not think this was said of the Lord, but of Judas his betrayer. For they say that it was not said, "Cursed is everyone who is fixed to a tree," but "who hangs on a tree," because it was not the Lord who was signified, but the one who hung himself with a noose. They err greatly (he says), nor do they notice that they are arguing against the Apostle, who says: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us." Because it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." Therefore, He who became a curse for us surely hung on the tree—that is, Christ—who liberated us from the curse of the law so that we might no longer be justified through fear in the works of the law, but <margin>Galatians 3:b</margin> by faith before God, which works not through fear but through love. For the Holy Spirit, who spoke this through Moses, foresaw both: that those who could not yet live by invisible faith might be guarded by the fear of visible punishment, and that He Himself might dissolve this fear by taking upon Himself that which was feared, so that, once fear was removed, He could give the gift of charity. Nor should it be thought an insult to the Lord that He is called "cursed" because He hangs on a tree. Indeed, He hung on the tree according to His mortal part. Whence mortality comes is well known to believers: it is surely from the penalty and the curse of the first man's sin, which the Lord took up, and He bore our sins in His own body upon the tree. If, therefore, it were said "death is cursed," no one would shrink away. But what else but the death of the Lord hung on the tree, so that by dying He might overcome death? Therefore, that same thing which was conquered is called cursed. Likewise, if it were said "sin is cursed," no one would wonder. But what hung on the tree except the sin of the "old man," <note>In Pauline theology, the "old man" refers to the unregenerate human nature prone to sin.</note> which the Lord took up for us in that very mortality of the flesh? Whence the Apostle did not blush or fear to say that He was "made sin" for us, adding: "so that He might condemn sin by sin." For would our "old man" not also be crucified together with Him—as the same Apostle says elsewhere—unless the figure of our sin hung in that death of the Lord, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin? In the figure of that sin and death, Moses also exalted the serpent upon a pole in the desert; for indeed, by the persuasion of the serpent, man fell into the damnation of death. Thus, the serpent was appropriately exalted on the wood to signify death itself; for in that figure, the death of the Lord hung on the tree. Nor was that bronze serpent made for any other reason than to signify faith in the permanence of the Lord’s passion. For even the common people say that things made of bronze

<column-break/>

fo. xxvi.
# Book Three

are those whose number remains; <note>The author is making a linguistic or symbolic connection between the durability of bronze and the enduring nature of faith.</note> but now the faith of the cross remains as if made of bronze, so that while some die and others are born, they may find that same sublime thing remaining, by looking upon which they may be healed. It is no wonder, then, if he calls "cursed" that which comes from a curse—He who saw death from death, sin from sin, and the serpent from the serpent. For death is cursed, sin is cursed, the serpent is cursed: and all these were triumphed over on the cross. Therefore, "cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." Because Christ justifies those believing in Him—not by the works of the law but by faith—the fear of the curse of the cross has been taken away.

<margin>Galatians 4</margin>
> ¶ You observe days and months and times and years. I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored in vain among you; become as I am, for I also am as you are.

### ¶ Exposition.

<margin>Saint Augustine on the Epistle to the Galatians.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'V' featuring a figure, possibly an angel or a scholar, within a scrollwork frame.</image-desc>
Very common is the error of the pagans, that either in performing tasks or in expecting the outcomes of their lives and business, they observe days, months, years, and times marked by astrologers and Chaldeans. <note>In this period, "Chaldeans" was a common term for practitioners of astrology or divination.</note> And not only do the pagans observe years and months, but also the Jews, as Augustine writes, <margin>Augustine in the book *Enchiridion*.</margin> they observe them slavishly in the carnal observation of the Sabbath, and the New Moons, <note>Jewish festivals marking the beginning of the lunar month.</note> and even the ninth month and every seventh year, which they call the Sabbath of Sabbaths. For those things which were shadows of things to come remained in superstition even after the arrival of Christ, since they were observed as if they were necessary for salvation by those who did not know better. And elsewhere he says: who would estimate how great a sin it is to observe days and months and years and times <margin>Augustine in the book to Januarius, book 1.</margin> as something significant, because they estimate times as favorable or unfavorable according to the vain doctrines of men? We must weigh the greatness of the Apostle’s fear; for he blames those (as the same Augustine writes elsewhere) who say: "Do not set out on a journey because it is the day after," or "because the moon is in such a phase," or "set out so that things may turn out prosperously because the position of the stars is such-and-hers." "Do not conduct business this month because that star is ruling the month for me," or "I will do it because it has taken over the month." "Do not plant a vineyard this year because it is an intercalary year." <note>A leap year or a year with an extra month added to the calendar.</note> However, no wise man thinks those who observe times are to be blamed when they say: "I will not set out today because a storm has arisen," or "I will not sail because it is the remains of winter," or "It is the time for sowing because the earth has been saturated by autumn rains." # The Theorems of the Divine Paul
## Book Four. Folio 27.

Other natural effects concerning the movement of air and moisture, which vary the qualities of the seasons, are noted in the most orderly rotation of the stars, about which it was said when they were created: "Let them be for signs, and seasons, and for days and years." <note>original: "Et sint in signis & tẽpibus & in dieb' & annis." This is a quotation from Genesis 1:14.</note> Days are observed (says Ambrose) when they say that one must not set out tomorrow, or that nothing should be started on the day after tomorrow. In this way, those who worship the months are often more deceived, such as those who scrutinize the course of the moon, saying, for instance, that on the seventh moon garments should not be made, or on the new moon a house should not be built or a slave bought. Because of these beliefs, misfortunes usually happen more easily. Seasons are observed in this way when one says "today is the beginning of spring," or "there is a festival," or "the day after tomorrow is the Vulcanalia," <note>The Vulcanalia was an ancient Roman festival in honor of Vulcan, the god of fire, held on August 23rd.</note> and such things; or "after such a time, one must not leave the house." They honor the years in this way when they say "on the Kalends of January <note>The first day of the New Year.</note> it is a new year," as if they were not completing a daily cycle, but rather to honor the memory of the two-faced one <note>original: "bifrontis." A reference to Janus, the Roman god of beginnings and transitions, usually depicted with two faces.</note>. This superstition is used by those who should be far from the servants of God. For if God is loved with the whole heart, and He is favorable, there should be no fear nor suspicion of these things; for whatever is done simply under devotion to God can turn out successfully.

### ¶ The Fifth Theorem.

#### ¶ The Vulgate and Greek editions differ very little.

<margin>Galatians 5</margin>
¶ **B**ut if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution? Then the scandal of the cross has been removed. I wish those who trouble you would even cut themselves off. <note>original: "abscindantur." St. Paul is using a harsh pun here; if they are so obsessed with the "cutting" of circumcision, he suggests they go all the way and emasculate themselves.</note>

#### ¶ Exposition.

<image-desc>A small woodcut of a bearded scholar or apostle, likely Paul, seated at a desk within a vaulted study.</image-desc>
What he says is clear: he was held as an enemy by the Jews, and they did not cease from persecuting him because he taught that circumcision no longer stood. Finally, with the Jews compelling him and frequently bringing false accusations against him, seeing a biased judge, he was forced to appeal to Caesar. Therefore, the scandal of the cross is made void. The preaching of the cross was a scandal <term>scandalum: a stumbling block or offense</term> to the Jews because it made void the Sabbath and circumcision. If he were to admit circumcision, there would be no scandal, and the Jews would be at peace with us. For they said of the Savior: "This man is not from God, who does not keep the Sabbath."
<margin>Augustine in his exposition on Galatians.</margin>
As to what he says, Augustine asks: "the scandal of the cross is made void." He repeats that sentence: "For if righteousness comes from the law, then Christ died for nothing." <margin>Galatians 2:d</margin> But here, because he names the "scandal," he calls to memory that the Jews suffered a scandal in Christ especially for this reason: because they frequently noticed him teaching to disregard and despise those fleshly observations which they thought they held for their very salvation. Therefore, he spoke as if he were saying: "Without cause, then, the Jews were scandalized and crucified Christ when he despised these things," if such things are still being persuaded to those for whom he was crucified. And he added with a most elegant ambiguity, as if speaking a blessing under the appearance of a

<column-break/>

curse: "I wish those who trouble you would be cut off." He says let them not only be circumcised, but cut off. For in this way they become eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and will cease to sow carnal things.

### ¶ Book Four of the Theorems on the Epistle to the Ephesians.

### ¶ The First Theorem.

#### ¶ The Vulgate and Greek editions are similar.

<margin>Ephesians 1</margin>
¶ Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavens in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless in his sight in love. Who predestined us to the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ in himself according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace.

#### ¶ Exposition.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a figure seated in an arched frame, similar to the previous image.</image-desc>
**H**e chose our leaders for us from eternity, before he made the beginnings of the world, who would be holy and spotless before God, burning with love for the Lord; so that through them all men might be adopted as sons of God in Christ the Lord, the proper and consubstantial Son. And through Christ, since the Father works all things, the foreknowing God (says Ambrose) knows all who would believe in Christ. 
<margin>Divine Ambrose.</margin>
Just as it says to the Romans: "Those whom he foreknew, he also called." And he called us, not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles. Those, therefore, whom God is said to call, persevere in faith; these are the ones he chose before the world in Christ, so that they might be uncontaminated before God in love. This means that the love of God makes their conduct holy. For no one obeys another better than the one who serves out of love. And he says that God foresaw that those believing in Christ would be adopted as sons to God, so that their head might be Christ, the true Son of God. But we have discussed predestination sufficiently in Book 1, Theorem 7.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul
->Exposition.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial U depicting a seated royal or divine figure, possibly God the Father, holding a globus cruciger and a scepter.</image-desc>
The soul of the people ought also to be one: because those things which he enumerates are of unity. For all things agree in one God as Father: because He owes what He is to no one. He said He is "above all," and "through all." He is through all because all things are from Him; and it remains necessary that He who is the source of all these things be above them. And He is "in us all," that is, in the faithful. For He is in us through confession, because we acknowledge Him, and because He gave us His Spirit, through whom He is undoubtedly in us. He is not in the pagans, because they deny that He is the Father of Christ. And lest the various gifts among men be thought to hinder unity, he clarifies that this is not the case; for in these gifts there is a diversity of duties, not of nature. He says that to each one, as much grace is given as the Lord deigned to bestow—yet not without a measure of equity, for He distributes to each according to their strength, so that each may drink <margin>h. 67. d.</margin> <margin>Saint Ambrose.</margin> as much as they thirst for. It is written in the Psalm: "Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." <note>A reference to Psalm 68:18, quoted in Ephesians 4:8.</note> However, these gifts (Ambrose says) He began to bestow after His triumphs; for He is the one who conquered death, being exalted on the cross, as He Himself said: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself." He despoiled the underworld when He took away those captives who were held in subjection due to the transgression of Adam or their own sins, provided they consented to Him, and ascending from there, He brought them into the heavens. From among these, some rising in their bodies appeared to many as a testimony to the defeat of death, so that those who perhaps would not have believed in Christ’s resurrection might be held accountable by the resurrection of those whom they knew were dead; for they saw those whom they recognized had lived long ago. Although captives are usually led unwillingly and as strangers, the Savior led His own even as volunteers. For by His appearance, while He stirs those desiring to be liberated, He is said to have "captured" them. "But that He ascended, what is it but that He also descended into the lower parts of the earth?" By judgment He was held among those in the underworld—a judgment that could not hold the Savior, because He conquered sin.

### Third Theorem.
->The Vulgate and Greek editions do not differ.<-

<margin>Ephesians 4.</margin>
> Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you are sealed for the day of redemption.

->Exposition.<-

<margin>Luke 15:b</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial C depicting a seated figure looking at an open book or scroll.</image-desc>
When we act well, the Holy Spirit given to us rejoices in us, seeing His warnings benefit our well-being, just as was said by the Lord: "So there shall be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance." Therefore, the Holy Spirit rejoices in our salvation, not for Himself—for He (as Saint Ambrose writes) does not lack joy—so, on the contrary, if we are not obedient to Him,

<column-break/>

He is "grieved"; not because He lacks progress, but because He wants us to belong to life. Yet He is not grieved in such a way that He suffers, since He is truly impassible <note>term: impassibilis. Meaning "incapable of suffering or changing," a standard theological attribute of God.</note>. But when He is said to be "grieved" because of our words or actions, it signifies this: that He abandons us because we have wounded Him by despising His warnings. Therefore, His "grieving" is our own indignation, which prevents us from being called children of God. For it is the Holy Spirit Himself who signifies the children of God by dwelling within us.

### First Theorem.
->The Vulgate and Greek editions are similar.<-

<margin>Philippians 2.</margin>
> For let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal to God: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and in habit found as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. For which cause God also hath exalted him, and hath given him a name which is above all names: that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth: and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

->Exposition.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial C depicting a bearded man in a scholar's cap reading a book.</image-desc>
When our Lord came into this world, He did not consider what was His own, but the interests of others and what would be our future goods. And He who was by nature the Lord of all came not to rule, but to serve those who are by nature servants. "The Son of Man," He says, "came not to be ministered unto, but to minister." Christ was always in the "form of God," because He is the image of the invisible God. But the Apostle (as Saint Ambrose writes) treats of the Son of God when He became incarnate as man, saying: "let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus," that is, concerning God and man. For although He was in the form of God, He certainly lived among men, appearing to be God by His deeds and works. For the "form of God" differs in no way from God. Therefore, He is called the form and image of God so that it might be understood that He is not the Father Himself, but is that which the Father is. Therefore, He "thought it not robbery" <note>original: "rapinam." The author argues that Christ did not "steal" equality with God, but possessed it naturally.</note> to be equal to God. For knowing Himself to be in the form of God, He did not commit a theft by saying, "I and the Father are one." And elsewhere, he says, for this reason they persecuted...

# The Theorems of Saint Paul
<margin>Saint Ambrose.</margin>
The Jews [persecuted] Jesus: because not only did he break the Sabbath: but he also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God. Therefore, by right, he equalized himself with God. For he who makes himself equal to one to whom he is inferior is considered to commit robbery <note>original: "rapinam" - a reference to Philippians 2:6, often translated as "a thing to be grasped"</note>. But to teach the law of humility to the Jews who were seizing him, not only did he not resist: but he emptied himself <note>original: "exinaniuit" - the theological concept of *kenosis*, where Christ sets aside his divine attributes</note>, that is, he withdrew his power from operation: so that, being humbled with his power idle, he might seem to be weakened, taking the form of a servant; while he is held and bound and driven by lashes even to the cross: made obedient to the Father to whom he knew he was equal. He did not maintain his equality for his own sake, but subjected himself. He teaches us to imitate this patience and humility, so that we do not prefer ourselves over our equals, but even bow ourselves down, following the example of our Creator. Yet the form of <margin>Ambrose says.</margin> God is said not to have been *received*, but rather that he *is* in the form of God; however, he *received* the form of a servant when he was humbled as if he were a sinner. For servants are made from sin: just as Ham, the son of Noah, who was the first to rightfully receive the name of servant. Christ truly has two natures in himself: divine and human. The divine is the "form of God"; the human—as our [scholar] from Étaples <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (Stapulensis), the author/editor of this volume</note> writes—is the "form of men." The divine is truth, the human is the divine image and likeness; the divine is the archetype and exemplar, the human is the figure. For it does not seem to me (Ambrose says), as it does to some, that he thus received the form of a servant merely when he was born as a man. For see what he says: "Have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus" [Philippians 2:5], that is, in God and man. For before the incarnation, he can be called either Christ or Jesus: because both names together signify both the Son of Man and the Son of God. For before his birth, it says among other things: "and the rock was Christ" [1 Corinthians 10:4]. And we do not tempt Christ as some tempted him; where, therefore, Scripture wants to signify either God or man, it places one of the two, either Jesus or Christ. For the Son of God, born as a man, was thus in the form of God: because although he appeared as a man, he performed the works of God, so that in the deeds accomplished it might appear that he was God, though he was thought by the Jews to be only a man. For the works signified his form, so that since his works are certainly not the works of a man, he who was in the work or form of God might be understood as God. For what is the "form of God" but an example? For he appears as God while he raises the dead, restores hearing to the deaf, cleanses lepers, and so on. But how is he said to have been "made like unto men" if he was only a man? And for what reason was he "found in appearance as a man," if he were not also God, except that whereas before he permitted himself to be lowered, he always appeared in power to the Jews; afterward he was weakened. He was found in the appearance of a man. For on the mountain <note>The Mount of Transfiguration</note> he appeared as if God: and walking on the sea with his feet, he was seen and understood not only as man, but also as God. Finally, what do those who were in the boat say? "Truly this is the Son of God." Therefore, when that power ceased, he was seen as a man. For this reason he says "as if" [quasi]: to signify this: that he is also God. For the sake of his weakness, he says that God was made like men, which he reveals in what follows, saying: he humbled <meta>catchword: himself</meta>

<column-break/>

# Book Four. fo. 29.
himself, being made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. This is what it means to be "found in appearance as a man": for retaining his power so that it might not appear in him, he was seen as a man and killed—he who does not know how to die.

Where the Vulgate edition says "and you, true companion" [germane compar], it seems that Paul is speaking to a woman rather than a man, which can be understood from what follows immediately: as to a woman, he commends other women living with her to be helped. Ambrose says he would not say "it is good for them to be as I" unless he were chaste in body. Nor would he say (he says) "I wish all men were even as myself." If he had a wife and said this, he would not have wanted them to be virgins: but let it be far from the truth! He [Paul] served the Spirit from his childhood so that he had no interest in this matter [marriage]. Indeed, as a young man he was anticipated by the grace of God; after saying that each has his own gift from God, he showed in which it is better to be more inclined: because a person is helped in that which they seem to desire with eagerness of mind. He said this here and elsewhere, that all the apostles except John and Paul had wives. <margin>The Holy Father Jerome.</margin> Likewise, another will object from the sayings of Jerome to Eustochium concerning the preservation of virginity, to whom writing he says: concerning virgins (says the apostle) I have no commandment from the Lord. # The Theorems of Saint Paul

[Paul] was a virgin not by command, but by his own will. And in the same place [Jerome] says that those who imagine he had wives are not to be listened to. Thus says the holy Jerome: "I would not deny that the most blessed Paul was a virgin and was a great and distinguished herald of virginity," for which cause he also endured bonds and prisons in Iconium <note>A reference to the *Acts of Paul and Thecla*, an early Christian story where Paul's preaching on virginity in Iconium leads to his arrest.</note>. But it is difficult to find this from the [original] author; neither could Ambrose or Jerome be considered primary authorities, writing as they did so many years after the memory of Paul. But does Paul not place himself among the virgins when he says to the Corinthians: *I wish that all men were even as I myself am*? And when he says again: *I say to those who are unmarried and to the widows, it is good for them if they remain even as I*? This is not entirely clear. For as Scapulensis <note>Possibly a reference to a specific commentator or a legal scholar of the period.</note> writes, in the first place he is speaking of those who had wives: who could not be like Paul in terms of virginity, but only in this respect: that even if they had a marriage bed, they might perpetually restrain themselves for the sake of prayer, the continual service of God, and the imitation of Christ the eternal king; just as Paul abstained from all female contact for those same reasons. and in the second place, he speaks of those who are without wives—which applies to the celibate and widows—and of women who are celibate and widows. Thus, from these passages, we do not find that he places himself among virgins any more than among those who are continent in marriage or among the celibate. Nevertheless, I frankly admit that Ambrose and Jerome were of the opinion that Paul did not have a wife. But those who defend the opposite view will deny that they are "imagining" that Paul had a wife. Should Paul not be heard, who seems to say this (as they clearly show)? Should the divine Ignatius not be heard, who was a contemporary of Paul and who saw Paul in the flesh? He places Paul among the married in his *Epistle to the Philadelphians*. <margin>Saint Ignatius.</margin> What then shall we do? We shall freely grant to Ambrose and Jerome that Paul was a lover of chastity and a virgin. But it is not so easy to claim he had no wife when the authority of the elders cries out against it. That point was also made more eloquently: the statement of Jerome or Ambrose there seems to have neither the authority of the elders, nor the reliability of eyewitnesses—such as the divine Ignatius was (which no one denies)—nor the reasoning of Scripture; but rather an arbitrary persuasion and a rhetorical style of speaking. Furthermore, Clement [of Alexandria], Bishop Eusebius, and almost all the Greeks wanted Paul not to be silent about the memory of his own wife, to whom he commends other women, especially so that he might be a help to those who labored in the Gospel. She is the one he greets along with the others in the farewell of the *Epistle to the Philippians* <note>Philippians 4:3, where Paul mentions a "loyal yokefellow" (Latin: *germane compar*), which some early fathers interpreted as his wife.</note>, adding what you can read in the new understanding from the Greek. For the Church does not condemn marriages, but subjects them [to God]; it does not cast them away but dispenses them, knowing that in a large house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Finally, the blessed Ignatius,
