in the fifth epistle cited just before, confirms the same opinion: namely, that marriage is to be honored, not rejected. "I do not disparage," he says, "the other blessed men who were joined in marriage, whom I now remember. For I pray to be found worthy of God following in their footsteps in his kingdom, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; as Joseph and Isaiah and the other prophets; as Peter and Paul and the rest of the apostles who were associated in marriage."

### The Third Treatise of the Fourth Book on the Epistle to the Colossians.

#### Theorem I.

#### The Vulgate and Greek editions are similar.

<margin>Colossians 1.</margin>
Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; for in him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and in him. And he is before all, and by him all things consist.

#### Exposition.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter F featuring a seated haloed figure, likely a Saint or Church Father, in a study or architectural setting with trees visible through an opening.</image-desc>
**T**he Son is the image of the Father, but a consubstantial <note>original: "consubstantialis" - meaning of the same essence or substance.</note> image; for you could not properly call him a "Son" if he were not consubstantial, and specifically so. For you would not call your image in a mirror a "son," because even if it is a natural image, it is nonetheless not consubstantial. Therefore, the Son of God is the image of the Father and a consubstantial image. And as Saint Ambrose writes: "The image of the invisible God cannot be visible, otherwise it would not be an image." For that which is invisible cannot be painted, nor can a visible person see an invisible one. For that which is seen is either a body, or a shape, or some formed substance which the sharp gaze of the eyes reaches—yet the whole is a body. But God, who is foreign to all these things, how can he have a visible image? But he is called so for this reason: so that the Son may be understood to be such as the Father is. Because he is from Him, and differs nothing from Him in the divinity of nature, he is called His image and form; this is so that another god might not be believed in by the unfaithful, since this [unity] is contained in the name itself. Therefore he is called the true Son of God, so that he may be believed to be from Him. But because of poor understanding, this was also added: that he be called His image, so that when he appears (though in human form, or certainly in fire, as he appeared to Moses), it is not the Father himself who is understood to be there, but the Son; and through the fact that he is His image, he is believed to differ in nothing from Him. Whence he says to Philip: "Philip, he who sees me, sees also the Father; why do you say, show us the Father?"

# The Theorems of Saint Paul | Book Four.

<margin>Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book One.</margin>
"Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me?" <note>original: "non credis quia ego in patre: et pater in me est"</note> This refers to the unity and substantiality of the Father and the Son, such that they exist within one another. Thus, whoever sees the Son also sees the Father. Certainly, by an understanding of divine works, they saw the Son—not with carnal eyes, but through the works the Son performed, which he declared to be the Father's, in order to show the unity of their power. In this same way, Jacob also saw [God], from which he received the name Israel, which means "one who sees God." <note>A traditional medieval etymology for the name Israel.</note> For this reason, he is called the "image of the invisible God," so that he himself might be understood as God, having been seen through the intellect. The Apostle testifies that the Son was begotten, not created, before every creature, in order to distinguish his birth from the making of a creature. And to make this completely clear, he added: "Because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth." This is so that the power of all things might be believed to be in him, and perfected by him, while all things are made through him. This means he is the head of all creation, because all things began to exist from him. Therefore, the things made by him are said to be "made through him," because he was already born so that he might create the world. He was in God and proceeded from God so that he might be one God; thus, there is neither a diminishing of the Father nor a development of the Son when he is born.

Ambrose says: He is "before all" in such a way that he alone is born of God the Father, from the unbegotten substance of God. These things, however, subsisted by his power which he has through his generation from the Father, not that they share a common substance with him. Rather, they began from nothing by the will of God the Father, with the Son acting as the agent. All things consist in him because without him they are nothing; for unless they are subjected to him, they wander in error and become liable to destruction. For he was born of the Father before all things so that he might create all things that did not exist. Furthermore, having taken on flesh, he was born of the Virgin, so that the sin which had entered the world through the virgin Eve might be abolished. Therefore, having been born and having died, he rose again, so that those things he first created he might later recreate. Because through error they were as if dead, he became the first and the prince in all things. According to his "form of God," it is said: "Before all the hills he begot me," <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:25, interpreted as the eternal wisdom of Christ.</note> that is, before all the heights of created things. And "before the morning star I begot you," that is, before all temporal things and time itself. But according to his "form of a servant," <note>A reference to the "Hymn of Christ" in Philippians 2:6-7, distinguishing Christ’s divinity from his humanity.</note> as Saint Augustine writes, it is said: "The Lord created me in the beginning of his ways." <note>Proverbs 8:22.</note> For according to the form of God, he said "I am the Truth," and according to the form of a servant, "I am the Way." Because he himself is the firstborn from the dead, he makes a path for his Church to the kingdom of God and to eternal life, for which he is the head, leading even the body to immortality. Therefore, he was created "at the beginning of the ways of God for his works." For according to the form of God, he is the "Beginning" <term>principium; the source or origin</term> who speaks to you, in which beginning God made heaven and earth. But according to the form of a servant, he is the bridegroom proceeding from his chamber. According to the form of God, he is the firstborn of every creature and he himself is before all and all things consist in him; according to the form of a servant, he is the head of the body of the Church.

<column-break/>

### Theorem Two.

#### The Vulgate edition differs little from the Greek.

<margin>Colossians 2.</margin>
> "Now I say this so that no one may deceive you with loftiness of words. For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your faith which is in Christ."

### Exposition.

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
He warns them lest their senses be led astray by the conversations of the wicked and by searched-out craftiness. For the "wise of the world" <note>referring to secular philosophers or sophists</note> strive to ensnare the souls of the simple with a certain art and with the minutiae of disputations, so that by the reasoning of worldly things they might draw them away from the hope that is in Christ. Whence (as Saint Ambrose writes), the Apostle says he is present there in spirit, so that having reverence for him before their eyes, they might abstain from such men. For if the spirit of the prophet Elisha saw the fraud of Gehazi, who went to Naaman the Syrian to receive in Elisha's name things that had not been commanded to him, and saw Naaman descending with a ready heart to give more than was asked—how much more could the Apostle see in the spirit those things he spoke of? <note>Ambrose compares Paul's spiritual insight to the biblical story in 2 Kings 5, where Elisha supernaturally perceives his servant Gehazi's greed.</note> For there was greater grace in the Apostles than in the Prophets. And to make them more ready regarding the tradition of the Gospel, he says he rejoices in the arrangement of their conduct, so that knowing how God is pleased, they might become firmer in that through which they were made worthy to learn the meaning for the benefit of their faith.

A response must be given to those men who seek to slander our books of salvation and learning: whatever they have been able to demonstrate about the nature of things with true evidence, we show is not contrary to our scriptures. However, whatever they have brought forth from any of their own volumes that is contrary to our scriptures—that is, to the Catholic faith—we should show [to be false] by some faculty. And as Augustine writes:
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
"Let us hold fast to our Mediator, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge," so that we are neither seduced by the loquacity of false philosophy nor terrified by the superstition of false religion.

### Book Five of the Theorems of the Most Blessed Paul
### on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.

### Theorem First.

#### The Vulgate and Greek agree.

<margin>1 Thessalonians 4.</margin>

# The Theorems of Saint Paul / Book Five.
### Folio 32.

For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a command, and with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord. <note>original: "Qm ipse dñs in iussu..." Reference: 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17.</note>

->Exposition.<-

<margin>Joshua 5.d. Saint Ambrose.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a male figure in academic or clerical robes seated at a desk, possibly representing a church father or the author.</image-desc>
For Christ the Lord himself, by the will of the Father, shall descend from heaven like the primary angel of God with a heavenly army—as is contained in the Apocalypse of John the Apostle—to wage war in the name of God against the Antichrist. Once the Antichrist is destroyed, the dead shall rise at his command. He is indeed, as he himself said to Joshua the son of Nun, the leader and prince of the Lord’s army <note>original: "dur et princeps exercitus dñi"</note>. For this reason (Ambrose says), he is called an "archangel." Furthermore, when he descends with the trumpet of God—concerning which both [the trumpet and the descent] are contained in the scriptures, such as in Exodus—we read that this "angel" appeared to Moses in a flame.
<margin>Exodus 3.b.</margin>
Immediately we recognize that God himself was present in those things—that is, the Son of God—as the same scripture says: "And Moses, going up, turned away because he could not look upon the face of God." He is called leader and prince because he is the head of all; for all things exist through him. But will those who are found alive at that time not die? This prophecy <note>original: "oraculum"</note> does not explicitly state this; rather, it says they will be caught up to meet Christ in the air. Nor does this contradict the article of faith left to us through the Holy Spirit, which says that he "shall come from thence to judge the living and the dead." By "the living," we understand those who will then be alive, and by "the dead," those who shall rise from the dead. Since it is appointed for all men to die once at the determined limit of death, is it any wonder if a dispensation is granted—due to the presence of Christ—to those who have not reached that limit, which by God's decree cannot be bypassed? Nevertheless, the Blessed Ambrose writes that in that very "catching up," death will occur as if through a sleep, so that the soul, having departed, may be restored in a moment; for when they are taken up (he says), they cannot be "dead" [in the permanent sense]. Concerning the resurrection of the dead, Saint Augustine writes that there will be a resurrection of all people; if it is for all, then all must die so that the death brought by Adam may rule over all his children. However (he says), there are other Catholic and learned men who believe that those found alive at the coming of the Lord will be changed toward incorruption and
<margin>Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.</margin>
immortality while the soul remains in the body; and this is counted as their "resurrection from the dead" because they lay aside mortality through a transformation rather than through death. Whichever view one accepts, he is not a heretic—unless he becomes a heretic through stubborn contention—for it is sufficient in the Church to hold to the resurrection of the flesh and to believe it will come from death.

### Second Theorem.

### The Vulgate Edition.

<column-break/>

Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. But test all things; hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every kind of evil. <margin>1 Thessalonians 5.</margin> And may the God of peace himself sanctify you in all things, so that your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

->Understanding from the Greek.<-

Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not look down upon the prophets. But examine all things; retain the good. Abstain from every appearance of evil. And may the God of peace himself sanctify you, having made you entirely complete, so that your whole spirit and soul and body may be kept without reproach at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

->Exposition.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' showing a man in robes inside a room; a window in the background reveals a landscape with trees and a building.</image-desc>
We should not extinguish the Spirit if anyone possesses faith, hope, and love, or devotion—which are gifts of the Holy Spirit. We must not quench them, but rather increase them if we can; for the graces of God, wherever they are found, must be magnified, and God must be worshiped in them. Let us not look down upon prophecies. For prophecies are for edification, and those who despise prophets despise the Spirit of God—the author of prophecy who searches the deep things of God and speaks mysteries through the prophets. Those prophecies which must especially not be disregarded are those contained in the Old and New Testaments; they are full of spiritual light regarding past and future times. All things (Ambrose says) <margin>Saint Ambrose.</margin> are said to be "tested"—the Apostle advises this—and whatever is found to be sober and blessed should be retained. For whatever is in harmony with the words of the Apostles and the Lord himself must be held as blessed and retained; but we must abstain from those things that appear hostile to the faith. For unclean spirits are accustomed to speak good things deceitfully, as if by imitation, and among these to introduce depraved things. They do this so that through the things that are good, the evil things might also be accepted; because they are thought to be the words of a single spirit, they are not distinguished from one another, but the illicit is commended by the authority of a name rather than the logic of virtue. They are accustomed to teach shameful and contrary things under the name of the Apostles and the Lord himself. Therefore, the Apostle advises that all things must be tested, because the words of the Lord cannot be contradictory—or as the Greek translation has it: "All things must be examined." From this also comes the Epistle of John the Apostle: "Do not," he says, "believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see if they are from God," because many may speak good things, but if they bring forth anything against God, it is known that it is not the Holy Spirit. For no error can be found in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the Apostle said that we should examine all things, and whatever is truly good—a true prophecy—we should retain. All things are therefore to be tried, tested, and examined; and if your own examination is not enough, trust the examination of others who are driven by the fear and love of God, and not by idle curiosity. And through examination (as is fitting and as God shall grant), if you find something good, follow the Apostle's sentiment.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul
## Book Five. Folio 34.

Hold fast; otherwise, reject it. For here there are dangers full of great horror and dread. Let us abstain from every appearance of evil <note>original: "Ab omni specie mali abstineamus." Reference: 1 Thessalonians 5:22.</note>: the "appearance" of evil is not a true form, but is rather a deformity. Therefore, he who commands this warns us away from all deformity and forbids every sin. Indeed, since all things that the Father has belong to the Son, the Apostle desires that the Son sanctify us, so that He may enlighten us with the piety of His mercy and direct our every vow toward perfection, so that the spirit given to us may be kept whole.

<margin>Ambrose</margin> For then (says Ambrose), the spirit is "whole" if we strive for a good life, possessing a clean soul and a body without reproach, so that the whole man may be perfect. For it is possible for the body to be clean while the soul is defiled by evil thoughts; therefore, he says the spirit in man ought to be clean. If, however, an evil life or thought intervenes, the spirit will not be whole, because it deserts a man who is subject to sins. For while the soul and body are in disagreement, those who lack spiritual sense are made strangers to it; and as if losing them, the spirit will not remain whole. For the spirit is given to man for this purpose: to remain and be, as it were, his head. Therefore, it will not be whole, because it loses its members when a man retreats from it by doing those things which the Holy Spirit hates. Whether indeed the spirit, soul, and mind differ from one another has been sufficiently discussed by us in the second book on the *Miracles of Sacred Scripture* and in the first book of the *Theorems*.

### ¶ The third Theorem of the fifth book, on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians.

<margin>2 Thessalonians 2</margin> ¶ Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, that you be not easily moved from your sense, nor be terrified, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by epistle as if sent by us, as if the day of the Lord were at hand. ### ¶ Exposition.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration showing a man in scholarly robes and a cap sitting in a high-backed chair, writing or reading at a desk or lectern.</image-desc>
This is Paul’s revelation concerning the coming of the Antichrist, which is obscure and veiled. And the holy Apocalypse of John reveals two Antichrists (as our Scapulensian <note>Likely referring to a specific commentator or a member of an order wearing the scapular.</note> prefers) by the names of the first and second beasts. The first beast has already come: and that was Muhammad <note>original: "mahumetes"</note>, who appeared under the emperor Heraclius and whose deeds still endure; though by God’s mercy, they shall shortly perish utterly. The second

<column-break/>

# Book Five. Folio 34.

beast has not yet appeared, of whom the Apostle seems to speak more directly. But the Lord will not come before, as Saint Ambrose writes, the falling away of the Roman Empire occurs <note>original: "regni romani defectio"</note> and the Antichrist appears to kill the saints. Once liberty is restored to the Romans—though under his own name—he, knowing the Lord is coming to suppress his name, will usurp it for himself. And so that his kingdom may seem true, he will draw along with him those who shall perish together with him, so that he may sit in the seat of Christ in the house of the Lord and assert that he himself is God—not the Son of God. Wherefore in the Gospel, the Lord said to the Jews: "I have come in my Father's name and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive." <note>John 5:43</note> On this account, it is expected that he will be of the circumcision, or circumcised in the womb, so that the Jews may have confidence in believing him.

Thus, when the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians, he teaches that everyone ought to be cautious in matters of this kind. And he says this specifically so that the one who is to come before the Lord may be revealed, so that the coming of the Lord may then be hoped for—which previously was made as if under a veil. He says "unless the falling away comes first," which Saint Ambrose previously mentioned should be understood as the abolition of the Roman Empire; so that when it has failed and the Antichrist has come, then the coming of the Lord may be believed to be imminent. The "mystery of iniquity" began with Nero, who in his zeal for idols killed even the Apostles at the instigation of his father the devil, continuing until Diocletian and most recently Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note>, who by a certain art and subtlety was unable to fulfill the persecution he began because it had not been granted from above. For Satan uses these ministers twice so that, in the meantime, under a crowd of gods, he might mock men with a manifestation against the one true God. As long as the Roman Empire stands, this is what he means by: "until he be taken out of the way" <note>original: "donec in medio fiat." Reference: 2 Thess 2:7.</note>. But concerning the Antichrist, enough has been said by us in the fourth book on the *Christian Religion*.

# The Theorems of Saint Paul
### Page 34

**Q** Whoever lacks the spirit of faith undoubtedly possesses an evil conscience. For such a person either preaches as a hypocrite or as an open blasphemer, just as were Hymenaeus and Alexander, who (as it pleases Saint Ambrose to say) suffered a shipwreck after abandoning the faith. <note>original: "naufra-gi facti sunt." Reference: 1 Timothy 1:19-20. Ambrose suggests that losing faith is like losing a ship, leaving the soul "naked" of truth.</note> That is, they were stripped of the truth or deprived of life. For what is truth if not life? The Apostle says he delivered these men to Satan so that they might be corrected regarding their blasphemy. This "handing over" is as follows: the Apostle, moved by their blasphemies, pronounced a sentence against them. Moreover, the Devil, who stands ready to receive into his power those turned away from God, seized them once the sentence was heard, so that they might understand they were being bound by punishments because they had blasphemed. Hence it is said in the Gospel, among other things: "Now, do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you," <note>original: "iam noli peccare ne quid tibi deterius contingat." Reference: John 5:14.</note> showing that infirmities are sometimes brought upon bodies because of sin.

<margin>John 5:c</margin>
<margin>Luke 13:d</margin>
And because these things are done by the service of the Devil, the Lord declared this, saying among many things: "Should not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound these eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?" <note>Reference: Luke 13:16.</note> Regarding Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom he delivered to Satan:

<margin>Chrysostom</margin>
Chrysostom understands this as excommunication and cutting off from the body of Christ <note>Saint John Chrysostom was a 4th-century Church Father known for his "golden-mouthed" preaching.</note>: so that there would be no communion of the faithful with them, and no sharing in spiritual prayers. This is a hidden delivery to Satan, occurring without the destruction and torment of the flesh. However, that delivery involving the incestuous Corinthian was manifest, terrifying in the destruction and torment of the flesh. <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 5, where Paul orders a man expelled for immorality.</note> And this was not so they might perish, but so that through this casting out from the society of the saints, they might learn not to blaspheme or speak evil of Christ and his faith, and that by repenting and performing worthy penance, they might be grafted back into the body of Christ. For one who is separated from it is like a sheep separated from the flock; in the presence of the wolf, it is immediately under the wolf’s power. So too is that person continuously under the power of Satan, from whose bites only Christ rescues us—He who is the King of ages, blessed forever, may He always protect, defend, and rescue us.

### ¶ Theorem 2

<margin>1 Timothy 2</margin>
¶ For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

### ¶ Exposition.

<column-break/>

# Book Five. Folio 34.

**S** <margin>Saint Ambrose</margin> If God, who is called omnipotent, truly wills all men to be saved, why is His will not fulfilled? But in every speech (says Ambrose), there is a meaning and a condition lies hidden. Whence Peter the Apostle says: "All Scripture requires interpretation." <note>original: "Omnis scriptu-ra indiget interpretatione."</note> For God wills all to be saved, but only if they come to Him. For He does not will it such that they are saved against their will, but He wills them to be saved if they themselves also wish it. For surely He who gave the law to all excluded no one from salvation. Does not a physician set himself up in public for this reason: to show that he wishes to heal everyone, provided he is sought out by the sick? For it is not true health if it is granted to one who does not want it, nor can one who receives medicine against his will—if that is even possible—rejoice in a salvation he has not perceived. I might even say the medicine cannot have an effect unless the sick person applies his mind to it; for this medicine is not corporeal but spiritual, which profits neither the doubting nor the envious.

For it is Faith that grants salvation; unless the mind receives it with total will, it will not only profit nothing but will even be harmful. For the grace of Faith has this power: it pours divine healing into those devoted to it, but to the undevoted, it brings a disease through which the whole man perishes. He signifies that God and Christ have one will in saving mankind; whence he confesses that God the Father—from whom all authority comes—is one, and the mediator between God and men is one: Christ Jesus. For having been sent by the Father and made an arbiter, he reconciled God and men by reforming them to the knowledge of Him. Because the Father and Son are one—not in person, but in an inseparable nature—so that He might be the arbiter of God and men, the Son of God took on flesh and was born a man. Thus the mediator of God and men was the man Christ Jesus—that is, not without divinity. For the man was in God and God was in the man, so that from both He might be a mediator, and He first did this to reconcile both in Himself.

For (says Ambrose) while preserving the unity of God, He could not be called a mediator of God and men as if He were a different God who called man back into grace after man had disagreed with God; rather, as a man who would not overstep the law that was given, He was made an arbiter between Him who sinned and Him who knows not how to sin, so that the latter might forgive and the man might henceforth remain in the faith of God.

Book Five. folio xxxv.

...the powerful King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in light inaccessible, whom no human has seen, nor indeed can see. To Him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen. <note>original: "potens rex regum & dominus dominantium..." This is a concluding doxology from 1 Timothy 6:15-16.</note>

### Explanation.

<image-desc>A small woodcut illustration depicting two men, possibly saints or scholars, holding books and engaged in discourse.</image-desc>

He alone, God, is the essence of all things and the life of all to whom He gives being; and to all who live, He gives life. He sent His Son to earth, who testified to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, as the one who gives life to all. "I am a King," He said, "for this I was born and for this I came into the world: that I might bear witness to the truth; everyone who is of the truth hears my voice." <note>Reference: John 18:37.</note> For He alone is the one who possesses His own blessedness, power, lordship, and kingdom, as well as immortality, received from no one else. The Father has all these things; likewise, the Son has them from the Father. However, "inaccessible light" belongs to the Father alone: which (as Ambrose says) has never appeared to anyone, and which no human has seen or can see. This is not because the Son's light is different—since it is written in the Psalm, "And in your light we shall see light" <note>Reference: Psalm 36:9. This is interpreted here to mean the Father's light is in the Son.</note>—but because (he says) no one sees the Father, and through this, He dwells in inaccessible light. There is (as the same Ambrose writes) no order for anyone to see the Father except for Christ, who is from God; He has seen God. But because the Son Himself performs all things, He is said both to appear and to be seen. Therefore, that which was mentioned above is unique to the Father. To Him be honor and eternal power. 

If we seek the manner (as Augustine says) in which God has spoken, we must hold most certainly that God speaks either through His own substance or through a creature subject to Him. But He does not speak through His substance except to create all natures; for spiritual and intellectual natures, He speaks not only to create but also to illuminate them when they are able to grasp His speech, such as is found in His Word, which was "in the beginning with God and the Word was God," through whom all things were made. <note>Reference: John 1:1.</note> To those, however, who cannot grasp Him, when God speaks, He does so only through a creature—either a spiritual one, whether in dreams or in ecstasy in the likeness of bodily things, or even through a physical creature when some appearance is presented to the bodily senses or voices sound out. For as he writes elsewhere, God cannot be seen by man in the same way that man sees physical things with the body. For if He were inaccessible even to the minds of the pious, it would not be said, "Come to Him and be enlightened." And if He were invisible to the minds of the pious, it would not be said, "We shall see Him as He is." <note>Reference: 1 John 3:2.</note>

### The fourth theorem on the Second Epistle to Timothy.

->The Vulgate edition and the Greek have the same meaning.<-

---

> In a large house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; and some indeed for honor, but others for dishonor. If anyone, therefore, cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work. <note>Reference: 2 Timothy 2:20-21.</note>

### Explanation.

<image-desc>A small woodcut illustration, identical to the previous one, showing two scholarly figures with books.</image-desc>

Someone may ask how God sustains among His own people those who name His name unworthily—and if they ought not to be there, why does He tolerate such unjust men, liars, and idle talkers? Paul satisfies this question and indicates that there are diverse people in the Church. Some are good and supreme men, whom he understands as "gold"; some are merely good, whom he designates as "silver." Others, however, are not good, whom he calls "vessels of wood and clay." <term>vessels of clay</term><note>original: "vasa fictilia." Earthenware or pottery, representing the fragile or less noble members of the community.</note> Saint Ambrose thinks there is no ambiguity here. <margin>Saint Ambrose.</margin> For (he says) the frequent speech of the rebuking Apostle proves this in the church of the Corinthians. Now, however, it is plain in our own Church; and it is proved by clear readings regarding the temple in Jerusalem, which was a type <note>In theology, a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality.</note> of the Church. For the Sadducees were there, from whose root came Hymenaeus and Philetus. When the Apostle had spoken concerning their depraved opinion, he immediately added this so that it would not be a marvel to see dissenting men in the Church. For even in the church of the Corinthians, there were some who, in their dissent, denied the resurrection. 

Nevertheless, the insane Novatian, <note>Novatian (c. 200–258) was a scholar and priest who held a rigorist view that those who lapsed in faith could not be readmitted to the Church. The author calls him "insane" for his schismatic views.</note> in order to flatter his own error, teaches that this must be understood differently: so that the "large house" is believed to signify the whole world. He does this because the Lord has diversity [within the world], though it is certain the Apostle used the example of a wealthy and opulent house which, however large it may be, still has vessels of wood and clay. In this way, the Church, although it is called holy, still has those who are vicious and of depraved opinions. He shows these are worthy of dishonor, yet not necessarily to perish, but to be purged through fire, because they are necessary to the house in some part. Novatian, however, lifted up by pride, decreed it should be understood this way so that he might defend the "general truth and holiness" of his own church, as if the Church existed only with him, and that he has only purified people—for which reasons he accuses us of being innocent. But what need was there in this place to say anything about the world? Or why would he affirm that the world is signified by the "large house"? For the Lord says to the apostles: "You are not of the world, but I have chosen you." How, then, are those who are denied to be of the world to be enclosed within the world? And the same Apostle says: "What is it to me to judge those who are outside?" For in one house, all are under one name, for all are counted under the one name of their Lord. The world, however, contains men of diverse professions, such that different people profess to have different gods and lords. Therefore, he did not call the world the "large house," but the Church, in which all are under one Lord...

### ->Fifth Theorem.<-

#### The Vulgate Edition.

The cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come, bring with you, and the books, especially the parchments.

#### Understanding from the Greek.

The *phelonēs* <note>The Greek word "phelonēs" refers to a cloak or a case for books.</note> which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come, bring [it] and the books, especially the parchments.

#### Explanation.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a man's face in profile, wearing a cap.</image-desc>
He wished to leave a memorial of himself to someone before his death. He had Luke with him. He commands that Mark be brought along with the parchments which were with Carpus—a most holy man of whom the divine Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> makes mention in *The Celestial Hierarchy*. But for what purpose, if not so that he might leave those [parchments] to Luke and Mark, the divine scribes chosen by the Holy Spirit, for the recording of the holy Gospel? 

<margin>Ambrose</margin>
The apostle, as Saint Ambrose writes, was a Jew by nature, and he possessed nothing that was foreign to him. From where, then, did he get a cloak? But because (he says) he was from Tarsus—and it is established that those people were received into the society of the Romans so that they might thereafter be called Roman citizens—it was therefore necessary for them to have a court dress <note>original: "curiam."</note> in which, according to the Roman custom, they would assemble wearing cloaks <note>original: "penulati."</note>. For whoever at that time had met the Romans with gifts were gifted with perpetual immunity and named Roman citizens and their brothers, as the same apostle testifies. It is possible, therefore, that even if it was not his own (since he had given himself entirely to the Law), he might have had his father’s cloak. Grammarians disagree whether a *penula* <term>penula: a heavy outer garment or traveling cloak</term> signifies that kind of garment which is put on over other clothes when it rains. Therefore, when it rains, a cloak is necessary; if it does not rain, there is no use for it. Unless perhaps, for the sake of office and the court, they assemble wearing cloaks in the manner of the doctors of Paris.

### ->Sixth Theorem.<-

The Vulgate edition and the Greek have the same meaning.

<header>Book Five.</header>
<page-num>folio xxxvi.</page-num>

<margin>2 Timothy 4</margin>
Greet Priscilla and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, but I left Trophimus sick at Miletus.

#### Explanation.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting two figures, a man and a woman, seated in a domestic interior.</image-desc>
According to Saint Ambrose, Aquila and Priscilla are those with whom the apostle stayed and worked with his hands. And this is the same Onesiphorus whom he testifies about in the first [part of the] epistle. Why is it, someone asks, that while the apostle was present—he who raised the dead—Trophimus remained sick? It is because (he says) signs were performed for the sake of unbelievers. And because merit with God is established for various reasons: so that whether a person gives thanks to God in tribulation or in sickness, and does not seek help from the opposing side <note>likely referring to magic or pagan remedies</note>, he may increase in merit before God. However, because of the rains and the cold, he urged him to come to him by autumn.

### ->Seventh Theorem<-
#### on the Epistle to Titus.

The Vulgate edition and the Greek have the same meaning.

<margin>To Titus 3</margin>
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. A man who is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid; knowing that he that is such an one is subverted, and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.

#### Explanation.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a bust of a man in a feathered cap.</image-desc>
He calls those questions "foolish" which have no effect on salvation nor provide any skillful knowledge for utility. How does one build up [the church] who makes people loud, contentious, and ambitious for victory—defending this point and attacking that—so that they fight for victory and not for truth? And it is a wonder that those who have chosen only the method of questioning regarding the matters of the divine law for their discipline have not read Paul's precept to Titus: *avoid foolish questions and genealogies and contentions and strivings about the law.* For they are unprofitable and vain. *Avoid a man who is a heretic after the first admonition.* 

There are also heretics, as Saint Ambrose testifies, who attack the Law through the words of the Law; for they attach their own meaning to the words of the Law so that they may commend the depravity of their own minds by the authority of the Law. For since impiety is very strong when fallacies are composed under the name of authority, a bad thing—which cannot be acceptable through itself—is commended by the goodness of a name. Therefore, such men ought to be corrected once so that they may be without excuse. For if they are corrected more frequently, they will become more practiced in evil. He who corrects them often seems to compel them to become more anxious for the destruction of many; therefore they are to be let go, so that having become more negligent, they may perish alone in their filth.

Theorems of Saint Paul / Book Six. Folio 37.

### Book six of the Theorems of the most blessed Apostle Paul on the Epistle to the Hebrews.

### First Theorem.

->The Vulgate and Greek editions have the same meaning.<-

<margin>Hebrews 6</margin>
For it is impossible for those who were once illuminated, have also tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, have nonetheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, recrucifying in themselves the Son of God and making him an example of shame. <note>The author is addressing a controversial passage in Hebrews 6:4-6 which was often used to argue that serious sins after baptism could not be forgiven.</note>

### Explanation.

<margin>Saint Augustine in his book *On Faith and Works*.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a scholar or saintly figure in robes, seated and gesturing towards a text.</image-desc> The very separation from the Egyptians signifies the departure from sins which those about to be baptized profess. For this purpose (as Augustine writes) they profess what was said by Peter: "Repent and let every one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." It is as if he were saying: "Depart from Egypt, cross through the Red Sea." Whence also in the epistle inscribed to the Hebrews, when the beginnings of those who are being baptized were commemorated, "repentance from dead works" was placed there. For he says: "Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Jesus, let us look towards perfection, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith in God, of the doctrine of washings <note>original: "lauacri doctrine." Referring to the Greek "baptismos," often translated as washings or baptisms.</note>, of the laying on of hands, and also of the resurrection of the dead and of eternal judgment." The Scripture testifies clearly enough that all these things pertain to the beginnings of "neophytes" <note>New converts or newly baptized Christians.</note>. Now, what is repentance from dead works but from those things which must be put to death so that we may live? After committing faults, the Hebrews were laying again the foundations of faith, of repentance, of baptism, of the laying on of hands, and of the rest, as if they had never been baptized before and had come anew to the knowledge of Christ and faith, and to the resurrection of the flesh and eternal judgment—which is called "eternal" because those who will be judged by it, whether to life or to death, shall remain so forever. Truly, they ought not to do this, but be carried toward perfection, which we obtain if, from the time of our regeneration <note>The spiritual rebirth through baptism.</note>, we live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. What does it mean that they were "once illuminated"? Certainly, that they were once baptized; for this was called by our ancestors the sacrament of *photismatum* <note>original: "photismatū," from the Greek "photismos," meaning illumination or enlightenment, a common early Christian term for baptism.</note>, that is, of illuminations. Those who received justification from sins tasted the "heavenly gift." Those who were grafted into the body of Christ and began to live by the Spirit of Christ were made "partakers of the Spirit." Those who were fed by the Gospel of Christ tasted the "good word of God." They also tasted the "powers of the world to come" who received the body and blood of Christ, through which the world to come can be possessed, and who also received certain spiritual gifts <note>original: "charismata."</note>

<column-break/>

of the Holy Spirit. And what follows—it is not simply said to be impossible to be renewed to repentance, but impossible to be renewed to repentance *by recrucifying in themselves the Son of God and making him an example of shame*. This they would certainly do: those who, having fallen after the illumination of baptism, thought they could be renewed through a repeated baptism for their lapses. For through baptism we die with Christ, are buried with him, and rise again with him; this can happen only once. For the Lord died once, was buried once, and rose once. Is it not a great example of shame to crucify Christ a second time in a second baptism? As if his being once crucified, dead, and buried were not sufficient to redeem the world. Therefore, repentance is not to be repeated through a multitude of baptisms, as if through a multitude of Christ's passions and burials. But come now, if there is a place for repentance for those who fall after baptism, what is it if it is not through the washing of baptism? There is, without doubt, a place for repentance. For if there were not, the Apostle would not have delivered the incestuous fornicator to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord. "Confess, therefore," says James, "your sins to one another, and pray for one another that you may be saved," just as if he who was sick, having brought in the priests, would have made a confession if he were in sin. This method was seen as easier and more universal for the salvation of all. For the "vicars of Christ" <note>The priests or clergy acting in Christ's place.</note> help certain simple people to make their confession, and they pray for those who otherwise would neither know how to accuse themselves in confession nor how to pray. Moreover, they correct, exhort, and teach with human kindness or, if necessary, even with severity; and this is done in secret, as if Christ alone were listening. But there is more on this in Book 2 of *On the Wonders of Holy Scripture*.

### Second Theorem.

->The Vulgate and Greek editions have the same meaning.<-

<margin>All these things are treated more extensively in Book 2 of *On the Wonders of Holy Scripture* in the chapter on blasphemy; read there.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 14:d; Hebrews 7:a.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' containing a figure, possibly an angel or a classical youth.</image-desc> For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him; to whom also Abraham gave a tenth of everything; who is first, by interpretation, King of Justice, and then is also King of Salem, which is King of Peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, remains a priest forever.

### Explanation.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting two figures, one kneeling or bowing before a seated person.</image-desc> We read of Melchizedek in the book of Genesis; regarding Melchizedek, it is also written in a similar way in the epistle given to the Hebrews. And so that the Apostle might signify who should be understood through Melchizedek, he added: "without doubt," he says, "the lesser is blessed by the better." Which indeed (as he sa<unclear>ys</unclear>)

<margin>Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, Question 76, near section A.</margin>
Augustine writes: He did not refer this to the tradition of the ecclesiastical office. "For who," he says, "would doubt that the rule of the Lord’s tradition, by which subjects are blessed by the Lord, is better than those who are blessed by it?" For the mystery of the Lord works in these words which encompass and commemorate Him, but He wished to demonstrate the personal merit and power of that individual. Who, then, is this man, and how great is he, in comparison to whom Abraham is called the lesser? For it is established that Abraham holds among all the faithful the sign of the testimony of nobility and faith. For Augustine says that Melchizedek possesses blessing by nature and substantially—whom the Scripture calls the priest of the Most High God—and he gives the blessing through his will. Therefore, he says, through this it appears that Melchizedek is beyond man; for there was no reason why he should be better than Abraham unless a superior nature preceded him. For an <term>impassible<note>In theology, "impassible" describes a nature that cannot suffer, change, or be affected by external pain or passion—a quality usually reserved for the divine.</note></term> nature possesses blessedness through its very substance; however, human necessity acquires blessedness through deeds. Because a human does not possess the perfection of divinity, he advances through practice and struggle so that he may become better, since he conquers more than he is conquered. For if he were to act in such a way—which he says is impossible—that he never sinned, he would be made better than God (may such a thought be far from us!). Because a nature that is able to sin as well as not to sin, if it always conquered, would have to be placed above that nature which does not sin because it is impassible. For it does not seem a great thing not to sin because one is unable; however, it is magnificent if one is able to sin and yet does not. This, therefore, is the difference between the substance of God and man: because the substance of God is always blessed by the security of its invincible eternity, while the substance of man becomes blessed through labor. For even the nature of men, although it attains blessedness through labor, will not however be untouched, nor will it lack scars. For how can it be that one who has often engaged in battle, and has sometimes been defeated, is not wounded? But the impassible nature always remains untouched, unhurt, and inviolable. Therefore, Abraham would not be called the least in comparison to Melchizedek unless the nature of Melchizedek were more powerful than that of Abraham. For these things we have said are seen to belong to a stronger intellect. But if we look back at the law, many more and more powerful things will be said: for this Melchizedek, King of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him; whose name is first interpreted as "King of Justice," and then "King of Salem," which is "King of Peace"; without father, without mother, and without genealogy; having neither beginning of days nor end of life; but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever. And so that he might commend these things to God in the places where he had signified them, he added: "See," he says, "how great this man is, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave tithes from the firstfruits." For as he showed by what power and how great Melchizedek was,

<column-break/>

<margin>Augustine’s opinion on Melchizedek.</margin>
he praises him by way of Abraham, saying: "Because he is the prince of the fathers" <note>The "prince of the fathers" refers to Abraham's status as the patriarch of the faithful.</note>—that is, Abraham is better than all others, but the least compared to Melchizedek. Is it not manifest, Augustine asks, that this is not a man, but something better? For what is it that he says of him: that he is the King of Peace and the King of Justice? Come closer and see. For seeing the sun from afar, you think it a lamp; and looking at silver, you estimate it to be tin. Can any of men be called the King of Peace and Justice? For peace is preached to men in a similar way to justice; but this one is called King of Peace and Justice so that from him justice and peace may be known to have their origin. For men are instructed by justice as a teacher and by peace to deserve God. Therefore, Melchizedek does not have a king as a teacher, since he himself is the Lord. How much better, then, is Melchizedek than man, when the governess of men <note>Referring to Justice/Peace personified.</note> is under him? This is what it means to be the King of kings. Therefore, when he is called the King of Justice and Peace, it signifies that he is their author; just as the Lord Jesus is the author of life, so also Melchizedek is the author of justice and peace. It is said of Melchizedek that he is the King of Justice and Peace. By what reasoning he should be set apart, I do not understand; for I think, says Augustine, it makes no difference as far as the matter pertains whether he is called the King of Peace or the God of Peace. For the King of God is justice, and he who transgresses it remains under God's judgment. Moreover, Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High God, appeared to bless Abraham as a presage of future holy things. Because a blessing was to be given in the future to the people of God through a prelate of God, whom we call priests; this Melchizedek, therefore, appeared as a precursor of the sacred future Son of God. For he who follows in order precedes for the sake of service. Therefore, the things we have said of Melchizedek should not be wondered at, when Scripture adds more to the confusion of those who clamor against it, and says after all things worthy of praise, to confound the malevolent: "but being made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever." But he cannot be like the Son unless he is of the same nature. And what, Augustine asks, seems incredible if Melchizedek appeared as a man, when he is understood to be the Third Person? <note>Augustine is exploring the theory that Melchizedek was a manifestation of the Holy Spirit (the Third Person of the Trinity).</note> For if Christ, who is the Second Person, was frequently seen in the habit of a man, why is there doubt about these things that have been said? For we read in the Psalm: "Because you are," it says, "a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." None of us doubts that this pertains to the person of Christ, because Christ is a priest forever in the same manner as Melchizedek. But Christ is the High Priest, and Melchizedek the second. This is Augustine’s opinion on Melchizedek. But others, such as Ambrose, Nicholas of Lyra, and <term>Stapulensis<note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536), a French humanist and theologian known for his commentaries on the Bible.</note></term>, as well as other authors, say that Melchizedek was a figure of Christ, and therefore...

Theorems of Saint Paul | Book Six. Folio 39.

They say that this divine Apostle inserts here a "symphony" <note>original: "simphoniam"; here meaning a harmonious correspondence or typological connection</note> between Christ and Melchizedek. Neither the name of his father, nor mother, nor a genealogy of Melchizedek is set down in the divine words, nor the beginning of his days, nor his end. This is because Christ, according to his humanity, had no father; and according to his divinity, he had no mother; and because his divine origin <note>original: "Genesis"</note> is an unknowable generation. For who (he says) shall declare his generation? Sacred discourse ought not properly to contain his human genealogy. For that which is commonly traced is properly the genealogy of Joseph, not of Christ. For his genealogy would have been a lineage derived from the Virgin, traced through David and Judah; but it was not the custom of the Hebrews for Moses to trace a genealogy through a woman. They say the beginning and end of Melchizedek's days are not written because Christ remains forever, having truly neither beginning nor end of days, being co-eternal with the Father, just as he himself said to the Jews: "Verily, verily, I say unto you: before Abraham was, I am." But indeed, it would be laborious and less suited to this place to review at present all the opinions of authors concerning that high priest Melchizedek, whom the Apostle mentions in the letter to the Hebrews. Nor can it be sufficiently clear to us which of those opinions is to be preferred over the others. Therefore, we must confess the scripture to be true, and seek its understanding either through reading or obtain it from God through prayers. But we have spoken more extensively about Melchizedek in Book One, Chapter 10, concerning the wonders of Holy Scripture; I advise the reader to refer to that place.

## Theorem Three.

### The Vulgate Edition.

<margin>Hebrews 11</margin>
Now faith is the substance <note>The Latin "substantia" implies a foundation or reality that stands under our hopes.</note> of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing. For in this, the elders obtained a testimony. By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that from invisible things, visible things might be made.

### Understanding from the Greek.

Now faith is the foundation of those things which are hoped for, the proof of things that are not seen. For in this, the elders received testimony. By faith we understand the ages were perfected by the word of God, so that from things not appearing, the things which are seen were made.

### Exposition.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'A' depicting a seated king with crown and scepter, possibly David or Solomon.</image-desc> For one man shines through faith, such as Abraham; another shines through chastity, such as Joseph. Likewise, another shines through gentleness, such as the man of God, Moses. Again, another through constancy and the endurance of vehement pains, like the admirable Job. However, in that place where it is said of Abraham that "faith was credited to him as righteousness," a perfected faith is declared. For just as Origen 

<column-break/>

writes, the Apostle says that knowledge and prophecy are "in part." And again, he says it is perfect in that place where he writes: "We know in part and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, those things which are in part shall be destroyed." In this way, we can also understand that faith is sometimes "in part" and sometimes "perfect." In the Gospel it is said: "Lord, increase our faith." And the Apostle himself, when he says, "If I have all faith, so that I could move mountains," by saying "all," he teaches that it is a whole composed of parts. But when I return to the scriptures, I do not find (he says) that faith is credited as righteousness for all believers. After all, it is written of the children of Israel that "they believed God and his servant Moses," yet it is not added—as was written of Abraham—that "it was credited to him as righteousness." For this reason, Origen thinks that there was not in them, as there was in Abraham, a perfection of faith heaped together from many parts into one, which would merit being credited as righteousness. Similarly (he says), it can be said of another that he has the faith of God, but not according to knowledge, if he is ignorant that faith without works is dead, and that the faith of God is not in words alone—which are sometimes learned as composed or written by another—but in the affection of the mind. Such a faith was held by that woman who said, "If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved." 

<margin>On the Epistle to the Romans, Book 10.</margin>
If anyone, therefore, does not hold faith in such a way that he shows he believes through his good acts, it can be said to him as well that he has the faith of God, but not according to knowledge. It can also be said of another (he says) that he has the charity of God, but not according to knowledge; and therefore, the works of knowledge must be given chief place, lest things turn out unhappily for us: that while placed in faith, we are frustrated by faith, or that having zeal for good things, we fall away from the good. Do you wish to know how one who does not have knowledge can vanish in his faith? Listen to Paul himself saying to certain people: "Unless you have believed without cause" <note>original: "nisi sine causa credidistis"; usually translated as "believed in vain."</note>. It happens, therefore, that those who do not apply themselves to the work of knowledge believe without cause, so that in that which they have believed, they might also receive the understanding of the truth. But now let us see if the discourse contains any secret: there are many (as the same Origen writes) and diverse studies of literature in this world. 

<margin>Origen in Homily 4 on Psalm 36.</margin>
And you may see many who begin with <term>Grammar<note>The "Liberal Arts" were the standard curriculum of the time, beginning with the Trivium (Grammar, Rhetoric, Logic) and moving to the Quadrivium.</note></term>, learning the songs of poets and the fables of comedies and tragedies, or commentaries, or the horrific narrations of history in long and diverse volumes; then they pass on to <term>Rhetoric</term> and there seek all the paint and polish of eloquence; after this, they come to <term>Philosophy</term> to scrutinize <term>Dialectic</term> <note>Logic and the art of argument.</note>, to inquire into the connections of syllogisms, to test the measurements of <term>Geometry</term>, and to scrutinize the laws of the stars and the courses of the constellations in <term>Astronomy</term>; nor do they omit <term>Music</term>. And so, being educated through all these diverse and various disciplines—in which they have learned nothing of the will of God—they have indeed gathered many riches, but the "riches of sinners." But look at one man of the Church, unskilled indeed in word and education, but filled with faith and the fear of God. He, because of the fear of God, dares to commit no wrong, but is altogether afraid to open his mouth lest perhaps an evil word proceed from it; and he observes himself even in the smallest transgression, from which that man who is rich in worldly learning cannot guard himself...

->Theorems of Saint Paul | Book Six. Folio 40.<-

such wisdom. Therefore, the divine word, comparing us to them, says: "Better is a little for the righteous than the many riches of sinners" <note>original: "melius est modicum iusto: super diuitias peccatorum multas"; a reference to Psalm 37:16</note>. For the wisdom of this world, in which they are rich and abundant in eloquence, is like the riches of sinners; yet they are not strong enough to restrain themselves from sin through it. But the "little" of the righteous man is he who has faith as small as a mustard seed, yet it is living and powerful; through it, he is generally kept from sin. Therefore, a little faith for the righteous is better than the many riches of eloquence and wisdom of this age which is being destroyed. And even if that man be unskilled and a layman <note>original: "imperitus & idiota"; in a Renaissance context, this refers to someone without formal university training rather than a lack of intelligence</note>, if he is faithful and God-fearing, that little bit of faith is better for the righteous man than the many riches they have acquired from the wisdom of this age. But above those is he who is rich in the word of God and the knowledge of truth: that is, he who, according to the Apostle, is rich in every word and in all knowledge, and is nonetheless rich in good works. For all our ancestors agree in asserting that faith is the beginning of understanding. For in every faculty, certain things are presupposed as first principles which are apprehended by faith alone; from these, the understanding of the matters to be treated is drawn out. For it is necessary for everyone who wishes to ascend to learning to believe those things without which he cannot ascend. For Isaiah says: <margin>Nicholas of Cusa, Cardinal, Book III, Chapter 11, *On Learned Ignorance*.</margin> "Unless you believe, you shall not understand." <note>original: "nisi credideritis non intelligetis"; a common Latin rendering of Isaiah 7:9</note> Faith, as Nicholas of Cusa writes, is in itself the enfolding <note>term: "complicatio" / enfolding. A philosophical concept from Cusanus where all things are contained within a unity before being "unfolded" (explicatio) into the world</note> of everything intelligible; while understanding is the unfolding of faith. Therefore, the intellect is directed through faith, and faith is extended through the intellect. Where, therefore, there is no sound faith, there is no true understanding. It is manifest what kind of conclusion follows from an error of principles and a weakness of the foundation. But no faith is more perfect than Truth itself, which is Jesus. Who does not understand that right faith is the most excellent gift of God? John the Apostle says that faith in the incarnation of the Word of God leads us into truth so that we may be made children of God; for the sake of this final conclusion, he adds, saying: "These things are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Son of God."

## Second Theorem.

<margin>Hebrews 12.</margin> The Vulgate edition and the Greek have the same meaning: Let no one be a fornicator or a profane person like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. For he found no place for repentance, though he had sought it with tears.

### Exposition.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a figure (possibly a scholar) seated at a desk with an open book, set within an architectural frame.</image-desc>
Esau, coming from the road, was failing from lack of food; and he was cast down so far by the madness of hunger that he traded his birthright for a meal of lentils. And who were these people? As Origen <note>A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> writes: The lineage of Esau, the son of Isaac and brother of Jacob, was a race, a tribe, a progeny, and occupied provinces and regions. For just as Jacob fathered a multitude, the nations of the Israelites and Jews, so Esau fathered a multitude of nations who were called Idumeans <note>Also known as Edomites</note>. And because he had brought to mind Abraham and Isaac, Esau himself was a worshiper of God; for although he may have violated it in some things, he nevertheless passed down that same worship of God to his sons. Rightly, as Origen writes, many of the Idumeans were worshipers of God, and some were very religious, such as Job or his friends who came to him. For certain regions of the Idumeans were named Arabia; in the borders of that Arabia, Job lived, for he also took a wife from Arabia, since they were of the same Arabian stock. Now, indeed, both the name and language of the Idumeans have perished; they are all called Arabs and all speak Syriac. 

As Saint Ambrose writes, Isaac had told his elder son to bring him food and receive the blessing; but while he delayed and sought wild and foreign food <note>referring to Esau hunting game</note>, the younger brother brought domestic food from the flock of sheep. Esau was therefore rejected, yet not simply rejected. For he also received a blessing—though in an inferior place—and a possession; but repentance did not avail him for that [original] place, even though it was held with many tears. What is shown in the sons of Isaac also happens in the children of Christ: many, because of intemperance and impurities, lose the chief place of inheritance. If they seek the inheritance afterward, they are rejected—not simply, but from that [primary] place—nor does repentance continued with many tears obtain that place of blessing. 

For example: you are a virgin, and for a long time you have lived blameless in the faith of the Son of God, uncontaminated in mind and body. If you persevere, a chief blessing and inheritance will be given to you; your place will be with the virgins, and you will retain the full right of the firstborn of Christ. But if a wicked error takes you away and you defile yourself with a woman, for a small and foul pleasure you have lost the chief inheritance. When you desire it afterward, you are rejected; and no matter how much penance you perform and how many tears you shed, you will not find that [original] place, and your lot will not be among the virgins. Yet if you perform penance, you will not be simply rejected; rather, you will receive a blessing and an inheritance just as Esau did, but not in that same place as before. For in the heavenly inheritance, there are many places and many mansions. Isaac also had many possessions and places. But if you do not repent, you will be deprived of both blessing and inheritance. For if Esau had not repented and shed tears, he would not even have obtained a blessing from his father. These things happened long ago as a figure <note>original: "in figura"; meaning a typological or symbolic foreshadowing</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the superiority of simple faith over worldly wisdom, citing Nicholas of Cusa, and provides an exposition on Esau as a cautionary figure who lost his primary inheritance through a lack of restraint.</summary>

# Theorems of Saint Paul

### Theorem Five.

<margin>Hebrews 13</margin>

->The Vulgate edition and the Greek version share the same meaning.<-
->Do not be led away by various and foreign doctrines. It is best for the heart to be established by grace, not by foods, which have not profited those who have walked in them.<-

### Exposition.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' containing a woodcut portrait of a tonsured man with a book, possibly a scholar or monk.</image-desc>The Apostle intended that not everyone should be reckless in pursuing human philosophy and the literature of the pagans. Therefore, one must exercise moderation, for many things are harmful if taken in excess. Indeed, many types of people cannot handle these subjects without harm. Some waver in their faith, or possess a habit of soul that is weak and infirm toward God, such that if they encountered things opposing our faith, they would easily fall into a trap—such as the arguments of Aristotle concerning the eternity of motion <note>Aristotle argued the universe had no beginning, which contradicts the biblical account of Creation</note>, or those of Averroes concerning the unity of the intellect <note>Averroes, an Islamic philosopher, suggested all humans share a single "active intellect," a view often condemned by Christian theologians who emphasized individual souls</note>, or Alexander of Aphrodisias concerning the corruptibility of the soul. There are also certain Platonic dogmas which, although long since exploded by our own thinkers, might nonetheless easily cause those who have not properly admitted the heavenly light to stumble in their darkness. Furthermore, even physicians and theologians themselves should not grow old merely in the commentaries of philosophers. I would rightly call "theologians" all those who apply themselves to the sacred scriptures: let them know, venerate, and worship God, obey His decrees, and be a help to others.

Nevertheless, I do not deny that many may return to their former studies, either for the sake of relaxing the mind, or to remember what has been forgotten, or for the sake of composing some work, or to help themselves and others in some other way. However, those who begin to explain Aristotle must be especially careful—I say careful, because this kind of business is most dangerous for those who falter in performing that duty. This danger arises partly from the distorted affections of the students, and partly from the insults with which rivals (whom they call "concurrents") attack one another. In this manner, they busy themselves trying to capture the favor of the ignorant masses, whose judgment is so corrupted by God that they cheer for envious shouting and hurl sophisticated slanders, believing the louder man to be more learned. Because of this, it happens that many, when they ought to be preparing or thinking out arguments, instead seek out certain theatrical gestures and new ways of belittling an opponent to provoke laughter from the unlearned bystanders. This brings shame to the one who had opposed or answered them, if he is of a mild nature; but if he is rigid, it drives him to fury and madness. 

It is a wonder that those who have chosen a purely "question-based" <term>questionarium: a style of teaching focused on debating specific logical or legal problems rather than studying a text as a whole</term> method for instruction regarding matters of divine law have not read Paul’s command to Titus: "Avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law." Just as the pious and profitable way of rightly instructing and teaching according to apostolic precepts is useful, so that contentious and (if I may say so) "questionary" way is useless, impious, and vain. I say useless because it does not build up. It is impious because it does not lift the soul to God

<column-break/>

# Book Six. Folio 41.

nor does it soften the heart. It is vain because it does not reach the goal, which is the perfection of love and the fruit of eternal life. If anyone is a sophist and a lover of word-battles, he should be struck down by the apostolic sentence. In human disciplines, there are both good and bad "sects" <note>original: "secte"; in this context, it refers to schools of thought or philosophical traditions</note>. The good ones are of little danger; I believe those are better which stay closer to the original authors. I consider those physicians better who stick to Galen and Hippocrates, and those more skilled geometers who stick to Euclid. Those are more learned arithmeticians who follow Jordanus and Nicomachus; and those philosophers who follow Plato and Aristotle in matters where they do not contradict our faith—and so on for the rest. However, the "perverse" sects are those of men who hand down their own ideas as if they were someone else's, and are furthest from the original authors. Thus the perverse Marcion <note>A 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament and much of the New Testament</note> utterly refuted whatever in the Gospels and Epistles did not support his own sect.

Therefore, just as in human affairs, "sects" occur in divine matters as well: both good and bad. Both are of great importance, leading either to salvation or to the danger of eternal perdition. They are good when they cling to God and acquiesce to divine understanding; they are bad, however, when they are "cut off" <note>The author plays on the word "secta," linking it to the Latin "secare," meaning "to cut"</note> and oppose the divine understanding (which belongs to the Holy Spirit). The sect of the Sadducees was perverse, but the sects of the Essenes and Pharisees—as far as most were concerned—were good sects. The "Nazprophete" <note>likely referring to the Nazarites or a specific prophetic tradition</note> were either Essenes or Pharisees; and Nathanael was of the Pharisee sect, of whom the Savior said: "Behold, a true Israelite in whom there is no guile." 

Indeed, as our "Scapulensis" <note>referring to a fellow member of the author's religious order or a specific scholar</note> rightly writes, as long as something is not cut from the foundation, it is not so much called "cut" (sect) as it is called "united." But that which is cut from the things that cling to the foundation is cast far off; it is entirely "sect" (cut) and not joined. Therefore, a "true sect" is called a sect not so much because it is cut, but because it is not cut off; for those who belong to it cling to God, who is the foundation and the spirit of understanding. They are therefore not "cut," but united and clinging. But a bad sect (which is the same as a false one) is entirely "cut off." 

When the Apostle says, "It is good for the heart to be established by grace," the "grace" that establishes the heart is the doctrine of Christ. The "foods" in which those who walked did not profit are the "various and foreign doctrines" that do not contain the word of God, but rather oppose it. For (as it is written) man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Furthermore, as Saint Augustine writes, there is no false doctrine that does not mix in some truth. Therefore, he says, truths mixed inordinately with falsehoods in a man's discussion or narrative appear like colors on a single body <margin>Augustine in the second book on the Questions of the Gospels</margin> signifying leprosy, as if spotting and staining human bodies with alternating patches of true and false colors. These people must be avoided; if it can be done, they should be moved further away from the Church. Let them call out to Christ with a great cry, like those ten lepers who stood afar off and lifted their voices saying: "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." For as to why they call Him "Master"—a name I know not if anyone else used to petition the Lord for me—

<sig>ff</sig>
