->¶ On the constant prayer to God.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'S' depicting two figures, one seated and one standing, in a room with a window.</image-desc>
But above all these good things, let us give thanks to God, the King and Author of such great gifts. Let us glorify Paul, through whom these things were completed; let us also pray that we ourselves may enjoy these same blessings. For we ought to pray that he might obtain this grace for us from Christ, so that we may be able to profit in his epistles to the honor and glory of God, and thus advance in spiritual understanding. May the light of the sacred scriptures shine upon us through this understanding, and may Christ, in the treasures of His wisdom, be celebrated spiritually by us along with all the saints. Through the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever.
->Amen<-

->¶ Conclusion.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'H' depicting a scholar seated at a desk writing in a book.</image-desc>
These things I have offered <note>original: "Hehabui," likely "Haec habui"</note> from the slender resources of my poverty, which I have given to the duty of our long-standing friendship and mutual charity. I know that more things could have been said, and more copiously and elegantly; but I had to spare the exhaustion of the reader's ears. You, most holy prelate <note>A "prelate" is a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop, to whom this work is likely dedicated</note>, out of the fertility and abundance of your own talent, and by the labor and industry of your work, will seek out more and better things. These, when joined to my own efforts, can serve as a vehicle for you and for me toward the heavenly fatherland. You also, most distinguished writers, who still lead a steady life in this mortal world, I call upon, I pray, and I entreat you: if we have performed anything in this little work that is less than worthy of your noble merits or your late-night studies, ascribe it not to our will, but to our lack of skill, and do not deny the forgiveness we seek.

->¶ On the Catholic Epistles which our people call<-
->Canonical, and why the author did not explain<-
->the theorems within them.<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'Q' containing a profile portrait of a man wearing a soft cap or beret, typical of 16th-century scholars.</image-desc>
Although the theorems of Paul have occasionally been explained and declared by ancient theologians, some most learned men of our own age have committed to writing very powerful arguments for interpreting and spreading those same epistles of Paul. Nevertheless, I did not think it at all out of place—moved by the authority of the most blessed Peter in the third chapter of his second letter—to bring forward some proofs by which faith itself might be defended and impiety defeated. But if human curiosity (in which a great part of the sophisticated <term>urbanorum; refers to the "city-dwelling" intellectuals of the Renaissance</term> are eager for almost all literature) should perhaps ask in what way you, Champier <note>The author, Symphorien Champier (c. 1470–1539), a French physician and humanist</note>, have only explained the theorems of Paul, when many theorems are also contained in the "Catholic Epistles" (which our people call "Canonical") and yet you have left them untouched. I do not deny this; rather, I frankly admit that I found many theorems in them. Indeed, I confess with a free voice that I have profited greatly from reading them. But since, as the poet says, "We cannot all do everything" <note>A famous quote from Virgil’s Eclogues (Non omnia possumus omnes)</note>, I leave the exposition of those epistles to those who come after, so that they may add from their own vein of talent where I, exhausted, have stopped. Furthermore, it will not be superfluous to note here that those seven epistles of the four holy apostles—James, Peter, John, and Jude—are rightly and fitly called "Catholic," that is, "Universal." This is because they are not written to any particular church or specific person, as are the epistles of blessed Paul, but are addressed indifferently and indiscriminately to the whole assembly of believers in Christ and the entire congregation of Christians, except for the second and third epistles of John. However, it happened through the unskillfulness of scribes (as some very learned men surmise) that by changing some letters of the middle syllables, these are commonly called "Canonical" epistles, when they ought to be called not Canonical, but Catholic. Therefore, let it cling <note>original: "bereat," likely "haereat"</note> more tenaciously to our minds that the theorems of the Catholic Epistles are true, but that one should achieve their understanding or reading through prayers obtained from God. For if the apostle John, who reclined upon the breast of the Lord at the Last Supper, did not fully explain the theorems and mysteries of his own epistles, who shall be sufficient to express them correctly unless he has been taught by the revelation of the Holy Spirit? Therefore, let that saying of the Wise Man cling more tenaciously to our soul: "Just as he who eats much honey, it is not good for him; so he who is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory" <note>Proverbs 25:27</note>. And again in another place: "Seek not the things that are too high for thee, and search not into things above thy strength; but think always on the things God has commanded thee, and be not curious in His many works. For it is not necessary for thee to see with thine eyes those things that are hidden. In superfluous matters, do not search manifoldly, and in His many works thou shalt not be curious; for many things have been shown to thee above the understanding of men" <note>Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 3:22–25</note>. For to many...

# Theorems of the Canonical Epistles.
## Book Six. leaf 43.

Their suspicion supplanted them and held their senses in vanity. Nor do those men in Genesis signify anything else, who wished to build a tower of confusion <note>original: "turrim confusionis"; referring to the Tower of Babel</note> whose top would reach all the way to heaven, but were forced to stop their undertaking by the introduction of a variety and division of languages. Those who dare to pry into the inaccessible secrets of divinity and climb the steep heavens usually fall into a confusion of errors and a pit of impiety. Therefore, the Apostle healthily warns us not to think too highly of ourselves, nor to <margin>John of Damascus, Book 1, Chapter 1, f.</margin> <note>Saint John of Damascus was an 8th-century monk and theologian known for his systematic summaries of Christian doctrine.</note> know more than is proper, but to know with sobriety. And Damascene likewise warns us that we should not transcend the limits of knowing the divine defined by the highest Deity. I leave, therefore, to posterity that province, so that they may add from their own vein where I, exhausted, have stopped.

->Theorems from the Epistle of the Blessed Apostle James.<-

->The First Theorem.<-

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin> Let no one say when he is tempted: "I am being tempted by God." For God cannot be tempted by evil, and He himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted by their own concupiscence <term>concupiscence: a strong desire or inclination toward sin</term>, being drawn away and enticed.

->The Second Theorem.<-

<margin>Chapter 2. This theorem is explained by Saint Augustine in the second book of *The Origin of the Soul* and in the letter to Jerome regarding the teaching of James.</margin> Whoever keeps the whole law, yet stumbles in one point, has become guilty of all. For He who said, "You shall not commit adultery," also said, "You shall not kill." If you do not commit adultery, but you do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law. So speak and so act as those who are beginning to be judged by the law of liberty.

->Theorems from the Epistles of the Blessed Apostle Peter.<-

->The First Theorem.<-

<margin>1 Peter 2; Isaiah 28; Psalm 118; Matthew 21; Mark 12; Luke 20; Acts 4.</margin> The Lord is sweet; coming to him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Because of this, the scripture contains: "Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, tested, chosen, and precious; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." Therefore, to you who believe, there is honor; but to those who do not believe, "the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner," and "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense." To those who <column-break/> stumble at the word and do not believe, for which they were also appointed.

->The Second Theorem.<-

<margin>Exodus 19; Hosea 2; Romans 9; Romans 13; Galatians 5; 1 Peter 3, 4; Proverbs 11.</margin> Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a slanderer, or one who covets what belongs to others. But if he suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name, since it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God. If it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God? And if the righteous person is saved with difficulty, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear? Therefore, let those who suffer according to the will of God commend their souls to the faithful Creator through good deeds.

->The Third Theorem from the Second Epistle of Peter.<-

<margin>2 Peter 1, 2; Timothy 3.</margin> No prophecy is made by one's own interpretation. For prophecy was not brought at any time by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit.

->The Fourth Theorem from the same Epistle.<-

<margin>2 Peter 2.</margin> For God knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the wicked to be tormented on the day of judgment.

->The Fifth Theorem from the same.<-

<margin>2 Peter 2; John 8.</margin> For if, having escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in these and overcome, their latter state is made worse for them than the former. For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of justice, than after knowing it, to turn back from that holy commandment delivered to them. For that true proverb has happened to them: "The dog returns to his own vomit," and "the sow that was washed returns to wallowing in the mire."

### ¶ The Seventh Theorem.

### ¶ Theorems from the Epistles of the Blessed Apostle John.

### ¶ The First Theorem.

<margin>1 John 2</margin>
¶ If anyone loves the world, the charity <term>charity: in this context, the divine love (caritas) of God</term> of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passes away, and its concupiscence. But he who does the will of God remains forever. Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that antichrist comes, even now many antichrists have appeared: whereby we know that it is the last hour.

### ¶ The Second Theorem.

<margin>1 John 3</margin>

### ¶ The Third Theorem.

<margin>1 John 5</margin>
¶ Everything that is born of God overcomes the world: and this is the victory which overcomes the world, our faith. Who is he that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ: not by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit which testifies that Christ is the truth. For there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit: and these three are one. <note>This passage, known as the "Johannine Comma," was a historically significant verse used to support the doctrine of the Trinity.</note>

### ¶ The First Theorem from the Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Jude.

### ¶ A Prayer to the Holy Apostles of God.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'F' depicting a robed figure, likely an apostle, seated with a book.</image-desc>
**O** happy and holy apostles of Christ's God, I beseech you by Him who chose you. You, the most beautiful gates who have risen to great height, intercede and pray constantly and unceasingly for us miserable and greatly negligent sinners. For we are exceedingly fragile, and the dominions of no virtue; we are slaves to the belly and the flesh, in whom scarcely any trace of virtue appears. Pray to the Lord, pray, O most pious ones; pray, all you hosts of saints and the entire assembly of the blessed, so that assisted by your prayers and merits—with the ship safe and the cargo intact—we may deserve to arrive at the port of perpetual salvation, of rest, of continuous peace, and of security that shall never end.

### The four golden books of Lord Symphorien Champier of Lyon regarding the Christian religion against Gentiles, Jews, Heretics, and followers of Muhammad.

### What is religion? Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'R' composed of ornate, scrolling foliate and floral patterns against a dark, textured background.</image-desc><margin>Cicero, Book 2 of the <term>Art of Rhetoric: referring to 'De Inventione'</term></margin>Religion, as Marcus Tullius [Cicero] says, is that which offers care and ceremony to some superior nature which they call divine. <margin>Plutarch in the <term>Life: specifically the 'Life of Numa'</term></margin>Plutarch indeed says that religion is the knowledge of divine things as named by philosophers. <margin>Masurius Sabinus</margin>Masurius Sabinus writes that "religious" is that which, on account of some holiness, is removed and set apart from us, the word being derived from "leaving behind" <note>original: "a relinquendo," an etymological argument connecting 'religio' to leaving something aside for sacred use</note>. <margin>Lactantius, Book 4</margin>Indeed, he shows that a religious place is one separated from the common use of the people by the difficulty of approaching it. Lactantius asserts that religion is named from "binding" <note>original: "a religando"</note>; he says we are born under this condition: that once created, we should provide just obedience to God; that we should know Him alone. Let us follow Him, bound <note>original: "religati"</note> and tied to God by this bond of piety, from which religion itself took its name—not, as Cicero interpreted it, from "re-reading" <note>original: "a relegando," Cicero’s view that religious people were those who carefully retraced or "re-read" the steps of divine ritual</note>. <margin>Augustine, Book 10 of *The City of God*</margin>Augustine, however, thinks that religion is named from "re-choosing" <note>original: "a religendo," from 're-eligere'</note>, when he says: "Choosing Him again—or rather re-choosing Him, for we had lost Him by neglecting Him—whence religion is said to be named." Therefore, even if religion is defined differently by others, it is truly and piously said to be a certain "re-binding" <note>original: "religatio"</note> of humans to God through pious works. This is joined to the sinew of holiness through piety, which is the same thing: and the recognition of the best and greatest God moves piety; piety moves holiness; holiness moves religion. Religion embraces both and, in a certain way, binds them back. First, therefore, human piety understands God and contemplates His nature, which is more excellent and distinguished than can be said. Holiness takes up this concept of the soul, and all the reasoning of the human mind fails in loving Him whom it has known in whatever way; from this arises that final method of pious works and the observation of the commandments which we call religion. This virtue is so proper to man, so fitting to this most noble of all animals, and finally so desirable, that there is no nation in all the lands so wild or so devoid of customs and things that it has not fashioned some religion for itself, even if not a probable one. For what was once simpler on earth than the Indians? What more empty than the Ethiopians? What more rigid than the Scythian people? Who more lying than the Greeks and Egyptians? Who softer than the Arabs? Who more treacherous than the Africans? What was more uncultivated than the Getulians? Who more light-minded than the Spaniards? Who more bellicose than the Gauls? What was more horrid than the Germans? Who milder than the Getae? Who more truculent than the Sarmatians? Yet in these human affects of the various nations, there is such a great [number] of bodies...

<header>The Bulwark of the Christian Religion.</header>

Despite the differences in minds and the diversity of worship and customs, there has been a single concern for religion among all people. It is, as it were, an innate longing. Thus it happens that even barbaric, uncultured nations—lacking laws, customs, and nearly all human refinement—felt this diversity, though it was perhaps known only to a few. Some invented gods for themselves, while others stubbornly continued to worship those they received from elsewhere. Yet, the same impulse was the cause: from the very beginning of life, mortals considered nothing more holy or venerable than those who were the interpreters of divine matters or the ministers of sacred ceremonies. Thus, India marveled at the **Brahmins** <term>Bragmagmas: a Latinized form of 'Brahmins,' the priestly caste of India</term>.

<margin>The mysteries of the ancients.</margin>
Assyria marveled at the **Magi**; Egypt at its priests; the Jews at their **Prophets**; and the Gauls at their **Druids**. Others were honored with the title of "Wise Men" by whoever deemed them worthy. Almost all their meditation was focused on the contemplation of divine things. From this, each nation's own religion arose, or was at least greatly increased. Thus, **Mercury Trismegistus** <note>A legendary figure often associated with the synthesis of Greek and Egyptian wisdom</note> delivered laws to the Egyptians; **Zoroaster** to the Bactrians and Persians (regarding the god Ozomasis); **Moses** most rightly to the Jews regarding God, the father of all nature; **Minos** to the Cretans regarding Jove <note>Jupiter</note>; **Canondas** to the Carthaginians regarding Saturn; **Lycurgus** to the Spartans regarding Apollo; **Draco and Solon** to the Athenians regarding Minerva; and **Numa Pompilius** to the Romans regarding the nymph Egeria. The Druids—or Barons—the priests of the Gauls, gave laws regarding Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Jove, and Minerva; **Ramolebis** to the Scythians regarding Vesta; **Plato** to the Magnesians and Sicilians regarding Jove and Apollo; **Muhammad** <note>original: "Macometh"</note> to the Arabs regarding the angel Gabriel. But the Apostles and Evangelists of Christ most rightly delivered the truth regarding the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is the true religion which Christian piety honors above all that ever were, are today, or could ever be. It is, without controversy, the most holy and by far the truest, because the truest Author—or rather, Truth itself—instituted it, sanctioned it, and handed it down to be piously observed. I urge and warn you to hold fast to this, for this is the direct path to heaven and the most certain way to those eternal goods which "no eye has seen nor ear heard."

<margin>The laws of the nations and the ancients.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 118. Psalm 118.</margin>
Other laws are merely evasions and fables, as the Psalm says: *The wicked have told me fables, but not like your law* <note>original: "Narrauerunt mihi iniqui fabulationes: sed non vt lex tua." This refers to Psalm 119:85 in modern numbering</note>. And again: *He has not done so for every nation, and his judgments he has not made known to them.* In the name of Jesus, as he himself predicted, demons were cast out, diseases were cured, the dead were raised, idols were smashed, temples destroyed, and finally the **orthodox truth** was preached throughout the whole world. This the apostles, the martyrs, and the holy confessors did—by invoking the name of Christ—not in corners, but openly in the presence of princes, kings, and peoples. No nation and no part of the world now serves idolatry, unless perhaps some at the **Antipodes** <term>Antipodes: literally 'those with feet opposite,' a term used for people living on the opposite side of the earth</term>—if indeed the Antipodes even exist—or other islands unknown to us, to which the fame of Christ has not yet passed. And who scattered this doctrine throughout the world? Who sowed this dogma through the islands, across the sea, and across the land? Indeed...

In the past, there were kings who, because of their royal memory, began to be worshipped by their people even after death. From this, temples were established for them, and statues were fashioned to preserve the likeness of the deceased. They would sacrifice victims and celebrate feast days to offer them honor. From this, what were originally intended as solaces for the living became sacred rites for posterity. To see if this truth holds for each case, let us teach more extensively about that wicked worship of idols, which is so abhorrent to the Christian religion. Although the story is difficult to tell, you will recognize that the madness of the ancients was not small. We read that **Venus** was greatly honored by Sicilian colonists. There was a famous temple of Venus on Mount Eryx, a high mountain in Sicily, crowded with a multitude of women dedicated to her service, many of whom were brought from Sicily and foreign regions. As the author **Diodorus Siculus** states:

For He made all things that He willed out of nothing; He Himself rules what He made. The gods of the heathens <note>original: "Gentilium dij"</note> are not gods precisely because they are commemorated: they can be both grasped and seen by these eyes. However, as Aurelius Augustine is the authority, those whom the vain worship in vain—Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Juno, Minerva, Venus, and other monsters—are not good names but bad names. Even the writings of those who delight in such errors cry out that these were mortal men. But it is helpful to hear the Apostle Paul regarding what kind of God our sacred scriptures proclaim: he says, "To the only invisible, incorruptible God be honor and glory" <note>1 Timothy 1:17</note>. Our God is not seen with the eyes of the flesh, but is seen with the eyes of the heart; He is not seen for a time, but is seen for eternity. But the pagan says: "Show me whom you worship." I respond: I indeed have someone even now to show you, but you do not have the eyes to see Him; for our Savior says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" <note>Matthew 5:8</note>. An impure heart shrouded in the darkness of sins seeks to see God? The light shines in the darkness, but the darkness has not understood it. Is it because the blind man does not see that the light therefore does not shine? If you knew, O infidel, how to say to the true God, "Enlighten my eyes," you would see with us now "through a glass darkly" <note>original: "per speculum in enigmate"; 1 Corinthians 13:12</note> so that you might later be able to see "face to face." If you understood the craftsman from his works, you would recognize the Creator from the creature. If you were awestruck within yourself because you do not fully grasp your own being, you would recognize the God who made you. We believe, therefore, in an immortal and invisible God—not the one whom you infidels imagine as a god who is both an adulterer and a thunderer—but the true God, the fabricator and ruler of the whole world.

### ¶ That the inventions of the Druids, which some want to understand mystically, are not to be regarded.
->Chapter 3.<-

<margin>Gallic priests according to Caesar.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial letter 'N' containing a portrait of a man in profile, wearing a soft cap and a high-collared garment.</image-desc>For the errors of the Druid superstitions, who imagined Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva to be gods, are not to be listened to. Caesar refutes them—and I do not know whether anyone among the Romans could be more learned or more curious regarding such matters. For he says in Book VI of the *Gallic War* that several gods were immediately adopted by the Celts. For we read in his work as follows: In all of Gaul, of those men who are of any account and honor, there are two classes. For the common people are held almost in the place of slaves, who achieve nothing by themselves and are admitted to no council. Most of them, when they are pressed by debt, the magnitude of taxes, or the injustice of the powerful, surrender themselves into slavery to the nobles, who have the same rights over them as masters have over slaves. But of these two classes, one is the Druids, the other the Knights. The former are concerned with divine matters, manage public and private sacrifices, and interpret religious rites. To them, a great number of young men flock for the sake of instruction, and they are held in great honor among them.

<column-break/>

# Book One. Folio V.

For they decide about almost all public and private controversies. If any crime has been committed, if a murder has happened, if there is a dispute about an inheritance or boundaries, these same men decide it and determine rewards and punishments. If anyone, either a private citizen or a public official, does not abide by their decree, they ban them from the sacrifices. This punishment is the most severe among them; those who are thus interdicted are held in the number of the impious and wicked. Everyone withdraws from them; they flee their approach and conversation lest they receive some harm from the contagion. Justice is not restored to them when they seek it, nor is any honor shared with them. One man is in charge of all these Druids, who holds the highest authority among them. Upon his death, if any of the remainder excels in dignity, he succeeds; but if there are several equals, he is chosen by the vote of the Druids. Sometimes they even contend for the leadership with arms. At a certain time of the year, they sit in the territory of the Carnutes <note>A region in central Gaul, near modern Chartres</note>, which region is considered the center of all Gaul. Here, all who have controversies assemble from everywhere and obey their judgments and decrees. The Druids are accustomed to be absent from war, nor do they pay taxes together with the rest; they have an exemption from military service and immunity from all matters. Driven by such great rewards, many come together for instruction of their own accord, and many are sent by their relatives and parents. They are said to learn a great number of verses there by heart; thus, some remain in training for twenty years. Nor do they think it right to commit these things
<margin>The Gauls use Greek letters.</margin>
to writing, although in almost all other matters, both public and private accounts, they use Greek letters. They wish to persuade people of this primary point: that
<margin>Immortality of the soul.</margin>
souls do not perish, but after death pass from one person to another <note>The doctrine of metempsychosis or reincarnation</note>; and they think that by this, men are most excited to virtue, having neglected the fear of death. Furthermore, they dispute many things concerning the stars and their motions, the magnitude of the world and the earth, the nature of things, and the power and might of the immortal gods, and they hand these down to the youth. The nation of all the Gauls is extremely devoted to religions, and for that reason, those who are affected by more serious diseases and those who are engaged in battles and dangers either sacrifice humans as victims or vow that they will sacrifice them. Because they think that the will of the immortal gods cannot be appeased unless the life of a man is given for the life of a man, they have established sacrifices of that kind publicly. They worship the god <margin>Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Jupiter.</margin> Mercury most of all; after him, Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva. Regarding these, they have almost the same opinion as other nations: that Apollo wards off diseases, Minerva teaches the beginnings of works and crafts, Jupiter holds the empire of the celestial beings, and Mars conducts wars. This is what Caesar felt regarding the priests of the Gauls. 
<margin>Pomponius Mela on the gifts of the Gauls.</margin>
Pomponius Mela wrote almost the same things regarding the mysteries of the Gauls in the place from which he speaks in the third book of *On the Situation of the World*: "The Gauls have their own eloquence and their masters of wisdom, the Druids. These men profess to know the magnitude and form of the earth and the world, the motions of the heaven and the stars, and what the gods want. They teach many things to the most noble of the nation secretly and for a long time—twenty years—in a cave, or..."

# The Bulwark of the Christian Religion.
## Book One.
### Folio 6.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus</margin>
In the secluded forests, they teach one principle above all, as the common people report: that they might be better suited for war, they believe that souls are eternal and that there is another life among the shades. Thus, when they cremate and bury their dead, they include things once suited to the living for their business. Even the accounting and demand of credit was deferred to the underworld, and there were some who would gladly cast themselves onto the funeral pyres of their kin as if they were to live together. So says Diodorus Siculus in the sixth book of his *Antiquities* regarding the Gauls. He says the Gauls are of sharp 
<margin>Bards, poets of melody</margin>
intellect and not at all averse to learning. Among them are also poets of melodies whom they call Bards; these sing with instruments like the lyre, praising some and censuring others. There are also philosophers and theologians 
<margin>Philosophers of the Gauls</margin>
whom they call Saronides <note>An ancient name for Druidic philosophers or priests mentioned by Diodorus.</note>, who are especially honored by them. They also employ diviners who, through sacrifices, predict the future; these are held in the highest esteem, with the entire populace obeying them. It is a custom among them to perform no sacrifice without a philosopher. For they believe that through those who are acquainted with the divine nature, sacred rites ought to be performed, as if these men were closer to the gods, and that good things should be sought from the gods through their intercession. They enjoy the counsel of these men in both peace and war. Indeed, poets are held in such high regard among them that when the battle lines are drawn and the armies have drawn their swords and cast their spears, the poets approach not only friends but enemies, and at their intervention, the fighting ceases. Thus, among the Gauls, anger yields 
<margin>Customs of the Gauls</margin>
to wisdom, and Mars <note>The Roman god of war.</note> reveres the Muses <note>The goddesses of the arts and sciences.</note>. For the opinion of Pythagoras <note>The Greek philosopher who taught the transmigration of souls.</note> flourished among them, in which he said that the souls of men are immortal, and that after a certain time, having left their bodies, they would return into other bodies. For this reason, they even cast written letters onto the funeral pyres of the dead, as if the dead were going to read them. Some even despise death so much that they fight naked. But these many points tend toward this: that while different mortal men may lack different proofs of life, religion is nevertheless a perpetual companion of humanity. Some barbarians lived their lives without women; the Amazons lived without men; many were without morals, without discipline, or without laws; others had no houses or any city; many did not even know the commerce of other nations, and some stubbornly fled from it. The Troglodytes and Garamantes <note>Ancient groups traditionally cited as living in primitive or "uncivilized" states.</note> lived naked. The Ethiopians indeed despised gold and gems, yet no one was ever without religion, either because they did not wish to be or because they could not. But almost all of these have ceased to be worshippers of false gods, and now their ritual is entirely different from what it once was.
<margin>Tertullian in the *Apology against the Nations*, Chapter 16.</margin>
The Gauls were once worshippers of the gods of the nations <note>original: "Gentilium... deorum"</note>, just like other peoples; now they are most observant of true piety. At that time, each of the peoples lived for themselves, and the cities were ruled by a few petty kings throughout the whole nation; now the empire of the King holds everything widely. For that which we Christians worship (Tertullian begins) is the one God, who from the 

<column-break/>

bodies of the elements, the spirits, by the Word with which He commanded, by the Reason with which He arranged, and by the Power with which He was able, brought forth out of nothing as an ornament for His majesty. From this, the Greeks also adapted the name "Cosmos" <note>original: "cosmon"; meaning "order" or "world-system."</note> for the world. He is invisible, even if He may be seen; He is incomprehensible, even if represented through grace; He is inestimable, even if estimated by human senses. Therefore, He is true and so great. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure often cited by early Christians as a "pagan prophet" of monotheism.</note> also (as Saint Cyprian is the authority) 
<margin>Cyprian in the treatise *On the Vanity of Idols*.</margin>
speaks of one God, and confesses Him to be incomprehensible and inestimable. These spirits (he says) hide within consecrated substances and images. They inspire the hearts of seers with their breath; they animate the fibers of entrails; they govern the flights of birds; they rule lots; they produce oracles; they always wrap falsehoods in truths. For they are both deceived and they deceive. They disturb life; they disquiet 
<margin>Demons lurking in images according to Cyprian.</margin>
sleep; creeping as spirits into bodies, they secretly terrify the mind, distort the limbs, break health, and provoke diseases to force people into worshipping them. Thus, being fattened by the steam of altars <note>original: "nidore altarium"</note> and the funeral pyres of cattle, they may seem to have cured what they had previously bound by ceasing their injury. This is the only "healing" from them: when their own injury stops. Nor is there any other aim for them than to call men away from God and to turn them toward the superstition of themselves, away from the understanding of true religion. And since they are themselves subject to punishment, they seek companions for their penalty, whom they have made sharers in their error through their crime. Yet these, when adjured by the true God, immediately yield to us and confess, and are forced to depart from the possessed bodies. There is, therefore, one Lord God of all, for that sublimity cannot have a companion since it alone holds all power. There is one king for the bees, one leader in the flocks, and one ruler in the herds. Much more is there one ruler of the world, who commands all things that exist by His Word, dispenses them by His Reason, and completes them by His Power. For He cannot be seen—He is clearer than sight; He cannot be grasped—He is purer than touch; He cannot be estimated—He is greater than sense. And therefore, we estimate God worthily when we say He is inestimable. Do not seek a name for God: "God" is His name. Those words are needed where a multitude must be distinguished by specific marks of titles. To God, who is alone, the title "God" is the whole name. Therefore, He is one, and He is diffused everywhere; God is mingled with man. This is our God, this is Christ, who, as mediator of two, put on man to lead him to the Father. What man is, Christ willed to be, so that man also might be what Christ is. That idols are not gods, and that there is one God, and that it has been given to believers to know that those whom the nations worshipped are not gods, is known from this, as the same Cyprian says. I think even regarding his Gauls, 
<margin><unclear>X</unclear></margin>
the idolaters may insultingly reproach us, saying that those who cut themselves off gladly suffer torture, as long as they obey the pretenses of their statues' standing.

# The Bulwark of the Christian Religion.
## Book One.
### Folio 7.

<column-break/>

Nevertheless, we should not shun music on account of the superstitions of the profane. If we are able to take anything from it that is useful for understanding the Holy Scriptures, we should not be turned toward their theatrical trifles. If we find anything regarding harps, organs, or the governors of public affairs that might serve to grasp spiritual things, let us discuss it with the <term>Saronides</term> <note>Ancient Gaulish philosophers/priests mentioned by Diodorus Siculus.</note> and the Bards and the Druids. For we ought not to refuse to learn through letters simply because they say Mercury was their discoverer, or because they dedicated temples to Justice and Virtue. They preferred to worship in stones what ought to be carried in the heart; yet for that reason, justice and virtue are not to be shunned by us. Indeed, whoever is a good and true Christian should understand that truth belongs to his Lord, wherever he shall find it. <note>original: "Domini sui esse intelligat vbicunq; inuenerit veritatem"</note> While confessing and acknowledging this truth even in sacred letters, he should repudiate superstitious fictions. He should teach men and warn them that, though they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God or give thanks. Instead, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish hearts were darkened. For claiming to be wise, they became fools; and they exchanged 
<margin>Romans 1:c</margin>
the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents.

### That idols are not gods: and that there is one true God
### and Lord of all, whom Christians worship.
### Chapter Four.

<margin>Augustine, Book 3 of "On the Symbol for Catechumens," Chapter 1.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial Q featuring a seated man in a hooded robe, likely a scholar or monk, pointing at a book.</image-desc>
That idols are not gods and that there is one God is known to all who are of sound mind. But sins and the author of sin, the devil, have separated the soul from God. And while the creature followed its seducer and deserted its Savior, a great ruin occurred and the soul wandered. Indeed, the soul, so that it might worship idols in place of God, adored the very things it made, deserting Him by whom it was made. By adoring a stone having no life, the soul itself perishes by deserting God, who is its true and eternal life. From this, as Augustine is the authority, comes all error and the desertion of good things; from this comes the worship of the pagans and the perversity of heretics. Souls wandered through various and perverse pleasures, so that some worshipped the sun, others the moon and stars, others mountains, others stones, and even thickets. Each believed he had found for himself not God as a helper, but the devil as a deceiver. Thus, through these various paths, the soul wandered from its Creator; so that everything God had given to it for its service, the soul worshipped as God. 
Were not all things created for the sake of man? Read the Holy Scriptures and you will find that God said to man, whom He formed from the mud of the earth: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it, and have power over the fish 

<column-break/>

<header>Book One. Folio 7.</header>

of the sea, and the birds of the air, and the cattle of the earth." And a little later He said: "Behold, I have given you all things for your use and for food." Moreover, those who refuse to read the Holy Scriptures, as the same 
<margin>Augustine in the same work.</margin>
Augustine reports, are convinced by the very nature of things and by the world itself, which serves them by its works; with its own voice, the world rebukes the incredulous and says to the perverse soul: "Why is it, O wretched one, that you wander within me? Having become degenerate, you have forgotten by whom and for what greatness you were created; you, for whom heaven and earth—this so beautiful home—was constructed without any preceding merits of your own." Each of the elements cries out in response, demonstrating their craftsman by their own works. Heaven cries: "I am not God; for if I were God, no clouding could have obscured me, nor would darkness succeed my light. Rather, my light would have remained whole, incorrupt, and inviolate, just as that true light remains which created this temporal light in me for your sake." The sun also cries out: "Why, O man, do you worship me as God, whom you see enclosed by rising and setting? God has neither beginning nor end; but you, by deserting Him, have incurred a great fall. Though you may consider me great and wonderful, I acknowledge that I have over me He who created me and you. Since my works, splendors, and heat serve you, why do you think I should be worshipped as God, unless it is because you do not know how to worship the true God?" Likewise, the moon and stars bring forth a similar voice. "Do you not see, O man," they say, "that we perform our nightly space, are excluded from the light, and do not overstep the established boundaries which the Almighty Craftsman fixed for the comfort of your rest? I am not God; we prove your falsehood by serving you to your own punishment." The sea cries out, and all things that are in it: "We are not God; for I offer service as I was commanded, taking up the journey of the ship's hull, directing the appropriate movements and the breaths of the winds, so that I may lead your steps to the desired port, even as greed hurries you along without delay. Indeed, you recognize that the animals born from me were given to you for food. Since, therefore, I acknowledge my limited measure through all things, why do you desert your proper order by deserting God, the Creator of all?" The earth cries out: "Why then, O man, do you ascribe the name of deity to me? You do not recognize what I am because you have forgotten who you are. You do not recognize your own material; you do not recognize that you are my mud, formed from me indeed, but not animated as I am. You do not recognize that among all animals produced from me, you alone were established under God as almost the lord of the world. Rightly do you not understand, because when you were in honor, you did not understand; you are compared to foolish beasts and have become like them." For God does not easily forgive idolaters; Moses in Exodus prays for the people but does not obtain his request immediately. He says: "O Lord, this people has sinned a great sin; they have made for themselves gods of gold. And now, if you will forgive them this great sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of the book which you have written." And the Lord said to Moses: "If anyone sins before me, I will blot him out of my book." Likewise, when Jeremiah [prayed] for the people...

# The Bulwark of the Christian Religion.
## Book One. Folio 9.

...you will find that it says in Latin: *Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.* <note>The author refers to a famous acrostic in the Sibylline Oracles where the first letters of the verses spell out "Jesus Christ Son of God Savior" in Greek.</note> Let us hear other Sibylline verses, delivered by the same Augustine, which more clearly demonstrate the passion of Christ:
Into wicked and unfaithful hands he shall later come.
They shall strike God with impure hands,
And with filthy mouths they shall spit poisonous saliva.
But he, entirely innocent, shall give his back to the lashes,
And receiving blows, he shall remain silent, so that no one may know
What the word is or from where it comes: that he may speak to the dead.
And he shall wear a crown of thorns.
They gave him gall for food and vinegar for his thirst;
They showed this table of inhospitality.
For you, foolish one, did not recognize your God,
Playing with mortal minds, but with thorns
You crowned him; you mixed a bitter crown and gall.
The veil of the temple shall be torn, and at midday
Extremely dark shadows shall hold us for three hours.
And the fate of death shall end when a three-day sleep is taken;
And then, having returned from the dead, he comes into the light,
The first to show the beginning of the resurrection to those called back.
I believe, O Gentiles, that you are so dazed by such great witnesses, and so refuted by the truth itself, that you ought to resist no further nor ask anything more. Did not even the heaven give testimony concerning Christ, when a new star <note>The Star of Bethlehem.</note>—at the new birth of the man—showed the God-man born to the nations, as if with a tongue and a finger? And I shall mention Plato, who is called a "divine man" among you; he spoke to the effect that one should follow his precepts only until someone more sacred than a human appears on earth, who may open the fountain of truth to all, and whom everyone shall finally follow. I show, furthermore, Calcidius <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato’s Timaeus.</note>, who predicted in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus* that a new star would shine at the birth of Christ. He noted that the wise men of the Chaldeans, practiced in the observation of heavenly things, would look for it on a night journey and seek the recent birth of God to offer prayers, vows, and gifts. Nor was Virgil <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Maro). His Fourth Eclogue was widely interpreted by medieval Christians as a prophecy of Christ.</note> entirely unmindful of this (as Augustine asserts), who in his *Bucolics* expressed the future birth of Christ from a virgin (even if he ascribed it to another) and the prophecy of the Cumaean Sibyl. For, as Augustine says, the truth did not remain silent, crying out even through the tongues of its enemies:
The final age of the Cumaean song has now come.
A great order of the ages is born anew.
Now the Virgin returns; the reign of Saturn returns.
Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven.

<column-break/>

Only you, chaste Lucina, favor the boy being born,
By whom the iron race shall first cease,
And a golden race shall rise throughout the whole world;
Your Apollo now reigns.

Does Virgil not bear testimony here concerning Christ? This might come into doubt, unless I introduce other witnesses suitable for the Gentiles who say even more. Did not Balaam the astrologer speak through a parable, saying: <margin>Numbers 24:c</margin> "A star shall rise out of Jacob"—that is, the glowing light of spiritual grace by which the night of the Gentiles' infidelity is illuminated—"and a rod shall rise from Israel, and shall strike the leaders of Moab, and shall lay waste to all the sons of Seth, and Edom shall be his possession. Out of Jacob shall come he who shall rule and shall destroy the remnants of the city." <margin>Origen, Homily 13 on Numbers.</margin> See (says Origen) how the wisdom of God made this vessel, which was prepared for dishonor, to be useful not only for one nation, but for almost the whole world; and to this man, who was accustomed to seeing demons, God appears, forbidding the path of evil work. Balaam is struck dumb and marvels at the authority of the one forbidding him. <margin>Saint Ambrose, Letter 37 to Theomastius.</margin> But do not wonder (says Ambrose) that the Lord poured into the augur what he should speak, when even in the Gospel he poured a word into the leader of the synagogue, one of those persecuting Christ: "That it is expedient for one man to die for the people." In this, there is no merit of prophecy, but an assertion of truth, so that by the testimony of adversaries, the truth might be manifested, and the treachery of those not believing might be refuted by the voices of their own augurs. Therefore, that Chaldean Balaam is brought to the faith so that the superstition of the Chaldeans might be silenced. It is not, therefore, the merit of the one confessing, but the oracle of the one calling, by the revealing grace of God. Augustine cries out: <margin>Augustine, Book 2 on the Creed to the Catechumens, chapter 4.</margin> "The star invites the Magi; the curiosity of the Magi is instructed by the tongue of the heavens. The Magi proclaim the King of the Jews; the Jews deny him. The former seek to worship; the latter seek to kill. The Magi tell King Herod whom they seek: the born King. The Jews tell from which city Christ shall rise to reign. Both proclaim, both confess, but the former in one way, the latter in another: the former so that, once found, he may be worshiped; the latter so that, once captured, he may be killed." Behold, the Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, offer gifts to Christ—not only gold, frankincense, and myrrh, but even their own souls. And as Saint Ambrose says, the Magi believed in one God, <margin>Ambrose, in the book On the Faith, chapter 2.</margin> and as suppliants, they brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the cradle of Christ. By gold, they confessed him as King; by incense, they worshiped him as God. For the treasure of the kingdom is the sacrifice of God; myrrh is for his burial. Why, therefore, did they want these mystical gifts among the lowly mangers, except that we might understand in Christ the distinction of divinity and flesh? As a man he is seen; as Lord he is worshiped. He lies hidden in swaddling clothes, but he shines in the stars. The cradle indicates him being born, and the stars indicate him ruling. It is flesh that is wrapped up; it is divinity to which service is rendered by angels. Thus the truth of the assumed flesh is proven, and the natural dignity of his majesty is not lost. This, indeed, is our faith.

# The Bulwark of the Christian Religion.

<margin>The oracle of Apollo.</margin> The Gentiles agreed that Jesus was God himself or certainly divine. When the Apollo of Miletus <note>original: "Mille sius appollo"</note> was consulted, he thus commended Christ: he was mortal in body, wise, a worker of wonders; but under Chaldean judges, he was seized with weapons, with nails and clubs; he suffered a bitter death. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and famous critic of early Christianity.</note>—the most wicked among the Gentiles—says in his book *On Oracles*:
<margin>Porphyry</margin> The gods declared Christ to be most pious and asserted that he had become immortal. Porphyry himself concedes that Christ was both wise and pious. Who then would call the Christians partly unlearned and partly sorcerers, thereby manifestly contradicting both the truth and himself?
<margin>Vespasian and Titus.</margin> The Emperors Vespasian and Titus, having heard of the works of Christ, feared even his power. 
<margin>Alexander Severus.</margin> Alexander Severus decided that temples should be built to Christ, but he did not succeed in this. As Capitolinus <note>A traditional author of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note> records, he used to pray in the mornings in his private shrine before a statue of Christ. 
<margin>Emperor Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.</margin> Hadrian, as the same author relates, decided to build temples to Christ and receive him among the gods. Therefore, he ordered temples without statues to be built in all cities. Antoninus Pius, when he heard that Christians frequently used the proverb, "What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another," investigated Christianity and consecrated a statue to him as if to a god.
<margin>Constantine the Great.</margin> Finally, Constantine, having clearly experienced Christ’s miracles in his own affairs, feared God more than the people; he worshipped only Christ openly, overturned the temples of idols, and built precious temples to Christ everywhere. These are the things the Gentiles felt concerning Christ, which we have narrated here, fortified by the authority of 
<margin>Augustine, Book 2, Chapter 40, On Christian Doctrine.</margin> Augustine, who says in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*: "If those who are called philosophers, especially the Platonists, have said things that are true and suited to our faith, they are not only not to be feared, but should be claimed from them for our own use as from unjust possessors." <note>This is the famous "Spoils of the Egyptians" argument, suggesting Christians can use pagan philosophy for holy purposes.</note> For what else have many of our good faithful done? Do we not see with how much gold and silver and clothing Cyprian—that most sweet teacher and blessed martyr—came out of Egypt? How much did Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary bring? To say nothing of those still living, and the innumerable Greeks. This is what the most faithful servant of God, Moses, had done before, of whom it is written that he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

# Book Two: On the Christian Religion Against the Jews.
## Christ was foretold by the Jews, but the people did not understand his coming. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' containing a portrait of a man's head and shoulders.</image-desc> The Jews knew that Christ was to come. For this was always announced to them by the warnings of the prophets. But the significance of his coming was twofold: one who would fulfill the duty and example of a man; the other who would manifest God. By not understanding the first coming—which then preceded in a hidden manner through his passion—

<column-break/>

<page-num>folio 10.</page-num>
<header>Book Second.</header>

they believe only in the one coming which will be manifest in power. That the people of the Jews could not understand this was the result of their sins; thus they were (as Cyprian is witness) punished with blindness of wisdom and understanding. As those who were unworthy of life, they had Life before their eyes and did not see it. And so, as was predicted before by the prophets, by his word and the command of his voice, he cast out demons from men, restored the paralyzed, cleansed the lepers, gave light to the blind, gave the ability to walk to the lame, brought the dead back to life, and compelled the elements to serve him. The winds served him, the seas obeyed, and the lower world yielded. The Jews, who believed him to be only a man because of the humility of his flesh and body, thought him a magician. Their masters and leaders—that is, those whom he refuted by his teaching and wisdom—provoked by anger and indignation, finally delivered him, once he was seized, to Pontius Pilate (who then governed Syria on behalf of the Romans). They demanded his cross and death with persistent votes. He himself had predicted they would do this, and the testimony of the prophets had preceded it: that it was necessary for him to suffer, not so that he might feel death, but that he might conquer it. And when he had suffered, he returned again to the heavens <note>original: "supos," likely *superos*</note> so that he might show the faith of his divine majesty. Thus he fulfilled the course of events. For having been crucified, he breathed out his spirit at the point of the executioner's act; he gave up his spirit voluntarily and on the third day rose again of his own accord from the dead. He appeared to his disciples just as he had been, and offered himself to be recognized by those watching. Seen at once as both the conquered and conspicuous in the firmness of his corporal substance, he remained for forty days, so that they could be instructed and learn the vital precepts anew. Then he was taken up into heaven in an enfolding cloud, so that he might present the man whom he loved, whom he put on, and whom he protected from death, to the Father as a victor. He is now to come from heaven for the punishment of the devil and for the judgment of the human race, with the vigor of an avenger and the power of a judge.

# Book Three of Lord Symphorian Champerier’s Bulwark of the Christian Religion Against Heretics.

## The refutation of the Arian heresy and the presumption of the Arians.
### Chapter One.

The assertion of our faith, as it pleases Ambrose, <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan and a key figure in the struggle against Arianism.</note> is this: that we say there is one God. lest we create several gods through the error of the pagans by assigning dissimilar powers; for it is written:

A foundational monotheistic statement known as the Shema.</note> For "God" and "Lord" are names of majesty and names of power, just as He says: "Lord is my name." Note that He says "in the name" <note>singular</note> and not "in the names." He also says: "I and the Father are one." He says "one" <note>Latin: *unum*, neuter gender</note> so that there is no division of power. He added "we are" <note>Latin: *sumus*, plural</note> so that you may recognize the Father and the Son, whereby it is believed that a perfect Father begot a perfect Son; and through the Father and the Son, there is a union not just of confession, but of the unity of nature.
<margin>Exposition of the Arian heresy</margin>
But now let us consider the questions which the Arians <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius (c. 256–336 AD), who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal or equal with God the Father.</note> bring against the Son of God. They say the Son of God is dissimilar to the Father; if this were said of a man, it would be an insult. They say the Son of God began in time, even though He is the creator of time itself. We are mere humans and do not wish to be temporal; we began in time, yet we believe we shall exist without time, and we hope to become eternal. And how can we deny that the Son of God is everlasting, whom nature—not grace—proves and demonstrates to be everlasting? They say He was "created." Who would rank an author among his own works, so that he appears to be the same as what he made? They deny He is "Good"—a sacrilegious voice that condemns itself so that it cannot hope for indulgence. They deny He is the true Son of God; they deny He is almighty, even though it is confessed that all things were made through the Son and all things were created by the power of God. For what is power <note>original: *virtus*</note> if not a perfect nature? They even deny that the divinity is one with the Father. Let them, therefore, delete the 
<margin>John 10:f</margin>
Gospel; let them delete the voice of Christ. For He Himself said: "I and the Father are one." It is not I who say this; Christ said it. Would He deceive so as to lie? Would He be so impious as to usurp what He was not? But these points shall be more fully arranged in their proper places. Now, since the heretic says He is dissimilar and strives to build this up with clever arguments, we must say what is written: "Beware lest any man cheat you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men and according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ; for in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." <note>Colossians 2:8–9.</note> For they place all the force of their poisons, as the same Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), a staunch defender of Nicene Christianity against Arianism.</note> reports, in dialectical dispute. This is defined as the opinion of philosophers: not to have the power of building up, but the zeal for destroying. But it did not please God to save His people through dialectics. For the kingdom of God is in the simplicity of faith, not in the contention of speech. Therefore, they say He is dissimilar. We deny it; rather, we shudder at this word. Tell me, heretic, you who dare to say that the wisdom of God is lesser: tell me the height of heaven, how great the breadth of the earth is, or the depth of the abyss. Count <note>original: *munera*, likely a scribal or OCR error for *numera* (number/count).</note>, if you can, the drops of rain, the sand of the sea, the days of the age; count even your own hairs. For all the hairs of your head are counted. Show

to me and explain those small, inferior things, and then I will believe that you can investigate the superior things. But you cannot; you are not able. For by teaching such things—or rather not teaching but blaspheming—you are shown to be doing an injury not to some powerful person, but to God the Father Himself in His Son. "The Father is greater, the Son is less; the Father is better, the Son is inferior"—not even any wise man would willingly accept such insults, who contends that he has a son as good as himself, or a father. Hence also that prophetic saying: "The father rejoiced in the son of wisdom; he lives in his life, and in his death he was not saddened. For the father is dead, and yet it is as if he were not dead." Why is he not dead? "Because he left behind one like himself." <note>A paraphrase of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 30:4–6.</note> Behold, the prophet says the wise son of a man is like his father; and you, heretic, dare to say that the very Wisdom of God, the Son, is dissimilar to the Father? The prophet says a dead man lives in the father because he left a similar son; and you dare to separate that very eternal life, which is the Son of God, from the Father who never dies. And what, he says, shall I do? He Himself said: "The Father is greater than I." 
<margin>John 14:d</margin>
Because you do not understand (says Augustine), what He said sounds wrong to you. For He Himself said it, and 
<margin>Augustine in the book against the Arians, ch. 8.</margin>
indeed confirmed it; He certainly said it: "The Father is greater than I." The Son Himself said it. See *when* He said this: He said this while situated in the assumption of human nature. He said "the Father is greater than I" at the time He said: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." <note>Matthew 26:38.</note> He said "the Father is greater than I" when He wept, when He was weary, when 
<margin>Matthew 26:d</margin>
He hungered, and when He thirsted. He said "the Father is greater than I" when the 
<margin>Psalm 8:f</margin>
Scripture also says He was "made a little lower than the angels." <note>Psalm 8:5.</note> Does insane pride really proceed so irreverently that you dare to say the Word of God, remaining with the Father, is lower than the angels in that divinity? If you do not dare to say this, heretic, observe these steps and your error will perish. The Son with the Father is equal with the Father, because He is eternal with the eternal, always remaining with the eternal; He remains equal, though sent and coming in the assumption of man, becoming "less" than not only the Father but even the angels. He is equal in the form of God, less in the form of a servant. Equal with the Father in creating the angels; equal with the Father in making mankind; equal with the Father in establishing the whole world; less than the Father in repairing the lost world. Equal with the Father in bestowing eternal life; less than the Father in undergoing our death. Now, therefore, we believe the Son is lesser in the assumption of man, but equal to the Father in divinity, made (as the Apostle says) from the seed of David. 
<margin>Romans 1:a, 1 Timothy 2:b</margin>
Whom the Virgin Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit, and in whose womb the Word took on flesh, becoming for us a mediator: fully man and fully God, truly soul and flesh, one Christ. Indeed, the order of this sacrament also declares this to us: that after we believe in God the Father almighty, we believe 
<meta>catchword: we believe</meta>

<meta>This page continues the theological defense of the Christian faith initiated in the previous section. # The Bulwark of the Christian Religion

We believe in God the Father Almighty and in Jesus Christ His Son, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. This birth disturbs all human thought, because a divine power brought it to pass. For our logic of generation does not admit how a virgin, conceiving and remaining a virgin after birth, should be seen with a son while her integrity remains inviolate. No ordinary man born could fulfill this; but He was able because He was not merely a man, but both God and man, who willed to be born as a man for the reason that every man had perished. Therefore, the first great and singular miracle of this Mediator was that He was born in such a way: so that He, who came to teach many and perform miracles—which He did through Himself and through others—might nevertheless possess something uniquely His own, having usurped nothing belonging to another. For He alone was born of a virgin: because He alone was conceived of the Holy Spirit without the embrace or seed of a man. He alone filled His mother's womb without corruption: just as He alone ascended above the heavens for us to sit at the right hand of the Father. The disciples came after Him to perform many great miracles, and they did so; yet no one is preached or believed to have been born of a virgin or conceived of the Holy Spirit, except that one who, being the Creator of time, was found in time, born even from the womb of a virgin; taking up that unstained human nature which He had formed, so that through it our Redeemer might, in a sense, repair our ruin. And He is both the Son of God and the Son of Man. The Son of God from the heart of the Father; the Son of Man from the womb of His mother. This is the one and the same Christ who proceeded from the virginal womb <margin>Psalm 18</margin> like a bridegroom from his chamber; in which womb spiritual nuptials were celebrated: God was joined to flesh and flesh adhered to God so that there might be one Christ, and as Augustine said, "wholly man." <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) was a foundational theologian who wrote extensively on the nature of Christ's humanity and divinity.</note> Therefore, you heretic, question the scriptures; question the apostles; question the prophets; question Christ. Why say more? Question the Father, whose honor the Arians <note>Arians followed Arius, who believed Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with the Father.</note> claim to study, even as the Son is judged by them to be "degenerate" <note>original: "degener," meaning falling away from the nature of the Father.</note>. But the injury of the Son is no honor to a good Father. A man cannot please the Father if he believes the Son has degenerated from the Father rather than being equal to the Father. In the beginning of the world itself, I hear that the Father and the Son exist, and I perceive one single work. I hear the Speaker, I recognize the One acting; but I read of one image and one likeness of both Father and Son. This likeness is not of diversity, but of unity. Why then do you claim for yourself what you take away from the Son, since you cannot exist "in the image of God" except through the Image of God? <margin>Divine Ambrose, On the Faith, Book 2, Chapter 4</margin> Let the "Image" teach you that He is not dissimilar; it signifies an expressed character; "Splendor" signifies that He is the Image, as Ambrose witnesses. This is not a bodily face, nor composed of dyes or wax, but a simple proceeding from God, expressed from the Father as from a fountain. Through this image, He demonstrated the Father to Philip, saying: <margin>John 14:b</margin> "Philip, he who sees me, sees the Father also." And why do you say, "Show us the Father"? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? For he who sees the Son sees the Father in the Image. That Image is Truth; that Image is Justice; that Image is the Power of God.

---

# Book Three
#### folio 14

It is not mute, because He is the Word; it is not unfeeling, because He is Wisdom; it is not empty, because He is Power; it is not vacant, because He is Life; it is not dead, because He is the Resurrection. You see, therefore: that when He is called the "Image," it signifies the existence of the Father whose image the Son is; for no one can be his own image. Arius says: "I have known God totally, not in part." But Paul says: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." Arius, as he confesses, comprehends the whole of God "face to face"; for he asserts that he searches even the deep things of God. Therefore, Paul is lower than Arius? The "Vessel of Election" <note>A traditional title for St. Paul, from Acts 9:15.</note> knows in part, while the "Vessel of Perdition" knows the whole? Paul says: "I know a man, whether in the body or out of the body I know not, God knows, who was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable things." Paul, caught up to the third heaven, did not know himself; Arius, wallowing in filth, claimed to know God. Paul says of himself: "God knows"; Arius says of God: "I know." But Arius was not caught up to heaven. Who followed him who, with damnable boasting, presumed to speak of divine things, saying: "I will place my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High"? <note>Quoting Isaiah 14:14, traditionally associated with the pride of Lucifer.</note> For just as that one said, "I will be like the Most High," so Arius wants the most high Son of God to appear like himself—whom he does not worship with the majesty of eternal divinity, but measures by the infirmity of the flesh.

### Chapter 2: Disproof of Pagan Error from Hermes Trismegistus and Augustine.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a circular portrait of a man in profile wearing a head covering, likely representing Hermes Trismegistus.</image-desc> What do you say, O Pagan? "If God," you say, "took delight in a son, He required a marriage; if He abhorred marriage, He is alone without a son." For what could be found similar to God to be joined to God, so that she might bear a son to God? Then you say: "If God has a son, you no longer worship one God." What shall we do? We have received a spear thrown from the whirlwind; what shall we send back? No matter what weapon that most miserable man throws, though it reaches Him, what does it profit? <margin>Psalm 115</margin> Why? Because he is hard; because he worships stone idols. For it is written: "All those who make them are like them, and all who trust in them." He does not accept the Holy Scriptures. Let us therefore seek a stone with which he may be struck, so that being struck he may be shaken; being shaken he may be crushed; being crushed he may be turned to dust; being turned to dust he may be watered; being watered he may be sown; being sown he may bring forth fruit—not that which the fire consumes, but that which is stored in the granary. <margin>Hermes</margin> Hermes, who in Latin is called Mercury, as Augustine testifies, wrote a book called *Logostelios* <note>original: "logoshelios." This refers to the *Logos Teleios* or the "Perfect Word," an alternative name for the Hermetic dialogue *Asclepius*.</note>, that is, the "Perfect Word." Great is the name of this book, because He about whom it is written is great. What is more perfect than the Word, who alone is "free among the dead"? <margin>Psalm 6</margin> "Let us hear," says Augustine, "what Mercury says concerning the Perfect Word." "The Lord," he says, "and the Maker of all things, made a second Lord from the gods." And after a few words, to show what he meant, he repeated and said: "Since therefore He made this one first, and alone, and one good; for He was most full of all goods..." <margin>John 1:b</margin> How "most full" he was, John the Evangelist says: "From His fullness we have all received grace for grace." He was "good," and "most full of all goods." And it follows: "He rejoiced in Him..."
