Bulwark of the Christian Religion. Book Three. folio xv.

[God] rejoiced. And He loved Him greatly as His only-begotten Son. He spoke of Him first as being "made," and afterwards called Him "only-begotten." Likewise in another place he spoke thus: "The Son of the blessed God and of good will, whose name cannot be told by a human mouth." You were seeking, O pagan, a wife for God <note>pagan critics often mocked the idea of God having a son by asking who the mother was; the author uses 'Mercury' to refute this</note>. Listen to Mercury: prepare your forehead, receive, O stone, the stone; fall so that you may be raised up; be broken so that you may be strengthened; be destroyed so that you may be built up. Let the strike of the stone not open the skin of the forehead, nor burst a vein of blood, nor make a pit of a wound: but let it make the sign of the cross. You seek a wife for God? Let such wicked depravity be cast out of your heart. The "wife" of God is His good will. How? That the Father is God and the Son is God, yet there are not two gods but one God; I ought not to dispute this with you, because unless you believe, you will in no way be able to understand. Nevertheless, confess the Son of God as Lord. Let Mercury, struck by this stone, cease to be a stone-like sacrilegious man. What are you doing, pagan? Open your ears; do not be like the deaf asp that stops its ear so as not to hear the voice of the charmer. I do not bring forward a Christian author for you. It is your own Mercury, to whom you have given such great honor and worship among the gods that you would call a day of the week by his name <note>original: "nomine diē domini vocaretis" — though usually meaning 'the Lord's day' (Sunday), the author likely refers to Wednesday, *dies Mercurii*</note>. Listen to him: let him convince you, let him defeat you; so that when he has conquered you, you may yield to him and believe me. Mercury said: "God loved His only-begotten Son"; he himself called Him "the blessed Son of God and of good will." And lest he should endure the weariness of questioning regarding His name, he followed by adding: "Whose name cannot be told by a human mouth." Why do you, O Mercury, say that the name of the Son of God cannot be told by men? Let it be told by you, who are not a man, but are esteemed as a god by men. Moreover, he speaks to his Son, saying: "For the Holy Spirit is the ineffable word of the wisdom of the Son." Is this not the same as "In the beginning was the Word"? Say, Hermes: does this word of wisdom have a mother? It follows that He comes from God alone. He is the Lord of all things, ruling over mortals. And because He cannot be tracked down by men, he adds and says: "He is above men." I cannot tell the name of the Son of God, because I am not God; let men say as men what I am not—a god; let men say as men what I am. The Word of wisdom is from God alone. Therefore, O pagan, do not suspect or imagine there to have been a human marriage there; He is from the Lord alone, and He is above men. The Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles were ancient texts believed by many early Christians to be genuine prophecies of Christ by pagan priestesses</note> rebukes you, saying: "Know that your Lord Himself is the Son of God." Him, and no other—not Mars, not Jove, not Mercury—but Him whom Mercury confesses. Why do you marvel, O Christian, that they say such things about the Father and the Son? 
<margin>Mark 1</margin>
Even the demons believe and tremble. 
<margin>James 2</margin>
Indeed, in the Gospel, as the Lord was passing by, they said: "We know who you are, the Son of God; have you come to destroy us before the time?" Augustine says: "Would that men recognized the Savior in the same way the demons recognized their Judge."

### Concerning the Heretics of Origen. Chapter iii.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial O featuring a bearded man in clerical robes seated at a desk or pulpit, framed by classical columns.</image-desc>
<margin>Psalm 82. The race of heretics.</margin>
**O**rigenists or Origenians, as Augustine prefers, were named after a certain Origen; not after the one who is known to almost everyone, but after another whom I do not know, of whom Epiphanius speaks when discussing his followers. The Origenians, he says, are of a foul operation; these are they who do unmentionable and wicked things, handing their bodies over to corruption. However, there are other Origenians, as the same Augustine testifies, who are followers of that famous commentator <note>Referring to the famous scholar Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD)</note>, and who deny the resurrection of the dead, introducing Christ and the Holy Spirit as "creatures," and allegorizing Paradise, the heavens, and all other things. Epiphanius reports these things about Origen, but his defenders say that Origen taught the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be of one and the same substance, and that he did not reject the resurrection of the dead. Although they strive to prove him innocent in these matters, those who have read more of his works contradict them. There are also other dogmas of this Origen 
<margin>Augustine, Book on Heresies, addressed to Quodvultdeus</margin>
which the Catholic Church does not accept at all. In these, as Augustine asserts, he is not falsely accused, nor can he be excused by his defenders—especially regarding the "purgation and liberation" and then, after a long time, the "revolution" of every rational creature back to those same evils. For what Catholic Christian, whether learned or unlearned, would not vehemently shudder at that which he calls the "purgation of the wicked"? That is, that even those who 
<margin>Epiphanius</margin>
finished this life in crimes, outrages, sacrileges, and the greatest possible impieties—and even finally the Devil himself and his angels—are, after a very long time, purged and liberated and restored to the kingdom of God and to the light; and again, after a very long time, all who were liberated fall back and return to these evils once more. And he claims that these alternating turns of blessedness and misery for the rational creature have always been and always will be. Regarding this most vain impiety, Augustine disputed very diligently in his books on *The City of God* against the philosophers from whom Origen took these ideas. In the time of 
<margin>Dialogues, Book 1, Chapter 3</margin>
Sulpicius Severus, as it is written in the first book of his *Dialogues*, foul struggles were carried on at Alexandria between bishops and monks for this reason or cause: that the priests, having gathered together, seemed to have decreed in frequent synods that no one should read or possess the books of Origen, who was held to be a most skilled commentator on the Holy Scriptures. But the bishops mentioned certain things written in his books quite foolishly, which his supporters did not dare to defend, saying instead that they had been fraudulently inserted by heretics; and therefore, they argued that the rest of his work should not be condemned because of those things which were rightly called into reproach, since the faith of the readers could easily distinguish them so they would not follow the falsifications, while still retaining what was discussed in a Catholic manner. It was not surprising, they said, if heretical fraud had been at work in modern and recently written books, since in some places it had not feared to attack the truth of the Gospels. Against these arguments, the bishops were more obstinate...

# Bulwark of the Christian Religion. Book Three.
## folio xvi.

...reverently by their power they compelled people even to live uprightly. Even then, they were already condemning the works along with the author himself, because the books the church had received were more than sufficient, and the reading of Origen should be entirely rejected, as it would do more harm to the foolish than it would benefit the wise. "To me, however," says Sulpitius <note>Sulpitius Severus (c. 363–425 AD), an early Christian historian known for his biography of Saint Martin.</note>, "many things from those books, investigated quite curiously, were very pleasing; but I discovered some things in which there is no doubt that he held perverse views, though his defenders contend they were falsified." I marvel that one and the same man could have been so different from himself: that in the part where he is approved, he has no equal since the apostles; but in the part where he is rightly criticized, no one is shown to have erred more hideously. For when many excerpts from those books were read by the bishops, which were clearly written against the Catholic faith, that passage prepared the greatest ill-will, in which it was read that just as the Lord Jesus came in the flesh for the redemption of man and endured the cross for man's salvation, he would also taste death for the eternity of the demon <note>Original: "pro demonis eternitate." This refers to Origen's controversial theory of *apokatastasis*, or universal reconciliation, suggesting even the Devil might eventually be saved.</note>, so that he would also redeem the devil in the same order of passion; that this was consistent with His goodness and piety, that He who had restored lost man should also liberate the fallen angel. While these and other things of this sort were being exposed by the bishops, a sedition arose from the zeal of the factions. When this could not be repressed by the authority of the priests, the prefect took it upon himself to rule the ecclesiastical discipline by force; by his terror, the brothers were dispersed, and the monks were driven to various shores, so that by issued edicts they were allowed to settle in no place. "That," says Severus, "greatly warned me that Jerome, a most Catholic man and most skilled in the sacred law, was at first thought to have followed Origen, though now the same man especially condemns him or all his writings." Nor indeed did I dare to judge anyone rashly; nevertheless, most excellent and learned men were said to disagree in this contest. "But yet," says Sulpitius, "whether that is an error (as I feel) or a heresy (as it is thought), it not only could not be repressed by many punishments from the priests, but it could never have spread so widely unless it had grown through contention." The blessed martyr Pamphilus wrote an apology for Origen. 

<margin>Rufinus in his apology for Origen.</margin>
Rufinus also wrote another book on the adulteration <note>Original: "adulteratione," referring to the claim that heretics corrupted the original manuscripts of orthodox fathers to make them seem to support heresy.</note> of the books of Origen, just as the books of the blessed Pope Clement, Clement of Alexandria, Dionysius, and other famous men were corrupted. He says it is customary for the entire body of the letters of Saint Cyprian the martyr to be written in one volume. Into this body, certain heretics who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit inserted a small book by Tertullian on the Trinity, which was written reprehensibly (regarding the truth of our faith). Writing many such volumes, they distributed them throughout all Constantinople at a very cheap price, so that men, enticed by the low price, might more easily encounter the hidden and lurking deceits, whereby the heretic might seek to gain credit for his treachery through the authority of such a great man's name.

<column-break/>

It happened, however, while the act was still fresh, that some of our Catholic brothers discovered and exposed the crime committed, and to some extent called back those they could from the snare of this error. Nevertheless, Rufinus teaches that many in those parts were persuaded that the holy martyr Cyprian held this faith, which was wrongly written by Tertullian.

### ¶ On the heresy of the Manichaeans. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'M' inside a square frame, depicting a figure in profile wearing a hood, looking toward the left.</image-desc>
The Manichaeans arose from a certain Persian named Manes. Although when his insane doctrine first took hold he was called Curbicius, his disciples in Greece, avoiding the name of "insanity" <note>The name "Manes" sounded like the Greek word for madness or insanity. To avoid this, they changed his name to "Manichaeus."</note> as if they were more learned and therefore more deceptive, doubled the letter "n" and called him Manichaeus—as if he were "flowing with manna" <note>Original: "manna fundentem." A play on words to make the name sound divine rather than mad.</note>—instead of Manicheus, meaning "insane." He composed that there were two principles, diverse from each other and yet eternal and co-eternal—that is, two spirits. Following other ancient heretics, he believed there were two natures and substances: namely, Good and Evil. The Manichaeans do not drink wine, saying it is the gall of the prince of darkness, even though he eats grapes. Nor do they swallow any unfermented wine, even the freshest. He thinks the souls of his <term>Hearers</term> <note>The "Hearers" (Auditores) were the lower class of Manichaean followers who served the "Elect."</note> are returned into the "Elect," or by a happier shortcut into the food of his Elect, so that being purged there, they are not returned into any bodies. Other souls, however, he thinks return into cattle and into all things fixed by roots and nourished in the earth. The Manichaeans falsely claim that the God who gave the Law through Moses and spoke through the Hebrew prophets is not the true God, but one of the princes of darkness. They say the promise of the Lord Jesus Christ regarding the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit</note> was fulfilled in their benefactor, Manes; whence he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ in his letters, because Jesus promised he would send the Holy Spirit and sent it in him. For this reason, Manes himself also had twelve disciples in imitation of the apostolic number. They claim that baptism in water brings no salvation to anyone, nor do they think any of those they deceive should be baptized. They make prayers to the sun during the day and to the moon during the night if it appears; if it does not appear, they pray toward the north. He asserts that two souls or two minds—one good, the other evil—contend with each other in one man, since the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. This vice is not healed in us, as we say, but he claims this evil substance will be separated and secluded from us, and when this age is finished, after the conflagration of the world, it will live in a certain globe as if in an eternal prison. He falsely affirms that the souls of the nature of man which could not be cleansed from the contagion of the evil nature will be added to and adhere to this globe as if it were a covering or a couch. Faustus was of this sect, as Augustine writes; he was African by birth, from the city of Mileve, sweet in eloquence, clever in wit, a Manichaean by sect, and thus perverted by this unspeakable error. Augustine wrote against him in thirty-two books; likewise, he wrote against Felix the Manichaean in two books, and against a certain Secundinus the Manichaean in one book. Therefore, if you wish to dispute against the Manichaeans who blaspheme the Law, the prophets, their God, and the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, read the books of Augustine.

# Bulwark of the Christian Religion. / Book Four.
### fo. xvij.
### ccc

The **Simonians** take their name from **Simon Magus** <note>Simon the Sorcerer, a figure from the New Testament (Acts 8) traditionally regarded as the first heretic.</note> who, after being baptized by Philip the deacon as one reads in the Acts of the Apostles, wished to buy with money from the holy apostles the power so that the Holy Spirit might be given through the laying on of his hands. This man had deceived many with the trickery of his magic. Moreover, he taught a detestable foulness regarding the indiscriminate use of women. Nor did he say that God had made the world. For he denied the resurrection of the flesh and asserted that he himself was the Word <note>Original: "rēz" likely "rem" or "verbum".</note>. Furthermore, he wished to be believed to be **Jove** <note>Jupiter, the king of the Roman gods.</note>. He made a certain prostitute, who was his partner in crimes, out to be **Minerva**, and he offered both his own image and that of the prostitute to be adored by his disciples. These images he had established in Rome by public authority as if they were statues of the gods (as **Augustine** reports); in which city the blessed apostle **Peter** extinguished him by the true power of the omnipotent God. For he had said that he, in the person of the Father, had given the law of Moses to the Jews on Mount Sinai; that in the time of **Tiberius** <note>Roman Emperor during the life of Jesus.</note> he had appeared in the person of the Son in a phantom-like way; and afterwards that he had come upon the apostles as the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire. But he claimed that Christ had neither come nor suffered anything from the Jews.

<margin>The Blessed Clement in his *Travels* <note>The *Itinerarium* or Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions.</note>, chapter 4.</margin>
This Simon the Magician, according to **Clement**, was a Samaritan from the village of the Gittonians. Finally, the apostle Peter said to this Simon—who, corrupted by the habit of the magic art, thought he could acquire the grace of Christ through the laying on of hands and the pouring in of the Holy Spirit with money:

> "You have neither part nor lot in this faith: for your heart is not right before God. Therefore, do penance for this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the bond of iniquity and the bitterness of gall."

<margin>Saint Ambrose, book 2 on *Penance*, chapter 4, section b.</margin>
**Ambrose** says: You see that he condemns by apostolic authority this man who blasphemed against the Holy Spirit with magical vanity—and all the more because he did not have a pure conscience of faith—and yet he did not close off the hope of pardon to him, whom he invited to penance. Therefore, let us cover our slips with later deeds; let us cleanse them with weeping, so that the Lord our God may hear us groaning, just as

Father of all. If, therefore, there is one faith—indeed, because there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all—I have already believed, I am already baptized, I already have God as my Father; why then do I suffer the murderous heretic? he says: the idle talkers and seducers of the mind, the **Arian** and the **Sabellian** <note>Arius taught that the Son was a created being; Sabellius taught that Father, Son, and Spirit were just different "modes" or masks of one person.</note>. He is empty of the Holy Spirit. For this reason God is called Love: because he does not divide the unity into parts, but ineffably (as **Augustine** says) he binds together the Trinity. For the Trinity itself is the one God, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy, who guards those believing in Him forever and ever. Truly, concerning Simon Magus, **Menander**, **Saturninus**, **Basilides**, **Carpocrates**, **Cerinthus**, **Ebion**, **Nicolaus**, **Lardon**, **Marcion**, the **Gnostics**, and such

## The fourth book of Lord Symphorien Champier on the Christian religion against the Mohammedans.

### The origin of Muhammad is uncertain among his own people. Chapter 1.

The year was six hundred and twenty-four of human salvation, the twelfth of the reign of Emperor **Heraclius**, and the sixth of the Persian expedition. Africa was recovered. So was **Egypt**, and whatever lands had been occupied by the Persians from the Roman Empire, from Mesopotamia to the coast of Syria and the Erythraean <note>The Red Sea.</note> Sea. Except for **Arabia**, however; its defection birthed a great fire for the human race. Thence arose that nursery of evils upon the earth with inextricable error, which led a far greater part of mortals into the oblivion of truth. **Muhammad**, the author of the born evil, was a man of whom it is doubtful whether he was an Arab or a Persian; for it is handed down by both—his father (as some relate) being a worshiper of evil demons, and his mother an Ishmaelite, and for that reason not ignorant of the Hebrew law. As a boy, he was sold...

...fashioned him as ambiguous while this one pleaded his law and that one hers. Therefore, the boy, imbued with both forms of worship, accepted neither as an adult. Instead, being a man of clever and crafty character who had long dwelt among men of Christian piety, he devised a thing ruinous to the human race out of the two laws. First, preaching among the Arabs, he detested the deeds of **Khosrow** <note>Khosrow II, the last great king of the Sassanid Empire.</note>, who had wished to be adored as a god by edict; it should seem a wonder to no one, Muhammad argued, if after the wealth of his kingdom was afflicted, Khosrow had been unhappily consumed along with almost his entire house. Then, standing midway between the two laws, he said the **Hebrews** acted impiously by denying that Christ was born of a virgin, since the prophets—men of exceptional holiness and inspired by the divine spirit—had sung that this would happen and had predicted it should be expected long before. On the other hand, he claimed the **Christians** believed foolishly that Jesus, the greatest friend of God and born of a virgin, would have wished to endure insults and torture from the Jews. When this pseudo-prophet had imbued his own nation with these evils, he brought forth a law. To ensure that men of sound mind would never oppose or abrogate it, he inscribed a capital penalty—foul and pestilential—and sanctioned it in his **Quran** <note>Original: "alcorano"</note>: if anyone dared to dispute it. By this sanction, he made it clear there was nothing sincere in that law, which he covered like some mystery and forbade from being examined, so that the people could not know the true nature of what he was bringing them.

There are some, as **Filelfo** <note>Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481), an Italian Renaissance humanist.</note> writes, who record that he was an Ishmaelite. Born in Arabia to obscure parents and in a sordid place, he lived his childhood years by thievish gain, seeking a living by hiring out and leading camels to carry merchandise; then as an adult, he practiced brigandage. Having gathered a band of robbers, he became famous for one or two outrages. He secured a marriage to a widow, through whom he obtained a vast sum of money and certain castles; he then raised his mind to greater things and was thereafter hostile in treacherous matters. He was among the factions of **Heraclius** <note>Byzantine Emperor from 610 to 641.</note> and was present in that battle in which the power of Khosrow collapsed. As some of the Greeks write, he was wounded by a common soldier named **Turco**, after which the power of the Persians was broken. Catching sight of the sloth of Heraclius, to which the Emperor was devoted after the Persian victory, Muhammad became much greater. No longer contemptible through various successes, he reached the point where he gave rights and laws to his nation. In bringing these forth, he was chiefly aided by **Sergius**, a monk and follower of the Nestorian impiety <note>Nestorianism was a Christological doctrine considered heretical by the mainstream Church.</note>. This man had lived a monastic life, but when he found no high regard among his own people for his current state of life, he went to Byzantium. Using this man’s counsel, Muhammad proposed a law that, in order to be popular, assumed something from the sects of all nations. The law of Muhammad itself began to become famous during the Roman papacy of **Boniface V**, at the time when **Eleutherius** the Exarch attempted to seize the kingdom. Others say that this deadly poison began to be offered to mortals during the reign of **Honorius**, who was Pope after Boniface, and that the beginnings of his papacy...

Heraclius, twice dismayed by the successes of Muhammad and his people, then finally turned away from the true faith to the **Monothelites** <note>A heresy suggesting Christ had two natures but only one will.</note> at the persuasion of Pyrrhus and Cyrus. However, because there was no doubt that the Saracens, having treacherously subdued it, would shortly invade Judea, he sent men to Jerusalem to carry the **Cross of the Lord** to Byzantium, lest it should fall into the hands of the **Agarenes** <note>Descendants of Hagar, Sarah's handmaid; a term often used pejoratively for Muslims in the Middle Ages to deny their claim to Sarah.</note>. Thus the Greeks then called the Saracens by that name as a term of reproach, as if they were descended from Hagar, the handmaid of Abraham.

Nor was Heraclius deceived in his opinion: after the Persians were defeated in war, the barbarians attacked **Antioch** and shortly captured that most noble city. Not much 
<margin>Regarding the years of Muhammad’s life.</margin>
later, they also gained possession of Jerusalem. Muhammad did not long survive this victory. He died at the age of thirty-four <note>Historical sources generally cite Muhammad's age at death as 62 or 63; the "34" here may be a transcription error in the original manuscript or a different tradition.</note>; he had carried that [violent] face across the human race for about that long. It was the year in which that most foul plague was extinguished from the earth: the 632nd year of human salvation. There is a city in the land of the faithless named **Mecca**; here is seen his iron ark <note>Tomb</note>, which the whole East worships. A **Caliph** succeeded Muhammad, but because of excessive superstition, his command was annulled, and in his place another leader of the same name was created, at the time when **Severinus**, the Supreme Pontiff, departed this life after having sat for a little more than a year.

A cruel judge and a savage tyrant will judge his people. Like a serpent sitting in the way, he will try to cast down those walking the path of truth, desiring to trip up the truth—for this is what it means to "bite the horse's heel"—so that the horse, wounded and pierced by the serpent’s tooth, might wash its heel with the spreading of the venom. Just as Judas the traitor, tempted by the devil, lifted his heel against the Lord Jesus to cast down the rider who had lowered Himself to raise all people. He fell, therefore, not prostrate on his face (as if sleeping), but backward, so that by stretching from higher things toward earlier things, he might not expect salvation. For he knew he was to be raised again, and thus Adam waited to lift up the one who was lying down. But the Lord will come in His second coming, though 
<margin>2 Thessalonians 2</margin>
He will not come until the number of the elect, known to God, has been filled, and the "man of sin, the son of perdition," who is the Antichrist, has been revealed. This is the revelation of Paul the Apostle concerning the second coming of the Antichrist in the second chapter of the Epistle to the Thessalonians—a passage veiled and obscure. And the Holy Revelation of John <note>The Book of Revelation / Apocalypse.</note> reveals two Antichrists under the names of the first and second beasts. The **first beast** has already come; that was **Muhammad**, prince of the Arabs, who appeared under the Emperor Heraclius, and whose sect still endures, though it shall soon be utterly destroyed by the mercy of God. The **second beast** has not yet appeared, of whom the Apostle seems rather to speak. This is no wonder. For at the arrival of the first 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
beast, the "apostasy" was not yet complete. "Apostasy" is interpreted as defection, repudiation, and rebellion. The holy Athanasius interprets this apostasy as the defection of the Roman monarchy <note>The Roman Empire.</note> in the Epistle to the Thessalonians. Saint Jerome does the same in his *Eleven Questions* addressed to Algasia regarding the Apostle. Furthermore, the first beast did not sit in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God; instead, he called himself only a prophet and messenger of God. Again, his coming, though indeed in falsehood—as one full of the spirit of Satan who lied about his familiarity with the angels of God and God himself, his "ascent" into heaven from the holy city even to the throne of God, his knowledge of heavenly secrets, and countless such things unworthy of being told—was done with a false ecstasy <note>Original: "ettasi," likely a typo for "extasi."</note>, a diabolical invention. By this, he was led through fantasies even to the prince of demons. By the touch of his hand (as he himself says), he felt a lethal cold, as if he who was being touched were declaring himself the prince of death—whom he even adored as the true god, led by the angel of darkness who transformed himself into Gabriel, the angel of light. He was carried on a beast (such a beast befitted him, and the sender who is the prince of bestiality, and the bestial man to whom he was sent) through the fictitious heavens of darkness, through multi-headed, multi-lingual, monstrous, and multi-formed apostate angels hanging in punishment, who even feigned that they needed his help. And—O what a crime! A horrific, unspeakable crime!—in that sacrilegious vision, one of them transforms himself into Christ, as if he were unworthy of his help and were begging for his prayers; he sees chains...

<column-break/>

...he sees punishments; he thinks he is praising God while speaking blasphemies, attributing to the prince of darkness those things which are owed to the Lord, the inhabitant of the immense light of all majesty. While he sees the hidden secrets of the deep night, he thinks they are heavenly. This is the truth and true interpretation of that vision and diabolical scene, which we have explained more extensively in our dialogue regarding the Muhammadan law. Therefore, the arrival of that beast and first Antichrist was in the spirit of Satan and in falsehood; however, he did not perform signs and wonders, as he himself testifies of himself. But the **second beast** will have the power of signs, and "it seduces," it says, "those living on the earth because of the signs which were given to it to perform." Nevertheless, the first beast and first Antichrist have a great similarity to the second (as is recognized in the Apocalypse) and run before him, so that the second may say he was announced by the first, and that he is the one whom the first commanded to be adored. For he will give spirit to the image of the beast, and the spirit of the image of the beast will be in the spirit of Satan. Moses and Christ: man and man-above-man through the fullness of God. The first and second beasts: beast and beast-below-every-beast through the fullness of Satan's wickedness. After the empire of the Greeks was taken away, Christ came. Likewise, after the Roman empire is completely removed, the second beast, who is the Antichrist, will come. Therefore, the Thessalonians did not have as just a cause for fear as we, who ought to fear the near arrival of the "man of sin" and "son of perdition," since we turn our eye to the sign of the Roman monarchy mentioned by Paul. Where is the monarchy now, I ask? Where is he who holds the reins of the world in it? We see even the head of the monarchy falling away from it. To whom, I ask, does Rome offer obedience to its king, its monarch? I do not know in what times a greater defection could appear. But since Muhammad is the "beast of the beast" and the "Antichrist of the Antichrist," it would not be absurd if almost everything the Apostle added seems to fit him. Who will deny that he is a man of sin and a son of perdition, who dragged Asia, Africa, and a great part of Europe away from the kingdom of Christ and God into eternal perdition? Who made such a great apostasy from the Roman empire across so vast an expanse of land? Who ever rose up as such an adversary to Christ? Who is so "exalted above all that is called God"? The Father is called God, and truly is; the Son is called God, and truly is; the Holy Spirit is called God, and truly is; and these three are in truth God and one God. But Muhammad denies the Father is God; he denies the Son is God; he denies the Holy Spirit is God. Muhammad denies the Three and denies Christ is God; he exalts himself above Christ. He exalts himself above the angels, claiming that Christ and the angels (and even demons) prayed for him as their superior. Is he not, therefore, exalted above everything that is truly called God? And since he is above angels and demons, he is even above those who are held to be gods by opinion.

# ¶ What Muhammad judged concerning Christ in his Quran. Chapter 3.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a man, possibly a scholar or a saint, seated in a high-backed chair at a lectern or desk with an open book.</image-desc>

In the Quran, Muhammad confesses Jesus Christ to be the power and wisdom of God, the soul, the breath, the spirit, and the Word [of God], born of the perpetual Virgin Mary by a certain divine inspiration which they call *rubela* <note>original: "rubela"; likely a corruption of the Arabic "Ruh-Allah," meaning "Spirit of God."</note>. He affirms that Christ is holy and outstanding in every virtue, preaching that he is above the heights of humanity—calling him now "the Word," now "the Spirit," and "the Soul of God"—born from the womb of a virgin. He extols the Virgin herself with wondrous praises and supports her with miracles. He accepts the Gospel history insofar as it does not disagree with his own Quran, claiming that the Gospels were corrupted by the disciples of the Apostles and had to be corrected through his Quran. Seeking to flatter the great number of those bearing the Christian name, he wished to be baptized by Sergius <note>Sergius was a legendary Nestorian monk who, in medieval Christian polemics, was said to have tutored Muhammad.</note>. From there, to win over the zeal of others, he joined with the Sabellians in denying the Trinity; with the Manicheans in placing a dual number in divine things <note>The Manichean belief in two opposing principles, Good and Evil.</note>; and with Eunomius in denying the equality of the Father and the Son. He called the Holy Spirit a creature, alongside Macedonius; with the Nicolaitans, he approved a multitude of wives; and so that something might be granted to the Jews, he preached and approved both circumcision and baptism together, along with the Old Testament, even though he said that it too was not without fault in certain places. In addition to these evasions, he offered an incredible lure by which life is easily captured: he loosened the reins of lust and all pleasures for his people. Such was he in the bringing of his law. Moreover, this most wretched thing has seen luxurious growth, for life is more prone to falling than to standing firm in the good. That plague creeps through vast, almost innumerable lands, so that one might ask how small a part of the world now serves the Lord compared to that multitude of wanderers. The beginning of so great an evil was in Arabia, as demonstrated above; for that land has always been a pestilence to the human race. So it was then with Muhammad, and so it was once with Ham and his progeny, who introduced the worship of evil demons. Muhammad, however, overthrew what had been established by the wondrous power of the true God.

# ¶ What Muhammad thought concerning idols. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure similar to the previous one, seated at a desk with books, framed by an architectural arch.</image-desc>

There is no need to make mention of idols, for he condemned every statue. Yet his own idol—that is, his hanging sarcophagus full of unhappy bones—became an object of veneration more ruinous than many idols for his foolish and beastly people. They call this place of veneration "unhappy Arabia," or rather, Mecha <note>Mecca.</note>. Truly, just as Christ shall dissolve and destroy it with the spirit of his mouth in the future, so has he already cast down that idol with a lightning-spirit (if the things are true which our Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Iacobus Stapulensis"; a famous French humanist and theologian (c. 1455–1536).</note> heard, and which I have read as written by him). The machinery of the world obeys Christ, ready always to serve him in whatever he wills. Lefèvre himself saw a man—it is now nearly the twenty-second year since—who wore sackcloth and always walked with a bare head and bare feet, girded with a twisted vine, 

<column-break/>

carrying a wooden cross in his hand. This man feared no cold and no snows (which were then at their peak), running from chapel to chapel; if the doors were closed, he would kneel in the snow and pray. His food was herbs and bread, and after many days of fasting, his drink was water and the earth his bed. They say this man served in Constantinople for seven years. He persisted in the confession of the name of Christ, after which time he went to Mecca with Turkish merchants who knew him and followed him because of his simple character and the faithfulness of his service. When they entered the temple, he entered with them, and when they bent their knees before the bier of the beast, he also knelt. They adored the beast, but he, with a silent prayer, prayed to Christ with tears that He might show a sign of His power and cast down that body which had seduced so many people into perdition, and that He might illuminate that land with the light of His grace so that men might know Him and give glory to the true God, who alone is worthy of glory. As he was leaving the temple, scouts seized him so that they might saw him in half with a wooden saw. For this is the penalty for those who dare to enter the temple who are of a sect other than Muhammad’s. He, however, exulting for the name of Christ, waited patiently for the sawing; but the merchants wept bitterly and, with prayers and gifts, received him back unharmed, for he had provided much service to them and their camels on the journey. Therefore, as they were leaving, a bolt of lightning sent from heaven struck, shook, and diminished the bier (just as he had asked the Lord of power for a sign). Lefèvre heard these things, and I also have read them in writing. Furthermore, even the Turks guess that their law will shortly come to an end. Behold (if these things are true), he who sat as a type in the temple and was adored as if he were God, and was extolled above Christ and everyone who is called God, has now been cast down; he has already fallen, crushed by the spirit of Christ. His coming had been according to the working of Satan, with lying signs and wonders, all for the seduction of iniquity in those who perish. For that sign was indeed a lie that hurried many to their destruction: seeing that hanging sarcophagus and thinking it was supported by divine power. (I say "hanging" in the air, a thing for which the simple people did not know how to recognize the cause, or if they were not simple, they did not dare to think of it because of superstition <note>This refers to the medieval legend that Muhammad's coffin was made of iron and held suspended in the air by powerful magnets in the roof and floor.</note>). Thus, for both the simple and the non-simple, it was a lying sign and wonder leading to the perdition of souls. But now, after the lightning-conflagration of the tomb and the unhappy bones, they say his body is in Medina <note>original: "medinatalabi"; likely a corruption of "Madinat al-Nabi," the City of the Prophet.</note> in Desert Arabia, where his shrine is visited. It is a hundred paces long and eighty wide, supported by four hundred columns, with hanging lamps perpetually lit to the number of three thousand. But is he not extolled here above the Most Holy object of worship, above the Holy of Holies which is truly worshipped, and to whom honor and reverence are due? Where else among nations does such a height of prideful veneration appear? Those admitted to this funeral spectacle have their eyes plucked out—and rightly so, as those who are never to see God. But Christ does not need these corruptible lights, He for whom innumerable eternal lights always shine, and the eyes that see Him are blessed and shall by no means be plucked out, as they are to see God perpetually. Those who worship the god of Muhammad worship the Prince of Darkness; this is their god: him Muhammad adored, and of him alone was he the messenger.

# Bulwark of the Christian Religion.
## Book Four. Folio 21.

Nor should anyone wonder at the great magnitude of these fabricated sights. For (as Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher whose works were often used by Christian scholars to explain biblical history.</note> relates) some of the children of Israel, tempted by a devilish curiosity, were deceived by similar fictions of the Canaanites. They believed they truly saw the sun in the middle of the night; and so, having abandoned the true Creator of the sun, they worshipped as the true God the one who had made that artificial sun appear. Nor should you wonder at these artificial angels or at the Christ simulated by the cunning of Satan, since it is known from the history of Heraclides <note>Refers to the *Lausiac History* by Palladius, though often attributed to Heraclides; it contains stories of the early Desert Monks.</note> that a similar thing happened to the monk Valens.

A demon (he says) transformed into the likeness of the Savior and came to him at night with a certain choir of a thousand angels—or so he feigned—carrying lit lamps and a flaming wheel in which he had simulated the Savior sitting. One of these went before him and said: "Go out of your cell and do nothing else except, when you see him coming from a distance, hasten to bow down and worship him; then you may return to your own dwelling." Having gone out of his cell, believing he was seeing the divine offices of the celestial ministry and everything glowing with the brightness of lamps, and seeing the Antichrist himself stationed no further than the distance of a stadium <note>A classical unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>, he immediately fell prone on the ground and worshipped him whom he believed to be the Lord. Thus says Heraclides.

Behold how the proud and foolish Valens, having left the true Christ, worshipped the adversary of Christ, taking a simulated phantasm and a false image for the truth. For the works of God are the truth for salvation, but the appearances of the devil are for damnation. Therefore, the coming of that beast and of the first Antichrist in the spirit of Satan was in a lie; he performed neither signs nor wonders, as he himself testifies, as has already been said. But the second beast will have the power of signs. And it "seduces those dwelling on the earth," as it is written, "because of the signs which were given to him to perform."

The first beast—that is, Muhammad—not only lied, but he speaks smoothly, unlearnedly, imprudently, and tastelessly in his Quran. He is often contrary to himself, as any examiner of his law will clearly understand. Innumerable are his follies, old wives' tales, and childish trifles, of which I wish to relate a few here to provide a judgment of the rest. Explaining a chapter of the Quran called *Israel*, he provides the first fable, which we told in the second chapter of this book. He fills the ears of the people with other trifles and ravings from the book titled *On the Doctrine of Muhammad*, saying thus:

Two angels named Arathes and Narrathes <note>original: "Arathes t̄ narrathes"; these are Harut and Marut, fallen angels mentioned in Sura 2:102 of the Quran.</note>, he asserts, descended to earth by the command of God to rule and instruct the human race, having received three mandates. First, that they should kill no one. Second, that they should judge nothing unjustly. Third, that they should drink no wine. After they had ruled for some time and judgments from the whole world were brought to them, a certain woman of graceful form and the most beautiful of all, having a legal case against her husband, sought a judgment from them. So that she might have favorable judges, she invited them with many prayers to have lunch with her.

<column-break/>

The angels do not refuse. A splendid banquet is prepared; the woman herself serves the food and drink. Multiple courses are set out, and with them wine. When the angels refused it, the woman insisted repeatedly and used many flatteries; at last they drank, and, becoming drunk on the wine, they grew heated toward their hostess and demanded to sleep with her. The woman promised on one condition: that one of them should show her the way to ascend into heaven, and the other the way to descend. The condition pleased them. But when she truly learned the way, she immediately ascended into heaven, leaving the angels behind and mocked. God, recognizing her, placed her among the stars, and her name is Lucifer <note>The author likely refers to the planet Venus, known as the Morning Star or "Lucifer" in Latin.</note>. The angels were called to judgment and were bound with iron chains in a very deep pit, to remain there until the day of judgment, since they chose to be punished in this life rather than the next.

This is the "wisdom" of Muhammad, which his theology teaches to children. This is "divinely revealed doctrine!" With what wondrous audacity—not to say stupidity or madness—one must view the laughable dreams in these fables. Who could listen patiently to the claim that the angels of God, drunk with wine and deceived by the beauty of a woman, sought to lie with her? Or that she, having been taught the way to heaven, reached the sight of the Great God and was honorably received and given a place among the stars? And that the angels suffered punishment, and for that reason wine was forbidden to man because it was the cause of such great evil?

Muhammad commemorates these things and presses them upon men as if they were received from the storehouse of God. See how weightily, how truly, and how skillfully he speaks of the fictions of poets that are read to children! Among the secrets of his law, Muhammad inserts things that Christian boys cannot hear without laughter—when women are said to be snatched into heaven and changed into the stars that are called the Greater and Lesser Bear <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.</note>. With such trifles Muhammad fills the ears of the people. 

But this is not the "Law of the Lord," as the Prophet says: "The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, providing wisdom to the little ones" <note>A quotation of Psalm 19:7 (Psalm 18 in the Vulgate).</note>. The law of the Lord is immaculate because it excludes all evil and admits no lust or any foulness. Thus, in the same Prophet, the words of the Lord are called "chaste"; and in Job we read, "you shall not find iniquity in my mouth, nor shall foolishness resound in my jaws." And the Apostle <note>St. Paul.</note> says, "the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good."

But how is the Muhammadan law "immaculate," when it admits debauchery, adultery, and all the stains and filth of lust? He will say, perhaps, that it commanded certain fasts, prayers, and alms. Far be it from us to call those things evil! But we deny that Muhammad was their inventor; we knew these things were good without Muhammad. Moses fasted, Elijah fasted, Christ fasted. To pray and to break one's bread for the hungry and the needy is much more ancient than the invention of Muhammad. Many legislators have invited us to works of piety; but to commit adultery, to fornicate, to serve the belly, and to lie in the filth of pleasures—only Muhammad places these among the "good things." Muhammad says: "Take wives and concubines as it pleases you. For I have the strength of forty men in my loins and for my wives."

### ¶ Concerning the second beast, that is, the Antichrist, and his coming. Chapter 5.

<margin>Six ages after Christ</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'U' depicting a scholar or cleric seated at a writing desk with an open book and inkpot.</image-desc>
There have been those who said that from Christ until the Antichrist, the world would have six ages: the first was that of the **Apostles**; the second, of the **Martyrs**; the third, of the **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to the great Teachers or Church Fathers who defined doctrine.</note>; the fourth, of the **Anchorites** (that is, those who withdraw, such as Paul the first hermit, Hilarion, Anthony, and their like); the fifth, of the **Monks**; and the sixth, of the **Mendicants** <note>The "Mendicants" refers to the begging orders like the Franciscans and Dominicans.</note>. When this last age has unfolded, they think the time of the Antichrist will be near. What then remains, unless—when the apostasy and the falling away of the Roman Monarchy has been completed—the second beast comes, the second "man of sin" and "son of iniquity" of whom the Apostle speaks in the second letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 2? To him is given the power of signs, in which all these things will be more manifest than in the first beast (which was a type of this malice). The Lord Jesus shall strike him down with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming, once the Gospel of peace has been preached in the whole world. Truly, once it is known and received, happy are those who will then be chosen ministers of God for such great happiness; great also is the happiness for those who will stand immovable in the faith of Christ, both in life and in confession. Nor, when those times press upon them, will they be moved from their minds or disturbed, but they will firmly adhere to Christ as to an immovable mountain, retaining his peace and serenity, and always giving thanks to him for the great mercy of God toward them. St. Paul exults in spirit regarding the Thessalonians for this being so, and he exhorts them to stand immovable and prays for divine help for them to this end. Nothing therefore 
<margin>Augustine in the book on the Antichrist.</margin> 
remains once the falling away of the Roman Monarchy is completed, but for this second beast to come. Hence the Apostle says that the Antichrist will not come into the world 
<margin>The last king of the Franks according to Augustine.</margin>
unless there first comes a "departure" <note>original: "discessio"; often translated as "apostasy" or "rebellion" in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note>; that is, unless all the kingdoms that were previously subject to it depart from the Roman Empire. However, as the blessed Augustine relates, this time has not yet arrived, because—as he says—although we see the Roman Empire destroyed in great part, nevertheless as long as the Kings of the Franks <note>The "Franks" refers to the French monarchy, which many medieval thinkers saw as the true successors to the Roman imperial title.</note> shall endure (who are said to hold the Roman Empire), the dignity of the Romans will not perish entirely, because it will stand in their kings. Indeed, some Doctors, as the same Augustine relates, say that one of the 

<column-break/>

Kings of the Franks will hold the Roman Empire in its entirety, who will exist in the very last time; and he himself will be the greatest and the last of all kings. After he has governed his kingdom successfully, he will at last come to Jerusalem and lay down his scepter and his crown on the Mount of Olives. This will be the end and the consummation of the Empire of the Romans and of the Christians. And immediately after, according to the aforementioned sentence of the Apostle Paul, they say the Antichrist will come—so says Augustine. There are even in our own times those who say the time of the Antichrist is approaching, and that a certain prophet will shortly be born who will introduce a great variety of customs and laws. But since all things are uncertain and full of fables, this response must be held: "Be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect." For the sign is given to be foreknown in no way unless it is revealed by God himself; and when the Apostles, desiring to know this and questioning him upon it, were answered: "It is not for you to know the times and the moments which the Father has placed in his own power." I believe it is spread in vain by posterity, and it is better to desist from such curious temerity. These are the things which, if you hold them in memory and meditate on them frequently as if ruminating, you will constantly despise the goods as well as the evils of this mortal life, which are destined to perish.

### ¶ Concerning the authority and excellence of Christian doctrine. Chapter 6.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'T' showing a scholar or saint seated at a high-backed desk, holding or pointing to a large open book.</image-desc>
The Christian law is as much more excellent than others as those who followed it were more learned—and more learned, more eloquent, and holier than other learned men. If dialecticians, orators, or poets had laid the first foundation of this religion, we would suspect that the common people had been deceived by human cunning. If all the learned had always rejected it, we would judge it to be fruitlessly held in contempt. If princes had favored this law entirely from the beginning or shortly thereafter, we would think (as we judge regarding certain other religions) that the weaker had been coerced by the more powerful, and that their successors then (as happens) sucked in that law with their mother's milk. Therefore, Divine Providence willed that the simple truth of His religion should take its first origin from men who were at first unrefined and simple, and He permitted the cunning and the learned to be happily ensnared by the simple and unrefined. Furthermore, He permitted His religion to be cruelly attacked everywhere by the powerful of the nations for more than three hundred years, so that the number of teachers, witnesses, and faithful might be greater, and the authority of the thing itself might be truer, more certain, and firmer. For it is easy to maintain faith in prosperity, but difficult in adversity. I shall pass over foreign histories, but Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman historian often critical of early Christians.</note> testifies that the Christians were tortured with the most exquisite torments. However, he disparaged the Christians, I believe, to flatter his own age. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author and apologist (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note> shows that Tacitus even lied in his history, because he said that the Jews worship the head of an Ass <note>original: "caput Asini"</note>, whereas history records that when people spied upon the secrets of the Jews, they found no idol among them. Therefore, from this one lie, the rest may be judged. Added to this is that our Irenaeus <note>St. Irenaeus of Lyons, a 2nd-century bishop and martyr.</note>, the martyr and most famous prelate of Lyons, testifies in his fifth book *Against Heresies*. It was for no other reason that suspicion then arose against the lords <insert>of the empire</insert>, as if against the innocent and pure, than because of the incestuous filth of certain Gnostic heretics...

Next, the holiness and miracles of Christ, the apostles, and the martyrs. To this is added that extraordinary depth and majesty which is perceived in their sober style—men who were previously unlettered fishermen. This is especially true of Peter, James, and John. I shall remain silent regarding Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles and a bulwark of the Christian law; though he was a most learned man before his conversion, he nevertheless rises in his epistles far above human capacity. What could be more concise than the epistles of Peter? What more venerable than the epistle of James and that of Jude? What shall we say of the Revelation of John? That book displays a heavenly countenance, containing as many mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta"</note> as it does words. And what of his epistles, in which there is a sweetness like nectar and a divine sense without any artificial veneer of words? Let one see his Gospel as having been written by the hands of God, not of man. When Amelius the Platonist read it, he swore by Jove that that "barbarian" <note>original: "barbarum"; Amelius, a Greek philosopher, used this term to refer to John as a non-Greek or a Jew</note> man had discussed briefly and concisely the divine nation, the principle, and the arrangement of things, about which Plato and Heraclitus had disputed. Simplicius, moreover, said he heard a certain Platonist say that the prologue of this Gospel ought to be written in letters of gold upon the highest peaks of the temples everywhere. Finally, all their speeches were like their lives; for just as they were most mild in conversation, yet most brave and constant in dangers and labors, so in speaking they were equally humble and sublime. Such combinations are judged to be above nature.

Thus, their master Christ rendered those rustics and fishermen "fishers of men," as he had promised. What is even more wonderful is that after his ascension into heaven, he suddenly taught them—still unrefined as they were—from heaven by a certain miraculous inspiration, so that they immediately excelled in all languages and doctrines before the whole people. A sign of this is that they themselves taught many learned men, and those excelling in the highest wisdom most willingly subjected their necks to the yoke of the apostles. These included Hierotheus, Dionysius the Areopagite, and Justin the Platonist <note>Justin Martyr</note>, whose writings are all full of wisdom. They underwent the Cross of Christ alongside the apostles. Furthermore, there were Quadratus, Agrippa, Pantenus the Stoic, Luke, Aristides, and Marcus the philosophers, as well as Tenas and Apollo, who were most skilled in the Jewish law. What shall I say of the wise Ignatius, a disciple of Christ and bishop of Antioch? What of Polycarp, bishop of the Smyrnaeans, a great companion and teacher of John the Evangelist? But behold, there now presents itself to me a great multitude of men excelling in every doctrine: Barnabas, Clement of Rome, Titus, Timothy, Sosthenes, Aristion, Clinanus, Philip, Dorotheus, Demophilus, Philemon, Lucius, Jason, Andronicus, Urban, Linus, Crescens, Cletus, Paul, Sergius the proconsul of Cyprus, Demas, Silas, Crispus, Hegesippus the Jew, Epaphras, Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphroditus, Onesimus, Tychicus, Papias, Justus, Hermas, Gaius, Enodius, and Mellitus the upright Asian. Cease your raving now, you Jews, so wretched and insane! Do you not believe in that divine man whom the whole world honors without controversy—John the Baptist? He who (as Josephus says) was truly and publicly held as a model of all virtues. To him, as if to an oracle, a great multitude of Jews and others flocked from every side. John, however, openly and without doubt affirmed that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah and commanded everyone to follow him. Otherwise, all those who then spoke of Jesus would not have made their beginning from the testimony and confirmation of John, nor celebrated him with such wonderful praises; it is clear to everyone that the life of Jesus and the life of John are narrated together by the Evangelists.

Cease your raving also, you Turks and followers of Muhammad. For your Muhammad was not ignorant of the friendship between these two, namely the birth, life, and praises of both John the Baptist and Jesus. In the same chapter of the Quran <note>original: "alcorani"</note> he sang their praises. He called Christ the "Spirit and Word of God." In the same place, he says that John was a great prophet and a confirmer of the divine word. And certainly, he confirmed it so well that Christ had his first disciples from John. Muhammad greatly approves of those first Christians. He confesses that Christian doctrine—that is, the books of the Evangelists and Apostles—received a miraculous authority from God himself, and he places it above the Old Testament; but he claims these books were corrupted by Christians after the time of the apostles.

All of this was devised by that man, so cunning and warlike, because he asserts that he himself was promised by Christ in the clearest words. He claims Christ said in the Gospel: "I predict to you that after me a certain messenger of God will come, named Muhammad, namely that Spirit of Truth who will teach you all things." <note>This refers to a common Islamic interpretation of the "Paraclete" or "Spirit of Truth" promised in the Gospel of John as a prophecy of Muhammad</note> In the beginning, such a device, though it might find a place through trickery among unlearned and un-warlike men (such as the followers of Muhammad are to him), is nevertheless utterly ridiculous to great and prudent men. For before the arrival of Muhammad, there was no reason why they should have subtracted the name of Muhammad from the Gospel rather than the names of Layphe, Nero, Domitian, or the Antichrist. After the arrival of Muhammad, Muhammad himself would rather have been worshipped by those who cherished the Gospel than have his name removed. But he falsely wished his own name to be subjoined where, in the Gospel of John, Christ promises the Holy Spirit, whose infusion was promised to the apostles themselves not long after the resurrection. Furthermore, in what way is it likely that all Christians would have dared to change those volumes which they so greatly venerated at that time as if given from heaven? If any impious men had dared to do so, being few and imprudent, they would have been immediately convicted by the many prudent ones, and would not have prevailed.

This Muhammad seems to have by no means understood the profound mysteries of the Christians, even if he read them. For when he reads that Jesus is the Son of God and God, he thinks the Christians are introducing two gods there, namely a Father and a Son. And this "binary" of gods in the Quran...

—though they are rooted in it, they can be eradicated. It is not necessary to say more of the followers of Muhammad, since it is obvious without any inquiry that their laws and institutes are contrary to the law of nature and the morals remaining from it. If these were cast aside by them, they would become fit and ready to drink in the divine light, to whom that could be said which Photinus, Bishop of Lyon and martyr, once replied to a faithless man questioning him about the God of the Christians: "If you are worthy," he said, "you shall know."

Indeed, he did not give a laugh like Simonides <note>A Greek poet who, when asked by King Hiero "What is God?", kept asking for more time to think because the more he deliberated, the more obscure the subject became</note>, who said he did not know what God was; nor like that other man who frustrated a tyrant by asking for a delay to deliberate. Rather, the martyr showed that he knew, but he was unwilling to teach for no other reason than that the one asking was unworthy. For a cruel, faithless, and dark soul full of errors could not admit the radiating light of truth; nor (as it is written) will wisdom enter into a malevolent soul. Therefore, he replied most correctly: "If you are worthy, you shall know." This means: if you depart from malice, if you burn with the love of truth, and if you struggle against proud obstinacy, you shall know. If you are worthy—that is, if you keep the laws of nature untainted—you shall be taught by divine grace. All who are enemies of the Church would achieve the same in a divine manner, if only they did not oppose the divine impulse frequently shaking their souls so that truth might enter; and if, relying on their own resources, they did not resist the queen of vices, Pride, but strove against her. Enough has been said of these matters for now.

I, however, give thanks to our God that in these four books I have discussed—not according to what I am (for I lack much), but according to what a person ought to be who strives to labor in Christian doctrine not only for himself but for others—to the best of my limited ability.

### ¶ A description of the customs and wonders of the regions and provinces according to the maps of Ptolemy. And first, regarding the first map of Europe.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'B' containing a portrait of a man in profile facing left, wearing a scholar's cap and robes, holding a book or tablet.</image-desc> The British Isles contain extremely fierce peoples who are very well-suited for war; though they have beautiful and tall bodies with very robust limbs, their complexion is pale. They also excel greatly in character and in their facility of language. However, they provoke disputes and wars, and thus frequently harass one another in turn. They fight as cavalry and infantry—formerly with <term>bigis</term> <note>original: "bigis et curribus," referring to two-horse chariots and carts</note>—armed in the Gallic fashion. They produce very many horses, and these are of such a kind that they seem to have learned from nature to walk only with a certain most pleasant gait, and to proceed with a kind of rhythmic modulation in a royal manner. They have sheep covered in such soft wool that it can easily be drawn out into a thinness resembling a spider’s web. The inhabitants are indeed rich in livestock and territory. They abound in pastures and the most fertile and sweet grasses. This is especially true of <term>Ireland</term> <note>original: "Inuerna... que et ihernia dicitur." Known to the Romans as Hibernia.</note>, to such an extent that the cattle fill themselves in a small part of the day; and unless they were kept from the fodder, they would burst after grazing for a long time. They produce a terrestrial mass—though mixed with sulfur—similar to <term>coal</term> <note>original: "carbonum." This likely refers to sea-coal or peat found in the British Isles.</note> which blacksmiths and the entire region, as well as those nearby, use extensively for lighting fires. There are massive rivers flowing through alternating mountains, sometimes into the sea and sometimes back again due to the tide, and some produce gems and pearls. These rivers emerge without springs. They lack lakes and mountains, except for very small ones. There is a large and varied abundance of metals which is easily extracted from the earth’s bowels. For they excel greatly in <term>tin</term> <note>original: "Stanno."</note> and <term>lead</term> <note>original: "plumbo," specifically black lead</note> and various forms of copper, as well as gold and silver. The island of <term>Thanet</term> <note>original: "Thanatos insula." The Isle of Thanet in Kent.</note>, separated from Britain by the Gallic Strait by a narrow and varying distance, took its name—amidst fields of grain and fertile soil—from the death of serpents; for while the island itself knows no snakes, earth carried from there to whatever nations it is brought kills snakes instantly. The same is reported of Scotland or Ireland: that there, a bird is rare and there is no bee. And if anyone elsewhere should scatter dust or pebbles brought from there among beehives, the swarms would abandon the honeycombs. <term>Thule</term> <note>original: "Thile." A semi-mythical northernmost location, often identified with Iceland, Norway, or the Shetland Islands.</note> is the furthest place, having its name from the sun because there, during the summer solstice, a continuous day is seen, and a perpetual night during the winter solstice—a place celebrated indeed in Greek and our own poems. One day’s sail north from Thule is the sluggish and frozen sea.

### ¶ Regarding the second map of Europe.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'H' depicting two figures: one seated figure on the left appearing to hold a scepter or tool, and a standing figure on the right.</image-desc> Spain—or Iberia, or Hesperia—is inhabited by the Iberians, a race of men who are extremely proud, gifted with intelligence and very ready for war, and industrious with the sling and hand. The land is equal to all others in the healthfulness of its climate and second to none in all kinds of crops; it is so abundant in men, horses, iron, lead, copper, silver, and gold...

so fertile that even where it is exhausted by a lack of water and unlike itself, it nonetheless nourishes flax or <term>esparto</term> <note>original: "spartū," a fiber grass used for ropes and mats</note>. The <term>Tagus</term> <note>original: "Tagus," the longest river of the Iberian Peninsula</note> river is considered rich in golden sands and is said to produce gems. The <term>Baetis</term> <note>original: "Betis," the modern Guadalquivir</note>, flowing down from the <term>Tarraconensis</term> <note>Northern and Eastern Spain</note> region, runs for a long time as a single river; then, not far from the sea, it forms a great lake and rises up as a twin from a single source, each branch flowing out as large as the original single channel. On the bank of this same Baetis is a town whose wells decrease as the sea tide rises and increase as it recedes, remaining motionless in the intervening times. This same nature is found in one well in <term>Seville</term> <note>original: "ispali," referring to Hispalis</note>, though the others are ordinary. The <term>Balearic Islands</term> <note>original: "Baleares"</note> are named from the throwing of slings, at which these men themselves greatly excel. Indeed, the boys do not receive food from their mothers unless they have struck it with a stone at their mothers' direction. <term>Ebusus</term> <note>original: "Ebusos vel ebyssus," modern Ibiza</note> is found under various names; it lies across the region and, though not favorable for grain, is more abundant in other things and is free from all harmful animals; it neither produces even the mildest of wild creatures nor sustains them if they are brought in. <term>Colubraria</term> <note>modern Isla de los Columbretes</note>, which is also called <term>Ophiusa</term> <note>original: "opnissa," likely a corruption of Ophiusa, meaning "Snake Island" in Greek</note>, is the opposite, for while it swarms with a many-headed and malicious kind of serpent and is therefore uninhabitable, nevertheless, for those who enter it within the space of soil brought from Ibiza, it is safe and without danger; those same serpents, which usually attack men, flee far away in fear at the sight of that dust (or rather, its scent). The shores of Europe and Africa, very close to one another, form mountains: <term>Calpe and Abyla</term> <note>The Pillars of Hercules, modern Gibraltar and Jebel Musa</note> are both columns of Hercules, but Calpe is more prominent and almost entirely projects into the sea. From there is the <term>Herculean Strait</term> <note>Strait of Gibraltar</note>, which is also called the <term>Gaditan Strait</term> from the island of <term>Gades</term> <note>modern Cádiz</note>, which meets those exiting the strait. From this island, the aforementioned mountains took the name of Gadium, as did another smaller island of the same name on which the Romans once founded the Julian city.

### ¶ Regarding the third map of Europe.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'G' with a profile portrait of a man wearing a cap, facing left, within a square ornate frame.</image-desc>
The Gauls are proud and especially spirited. They are strenuous in war and fiercer at the first onset. They love novelties and are sophisticated and liberal. Truly, they were once superstitious and sometimes so monstrous that they believed a human being to be the best and most pleasing sacrificial victim to the gods. A trace of a now-abolished truth remains in the name of the <term>Druids</term> <note>original: "druidarum"</note>, who were their masters of wisdom and professed to know whatever the gods willed. The land is especially fertile in grain and poppies, abounding in nectar-like vines and pleasant with vast groves. However, the field is impatient of any cold and does not nourish life everywhere; it is least frequent in harmful kinds of animals. The royal courts of these people are decorated with <term>gymnasia</term> <note>places of study or schools</note> of divine and human literature, a wonderful variety of artisans, and a gathered society of diverse languages. They abound in rivers most suitable for sailing, flowing to the north,

<header>Book one.</header>

west, and south, by which commerce can easily be imported and exported from and to any people anywhere. In the mountains of <term>Narbonensis</term> <note>Southern France</note>, acorn-bearing shrubs grow which, in the early spring, produce fragrant grains for dyeing textiles a purple or scarlet color, and which possess medicinal virtue. In <term>Belgica</term> <note>Northern Gaul</note> there are hot springs capable of curing many diseases in the territories of the <term>Leuci</term> <note>a tribe in the area of modern Toul</note>. Also in the parts of <term>Lugdunensis</term> <note>Central Gaul</note> among the <term>Bourbonnais</term> <note>original: "borbonioz"</note>. Mount <term>Vosges</term> <note>original: "Uosag⁹ mōs"</note> in that same climate of the Leuci possesses veins of silver. Lead and other kinds of metals are found there. In those same parts are the <term>chalcedony</term> stone and pearls. In Lugdunensis there is also silver where there is lead. But iron is dug up most abundantly there and in various places of the Gauls. In Narbonensis there is the fountain of <term>Salsuce</term>, which flows back with waters saltier than the sea. Nearby is a field very green with tiny and slender reeds. The rest is suspect, as a marsh lies beneath. For the sea, poured under, shows itself through those holes that are dug to the bottom. Fish are pulled out, having been killed through those openings by the strike of those catching them, so that they seem to be dug out of the earth. In Belgica also, far from any sea, there are very salty wells in which no fish are found, but from there salt is boiled down in pans, which the whole surrounding region uses.

### ¶ Regarding the name and antiquity of the Gauls.

<margin>Xenophon on homonyms.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'G' identical to the previous one, containing a portrait of a man in profile within a square frame.</image-desc>
In the Greek language, "Gaul" <note>original: "gallus"</note> signifies something white and milky <note>note: a reference to the Greek word "gala," meaning milk</note>, on account of their skin; in Latin, it means the husband of the hen <note>a rooster</note>. They were called <term>Celts</term> <note>original: "celtas"</note>, who are the ancient <term>Galatians</term> <note>original: "Galathe"</note>, from King Galathes the son of Hercules, from whom came the Galatians in Asia and the Gallo-Greeks in Europe. The ancient Gauls were said to be named from the "inundation" <note>referring to a flood myth</note>; Janus and the Janigenae were the fathers of the first and most ancient offspring of Italy, the <term>Imbrogians</term> <note>original: "ymbrozum," likely referring to the Umbrians or a legendary pre-flood people</note>, before Ninus in the first Golden Age, which was spoken of after the flood. These existed almost two thousand years before the burning of the city <note>Rome</note>. Indeed, the first Gauls who crossed the Italian Alps were called Celts from Galathes the son of Hercules; whom we commonly call "Frandigenae" <note>Frank-born</note>. However, they came into Italy, as <term>Livy</term> witnesses in his fifth book, <margin>The crossing of the Gauls into Italy.</margin> in the year of the city’s founding. They were enticed by the sweetness of wine by <term>Aruns of Clusium</term>. This was in revenge for the rape of his wife by a then-powerful <term>Lucumo</term> <note>an Etruscan prince or leader</note>, two hundred years before the burning of the city in the time of Tarquinius Priscus, and a little less than one thousand five hundred years after the Golden Age. Having crossed the Alps, they gradually devastated the <term>Tuscans</term> <note>Etruscans</note> from their empire, first from the Transpadane region, then from the Cispadane, until <term>Rhaetus</term>, driven by them even from the Cispadane, was forced to lead the Tuscan colonies into the Rhaetian Alps, as all historians agree. Thus, because of the rape of one woman, the empire of the Tuscans was lost in all of Gaul, which was called <term>Cisalpine</term> by the Italians; and finally, by the victorious <term>Lombards</term>, it became <term>Lombardia</term> <note>original: "longobardia"</note> through <term>syncopation</term> <note>the shortening of a word by dropping sounds</note>. The Lombards, however, are Germans, as is clear from Ptolemy. Indeed, the Gauls who occupied the empire of the Tuscans in the Alps and all of Lombardy—which was called Cisalpine Gaul by them—were the Boii, the Insubres, and the Senones, who changed the names of many towns. Therefore, the origin of all Trans-Apennine Italy, which is commonly called Lombardy, even as far as Ancona, is not Greek but Tuscan and <term>Phaethontic</term> <note>related to the myth of Phaethon and the river Po</note>, mixed with others from the neighboring Gauls and Germans. The Gaul of the Senones, as <term>Sempronius</term> witnesses...
