### On the origin of the Celts, their religion, and their letters.

<margin>Diogenes.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a bearded scholar in a cap, pointing toward an open book on a lectern, representing the transmission of ancient knowledge.</image-desc>
**C**ording to the author Berosus, Samothes founded the <term>Celts</term> <note>original: "Celtas," here referring to the French or "Francigenas"</note>. Samothes was the brother of Comerus and Tubal, born of their father Japheth. From him, the Britons first arose. Later, the Gauls were called <term>Samotheans</term> <note>original: "Samothei"</note>, and his followers were primarily philosophers and theologians. For this reason, <term>Diogenes Laertius</term> <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers</note> says at the beginning of his *Lives of the Philosophers* that many authors assert philosophy took its beginnings from the barbarians. It is well known that it flourished among the Persians with the Magi; among the Babylonians and Assyrians with the Chaldeans; and among the Celts and Gauls with the Druids and those called Samotheans. According to the testimony of Aristotle in his book *On Magic* and his second book of
<margin>The Gauls handed down letters to the Greeks.</margin>
fourteen successions, these were the most skilled in divine and human law, and for that reason, they were most devoted to religion. Because of this, they were named Samotheans. Thus, as many authors record, the use of letters and calendars emanated not from the Greeks, but from the most ancient Samotheans. Therefore, since the Gauls used the same letters as the Greeks—as Caesar testifies in the sixth book of his *Commentaries*—and since they had them from Samothes long ago, it follows that these letters did not come from <term>Cadmus</term> <note>The legendary Phoenician prince who supposedly brought the alphabet to Greece</note>. Rather, the Galatians, Meonians, Greeks, and all of Greece had these same letters from the Gauls, as argued by the authors Xenophon, Archilochus, and Josephus. Berosus also notes
<margin>The four Saturns.</margin>
what was done in the fourth year of Ninus by the <term>four Saturns</term> <note>The author uses "Saturn" as a title for ancient founding kings</note>. Three of these Saturns—Tubal of Spain, Samothes of Gaul, and Thubsco of Germany—shaped their kingdoms with laws.
<margin>Diodorus.</margin>
The fourth Saturn, Cametes, who had brought colonies from Egypt into Tuscany, proceeded to corrupt the Tuscans (who had already been formed by laws and letters by Comerus) with magic and vices. Concerning this, Diodorus says in his fourth book that this Saturn, the son of Heaven who reigned in Italy, Sicily, and Libya, was endowed with the greatest impiety and avarice. That letters and songs existed among the Gauls in those times
<margin>Samothes.</margin>
is recorded not only by Berosus the Chaldean, but also by others. Samothes, also
<margin>Dis.</margin>
surnamed <term>Dis</term> <note>The Roman name for the god of the underworld, whom Caesar claimed the Gauls believed was their ancestor</note>, gave wise letters which were Phoenician, from which the Greeks formed their own. The ancient Gauls first handed these down to the Galatians and Meonians.
<margin>Letters in Gaul.</margin>
For as Caesar is the authority in the sixth book of his *Commentaries*, the Gauls obtained their disciplines from Dis and retained them even until his own time, using letters which the Greeks also used. Xenophon, too, in his book *On Equivocation*, says that Cadmus brought into Greece letters more similar to those of the Galatians and Meonians than to the Phoenicians. Therefore, before Cadmus, there were letters, philosophy, theological songs, and laws, especially among the Gauls and Celts, through many centuries and ages. The name suggests that the learned Gauls were called <term>Sarronides</term> <note>A class of Druids focused on moral philosophy</note> from their leader Sarron, about whom Diodorus writes fully in his sixth book, as we have sufficiently reported in the first book of *On the Christian Religion*. Certainly, one must not think that letters, theology, and philosophy did not exist among the Gauls before Sarron, since it was shown above that they existed in the age of Samothes. But as Berosus says, there were no public <term>gymnasia</term> <note>In the ancient sense, a place of education and training</note>, which alone soften human ferocity. Among the Celts, music and poetry were taught by King Bardus.

->**On the people of Lyon, who are the true Celts.**<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a monk or cleric in a cowl, representing the religious and scholarly life of the city of Lyon.</image-desc>
**T**He name of the Celts has often varied. For in the beginning they were called Samotheans. Then, from Celtus, they were called Celts; later, from Galathes, Galatians; just as from Beligius they became Belgians. Afterward, both Celts and Belgians were called Gauls by the Romans, and finally, <term>Francigeni</term> <note>The "Frank-born" or French</note>. Thus Galates, the son of Hercules, gave his name to the Gauls and reigned among them in the age of the ancient philosophers. The metropolis of the Celts is the city of <term>Lyon</term> <note>original: "lugdunū"; Lugdunum</note>. For in the time of Macaleus, Lugdus reigned among the Celts, as Berosus pleases, from whom both the province and the people took their surnames. Regarding Berosus’s claim that the whole province and people were named after him, I think it should be understood that he means the entire region of Lyon, which is truly called <term>Celtic Gaul</term> by Caesar. In Lyon, song and music were taught by King Bardus of the <term>Bardic sect</term>. Diodorus Siculus says in his sixth book that among the Celts of Lyon there are "melody-making poets" whom they call <term>Bards</term>. These sing with instruments like the lyre, praising some and disparaging others.
And a little later, he says there are poets of such great standing among them that when armies approach with swords drawn and spears readied, not only friends but even enemies cease from fighting at their intervention. Thus, among the Gauls,
<margin>Suetonius</margin>
anger yields to wisdom, and Mars reveres the Muses. Suetonius, however, writes concerning Caligula that he established a contest of Greek and Latin eloquence in Lyon. In this contest, it is said that the losers were forced to provide prizes for the victors and to compose their praises. Those who displeased the most were ordered to erase their own writings with a sponge or their tongues, unless they preferred to be beaten with rods or submerged in the nearby river; the orators there would turn pale with the fear of punishment. Whence <term>Juvenal</term> <note>A Roman satirist</note> says in his first satire: "Let him turn as pale as one who has stepped on a snake with bare heels, or an orator about to speak at the altar of Lyon." The site of that
<margin>Juvenal</margin>
altar was called <term>Athanacus</term> <note>Modern Ainay</note> by the Athenians, where there is now a monastery of the monks of Saint Benedict. This temple was destroyed by the Romans.
<margin>The Altar of Lyon.</margin>
Secondly, it was designated by all the Gauls at common expense and dedicated as a sacred site to Augustus. At Lyon, as Strabo records, there is an altar of exceptional dignity having the names of sixty tribes inscribed upon it, and a statue for each of them; another immense altar was placed nearby. On one, as it pleases some, were the Bards, the melody-making poets. On the other was the exceptional temple of the Sarronides and
<margin>Athanas.</margin>
Druids. One was a gymnasium for philosophers; the other for poets and orators. Where the <term>Arar</term> <note>The Saône River</note> mingles with the <term>Rhone</term>, the altar of the Bards was located, which was called Athanacus. Another was on the mountain whose
<margin>Strabo.</margin>
name is the Forum of Venus. And just as Suetonius testifies that they gathered at that former altar of the Bards from all sides to obey the judgments and decrees of the orators, so they gathered at this one, called the Forum of Venus, from all sides to receive the opinions of the Sarronides and Druids on divine and civil matters. That was then the first seat of all. And it is recorded in memory that this city, famous among the other cities of Gaul, has produced a great many men both in various human sciences and in the perfection of the Christian religion. <meta>This page continues the history of Lyon (Lugdunum), moving from the general origins of the Celts to the specific cultural and religious luminaries of the city. It introduces the "Lyonese Sibyl" and her allegorical prophecy regarding Pontius Pilate and the Passion of Christ.</meta>

### On the wonders of the world

Lucius Plotius Gallus <note>A 1st-century BC teacher of rhetoric</note> is said to have been [here]; he was the first to teach Latin rhetoric to the Romans, and they say he traced his origin to Lyon. Regarding him, Cicero records the following in Suetonius's book *On Famous Orators*: "Indeed, I remember that when we were boys, a certain Plotius first began to teach in Latin. When many flocked to him and every most studious student practiced under him, I grieved that I was not allowed to do the same." However, he was restrained by the authority of most learned men, who thought that minds could be better trained by Greek exercises. In this city, forty-eight martyrs became famous, the first of whom was Pothinus, Bishop of Lyon <note>Pothinus (c. 87–177 AD) was the first Bishop of Lyon and died during the persecutions under Marcus Aurelius</note>, a disciple of the martyr Polycarp. Also famous in this city were Irenaeus, Justus, Bardomarus, Stephen, Desiderius, Nicetius, Epipodius, Alexander (a doctor and martyr), Agobard the pilgrim, Elpidius, Lupus, Annemundus, Eucherius, Antiochus, Sacerdos, Augendus, Aurelianus, and Domitian the abbot—all most holy men. And finally, the most celebrated poet Faustus flourished, a contemporary of Boethius, Claudian, Mamertus, and Cassiodorus, most learned men. Faustus wrote epigrams for the establishment of Christian progress and hymns on sacred matters, as is gathered from the letters of Ennodius. From these, it is established that Lyon once flourished with famous men. For as Strabo <note>A Greek geographer of the 1st century AD</note> testifies, this city also flourishes above others in its rank of illustrious men.

¶ The prophecy of the Lyonese Sibyl: the final chapter on the Gauls.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
The Lyonese Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; here, the author invokes a local legendary Sibyl to give the city of Lyon a prophetic heritage</note> sang some verses concerning the life-giving Passion of our Redeemer, but listen to what they mean. When Pontius Pilate <note>original: "Potius pylatus"; the text identifies the Roman governor of Judea as having origins or a legendary connection to the region of Lyon</note> wandered through foreign lands far from his ancestral home, he finally retreated into Italy, where, led by Fortune, he discovered the Grove of Fortune. This grove was planted with all kinds of trees, such as plane trees, cypresses, and others of that genus. In it, he saw one tree standing out above all others, which is called a beautiful apple tree <note>original: "malus arbor"; in Latin, "malus" means apple tree, but the author is playing on the word's similarity to "malus" meaning "evil"</note>—and a wonder indeed—endowed with tall foliage and pleasant fruits. He stood there for a moment; and as the ambition of mortal minds is ever-present, he tried to pluck away its honors (which I call the apples) with his fingers, and finally to seize the very top of the tree. As he was attempting this, our Lyonese Sibyl, aware of things to come, approached him with these words: "What are you doing, O Demas?" etc. But unmoved, he did not cease to proceed where his hope called him, and thus things turned out most poorly for him, because he refused to have faith in the Sibyl's words. I believe this is hidden from no one. Allegorically, I understand the present world by the "Grove of Fortune." By the "fruits," I understand the riches by which Pontius, though born very poor, finally became powerful. Led by pride and being most ambitious for things and honors, he claimed for himself the "apple tree" residing in the grove with his own wicked natural gifts, though he received nothing from it. By this tree, you must understand our Redeemer <note>Christ</note>, to whom he had given such great goods, but being ungrateful, he finally added him to a horrendous death. You yourself will recognize the rest on your own.

### Book One. Folio 5.
¶ Verses of the Lyonese Sibyl prophesying the Passion of our Redeemer.

> The grove of Fortune is a place enclosed on all sides by dense
> Trees, with wide-spreading, lush foliage.
> Here one may see spreading plane trees and tall cypresses,
> And the sacred coverings of Idean Jove <note>The oak tree, sacred to Jupiter/Jove</note>.
> Here the most beautiful laurel lifts its head to the stars in the sky
> To ward off the strokes of lightning.
> Here flourish scented cedars and many varied stores 
> Of nard, flowing in different ways.
> But in the middle of the grove, celebrated Gaul shines,
> Through which the slender Loire <note>original: "liger"</note> flows in various directions.
> A very great apple tree stands there, tawny with its tall trunk,
> Bearing fruits—apples owed to good leaders.
> Around it bloom most brilliant lilies, pleasing to the
> Highest God, never to be nipped by any snow.
> Many ages ago, the Lyonese Sibyl 
> Prophesied that this tree would be a wonder to the people.
> While Pontius, born of a poorer house, happened
> To wander alone through this grove—
> Being one who had to protect himself with modest means,
> Taking small profits from a great God—
> While he is amazed by the tree's fruit and green leaves,
> And judges this grove to be sacred to the gods above,
> He finally reaches the apple tree and grasps at the shining
> Lilies, taking up the golden apples at the same time.
> Such fruits as neither wealthy Phaeacia sends, nor 
> That ever-watchful dragon guards for the Hesperides <note>Refers to the golden apples of Greek myth</note>.
> While he praises, loves, cherishes, admires, and adores these,
> He thinks he can pluck them with an easy hand.
> For here there is no Hesperian dragon to be deceived,
> Nor was there a sister here to be tricked.
> Mercury hates him; Juno is unwillingly greedy;
> He damns the ancient way and finds fault with his [former] status.
> The goddess Fortune <note>original: "dea rubrica"</note> smiles a little and shows him 
> A serene face; with her right hand, she lifts the man up.
> He, first creeping up the trunk and then the middle of the tree,
> Raises his greedy hands to the golden gifts.
> At last, great-souled, reaching toward the very summit,
> He rolls a great burden of apples with his fingers.
> Now conspicuous here with his staff and two-pointed mitre <note>The "mitra biconi" refers to a bishop's mitre, suggesting Pilate's rise to power is an allegory for corrupt ecclesiastical or worldly ambition</note>,
> He alone, so wealthy, possesses the entire grove.
> He proceeds, despising his equals and his former life.

The story uses a "Grove of Fortune" and a Great Tree to symbolize the world and Christ, interpreting Pilate's actions as a warning against worldly ambition and ingratitude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Lyon, transitioning from its historical figures and the prophecy of the Sibyl regarding the fall of the ambitious—specifically aimed at the legendary figure of Pontius Pilate—into a broader geographical survey of Europe, beginning with Germany, the Danube regions, and Italy.</meta>

# On the wonders of the world,

Each thing (besides itself) considers this prophetess to be a god,
Against whom if anyone attempts to speak, she swears
That she holds nothing sacred from the wicked.
Yet the blind goddess does not cease from her usual favor,
Rather, with greater daring, she stirs proud hearts.
The far-seeing prophetess, kindled by Phoebus's <note>Apollo, the god of prophecy</note> heat,
Left these things carved in white marble.
Behold, the Rhone resounds with the melodious applause of Lyon,
But suddenly, bodies submerged in the Saône <note>The Arar river</note> groan.
Pontius <note>Referring to Pontius Pilate, who according to legend was exiled to Lyon and died there; his name was often used as a cautionary tale for fallen pride</note>, alas, strives to join the Sicilian forests to Gaul,
Divided by mountains and the sea.
Jupiter, keep these wicked attempts far from here!
Alas, the bright iron [ax] scatters the sacred grove.
What are you doing, O madman? To what end does your insane
And swollen mind tend? Do you believe this is the way to the stars?
Although this is a firm tree to have climbed the summit,
It is not safe; the leaves are fragile and thin.
If by chance you burst through with your weight, O Pontius,
See for yourself where and from where you might fall (if you are wise).
Consider this at the same time: the higher you reach,
The more heavily you will strike the ground with this weight.
Furthermore, falling, you must expect a huge crowd;
You alone will be prey for very many men.
Hence I see your greedy kinsmen standing by you in blood,
Whom at the same time a black hunger for gold tortures.
Hence your long life, O Pontius, is a grief to those
Whose goods you alone possess.
Therefore, beware of decorating your miter with too much gold,
So that you may be better able to stand upon light leaves.
The prophetess forewarns: believe the persuasive prophetess;
The true Apollo does not pour out empty sounds.

### ¶ Concerning the fourth map of Europe.

<image-desc>Circular woodcut portrait of a tonsured cleric or scholar in profile, wearing robes and holding a closed book.</image-desc>

Germany <note>original: "Ermania"</note> is named from "germinating" peoples, who are numerous within it. They are immense in spirit and body. They exercise both for the sake of ferocity: their spirits in warring and their bodies especially in the habits of labor. They contend with their neighbors, however, not out of a desire for ruling or extending what they possess, but so that the lands around them may be desolate <note>This echoes the descriptions of Germanic tribes found in Julius Caesar and Tacitus</note>. Right lies in strength among most of them, so much so that they are not even ashamed of robbery. They are good to guests and gentle to suppliants. They endure the cold almost naked; they are harsh and unrefined in their diet. They do, however, nourish their hair and curl it in a certain way. But formerly, before they were adults (for they led a very long childhood), the men were covered with cloaks <note>original: "sagis"</note>

<column-break/>

# First Book folio vi.
fo. vi.

or the bark <note>original: "libris"</note> of white trees, even in the harsh winter. Now also they cover their youths with the coarsest cloths and mostly retain their former customs, which did not permit more refined garments for them (unless they had earned them through skill, service, or strength). Beyond custom, they have much less shame, as they are unburdened from a soft upbringing (not without great harm). The land is obstructed by many rivers and rugged with many mountains, and for the most part is impassable due to forests and swamps. The Orcinian forest <note>The Hercynian Forest, a vast ancient woodland of central Europe</note> is said to occupy sixty days' journey in circumference; among some it is called the Hercynian forest. The Rhine river <note>original: "Rhenus"</note>, bursting from the roots of the Alps, flows into the northern ocean; at first a torrent and headlong in its course, soon becoming calmer, and finally increased by other rivers, it flows in a very wide bed and closes the province from the west. The Danube <note>original: "Danubius"</note>, which is also the Ister, born in the same mountains near the borders of the Helvetians, flows toward the east; it irrigates many and various nations and makes them navigable for merchants; finally, having received many other rivers, foaming and covered in mist, it is poured through five huge channels into the Euxine [Black Sea]. Hercynian birds are born among the Germans, whose feathers glow at night <note>A common medieval legend, possibly based on bioluminescent fungi or misidentified migratory birds</note>.

### ¶ Concerning the fifth map of Europe: which contains Raetia, Vindelicia, Noricum, both Pannonias, Illyria, Liburnia, and Dalmatia.

The temperaments, cultures, and customs of these nations differ as much in reality as in name; for those near the Danube strongly resemble the Germany which they touch. Those, however, who are washed by the Adriatic have different and dissimilar rites. Some are mixed, such as those who look toward Germany, Italy, and Greece; and among three very great nations, they are as varied as they are few. The Raetian land is fertile with crops; Noricum is cold; Illyria or Liburnia is read to be oppressed by vast darkness.

### ¶ Concerning the sixth map of Europe, which contains Italy and the island of Corsica <note>original: "Cirnum", the Greek name for Corsica</note>.

Many races inhabit Italy, and very many peoples, especially the Latins, a glorious race in our literature, second to none in the fertility of the soil and the excellence of their talents. But every region has excellent men, and is pleasant enough, being most fertile in oil, grain, and nectar [wine]; it nourishes outstanding horses, herds, and flocks. Nothing is lacking there that would please or be suitable for man. The Apennine [mountain range] bisects the middle and protects the maritime regions; it makes them wonderfully pleasant, for since it is not too high nor stretched to the stars with lighter snows, it provides shade against the rigor of both heat and cold in turn. By these, the surrounding plains receive moderation and are most aptly irrigated by the many rivers flowing from it. The Tiber <note>The text says "Liberi", likely a typo or variant for "Tiberis"</note> especially, which flows through Rome, the head of all provinces, and fertilizes the whole area where it flows with its width; it is finally received by the nearby sea in a most peaceful bay at Ostia. What the city itself once was is clearly evident from its ruins and writings. But even now it shines as the most famous of all, both for the glorious seat of the supreme pontiff <note>The Pope</note> of our most holy faith and the chosen columns of the Church, and for its most worthy victories, and so many blessed soldiers [martyrs] of that same faith whom the impious sword—breaking their bodies but stabilizing the faith itself—transferred with Christ into glory; also for the learning and assembly of all kinds of letters and men of whatever nations. And if Rome is to be preferred to all others...

<meta>This page continues the geographical survey of the world, moving from the general description of Italy and its famous cities into specific details regarding the islands of the Mediterranean (Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily) and the remote regions of Eastern Europe (Sarmatia and the Crimea).</meta>

fo. vij.

-># On the wonders of the world.<-

Who would not speak with admiration of the city of the Venetians, which placed its foundations among the waves of the sea? It possesses streets on the deep itself and makes perpetual use of ships for the import and export of goods. It lacks walls and has no space except for the waters, yet it has been able to rule magnificently over various nations, even those located far away. The Eridanus <note>original: "Eridanus", the poetic name for the River Po</note>, which is also called the Po, rises from the lowest roots of the Mount Viso in the Alps and, swollen by all the other streams, flows into the Adriatic Gulf near the aforementioned city. It flows through an opening called the Great Po with such speed that it pushes aside the waves; those who sail through that sea can drink fresh water amidst the salt waves, as the river maintains the same quality for a long time as when it first poured out. Lake Benacus <note>The OCR reads "Acnacus," but this refers to Lake Garda, known for its sea-like storms</note> imitates the tempests of the sea. Lake Avernus <note>A volcanic crater lake near Naples</note> is so heavy with vapors that birds flying over it fall to their deaths. In the marshes of Rieti, the hooves of horses harden in the water; those who drink from the Clitumnus <note>A river in Umbria</note> develop a loathing for wine. There are also healing springs in Italy. Mount Vesuvius also emits fire, just like Etna.

<margin>On Cirnus, or Corsica.</margin>
Cirnus <note>The Greek name for the island</note> was named after Corsa, a Ligurian woman. Having marveled at a bull that was accustomed to swimming across the sea, she followed it and gave her name and cultivation to the land; for she brought men with her from the continent to settle there. The land is angular with many promontories, most joyful in its pastures, and highly regarded for the strength and abundance of its natural products.

### On the seventh map of Europe: which contains Sardinia and Sicily.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial S containing a portrait of a bearded man wearing a turban-like cap.</image-desc>The Sardinians drew their origin from the Africans; for the Sardis (procreated by Hercules), setting out from Libya under their leader, occupied the island and imposed the name of their leader upon it. The land is fertile but the climate is unkind; for as much as it is productive, it is almost equally pestilential. In it there are no wolves, but only the *solifuga* <note>original: "solifuga", likely referring to a venomous spider or shrew</note>, a tiny animal ruinous to cattle. No poison grows there except for a herb mentioned by many writers and poets called "Sardinian smallage" <note>original: "apia stro filis", likely *Apium risus* or the Sardonic herb</note>, which contracts the mouths of men and kills them while they appear to be laughing. It has hot springs which heal the eyes and expose thieves. For if they touch their eyes with these waters after swearing an oath, their crime is revealed by blindness.

The Sicilians excel in wit and ease of mind but are high-spirited and fierce; so much so that once, when the Gauls <note>referring to the French during the Sicilian Vespers of 1282</note> (who had occupied their island) behaved immodestly toward their women, the Sicilians killed them all on a single day at dusk, following a signal of bells rung across the whole island in every location. This island was once part of the continent but was later cut off by the strait of the Sicilian sea. This narrow and dangerous passage flows with an alternating current, now into the Tyrrhenian and now into the Ionian sea; it is fierce, cruel, and famous for the names of Scylla and Charybdis <note>The legendary sea monsters of the Straits of Messina</note>. Scylla is a rock; Charybdis a whirlpool. The soil is fertile for crops, abundant in gold, and nourishes great horses. It is pierced with caverns and pipes, through which Etna burns with perpetual fire, yet it also displays mixed snows and maintains the appearance of winter; the heat is not mitigated by the cold, nor is the cold dissolved by the heat. In the same island are two springs: one of which makes a fertile woman sterile, and the other makes a sterile woman fertile. There is also the spring of Arethusa, celebrated by poets; it produces the agate stone and coral. It has salts from Agrigento which dissolve in fire but crackle in water. The Romans and Carthaginians fought over this island for a long time (while Carthage was still standing); because it was placed in the middle, it served as a rampart for both and was stained by the greatest turmoils of war.

<column-break/>

-># Book One.<-

### On the eighth map of Europe: which contains Sarmatia in Europe and the Tauric Chersonese.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial S containing a portrait of a man in profile facing left, wearing a soft cap.</image-desc>It is a marvel how an innumerable multitude of various nations fills Sarmatia <note>A vast ancient region covering parts of modern Poland, Ukraine, and Russia</note>, that region near the farthest part of the world, stretching from the Sarmatian Ocean to the River Tanais <note>The Don River</note>. The men are diverse in appearance and customs. Yet among them (though they surpass all in barbarity), something commendable is also found. For those properly called Sarmatians are ignorant of gold and silver (those greatest of plagues) and carry out the exchange of goods through barter. The Astrace, at the source of the River Tyras <note>The Dniester</note>, do not know what it is to steal. Therefore, they neither guard their own things nor touch the things of others. The Agathyrsi use wagons for homes. They paint their faces and limbs according to how their ancestors excelled; thus, some are marked more and some less. However, all have the same marks, and they cannot be made or washed away. There are those who inhabit shameful caves and dug-out pits during the winter, their whole bodies covered in trousers, and even their faces covered except for where they see. The Riphean Mountains <note>A mythical or semi-mythical range, often identified with the Urals</note> divide the region, on the highest part of which the Griffins—a fierce and persistent race of wild beasts—live. They say the earth produces gold deep within, which the Griffins love marvelously and guard, being most hostile to those who touch it. The Essedones celebrate the funerals of their parents with joy, with sacrifices, and with a festive gathering of kinsmen. They are accustomed to consuming the mangled bodies themselves, mixed with the entrails of slaughtered cattle, during their feasting. They carry expertly polished heads to use as drinking cups. Those living further inland love wars and slaughter; it is the custom for those at war to drink the blood from the wounds of the first man they kill. And the more men each has killed, the more distinguished he is considered among them. Moreover, to be without experience in slaughter is among the greatest of reproaches. Not even their treaties are without blood. Those who make an agreement wound themselves and taste the drawn blood after they have mixed it. They believe this to be the most certain pledge of lasting faith. Like the Essedones with their parents, these people polish the heads of their greatest enemies for cups. Some drape themselves and their horses with the skins of their enemies. The Neuri, at a certain time, can change into wolves if they wish, and then back again into who they were. There are people with only one eye, and these are man-eaters. The River Hippanis <note>The Southern Bug in Ukraine</note> rises from a large marsh and flows for a long time just as it was born. Only not far from the sea, from a small spring named Exampheus, it receives such bitter waters that the river itself becomes unlike its former self; it no longer flows sweet but becomes most bitter.

### On the aforementioned eighth map: regarding the Taurians.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial T containing a portrait of a man in profile facing right, wearing a cap.</image-desc>The Taurians <note>People of the Crimean Peninsula</note> are monstrous in their customs. They have a monstrous reputation for being accustomed to slaughtering strangers as sacrifices. But although they are not unequal to the Sarmatians in their barbarity, the law of friendship nonetheless once had such power among them that when Orestes and Pylades <note>Famous pairs of friends from Greek mythology</note>, the closest of companions, were driven there—one of whom was to be sacrificed or...

-># On the wonders of the world. Book One.<-

### ¶ Regarding the ninth map of Europe, which contains the Iazyges, Dacia, both Moesias, and Thrace.

<image-desc>Decorative initial H featuring two rustic figures, one standing with a staff and one seated, possibly representing the tribes of Sarmatia or Dacia described in the text.</image-desc>
**T**he customs and rituals of these nations are not the same; the greatest part of them are unrefined and entirely foreign to human community. Those bordering the north belong to the Sarmatians. Those to the west belong to the highest Germans. Those, however, to the south and the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note> imitate the customs and rites of the Greek race. For the capital of Greece is Byzantium <note>Constantinople/Istanbul</note>, established by Constantine, but formerly Athens was the seat of philosophers and the greater place of study. Regarding the Getae <note>a Thracian tribe</note>, whom Ovid mentions in his *Letters from the Black Sea*, some believe their souls return; others that they are not extinguished but pass to a more blessed state. Others believe they truly die, but that this is better than living. Thus, among some, births are mourned and newborns are wept for. Funerals, by contrast, are festive occasions. Women consider it a great honor to be killed over the bodies of their dead husbands and buried together with them. And because several are married to a single man, it is a cause of great joy when they compete to win this honor. Maidens are not given away by their parents but are publicly either hired out or sold. Those of good character and beauty fetch a high price; for the others, husbands are sought by paying a fee. The city of Tomis (widely known for the exile of Naso <note>The poet Ovid</note>) is seen on the shore of the Euxine <note>The Black Sea</note>. Beyond it lies the island of Leuca <note>Snake Island</note>, where all livestock are born with white fleece. In that place, it is said that the souls of Achilles and other heroes who were slain in the Trojan War dwell. The Thracian Bosphorus <note>original: "Hospozum thracium"</note> was named (as they say) by the crossing of Io, the mistress of Jove, when she was changed into a cow (fleeing the jealousy and anger of Juno). There they say certain "shameless" rocks wander through the midst of the waves and join and couple together with sound and murmuring <note>A reference to the Symplegades or Clashing Rocks</note>. The Hellespont <note>The Dardanelles</note> still and forever preserves the memory of the fall of Helle, daughter of Athamas, King of the Argives; this place is notable for the crossing of the Persians, who dared to bridge that sea and cross on foot.

### ¶ Regarding the tenth map of Europe, which contains Greece, Crete, Euboea, and Achaia, and the other islands of Greece.

<image-desc>Decorative initial G with a seated male figure, likely a scholar or author, gesturing toward the text, consistent with the mention of Aristotle and Homer.</image-desc>
**T**he Greeks are an imperious people and are greatly enticed toward the things they desire. Once they were the masters of the liberal arts. They raised that monarch Alexander, who was even then the pupil of Aristotle, the greatest of philosophers. Homer stands supreme as the father or most renowned prince of their literature. They have Athens as their chief city, the parent and nurse of most famous men and excellent geniuses. They also have the mountains Olympus, Pelion, and Ossa, famous in myth and war. Where the haunts of the Muses, the Pierian home, the noble Vale of Tempe, and the springs of songs lie nearby. The Peloponnese,

<column-break/>

the most famous land, which poets called Arcadia. Crete, the nurse of Jove. Euboea and various other fertile islands scattered throughout the sea. But so many mountains, rivers, cities, and harbors commend the continent itself by the grace of its soil and sky, that if anyone sought to find another part of the world to prefer, they would hardly find it. Only the Aegean, due to the crowding of islands, often shrieks and roars, murmuring from the deep, and presents no small dangers. Otherwise, it is most placid. Mount Athos rises above the very clouds from which rains fall. And the peak of Olympus is so elevated that the inhabitants call its summit "heaven." For there it is always serene and there is perpetual silence from the winds. Belief gained credit when it was discovered that ashes were not washed away from the altars once placed on that summit, but remained in the heap where they were left; and the following year, even letters traced in the dust were found in the same order, untouched and unchanged. In Epirus, there is a spring which, although it is cold and extinguishes submerged torches like any other, sets them alight when they are moved near it without fire. One reads of this land of wonders being once devastated by mobs: first by internal wars when they contended for dominance, then by others invading them because they were divided—namely the Thracians, Persians, and Asians. Sometimes they were victors and even dared to attack foreigners; but they did not rule long over an ungodly part of the world. They stubbornly waged that famous Trojan War, in which the victors emerged almost equal to the vanquished. They were conquered, like other nations, by the Romans, whose horrendous civil wars they also endured. Finally, the imperial power (which had been won among them on the plains of Thessaly <note>The Battle of Pharsalus</note>) and which persisted among the Romans for a long time, had its seat in Constantinople. They lost this city, along with almost their entire empire, to the hands of the most savage Turks who now hold it (except for three periods of sorrow <note>likely referring to the fall of the city in 1453 and its consequences</note>). The head of Greece: the helmet of Europe, the shield of our Church Militant. O princes of heaven and earth: why are you troubled in turn?

### ¶ Regarding the map added outside of Ptolemy, which contains the Goths and many other northern peoples.

<image-desc>Decorative initial T showing a man (a geographer or scholar) seated at a desk with an open book, representing the modern additions to Ptolemy's geographical tables.</image-desc>
**T**he map recently published outside of Ptolemy contains the Goths and peoples near the North Pole <note>original: "cardini", the "hinge" or pole of the world</note>, who are indeed barbarians, harsh in culture and diet, huge in body and robust (because they were once provoked by the Romans, they made various eruptions and remarkably wore down the Empire and the Catholic faith). Moreover, the gulf extending from the Germans to those parts is called the Codanus <note>The Baltic Sea</note>; it is a vast and sharp sea. It is never open but, with waters flowing between and often overflowing, it spreads a wandering and diffused appearance to the mind; and because of the alternating tides of the sea, sometimes they appear as islands, sometimes as one continuous land. In these places are the Oeonae <note>original: "ceneas"</note>, who live on the eggs of marsh birds and oats; yet there are others with horses' feet called Hippopodes, and the Sannali <note>original: "scmalos"</note> who have large ears spread out to cover their whole body. The part toward the North Pole bristles with hardened ice. And there, as the degrees of the world rise, the sun in summertime rises long before it is due to set, making the nights so brief that they do not lose the brightness of the sun.

-># On the wonders of the world.<-

but through longer winters and, just as elsewhere, in darkness: differing from other places as they are closer to the pole. So much so that the longest day increases to a month, then to two or three, or more according to the degree of latitude. Likewise, the night lasts as long in the wintertime. Around the pole itself—that is, directly under the pole—it is day from one equinox to the next, and in the same way, night from equinox to equinox; so that our year there consists of only one day and one night. Furthermore, this part of the world cannot be reached because of the extreme severity of the frozen sea and the cold; its violence is so great that it does not even allow the sight of those trying to look upon it.

### Regarding the tide of the ocean.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' containing a portrait of a crowned king holding a scepter, representing a ruler or the personification of the Ocean.</image-desc>

The Ocean is a vast and infinite sea, stirred by great and continuous tides, now flooding the plains, now baring them far and wide as it retreats. It rushes first into some and then into others, not by separate approaches but turning its force now here, now there. Yet when it has poured forth equally from its center onto all shores, however diverse the lands and islands may be, it gathers itself again from them into the middle and returns into itself with such immense force. It even drives back vast rivers and either traps land animals or strands sea creatures. It is not yet sufficiently known whether the world accomplishes this by its own breathing—drawing back and regenerating the water from all sides with its breath, if (as scholars believe) the world is a single living creature—or if there are some deep caverns into which the receding seas fall back and from which they rise again in abundance. Or perhaps the moon provides the cause for such great movements. Certainly, the tides vary with its rising and setting; it is observed that the water retreats and approaches not always at the same time, but just as the moon rises and sets.

### Regarding the first map of Africa, which contains the Mauretanias. <note>Mauretania: A region in Northwest Africa, roughly modern Morocco and Algeria.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting two men in conversation, one in a hood and robes, possibly scholars or travelers.</image-desc>

The Moors are for the most part a sluggish and obscure people, and the land is better than its men. The region is undistinguished and has fallen to men who are hardly illustrious. Among them are the Maseli or Massyli, a truly wild race of humans who have absolutely no knowledge of cultivating the field nor any use for the plow; instead, wandering only through woods and glades in the manner of wild beasts, they live on acorns and hunting. The very ancient town of Tingi <note>Modern Tangier</note>, founded (as they say) by Antaeus, long preserved his shield made of elephant hide, which was huge and, because of its size, unusable by any other man. In that place is a high mountain, and opposite it, Spain raises another facing it; they call the former Abyla and the latter Calpe: both are known as the Columns of Hercules. <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note> There also...

<column-break/>

->Book One. fo.ix.<-

the mound of the previously mentioned Antaeus <note>A giant in Greek mythology, son of Gaia and Poseidon</note> at the shore of the ocean sea: a modest hill in the shape of a man lying on his back. They say that when any part of it is dug up, rain begins to fall, and it continues until the excavated parts are refilled. The island of Erytheia <note>Often identified with Cadiz or a nearby island</note>, once sown with grain, renews its crops seven times from self-seeded stalks, blessed with such a mild climate that it even brings forth men of very temperate and long—almost immortal—lives, as they live for a very long time. The neighboring Ethiopians occupied it; they say they advanced there after Geryon <note>A three-bodied giant whose cattle Hercules stole</note> was slain by Hercules.

### Regarding the second map of Africa, which contains Lesser Africa, in which Carthage once stood. <note>Lesser Africa: The Roman province of Africa Proconsularis, centered on modern Tunisia.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a soldier or knight in full plate armor, holding a sword and looking towards the text.</image-desc>

The Punic race <note>The Carthaginians</note> was most ready for ferocity and arms, as the Punic Wars declare more than enough. Its capital was Carthage, founded long ago by Dido. Already flourishing then, but eager for extended empire and a persistent rival of Roman power, she provoked a miserable destruction for herself, though she was once again wealthy. Rome later destroyed her even more miserably during the downfall; while the fear of the warlike city was removed, they turned to pleasure and luxury and disagreed among themselves even to the point of civil wars and monarchical rule. The Altars of the Phileni <note>A monument marking the border between Carthage and Cyrene</note> signify a deed worthy of being told. For the Phileni brothers, sent from Carthage against the Cyrenians to end a war over borders—a war long waged with great slaughter on both sides—made an agreement after a previous pact had failed. It was agreed that where the envoys, sent from both sides at a certain time, met, the borders would be established. Here, to secure the borders forever, they endured being buried alive. Further inland and quite far from the shore (wonderful to behold), they find fragments of fish spines, murex shells, and oyster shells, worn stones (as is common from waves), and anchors fixed in sea-cliffs that are no different from those in the sea, along with other such signs and traces of the sea having once overflowed into those plains where nothing now grows. Cirta, far from the sea, was once the home of Kings Juba and Syphax, who held the region near the Ampsaga. For the rest, the cultivation of all Africa is quite sufficient; the soil abounds in grain and has wealthy peoples. Many rivers flow from the ridges of the Atlas Mountains, by which the region itself, though very close to the scorching heat, is irrigated and cooled by the chill of the mountains.

### Regarding the third map of Africa, which contains Cyrenaica, Marmarica, Libya, and Egypt.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' showing a scholar or scribe seated at a desk, surrounded by books or scrolls, representing Egyptian learning.</image-desc>

Egypt is known to have had the greatest men. They were of various and marvelous genius, and they are said to have loved letters so much that four hundred thousand volumes were once gathered there, which we read were consumed by fire. <note>A reference to the destruction of the Library of Alexandria.</note> Indeed, tradition holds that the Egyptians were the first to compose a way of life and the discipline of morals. They were also the first of all to invent the plow and to furrow the earth...

ran. Then also the first ones who measured the heavens with a surveying rod <note>original: "radio," a staff used by ancient astronomers</note> and worked out the slanted path of the sun itself. These are they who opened up this knowledge of the earth. Ptolemy himself was an Alexandrian mathematician and an extraordinary philosopher of the known stars, as well as a most renowned investigator of natural things. It must be admitted that all studious and illustrious minds, eager for marvelous and foreign things, owe much to him. For with his book placed before them, they are able to survey and come to know—without labor or expense—the individual provinces, cities, seas, mountains, rivers, and other notable places of the known world, each positioned correctly according to its degrees relative to the equator and its set boundaries.

Egypt is a land devoid of rains, yet it is wonderfully fertile, so much so that even the wheat returns a hundredfold. It is itself a very prolific breeder of humans and other animals. This is due to the waters of the Nile, which are effective for generating and nourishing (swelling most greatly in the springtime), by which the land is irrigated in a truly marvelous way. Indeed, this Nile, descending from the mountains of Ethiopia, increases because of melting snows, or from erupting veins of springs, or from the Etesian winds <note>original: "ethesijs," referring to the Mediterranean winds believed to blow water back up the Nile</note>, or from other causes yet undiscovered. It is reported that Thebes in that land had a hundred gates, or as others would have it, a hundred palaces or princely houses; it was customary for each of these to pour out ten thousand armed men whenever business required it. 

The Labyrinth, a complex of a thousand houses and twelve royal palaces enclosed within a continuous circuit of walls, built and roofed with marble, has a single entrance leading down into it. Inside are innumerable paths made uncertain by continuous winding; this was the work of Psammetichus. Alexandria, most wealthy in resources and most fortunate in all things, holds the Egyptian shore. From there, those coming from afar can see those most distinguished and beautiful lookout towers of the Pharos <note>original: "pallenidis," likely a corruption referring to the Pharos lighthouse</note>. The inhabitants of the town of Pelusium at the mouth of the Nile are so skilled in navigation that they are judged divine by other Libyans. Those who are far from the coast use huts called *mappalia*; they are harsh in their way of life. They are uncultivated, and their banquets are [rude]. Lake Moeris was once a plain but is now a huge lake, deeper than is sufficient for the navigation of great and laden ships. When the most beloved of their people die, the inhabitants mourn, and having embalmed them <note>original: "medicatos," literally 'treated with medicine/preservatives'</note>, they place them within the inner chambers of their homes. In a certain lake of Egypt is the island of Chemmis, which, supporting groves, woods, and a large temple, floats and is driven by the winds. There are the Macrobii <note>original: "macrobij," meaning 'long-lived'</note> who have a life twice as long as ours. The Pyramids in Egypt are of wonderful workmanship. In Syene there is a fountain which they call the Fountain of the Sun. Its water boils at night and is extremely cold during the day. There is also a rock there which, when touched by a human hand, the spring itself emits sand and rages like a horse.

### On the fourth map of Africa: which contains Ethiopia.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a figure standing in a landscape, representing a person of Ethiopia.</image-desc>

The Ethiopians are for the most part unstable and wandering; they fix their tents and huts wherever the daylight fails them. They drive their cattle and whatever else they possess; they are very harsh in their food and lifestyle. Among those inhabiting cities, there is a milder way of living, though not the same for all, but each has his own. All are barbarians. The Troglodytes <note>meaning 'cave-dwellers'</note> possess no wealth; they enter caves

---

<page-num>f. r.</page-num>
<header>Book One.</header>

and feed upon serpents. The Atlantes curse the sun both when it sets and when it rises, as if it were a pestilence to themselves and their fields. They do not have individual dreams, nor do they eat animals, nor do they see in their rest the kind of visions granted to other mortals. 

The Blemmyes lack heads; their faces are on their chests. The Satyrs have nothing human about them except their outward appearance. The Aegipanes <note>goat-legged creatures of myth</note> have the form that is commonly celebrated. The inhabitants of Augila consider the ghosts of the dead to be gods; they swear by them and consult their oracles. Having prayed for what they want, they consider the dreams they have while sleeping on the burial mounds to be the responses. Among their women, it is a solemn custom on the night they marry to be open to the debauchery of all who come with a gift; to have slept with the most men is considered the greatest honor. For the rest of the time, their modesty is remarkable. 

The Gamphasantes are ignorant of all weapons; they know neither how to hurl spears nor how to avoid them. They live alone among themselves and flee from those they encounter. There are also those who are mute and use nodding for speech. Some are without the sound of a tongue; others are without tongues at all. Others have their lips joined together, with only a small pipe under their nostrils. There are also women whose whole bodies are hairy, who are fertile of their own accord without the company of males, and who are of such harsh manners that some can scarcely be held back from resisting even with chains. 

The Bynaptodes crawl with bent, supple legs rather than walking. Others are half-human, or more like beasts. Among the Garamantes, there are cattle that graze with their heads turned backward, for their horns, pointing downward, would otherwise be in the way. The mountain Theon <note>likely "Theon Ochema," or 'Chariot of the Gods'</note> blazes with perpetual fires like Etna or the Chimera. Beyond this, green fields lie open further than can be seen. By day there is a vast solitude and a vaster silence. At night, frequent fires are seen, and the sound of cymbals and drums is heard, louder than human voices. Elsewhere there is a place always filled with prepared banquets, and whoever wishes may eat as they please; they call this the "Table of the Sun" <note>original: "trapezā solis," a legendary place mentioned by Herodotus where the earth was said to produce food spontaneously</note>. And they affirm that what is placed there everywhere is born of divine power. There is a lake in which bodies, when bathed, shine as if anointed with oil. The same water is drunk, but it is too weak to support anything that falls into it, so that not even the lightest leaves of trees can float. 

In Ethiopia there are Lycaons (very fierce beasts), Sphinxes, horned birds, the Tragapomenes <note>likely a creature with goat-like features</note> with horse-like ears, Pegasi, and Catoblepae with heavy heads which they can barely support, whose eyes it is fatal to have seen. There are also serpents and huge lizards, and innumerable other kinds of wild animals and beasts, some of which wander the mountains and solitudes, and some around the rivers. The Nile, among other things, besides being full of fish, gives birth to hippopotamuses and crocodiles.

### On the first map of Asia: which contains Asia Minor with several adjacent provinces, and also Armenia Minor.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a male figure in profile looking toward the right, representing an inhabitant of Asia Minor.</image-desc>

The customs and the locations of the nations on the map of Asia Minor and the others differ. Some are of the Greeks. Several are of the Syrians. Others are of the Scythians. There are also those who have various Asian rituals mixed with these. This was once a Catholic <note>meaning Christian or universal</note> region, but it is now Turkish enough to threaten our Europe, and they are conquering it while we do not hold together. The land they inhabit is very fertile and notable for its rivers, cities, and mountains. The Taurus mountain range, beginning especially from Pamphilia, assumes various names here and there, finally retaining the name Imaus among the Indians; it makes another base for the sky along with Atlas. The Cappadocians are men...

The most excellent riders of horses feed in the open. They once used to sleep together promiscuously. However, they are harsh and uncultivated, spending the night with their horses driven near. They choose their king openly by vote and punish him with hunger if he rules poorly. The Chalybes <note>original: "Ebalibes," a people of Paphlagonia famous in antiquity for iron-working</note> (a people of Paphlagonia) are never free from hammers or anvils. Their region seems to burn with smoke and flames, and thunders with the clatter of iron tools. They go about naked; in face and skin they are almost like Ethiopians. In battle they are warlike and pugnacious, trained in military discipline. They are very rich in the abundance of things. In Pompeiopolis lies the tomb of the poet Aratus, where stones thrown upon it jump apart <note>A legendary phenomenon mentioned by ancient geographers, suggesting the earth rejected offerings to the poet</note>. In Lycia, Mount Chimera burns like Etna in Sicily, like Theon in Ethiopia, and like Vesuvius in Italy. Among the Mariandyni is the Acherusian cave, which is a passage—as they say—to the spirits of the dead, and they believe Cerberus was dragged out from there. In Halicarnassus is the Mausoleum, the monument of King Mausolus, one of the seven wonders, the work of Artemisia. In Cilicia is the Corycian cave, which does not fail to charm those who enter; however, for those who reach the depths, another cave opens up that must be mentioned for other reasons. It terrifies those entering with the sound of cymbals—produced by divine power—and with a great crashing noise clattering inside. Then for some distance it is clear. Within, a rushing river rises, and where it has pulled its great force through a short channel, it is submerged and hidden. The interior space is more than anyone would dare to enter; it is horrific and therefore unknown. There is another cave beyond which they call Typhonian, filled with perpetual night, with a narrow mouth that immediately kills anything lowered into it. By the Rhyndacus river, immense serpents are born which emerge from there and gape, swallowing birds flying overhead. From Mount Ida, at midnight, scattered fires are seen to flicker toward the east; as light approaches they gather and become a huge globe, and as it decreases it becomes brighter and puts the night to flight, and with the day it rises, having now become the sun. The same is reported to happen on Mount Olympus in Arabia.

### Concerning the second map of Asia: which contains Asiatic Sarmatia.

<image-desc>Woodcut portrait of a man wearing a soft, peaked cap and a high-collared garment, depicted in profile within a simple square frame.</image-desc>

Armed women are described in the eighth map of Europe, a barbarous and cruel race. Near the mouth of the Tanais <note>the Don River</note> dwell the Ramatae, among whom the women practice the same arts as the men. So much so that the men are not even free for military service; the men stay on foot and fight with arrows. The women enter battle on horseback, and they do not fight with iron, but they kill those they have caught with nooses by dragging them. They marry, however, and so that they may be considered noble, there is no limit on age, but the virgins remain so until they have killed an enemy. The Tanais itself, having fallen from the Riphean mountain, rushes so headlong that while the neighboring rivers—both the Maeotis <note>Sea of Azov</note> and the Bosporus—and some parts of the Black Sea are hardened by winter cold, it carries heat alongside the winter and runs down lofty and swift like a lightning bolt. The Sauromatians <note>Sarmatians</note> hold its banks, comprising several peoples and several names. Then come the first kingdoms of the Amazons, and of the Geloni, where they live in wooden houses. The Budini <note>original: "Burra"</note>, Thyssagetae, and Turcae occupy vast forests and sustain themselves by hunting. Then, through continuous cliffs, a broadly harsh and 

<column-break/>

deserted region stretches as far as the Arripheans <note>original: "arrepheos," likely the Argippaei described by Herodotus as a sacred, bald-headed people</note>. These people have most just customs; their homes are the groves, their food is berries, and the women go with heads bare. They are held sacred, and thus no one from such wild nations violates them, so much so that it is considered a refuge for those who have fled to them. Beyond them rise the Riphean mountains themselves. However, for those who have been allotted the region around the Maeotis and the mouth of the Tanais, the habitation is harder. For as often as the cold has grown settled while the North Wind <note>original: "borea"</note> blows, one sees either horses or mules, or the herds themselves together with their gear, perish before one's eyes. Neither can men safely remain outside of protected and dark dwellings, since they themselves would perish along with their gear unless they observed the weather; they flee to the interior regions with closed wagons, leaving their furious fatherland of the North Wind. Near the Ceraunian mountains, certain monuments coiled in spirals are seen, which are said to be of Cadmus and his wife Harmonia. There also two columns are fixed, which as often as some adversity threatens the neighboring people, both immediately collide with each other, as if they were fighting.

### Concerning the third map of Asia, which contains Colchis, Iberia, Albania, and Greater Armenia.

<image-desc>Woodcut portrait of a king wearing a stylized crown and regal robes, facing slightly right, framed within a simple square border.</image-desc>

The Colchians, having formerly set out from Egypt, occupied the narrow part of the Black Sea from the frozen regions to the Caucasus; here is the Temple of Phrixus and the grove famous in the story of the Golden Fleece. The Iberians <note>Caucasian Iberians, living in modern Georgia</note> long ago set out from the Pyrenees and broke into that part of the world. They are most warlike men, very hostile to the neighboring Hyrcanians. The Albanians are so called because they are born with white hair <note>A common medieval etymology; "albus" means white</note>; they are fierce by nature and driven by a greed for war. There, the dogs are almost equal to bulls, and they even bring to the ground the bulls themselves (which are huge among them). The Caspian Sea is atrocious and cruel, without ports, exposed on all sides to storms; when the North Wind blows sharply, nothing else is more dangerous. It is navigated in the summer months, but hardly at all in the others. The Armenians are very robust and (as has been said) trained in military discipline, such that they are superior to the Medes and Syrians and other peoples subject to Asia. The land is rich in wild beasts and fodder, the mother of great rivers. It sends forth the Tigris and the Euphrates through long windings into the Red Sea at the Persian Gulf; and it sends the Aras <note>original: "arareē," referring to the Araxes river</note>, which cuts through the fields of Armenia and glides along peaceful and silent, so that it is not manifest which way it goes (until you look closely). When it reaches rougher places, pressed on this side and that by rocks, the narrower it is, the more it foams, breaking itself repeatedly against the opposing crags. Because of this, it rolls down with a huge murmur and sound, so swift that where it is about to fall from a precipice into the water below, it does not immediately drop. Beyond this, it even has a channel carrying it high for more than the space of an acre <note>original: "ingeris spacio"</note>, supporting itself with hanging waters as if it were its own riverbed. Then, where it descends in a curved and arched stream, it becomes tranquil. Again, silent and scarcely flowing through the fields, it slips away into the Caspian.

### Concerning the fourth map of Asia: which contains Syria, Mesopotamia, Petraean and Desert Arabia, also Palestine and Judea.

# On the wonders of the world.
## Book one.
### Leaf 12.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'S' depicting a scholar or cleric seated at a desk, writing in a large book placed on a lectern.</image-desc>
**Syria** is entirely filled with abundance, situated in a most temperate climate and perfectly suited for exchanging the various riches of the land and sea; it is a very wealthy and highly populous land. The **Phoenicians** (who formerly set out from Egyptian Thebes) hold the middle ground. They are a skillful race of men, trained for the duties of both war and peace; they cultivated letters and literary works, as well as other arts, with the greatest diligence. They were the first to test the sea with ships, to command nations with a gathered fleet, to organize kingdoms and battles, and they also invented the use of commerce and many other things which writers have not kept silent. **Mesopotamia** is most joyful for the grazing of cattle; it is fruitful with a variety, abundance, and sweetness of fruits, and no less rich in crops, so much so that men considered that region to be blessed and most pleasing to the gods. **Babylonia**, once arid, was afterwards made quite fertile and pleasant by rivers diverted into many channels; it has a city of the same name which **Semiramis** <note>A legendary queen of the East, often credited with the building of the Hanging Gardens and the walls of Babylon</note>, formerly queen of the Medes, surrounded with an impregnable wall of baked brick. The **Euphrates** is born in Armenia and for a long time flows widely in marshes; with its waters sitting still, it is sluggish and spreads out without a channel. Later, where it breaks the bank, it is narrowed into a channel like a true river and, having received banks, it becomes swift and clear; it strives on its way to come into our sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>. From here, through the Syrians and Arabs, sometimes huge and sometimes smaller than itself, it finally descends into the **Tigris**, with which it will glide into the Persian Gulf. **Palestine** itself is Judea, once the most blessed of lands, flowing with milk and honey, which God promised and gave long ago to the fathers: to Abraham and his descendants, from whose royal lineage the son of God, **Jesus Christ**—who is blessed forever—deigned to be incarnated in the womb of the glorious Virgin. He trod that land with his feet, which were beautiful as he preached peace to believers and promised eternal life, especially to those doing good works. His glorious Sepulchre still remains there, along with many signs of our redemption.

->¶ Regarding the fifth map of Asia: which contains central Assyria,<-
->Parthia, and Persia.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'A' depicting a man in profile wearing a high, pointed cap, possibly representing a Parthian or Eastern ruler.</image-desc>
The **Assyrians**, **Medes**, and **Persians** are very well known for the wars they have long waged against each other and against other nations. There are various peoples and various customs. The **Parthians** are a most hardy race of men; they never dig or plow the earth, nor do they cross over to other nations, nor do they raise herds or flocks. From their first age, they twist the bow with their hand and are worn out by the study of archery, or by the running of feet, or by continuous riding. The whole region rattles with the throwing of javelins and broken spears, nor is it lawful for anyone to approach dinner unless the labor of competing has drawn sweat from his whole body. They are nourished mostly by hunting, which they pursue either by javelin or by arrow. Once they despoiled the Medes; from then on, they were accustomed to use golden arms in war, as well as trappings and bridles for their horses, and silver spurs. They drew their origin from the **Scythians**. The **Medes** (who mostly inhabit the mountains) are read to be devoted to magic arts and dire poisons. Those who choose and build for themselves irrigated pastures and joyful estates on the plains

<column-break/>

find the region indeed burdened everywhere with many different flocks of cattle. **Persia**, on account of its temperate air, always has new fruits; the region is always green and always blooms. It is irrigated by many rivers, and the fertile soil overflows with an abundance of all things. **Assyria** is said to have first invented the use of purple, ointments for the hair and body, and scents for which the luxury of the Greeks and Romans raved; this land produces the **Median tree** <note>original: "medicam arborem," likely the citron (Citrus medica), known to the ancients for its medicinal properties and scent</note>, which grows nowhere else.

->¶ Regarding the sixth map of Asia: which contains Arabia and Carmania<-
->and the islands of the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'A' depicting a figure wearing a crown and royal robes, representing a king or the ruler of Arabia.</image-desc>
The **Arabs** inhabit the most precious region of all. For it is higher and surrounded by a twin sea. The whole land blazes with frankincense or myrrh or fragrant reeds, which are thrown into fires everywhere and burn, pouring out a most pleasing sweetness. The sheep (with which the land overflows) are clothed in the softest and thickest fleece. The lakes and rivers are filled with a multitude of fish. Frankincense, gum, and innumerable liquids flow from the bark of trees. Honey comes from the leaves. Spices grow of their own accord. Some live wearing miters <note>pointed or ceremonial caps</note> or with unshorn hair, but the beard is shaved except on the upper lip. For others, even this is unshorn. It is wondrous to say that out of innumerable peoples, an equal part lives in commerce or in robbery; as a whole, they are the wealthiest nations, as the greatest riches of the Roman fathers and other widespread nations remain among them. They sell what they take from the sea or the woods or the soil itself, buying nothing in return. Some live within caves and steep rocks, entirely naked and possessing nothing of human happiness; dried out by the excessive harshness of living, they have contracted a black color and burnt skin. If anything bad or adverse happens, they perish there; if enemies come upon them, they flee around like wild beasts, wandering and out of the way through the hills and deserts. They are by no means like the other Arabs who protect and guard their borders, endowed with such great gifts, with arms and weapons. There is a forest in Arabia that produces **ebony**, or (as they say) it grows on the islands of **Cocconati**. In that same Arabia is the **Phoenix**, a bird that is always unique; it is not generated by mating or birth, but when it has endured for a lifespan of five hundred years, it broods upon a pile heaped up for itself with various scents and is dissolved. Then, growing together from the decay of the rotting members, it conceives itself and is born again from itself. When it has grown up, it carries the bones of its former body enclosed in myrrh to Egypt, into the city they call the **City of the Sun** <note>Heliopolis</note>, placing them on fragrant altars of nard; it consecrates them in a memorable funeral. The **Carmanians** live without clothing or grain, without cattle or fixed homes; they clothe themselves in the skin of fish and feed on the flesh. Except for their heads, they are hairy over their whole body.

->Margiana, Bactriana, Sogdiana, and the region of the Sacae.<-

# On the wonders of the world.
## Book one.
### Leaf 13.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'C' featuring two men in classical or academic robes, one pointing toward the text.</image-desc>
The regions toward the east by the **Caspian Sea** are of renowned fertility. **Margiana** <note>An ancient region in modern-day Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan</note> is sunny and enclosed by mountains, the only place in that territory where vines grow. It is the pursuit of the **Massagetae** <note>A nomadic confederation of Central Asia</note> to be constantly worn down by the chance of archery. They are quite hostile toward guests and are not accustomed to keeping faith with neighboring peoples for long. They are completely ignorant of the use of grain and wine; they drink milk mixed with horse blood. The **Sacae** <note>Scythian nomads of the Eurasian Steppe</note> are also most skilled in the art of archery and are so well-trained by constant practice that it seems they cannot be surpassed or even equaled by anyone else. Indeed, it would be considered a great disgrace if anyone should shoot an arrow in vain and not strike the prey or the target. **Bactria** <note>An ancient region in modern Afghanistan/Uzbekistan</note> has very strong camels, specifically those that do not wear down their feet. Nearby to the north is the uncultivated cruelty of various tribes. There one encounters the **Anthropophagi** <note>A Greek term meaning 'man-eaters' or cannibals</note> who feed on human flesh. Therefore, adjacent to them are vast wildernesses and a multitude of wild beasts, possessing a savagery not unlike that of the men. All the men grow their beards long out of ferocity and great strength, though authors say they possess no true courage. The draft of the **Caspian Sea** is indeed sweet; its great size is undoubtedly overcome by the influence of fresh water over the salt. It is called Caspian from the nearby Caspian Mountains; it is also called the **Hyrcanian Sea** from the region of Hyrcania that lies below it. This land is abundant in forests and teems with panthers, tigers, and wild beasts of various kinds.

### ¶ On the eighth map of Asia: which contains Serica.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure standing in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
Regarding the barbarity of the **Scarians**, it has already been touched upon above. They inhabit forests and caves almost exclusively, dressed in skins, and they eat the flesh of horses and many other beasts (which we usually avoid). Whatever they catch is considered game. The **Seres** <note>The Latin name for the Chinese, meaning 'the Silk People'</note> are the first of the people born toward the north beyond the Indians; they are mild and very unlike the Scythians in their customs. Indeed, they loathe unclean meats. They are clothed in the **wool of trees** <note>A common classical description of silk, which was thought to be harvested from trees like cotton</note> and silken garments. They abound in textiles of this sort, and therefore they devote themselves to no other pursuit more intently; they also dye these same clothes with various flowers. They are a people full of justice and observe a silence <note>original: "omertio"</note> in trade that is conducted in absence, with goods left in the wilderness. Indeed, this nation is to be preferred above all others in this matter, and also in the honesty of the natural union of marriage, which they guard so strictly that no one knows anyone but his wife; no one touches her after conception, nor when she is being purified. Thus, among them, neither thief nor adulteress nor harlot is found, nor is it ever reported that a man was murdered. They have no judges or officers of the law so long as they live without crime or wickedness. Following justice, all impose the judgment of reason upon themselves. And because they live most justly and chastely, they are never punished by the decay, pestilence, or plagues by which we are worn down. Lasting for a very long time, they end their lives without sickness. However, those of morbid or unclean nature are usually killed for their sin.

### ¶ On the ninth map of Asia which contains Arachosia, Gedrosia, and other regions surrounded by mountains.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'E' containing a bearded figure, possibly a philosopher or traveler.</image-desc>
The needy people who are enclosed by mountains (which serve as a wall for them so they do not fight one another, and protect them against other nations) maintain a mixed barbarity, since they border the Scythians, the Indians, and both groups of Carmanians. **Aria** <note>An ancient region centered on the city of Herat in modern Afghanistan</note> is a forested region, sandy and (for the most part) sterile. Nevertheless, by a most excellent gift, crusts of **sapphire** <note>original: "sap bicee"</note> are gathered from the veins of the mountains and other gems are dug up; it also abounds in wild beasts and river fish. In other respects, the region, living according to its own custom everywhere, protects its own borders and keeps itself to itself. They are not read of as being conquered except by **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great</note>, who established cities of his own name among them and penetrated as far as the Indians.

### ¶ On the tenth map of India which contains India within the Ganges.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'I' (rendered as a decorative letter resembling an 'M') depicting two figures together.</image-desc>
The **Indians** have never exceeded their own borders, being content within their own limits. If other nations were to imitate this, they would not infest one another with horrific and unnecessary wars. The Indians are naturally black and stout. They have very thick hair, not unlike the color of the **hyacinth** <note>likely referring to a deep, blue-black luster</note>. Since gold is dug out of many places, many of them seek profit from that source. Others weave linen cloths; others scrape the tusks of elephants. Others, walking through the courses of rivers, search to see if any **beryl**, or **diamond**, or some **jasper** shines among the sands, or if any grey-green **topaz** occurs, or if they happen upon a certain purple **amethyst** similar to blood. For these are their most important pursuits, since that entire region is bathed in rivers that make the fatherland rich and powerful with riches of this kind. There are also gardens among the Indians that are always green and always filled with an abundance of fruit. There are also fertile fields, very rich pastures, mountains, forests, springs, and celebrated rivers, famous cities, and finally all the first and most excellent things that could be told or wished for, so much so that whatever unique or excellent thing is found in other lands seems to have come together in these regions at once. The inhabitants are veiled in linen or in the wools which the forests especially bear. Among so many gifts of heaven and soil, they abound in various species of beasts: elephants, lions, marvelous bulls, the **eale** <note>A mythical beast with movable horns</note>, the **monoceros** <note>The unicorn or rhinoceros</note>, and certain horrific serpents, eels thirty feet long, and **ants** no less than the largest dogs, which (in the manner of griffins) guard the gold dug deep from the earth with the greatest danger to those who touch it. The region is in some places so rich and of such fertile soil that the split sections of reeds can carry two or three sailors. The **Brahmins** <note>original: "Bragmanni"</note> are of a wonderful religion and an innocent life; they say that God loves nothing but a pure mind. The **Pandea** people among the Indians are accustomed to being ruled by women. There are those at the source of the Ganges who are nourished primarily by the scent of wild apples.

### ¶ On the eleventh map of Asia which contains India beyond the Ganges.
