# On the wonders of the world.
## Book one.
### Leaf 43.

<image-desc>Decorative initial E containing a woodcut portrait of a man in profile wearing a soft cap.</image-desc>
The outer Indians partly agree with the interior ones, and partly with those they border. For there are some who are dressed in linen and "tree-wool" <note>An early term for cotton</note>. And there are those who cover their bodies with the skins of wild beasts and birds. Others veil only their private parts. Some go about naked. Some are humble and small. Others are so tall and huge of body that they use elephants—even the largest ones—as easily and skillfully as we use horses. Some think it best to eat no meat. Some are nourished only by fish. There are those who, before their parents waste away from age or sickness, slaughter them like sacrificial victims; they judge it most pious to feast upon the entrails of the slain. Some, when old age or disease approaches, go far away from others and wait for death in solitude, not at all anxious. Truly, those among them who are wiser and devoted to the study of wisdom <note>Likely referring to the Gymnosophists or "naked philosophers" described by classical authors</note> do not wait for death, but joyful and with glory, they light fires and throw themselves into the flames. India experiences a reversal of winter and summer. Or they are at the edge beyond which, they say, lies the region of darkness—namely, clouds condensed in a perpetual state.

### Concerning the twelfth map of Asia, which contains the island of Taprobana.

<image-desc>Decorative initial A containing a woodcut portrait of a man wearing a peaked hat.</image-desc>
**Taprobana** <note>The ancient name for Sri Lanka</note> is filled with many riches of various things, and many of the elephants transported from there are bred there. It has happy elephants wandering everywhere along the shores, which are accustomed to feed in the Red Sea <note>original: "mari rubro"—in ancient geography, this term often included the entire Indian Ocean</note> and then carry themselves across those very waters. These animals are truly monstrous and of such magnitude that they look like hills brought to the shores. Their backs are roughened over a long stretch in the sea. They are extremely hostile toward humans; they have a hideous and huge gap for a mouth, so much so that they frequently swallow small boats along with the men. Indeed, the malice of men requires them to be afflicted and punished by the bites and blows of such wild beasts and monsters.

### Catalog of the cities of the whole world
And especially those held by Christians. For all those eager for human affairs, a most fruitful work by Lord **Symphorien Champier** <note>original: "Simphoriani champerij"—a famous French humanist physician and historian (c. 1471–1538)</note>, primary physician to the most illustrious prince, the Lord Duke of Calabria, Lorraine, and Bar.

<image-desc>Decorative initial G containing a woodcut portrait of a man in profile.</image-desc>
**Gaul** <note>Modern France</note> is named from the whiteness of its people; for in Greek, Gaul is called "milk" <note>The author is using a popular but incorrect etymology, linking Gallia to the Greek "gala," meaning milk</note>. For the mountains and the harshness of the sky exclude the heat of the sun from that part, which results in the whiteness of their bodies not being colored by tan. The ridges of the Alps protect this land from the east. The Ocean encloses it from the west; the steep Pyrenees from the south; the currents of the Rhine and Germany from the north. Its beginning is **Belgica**; its end is **Aquitaine**. It is a region with fertile and lush soil, 

<column-break/>

suitable for the use of animals. It is also well-watered by rivers and springs; poured through by two great rivers, the **Rhine** and the **Rhone**, it has many provinces: **Burgundy**, the **Province of Provence**, **France**, **Neustria** (or **Normandy**), **Aquitaine**, **Gascony**, and **Narbonne**. If we wish to truthfully distinguish the specific provinces of Gaul, there occur: France, Normandy, Lesser Brittany <note>Brittany</note>, Touraine, Picardy, Flanders, Holland, Zeeland, Burgundy, Lorraine, Luxembourg, Helvetia (or Alsace), and Provence. According to the witness of **Solinus**, the Dauphiné of Gaul stretches between the Rhine and the Pyrenees. Likewise, between the ocean and the **Cevennes** and **Loire** mountains, they stretch to the **Seine**. There is **Belgica**, from which the Belgians come; from there to the **Garonne** is **Celtica**, from which the Celts and those who are neighbors to the Spanish, the **Celtiberians**, come. The same is also called **Lugdunensis**, named after **Lyon**, the most noble and distinguished city of the Gauls. From there to the Pyrenean mountain is **Aquitaine**, which was previously called **Armorica**, from which come the Aquitanians and the region of Aquitaine. Indeed, the Gauls thrive everywhere among nations in the glory of their deeds. And not without reason, since the observance and religion of its ruler and those reigning under him toward the Roman Church is so great that they easily obtain whatever they ask from the Supreme King <note>The Pope</note>. Therefore, its kings are deservedly called "Most Christian" and the "Firstborn of the Church." No other prince in the whole world has deserved to be called by this name. Whence **Lodovico Bolognini** of Bologna <note>A noted Italian jurist and poet (1447–1508)</note> wrote thus concerning the happy empire and state of the Gauls:

->The kings of the Franks, born under a holy name,<-

> Have always been strong in counsel and always in arms.
> Supporters of holy goodness, holding the laws,
> The Roman Church calls them her own sons
> And her firstborn; they are worthy of such a name.
> God gave them empire and protects their laws.
> They are anointed and become holy, whoever are created kings.
> Under them are a hundred cities of noble name.
> Under them are peoples, nations, and the greatest kingdoms.
> To them, borders open without end; even the whole world opens.
> Innumerable lords are under them, and they are held by lords
> To offer faith to them by word and to defend them with arms.
> All agree; no one refuses arms twice
> For the holy empire of the Franks and for upholding the law.
> In the midst of these is wreathed **Louis**, great by name, <note>Likely King Louis XII of France</note>
> Who, as lord of war and peace, governs all things well.
> He increases the empire by his own virtue and that of the gods.
> By war, he first overcame the untamed **Ligurians** <note>The people of the region around Genoa</note>
> Under his guidance, he likewise subdued and captured the **Sforzas** <note>The ruling family of Milan</note>.
> But pious and merciful, he granted life to both;
> This was a noble victory, greater than the first.

### Concerning the cities of Italy.

¶ Italy is a region of Europe, the most celebrated in the entire world. It was first called **Hesperia**, named after Hesperus, the brother of Atlas. Later it was called **Oenotria**, after the excellent wine <note>original: "oenotrie," derived from the Greek word for wine</note> produced there. Finally, it was named **Italy** after Italus, a king of the Sicilians who came to these lands. In its territory, it yields to no other land in the fertility of its fields, and it possesses the most famous cities. Within its borders live various and diverse peoples; it begins at the Alps and rises high, and as it proceeds, it elevates itself in the middle by the perpetual ridge of the Apennine mountains between the Adriatic and the Tuscan <note>Tyrrhenian</note> seas. It runs out as a solid land for a long way, but where it goes further out, it splits into two horns. One side looks toward the Sicilian Sea, the other toward the Ionian; it is narrow throughout, and in some places much narrower than where it began—once the head and mistress of the world, possessing the most famous cities.

### ¶ In Transalpine Gaul.

There is one Gaul called **Cisalpine** and another called **Transalpine**. What is called Transalpine by the Italians is called Cisalpine by our people; that is, "across the Alps." Cisalpine means "this side of the Alps." Indeed, Transalpine Gaul is named by the Gauls themselves. For as it is found in the works of **Trogus Pompeius**, as **Justin** writes in book 20 of his *Epitomes*: When the Gauls had come into Italy, they expelled the Tuscans from their seats and founded **Milan, Como, Brescia, Verona, Bergamo, Trento, and Vicenza**; for which reason the region is rightly called Gaul.

### ¶ On Germany.

Germany is named "Germania" because of its fertility in "germinating" or producing populations <note>A common medieval etymology linking "Germania" to "germinare," to sprout or produce</note>. It lies after lower Scythia, starting from the Danube between the Rhine River and the Ocean; it is bounded to the north and west by the Ocean, to the east by the Danube, and to the south it is divided by the Rhine River. It is a land rich in men and numerous peoples. There are, however, two Germanies: **Upper Germany** near the northern Ocean, and **Lower Germany** near the Rhine. Germany has many cities.

### ¶ On Spain.

Spain was first called **Iberia** from the Ebro <note>Iberus</note> river. Later it was named **Hispania** from Hispalus. Now it is truly called **Hesperia** after Hesperus, the western star. It is situated between Africa and Gaul, closed to the north by the Pyrenees mountains. On all other sides it is enclosed by the sea. It has six provinces: **Tarraconensis**, **Carthaginensis**, **Lusitania**, **Galicia**, **Baetica**, and across the straits in the region of Africa, **Tingitana**. There are two Spains: **Hither Spain** <note>Citerior</note>, which extends as far as Cartagena, and **Farther Spain** <note>Ulterior</note>, which extends southward from the Celtiberians to the Strait of Gades <note>Gibraltar</note>. The shores are called "Hither" and "Farther" as if to say "this side" and "beyond": "this side" meaning this side of the lands, and "beyond" as if it were the end, or because there is no other land after it. It contains most illustrious cities.

In the Patriarchate of Antioch there are 152 cathedral churches, after the likeness of that word from the Gospel: *The net was filled with great fish, 152* <note>original: "clij." This refers to John 21:11, though the biblical text usually lists 153 fish</note>. Of which, in these times, it has the Archbishops who are noted below; these indeed are the suffragans:
**Babylon** <note>original: "Babuleñ"</note>.
**Latakia** <note>original: "Lardiceñ"</note>.
**Tartus** <note>original: "Anceradeñ" (Antarados)</note>.
**Tripoli**.
**Byblos**, which is called **Gibelet**.
The **Archbishop of Tarsus** has no suffragans.
The **Archbishop of Edessa**, who is otherwise called the city of the Medes <note>original: "rer moxorum," likely a corruption of "Rhoas" or "Rohais"</note>, has no suffragans.
The **Archbishop of Apamea** <note>original: "alpdanieñ"</note> has this suffragan: **Valania**.
The **Archbishop of Hierapolis** <note>original: "tulupeñ" (Eliosopolitanus)</note> has no suffragans.
The **Archbishop of Corycus** and the **Archbishop of Mopsuestia** <note>original: "manustreñ"</note> have none.

¶ According to the traditions of the ancients and also certain writings which hold no small authority among the Palestinians and Greeks concerning the Church of Jerusalem, until the time of Augustus it had a bishop enjoying no or very little prerogative. At that time, a general synod was assembled at Constantinople in the time of the Lord Pope **Vigilius**, [attended by] **Eutychius** of Constantinople, **Apollinaris** of Alexandria, and Lord **Eustachius** of Antioch, the Patriarchs, concerning the "Three Chapters"—namely, concerning the writings of **Theodore** [of Mopsuestia] and **Theodoret** of Cyrrhus <note>The Second Council of Constantinople (553 AD) which addressed the "Three Chapters" controversy regarding alleged Nestorian leanings in certain texts</note>. And the chapters [were sent] to Pope Martin. In this synod, after other ecclesiastical institutions which they had decreed were to be promulgated for the time, the aforementioned authority of the Holy Fathers who gathered there decided to honor the Church of God and give its bishop a place among the patriarchs by common holy will, showing reverence for the Holy Resurrection. And because the aforementioned City of God, Jerusalem, was located as if on the borders of the Alexandrian and Antiochian patriarchates, it was seen as expedient to carve out something so that they might ordain subjects for it according to the form of other patriarchates, without taking anything away from both patriarchs. Therefore, they withdrew the Metropolises of **Caesarea** and **Tripoli** from the [Patriarchate] of Antioch. From the Alexandrian—which is today of **Patras** or **Petra**, where today there is no Archbishop—they withdrew the Metropolises of **Rabba** and **Bostra** <note>original: "Beterreñ"</note>. And since it was necessary for the said Patriarch to have personal suffragans among the aforementioned metropolises, which the Greeks call *syncelli* <note>original: "cincillas"</note>, they withdrew certain bishops from the said metropolises and created some anew up to the number of 25, the names of which follow, with the metropolitans being counted first, in this order:

# Order of the Roman Church.

In the city of Rome there are five patriarchal churches:
First, the church of **Saint John Lateran**, which used to have a Prior of the Order of Saint Augustine, but now has a Dean.
In the church of **Saint Peter**, which has an Archbishop who must be a Cardinal.
In the church or monastery of **Saint Paul Outside the Walls**, which has an Abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict.
In the church of **Saint Mary Major**, which has an Archpriest who must be a Cardinal.
In the church or monastery of **Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls**, which has an Abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict; to this church are assigned the Lord Pope and the six Cardinal Bishops listed below to celebrate the divine offices, and they are these: first, the Lord Pope.
The Bishop of **Ostia** and **Velletri**.
The Bishop of **Albano**.
The Bishop of **Porto** and **Santa Rufina**.
The Bishop of **Sabina**.
The Bishop of **Tusculum** <note>Modern Frascati</note>.
The Bishop of **Palestrina** <note>original: "penestrineñ."</note>.
To each of the churches of the City are assigned the following Cardinal Priests, numbering twenty-eight. First, in the churches of the Cardinal Priests:
The Cardinal Priest of the title of the **Holy Cross in Jerusalem**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saints Marcellinus and Peter**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of the **Four Holy Crowned Martyrs**.
The Cardinal Priest of **Saints John and Paul**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Anastasia**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Sabina**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Clement**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saints Nereus and Achilleus** <note>original: "arcellet"</note>.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Susanna**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Pudentiana** <note>original: "potentiane"</note>.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Sixtus**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Peter in Chains**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Martin in the Mountains**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Eusebius**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Prisca**.
The Cardinal Priest of the title of **Saint Vitalis**.

->¶ Register of this work.<-

A. B. a. b. c. d. e. f. g. aa. bb. cc. dd. ee. ff. aaa. bbb. ccc. aaaa. bbbb. cccc. dddd. All are **quaternions** <note>original: "quaterni"; a gathering of four folded sheets of paper, making eight leaves</note> except for A and dddd, which are **ternions** <note>original: "terni"; three folded sheets</note>. B, ff, and cccc, however, are **duernions** <note>original: "duerni"; two folded sheets</note>.
